TOP-LEA-008Topic · Culture & Diversity

Safe To Be Yourself Here

✅ publishedCulture & DiversityIntermediate120 minCultural Safety in the Workplace (SKILL UP), Parts 1 and 2cultural-safetycultureleadershipbelonginginclusionidentitypacificmaori

Pillar: Culture & Diversity · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-008 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Cultural Safety in the Workplace (SKILL UP), Parts 1 and 2

"Real leadership doesn't take more room, it makes more room."

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A manager mispronounces a new staff member's name on her first day. Ordinary. It happens everywhere.

The next morning he comes back having learned it properly, macron and all, and uses it. He keeps using it.

Ask the room: what did she learn from that, that he never actually said?

Then the other version. Ask them to think of a time someone got something about them wrong at work, and never came back to fix it. A name, a pronunciation, an assumption about their family, their food, their faith.

How long did you keep noticing it?

Usually the answer is years.

Statement: Nobody decides they are culturally safe to work for. The people who work for them decide, and they decide from very small things.

➜ Facilitator note: never ask anyone to tell the second story out loud. The thinking is private. Ask only how long they kept noticing, and take the answer as a show of hands or a number.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Tell the difference between cultural awareness, competence and safety, and say who gets to

judge each one.

  1. Intervene early and kindly when something small signals something big.

3. About This Topic

Cultural safety means people can show up as themselves, including their identity, language, values and worldview, without fear of judgment, exclusion or penalty.

It goes beyond cultural awareness, which is noticing difference, and beyond cultural competence, which is knowing what to do, to the felt experience of respect: "I'm safe here. I belong here. I can contribute here."

Why it matters: cultural safety is the switch that turns diversity into performance. Teams think more creatively, speak up earlier about risks, and serve customers with genuine care when they trust they will not be punished for being who they are. In service industries and community-facing work it strengthens reputation, retention and results, because people remember how you made them feel.

Where it comes from matters too. Cultural safety, kawa whakaruruhau, was developed by Irihapeti Ramsden, a Māori nurse, with Māori nursing students in Aotearoa in the 1980s. It became part of New Zealand nursing education in 1992 and has since been adopted around the world. Teaching the idea without naming her is the exact kind of erasure the idea exists to name.

Common mistakes: treating culture as a tick-box training, confusing being nice with being safe, speaking for communities instead of with them, and tolerating small breaches such as jokes, interruptions or mispronunciations that signal big things.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Cultural safetyThe felt experience of dignity and belonging. Judged by the person receiving it
Kawa whakaruruhauThe Māori name for cultural safety. Literally, a protective protocol
Cultural competenceKnowing the protocols and being able to adapt. Necessary, and not sufficient
Protocol theatrePerforming a greeting or ceremony while daily behaviour contradicts it
DiacriticsThe marks that change a word, such as the macron in Māori. Dropping them changes the word

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-033 Cultural Safety — awareness, competence, safety

Origin: Irihapeti Ramsden (Ngāi Tahu, Rangitāne), Aotearoa New Zealand, 1980s onward. PhD thesis 2002, Victoria University of Wellington.

LevelWhat it isWhat the leader does
AwarenessNoticing that people bring different identities, languages, values and historiesLearn correct names and greetings. Notice who speaks and who does not. Ask "what would feel respectful here?" Check assumptions
CompetenceThe practical skill to engage across cultures accuratelyPronunciation in onboarding. Inclusive meeting rules. Checklists with cultural protocols. Rosters that flex for prayer or family
SafetyThe felt experience of dignity and belongingNorms that guard against jokes and interruptions. Intervene early and kindly. Confidential feedback, and close the loop. Pulse checks, and act on them
flowchart TD
  A["CULTURAL AWARENESS<br/>noticing difference"]
  C["CULTURAL COMPETENCE<br/>knowing what to do"]
  S["CULTURAL SAFETY<br/>how it actually felt<br/>to the other person"]
  A -->|informed interaction| C
  C -->|trust and inclusion| S
  A -->|sensitivity and protection| S

How to read it: awareness is what you notice, competence is what you can do, and safety is what the other person experienced. Only the first two are yours to assess.

The point that makes this different from every other diversity model: cultural safety is judged by the recipient, not the provider. You do not get to decide whether you were culturally safe. Your team does.

An honest refinement: Curtis, Jones, Tipene-Leach and colleagues (2019) argue safety is not simply more competence. Competence frames the problem as a knowledge gap. Safety frames it as a question of power: whose norms are the default, and who has to adapt. You can be culturally competent and still be unsafe, because you can know every protocol and still hold all the power.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Ramsden (2002), the founding thesis (PDF)
  • 📄 Curtis et al. (2019), why cultural safety rather than cultural competency

→ Full framework page

FRM-034 S.A.F.E Leadership (house framework)

What it is: four things a leader does, repeatedly, to turn intention into behaviour people can feel.

StepWhat it means
SShape the spaceSet respect norms at the start, not after something goes wrong. Consent rules for photos and filming stated before events. Rotate who speaks first
AApply curiosityAsk what would feel respectful. Ask people to help you say their names. Check intent and impact before taking offence. Invite two quieter voices before deciding
FFairness firstPublish decision criteria. Same standards for everyone including friends and stars. Rotate high-visibility tasks. Keep a decision log and share it
EEducate myselfLearn protocols and histories. Practise pronunciation. Keep a personal glossary with diacritics. One credible resource a month, one change made
flowchart LR
  S["S — SHAPE THE SPACE"] --> A["A — APPLY CURIOSITY"]
  A --> F["F — FAIRNESS FIRST"] --> E["E — EDUCATE MYSELF"]
  E -.->|next meeting,<br/>next shift| S

How to read it: a loop, not a course. The E step feeds the next S, which is why it is a practice and not a training day.

The phrase that carries the E step: "so others are not carrying your load." In most workplaces the cultural education of the manager is being done, unpaid and unasked, by the staff.

Worked example: a supervisor running a season briefing sets the norms and the filming rule up front, asks two people how to say their names and repeats them back, rotates who presents and says how shift preferences were decided, then afterwards notes one form of address she got wrong and fixes it before next time. No extra time. Different attention, applied at the start.

→ Full framework page

How cultural safety is broken (house content, and a strong list)

What it looks like
Token invitesPresent but not heard. Input is decoration, not direction
Assumption-led decisionsGuessing what is respectful instead of asking, so well-meant actions still harm
Protocol theatreCeremony for show while daily behaviour contradicts it
Name and language neglectMispronunciation, dropped macrons, bilingual staff used as unpaid translators
English-only spacesMeetings, signage and materials default to one language
Culture as a jokeSmall comments and mimicked accents left unchecked
Uneven consequencesHigh performers get a pass. Those who speak up pay quietly
Invisible risksSacred practices photographed, boundaries crossed for convenience

FRM-023 Psychological Safety

The close cousin, from a different lineage. Edmondson is about interpersonal risk in teams. Ramsden is about identity and power. Related, and not the same thing. → Full framework page

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-063 Cultural Safety Leadership Self-Assessment Eighteen statements on a 1 to 5 scale, scored in three separate sections so you get a profile rather than a number.

Section scoreWhat it means
24-30Strong and consistent
18-23Developing, with clear progress
12-17Early stage. Choose two habits to build now
0-11Starting out. Begin with simple daily practices

Read the shape, not the total. The important profile is Competence high, Safety low: you know the protocols and people still do not feel safe. That is a power question, not a knowledge one.

Statement 16 is a deliberate trap. "Team members say they can be themselves here without penalty." You cannot answer that. Only they can.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Who taught you what it feels like to belong somewhere? What did they do?
  2. Think of a time someone got something about you wrong and never fixed it. How long did you keep

noticing?

  1. Which of the eight breaches happens where you work, that everyone has stopped noticing?
  2. Whose job is it to learn how to say your team's names properly?
  3. When did you last ask someone "what would feel respectful here?"
  4. Who in your workplace is carrying your cultural education for you, unpaid?
  5. What would your team say if you asked them privately whether they can be themselves at work?
  6. What is the one thing you will change, in which meeting, and by when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-047 Name It In Ten Seconds

(8-10 min). The room learns each other's names properly. Then: put your hand up if someone at work has been saying your name wrong for over a month. The best possible opener for this topic.

  • ACT-065 Small Thing, Big Signal

(12-15 min). Eight situations rated 1 to 5 on fingers. The spread is the lesson.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min. This topic does not run well short. At 90, cut ACT-064 and set it as homework
  • Lead with Ramsden. Naming a Māori nurse as the originator changes how a Pacific or Māori room

receives the whole session, and it models the behaviour being taught

  • What usually goes wrong: the room hears "be nicer". Say early and plainly that being nice and

being safe are different things, and that the source itself names that confusion as a common mistake

  • Watch the load in the room. People who have experienced the breaches list are doing unpaid

emotional work while it is read out. Say so. Never invite anyone to share a story of harm in front of colleagues, and never cast someone from the affected culture as the target in a roleplay

  • Be honest about your own standing. If you are not from the cultures in the room, say so, say

where the frameworks come from, and hold it with care. It lands far better than confidence

  • ⚠️ Open gap: no video linked yet, and it should be an NZ or Pacific voice rather than an

overseas diversity-training clip

PS-CUL-001Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

You already have values, you just have never said them out loud

placeholder-storytikanga-maorivaluescultureidentityleadershipbelonging

Topic: TOP-CUL-001 The Values You Lead With · Pillar: Culture & Diversity

Point

Nobody arrives at work without values. They arrive without the words for them.

And the cost of having no words is not philosophical. It is that you cannot tell when your workplace is asking you to break one. You just feel bad on the drive home and cannot say why.

Model

Four values, and then seven roles.

Tikanga valueIn a workplace
WhanaungatangaRelationships built by doing the work together. People belong here
ManaakitangaLooking after somebody's mana. Everyone, not just the ones who are useful
RangatiratangaThe leader weaves the group together rather than controlling it
KaitiakitangaLooking after what you were handed, for whoever comes next

Then Tū Rangatira (Ministry of Education, 2010), seven leadership roles: He Kaitiaki, He Kaiwhakarite, He Kanohi Matara, He Kaiako, He Kaimahi, He Kaikōtuitui, He Kaiarataki.

➜ The finding worth a whole talk on its own: put those seven beside Kotter, Blake-Mouton and Bass and three of them have no equivalent in the Western canon. Guardianship. Staying a learner while you teach. Advocating upward for your people. Those are not decorative additions to the mainstream models. They are missing from them.

And the delivery move that makes it work in a mixed room: teach tikanga Māori properly and first, as the tangata whenua worked example. Then ask everybody else what they brought.

Metaphor

Water you grew up drinking.

You cannot taste your own tap water. Move somewhere else and you notice immediately, and then you cannot stop noticing. Values work the same way: invisible until they are contradicted.

Which is why the question is never "what are your values?" — nobody can answer that. The question is "when did work last ask you to do something that felt wrong?" People can always answer that one, and the answer is a value with the label torn off.

The stronger version, for a Māori or Pacific room: Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou, ka ora ai te iwi. With your food basket and my food basket, the people will thrive. The whole point of the session is that the room ends up looking at both baskets. Two half-empty kete become a meal.

Study

**Mead, H. M. (2003, rev. 2016). Tikanga Māori: Living by Māori Values. Wellington: Huia. The authoritative written treatment. Mead groups the values and their principles of application, and his framing is that all tikanga are underpinned by manaakitanga**: nurturing relationships, looking after people, being careful about how others are treated.

**Ministry of Education (2010). *Tū Rangatira: Māori Medium Educational Leadership.*** Developed with experienced Māori-medium principals, advisors and researchers. Freely available.

Mika, J. P. (Ngāi Tūhoe, Whakatōhea, Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Kahungunu), Māori enterprise research, on how Māori businesses hold cultural and commercial goals at the same time rather than trading one against the other.

⚠️ The attribution point is itself worth a segment. These roles circulate widely in New Zealand training material under the heading "traditional Māori leadership", with no reference attached. Zeducation first met four of them that way. A specific, named, collectively developed Māori framework presented as undifferentiated tradition loses the people who made it, and naming them takes one sentence. That is five minutes on any stage where the audience cares about doing this properly.

Story

The story on the page is Kāhui Tautoko Consulting nearly changing its Māori name before expanding to Canada, and Aunty Mate saying "just because you're going overseas, you don't stop being Māori." They kept the name and it became the reason indigenous communities trusted them.

But the better line is the second one, from the same director, about writing the values down:

"If you've been raised with those values, nobody gives you a booklet and says, 'This is how you have to behave!' It's just how you are."

The first quote is a good story about somebody else. The second one is about the person listening. Use the second.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who realised, in a session, that the thing they had been quietly resenting at work was a values collision and not a personality problem. Small, specific, and far more useful than an inspiring business case.

⚠️ Placeholder. No collected Zeducation story yet, and this topic will not reach its full weight without one.

TOP-CUL-001Topic · Culture & Diversity

The Values You Lead With

✅ publishedCulture & DiversityFoundation120 minLeadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 1 and 2tikanga-maorivaluescultureidentityleadershipbelongingwhanaungatangamanaakitanga

Pillar: Culture & Diversity · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120 min · ID: TOP-CUL-001 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Leadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 1 and 2

Ehara taku toa i te toa takitahi, engari he toa takitini My success is not my own, but that of the many

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A New Zealand consultancy is about to open in Canada. Small team, Māori-owned, Māori name.

Before they go, they seriously discuss changing the company name, because clients over there are not going to be able to pronounce it.

Their Aunty Mate says:

"Just because you're going overseas, you don't stop being Māori. Don't change who you are for anybody."

They keep the name. And what happens is the opposite of what they feared: it is the Māori identity and the Māori values that get them working with indigenous communities in Hawai'i and Canada. The thing they nearly hid became the reason people trusted them.

Then the harder part. Mara Andrews, the director, says the difficult bit was not keeping the name. It was writing the values down:

"If you've been raised with those values, nobody gives you a booklet and says, 'This is how you have to behave!' It's just how you are."

Ask the room: what are the values you were raised with, that nobody ever wrote down for you?

Statement: You already lead with values. You have just never said them out loud, which is why you cannot tell when your workplace is asking you to break them.

➜ Facilitator note: the second quote is the one that opens the room. The first is a good story about somebody else. The second is about them.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Describe four tikanga Māori values and say what each one looks like in a workplace.
  2. Name the values you personally lead with, and one place where holding them costs you

something.

3. About This Topic

Tikanga Māori is not a framework and nobody invented it. It is the body of values and protocols that guide how people behave and treat one another, developed over generations and handed down. It is based on long experience, and it applies to a modern workplace as readily as to a marae.

Four of those values come up constantly in New Zealand business:

  • Whanaungatanga, relationship. Built through shared experience, mutual respect, and working

together. It is what gives people a sense of belonging

  • Manaakitanga, care and hospitality. Looking after somebody's mana. Sir Hirini Moko Mead's

framing is that all tikanga are underpinned by manaakitanga

  • Rangatiratanga, leadership and self-determination. The leader's job is described as **weaving

the group together**, not controlling it

  • Kaitiakitanga, guardianship. You are looking after something that was here before you and will

be here after you

Then the second half of this topic, which is about the job rather than the values. Tū Rangatira is a 2010 Ministry of Education framework, developed with Māori-medium principals and researchers, naming seven leadership roles. Put it beside the Western leadership models and three of the seven have no clean equivalent: guardianship, staying a learner, and advocating for your people.

Why it matters: Zeducation's rooms are Pacific, Māori, migrant, Pākehā and young. Most learners have strong values and no vocabulary for them, which means they cannot name what is happening when a workplace asks them to act against those values. This topic is about getting the words.

⚠️ And the move that makes it work in a mixed room: teach tikanga Māori as the tangata whenua worked example, properly and first, and then ask everybody else for theirs. What comes back is fa'aaloalo, tautua, alofa, aiga, utang na loob, ubuntu, izzat, and "you finish what you start". Every one of them belongs on the same wall.

Common mistakes: translating the words and moving on; treating this as an icebreaker; producing another set of poster values nobody can name; and putting the Māori learner on the spot to teach the room.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Tikanga MāoriThe Māori values and protocols that guide how people behave and interact
ManaStanding, authority, dignity. Manaakitanga is about looking after somebody's
WhanaungatangaRelationship and belonging, built through shared experience
KaitiakitangaGuardianship. Looking after what you were handed
Ngā whenuThe strands. The seven roles in Tū Rangatira
KaupapaThe purpose, the reason the group exists

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-050 Tikanga Māori in Business

Full page, with sources and the cautions, at FRM-050.

ValueIn a workplace it meansYou can see it when
WhanaungatangaRelationships are built by doing the work together. People belong hereNew starters get introduced properly, not just shown a desk

Authority: Sir Hirini Moko Mead, Tikanga Māori: Living by Māori Values (Huia, 2003, rev. 2016). For the business application, MBIE's principles from te ao Māori and the Māori enterprise research of Professor Jason Mika.

FRM-051 Tū Rangatira — seven leadership roles

Origin: Tū Rangatira: Māori Medium Educational Leadership, Ministry of Education, 2010. Full page at FRM-051.

WhenuRoleThe leader who does this
He KaitiakiGuardianProtects the people and the kaupapa. Holds high-trust relationships
He KaiwhakariteManagerRuns the resources well
He Kanohi MataraVisionaryThinks and plans ahead
He KaiakoTeacher and learnerTeaches, and is still learning
He KaimahiWorkerLeads by doing, alongside people
He KaikōtuituiNetworkerConnects beyond this team
He KaiaratakiAdvocateSpeaks up for people. Holds culturally responsive practice, with te Tiriti as the foundation

⚠️ These roles are often taught as generic "traditional Māori leadership" with no reference. They are a named 2010 publication made by identifiable Māori educators. Cite Tū Rangatira every time you teach them.

FRM-027 The Team Charter (the tool that makes it stick)

Full page at FRM-027.

Values a room names and then never uses are worse than no session at all. The charter is how the wall built in ACT-088 turns into behaviour a team can hold each other to.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-089 Seven Roles, One Kaupapa is the self-assessment for this topic. Seven roles, rated often / sometimes / never, with a second column for "when did you last do it".

The second column is the whole instrument. It is very easy to believe you are a guardian and very hard to name the last time you guarded anything.

The pattern that comes back:

Usually strongUsually weak
He Kaimahi. New Zealand supervisors lead by working harder than everyone elseHe Kaiarataki. Advocating upward carries risk, so most people avoid it
He Kaiwhakarite. It is what they are paid forHe Kaikōtuitui. Nobody has time and nobody was told it was part of the job
He Kaiako, the learning half. Ask when they last learned something from someone junior

⚠️ Not a validated instrument, and not a measure of anyone's cultural competence. It is a mirror for leadership behaviour. Never score anybody on how Māori they are.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Who taught you how to treat people? What did they actually teach you?
  2. Is there a word in your family's language for it?
  3. Where does that value cost you something at work?
  4. Which of the four tikanga values does your workplace talk about and not do?
  5. Have you ever had to leave part of who you are at the door to fit in at a job?
  6. Which of the seven roles have you genuinely never done?
  7. Tū Rangatira has guardianship, learning and advocacy. Why do you think the Western models do not?
  8. What is one value you will name out loud to your team, and when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-092 Say My Name

(10-12 min). Everyone says their name properly, where it comes from, and what people get wrong. Then the room says it back, together, until it is right. The best opener in the library for a culture session and the correct one for this topic.

  • Whakataukī round (8 min). Put Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou, ka ora ai te iwi on the board

with the translation, and ask what the food baskets are on their team. Gentle, and it sets up ACT-088 exactly.

  • Where's the value? (10 min). Read four short workplace situations. The room calls out which of

the four values is being kept or broken. Fast, and it stops the values being abstract before the worksheet starts.

Source Trail

Built from SRC-009 Leadership Kōnae Ako 1, Te Wānanga o Aotearoa, ingested 2026-08-01. The te ao Māori content is the strongest material in that source and the reason it was worth ingesting.

⚠️ Both frameworks were traced to their sources during the ingest. The seven leadership roles are credited here to Tū Rangatira, Ministry of Education, 2010, and the full set of seven is carried rather than the four Zeducation first met. The four tikanga values are grounded in Mead (2003), MBIE, and Jason Mika's Māori enterprise research.

The Mara Andrews quotations are used under review and attributed. The whakataukī are traditional. The mixed-room move in section 3, all four activities and the wall build are Zeducation's.

  • ⚠️ Same for everyone else. Nobody becomes the representative of their ethnicity for the

afternoon. Invite, never call on

  • Be honest about your own standing. If you are not Māori, say so, say where the frameworks come

from and who made them, and hold it carefully. It lands considerably better than confidence

  • The "I don't have a culture" learner. Common, usually Pākehā. The answer is: what did your

family teach you about work? That is the culture, and it is invisible to you because it is the default around here

  • Tū Rangatira was written for kura, not warehouses. Every workplace example is Zeducation's

translation. Say so

  • ⚠️ Open gap, and it is the important one: neither framework page has been read by a Māori

educator. Get that done before this topic is delivered, and change whatever they tell you to change

PS-LEA-009Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Values are the warp, stories are the weft

placeholder-storytalanoateu-le-vapacificcultural-safetylisteningleadership

Topic: TOP-LEA-009 Weave Before You Decide · Pillar: Culture & Diversity

Point

A set of values with no one's story running through it is not a culture. It is a poster, and it falls apart the moment you pick it up.

The weaving is a conversation, and somebody has to actually have it before the decision, not after.

Model

The mat:

ThreadWhat it is
Warp — the strong parallel threadsThe shared values. Necessary, and on their own just parallel lines
Weft — the threads woven acrossPeople's lived stories and knowledge
The weavingTalanoa. The act that turns two sets of threads into something that holds weight

The three-part flow:

flowchart LR
  T["1. TEU LE VĀ<br/>prepare the<br/>relational space"]
  A["2. ASK<br/>open questions<br/>that invite story"]
  L["3. LISTEN & SHARE<br/>mirror back,<br/>then give back"]
  T --> A --> L
  L -.->|return next time<br/>saying names correctly| T

The dotted return is the proof. Anyone can hold one good conversation. Coming back having learned the names, and echoing one thing you heard, is what makes it a practice rather than an event.

The four questions: What would feel respectful here? · What meaning sits behind this practice? · When has this gone well for you? · Who else's voice should we include before we decide?

Metaphor

The woven mat is the metaphor, and it is the source's own, so it stays.

The second one, for the vā: most people treat the space between two people as a corridor. Something to walk down quickly on the way to the room where the business happens. Teu le vā says the corridor is the room.

Study

**Timote M. Vaioleti, Talanoa Research Methodology: A Developing Position on Pacific Research, Waikato Journal of Education 12 (2006). Vaioleti (Tongan) was the first to theorise talanoa as a research methodology. He breaks the word open: tala to talk or tell, noa** a space without a fixed framework. His central claim is that knowledge is produced through the relationship, not despite it, which is why an open technique with no predetermined questions gets further than a survey.

📄 Paper · 📄 Full text PDF

**Melani Anae, Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics; and Airini, Anae & Mila-Schaaf (2010)**, Teu Le Va: Relationships across research and policy in Pasifika education, NZ Ministry of Education. Teu le vā entered New Zealand education guidance in 2010 as a relational ethic: value, nurture and tidy the sacred relational space.

📄 Anae (PDF) · 📄 Airini et al. (PDF)

⚠️ Two nations, two concepts. Talanoa is Fijian, Tongan and Samoan practice. Teu le vā is Samoan. The source workbook was written for a Fiji client and uses both without naming either origin. Name them, and note the gap: Fijian-authored talanoa scholarship, and Sitiveni Halapua's work on talanoa in Pacific dialogue, would ground this properly in the client's own context.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a decision that changed because someone sat down properly first. The tour route example in the topic is illustrative, not documented. The real version needs a Zeducation client who ran a talanoa, heard something they would never have found in a survey, and acted on it.

What makes the story work is the specific thing that surfaced. Not "we had a great conversation", but the one constraint, protocol or reason nobody had written down. Collect that detail or the story is just a feeling.

TOP-LEA-009Topic · Culture & Diversity

Weave Before You Decide

✅ publishedCulture & DiversityIntermediate120-150 minCultural Safety in the Workplace (SKILL UP), Part 3talanoateu-le-vapacificcultural-safetylisteningleadershipculturedecision-making

Pillar: Culture & Diversity · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-LEA-009 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Cultural Safety in the Workplace (SKILL UP), Part 3

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Hold up a set of parallel strips of paper. Say these are the values: respect, safety, integrity, whatever this workplace says it stands for. Lay them out neatly.

Then lift one end.

They fall apart, because parallel lines are not a mat. They are a poster.

Now weave a few strips across them, and say what each one is: what Losana knows about the site, what Ravi learned in his last job, why the family down the road does it that way. Lift it again.

It holds.

Ask the room: which half is your workplace missing?

Statement: Values are the warp. People's lived stories are the weft. Neither one is a mat on its own, and the weaving is a conversation somebody has to actually have.

➜ Facilitator note: the metaphor is the source's own and it is the best one in the SKILL UP series. Use it physically. Watching parallel strips fall apart does more work than any slide.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Open a conversation by preparing the relational space before you get to the business.
  2. Run a talanoa that ends in a gift back, not just a good feeling.

3. About This Topic

Talanoa is a Pacific practice of open, relational conversation where people solve differences and share stories, experiences and hopes in a spirit of trust. It puts relationship first, then understanding, then decisions. In simple terms it is listening to learn, speaking to connect, and weaving meaning together so everyone feels seen and heard.

It matters because it turns diversity into connection. When people can speak in their own voice and at their own pace, you uncover the why behind protocols, names and practices, not just the what. That reduces misunderstanding, prevents harm around sacred spaces, and builds dignity and belonging.

For a leader, talanoa is both method and mindset. You prepare the relational space, invite the right voices, and co-create meaning before deciding. Then you close the loop by returning value to the people who shared: what will change, and how it will be protected. The result is leadership that is accountable, fair and culturally grounded, where decisions carry the strength of many voices rather than the weight of one.

Where these words come from. Talanoa is long-standing practice across Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. It was theorised academically by Timote Vaioleti (Tongan) in 2006. Teu le vā is a Samoan concept, brought into education and research ethics in Aotearoa by Melani Anae and by Airini, Anae and Mila-Schaaf in 2010. These are different Pacific nations and the words are not interchangeable. Say where each one is from.

Key words

WordWhat it means
TalanoaTala is to talk or tell, noa is a space without a fixed framework. Conversation whose shape is not decided in advance
VāThe relational space between people. Real, shared, and somebody's responsibility
Teu le vāTo tidy, value and nurture that space
Gift backReturning value to the people who shared: what will change, by when, and how they will see it

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-035 Talanoa — the Pacific relational conversation

Origin: Pacific practice. Theorised as a methodology by Timote M. Vaioleti, Talanoa Research Methodology, Waikato Journal of Education 12 (2006).

StepWhat you do
1Teu le vā — prepare the spaceCalm, relational tone first. Circle, purpose and consent, names checked with correct pronunciation. Agree norms, including how filming or sharing will work
2Ask open questionsPrompts that invite story, not short answers. Spacious: how, what, when
3Listen and shareFull attention, mirror back, one curious follow-up. Invite quieter voices before anyone speaks twice. Check consent in the moment. Close by gifting back
flowchart LR
  T["1. TEU LE VĀ<br/>prepare the<br/>relational space"]
  A["2. ASK<br/>open questions<br/>that invite story"]
  L["3. LISTEN & SHARE<br/>mirror back,<br/>then give back"]
  T --> A --> L
  L -.->|return next time<br/>saying names correctly| T

How to read it: the dotted return is not decoration. Coming back having learned the names, and echoing one thing you heard, is what proves the first conversation was real.

The four questions, from the source:

  • "What would feel respectful here?"
  • "What meaning sits behind this practice?"
  • "When has this gone well for you?"
  • "Who else's voice should we include before we decide?"

The last one is the leadership question. It is the difference between consulting and weaving.

Worked example: a tourism operator wants to add a site to a tour route. The fast version: check it is legally accessible, add it, brief the guides. The talanoa version: sit with the local families first, no agenda paper, ask what the place means and when it has gone well. It emerges that the site is fine to visit but not to photograph, and that a particular month matters. The route goes ahead with two rules nobody would have thought to write, and the guides can explain the why to guests, which is a better tour. The relationship produced the information. A survey would not have.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Vaioleti (2006), Talanoa Research Methodology
  • 📄 Full text PDF, University of Waikato

→ Full framework page

FRM-036 Teu le vā — caring for the relational space

Origin: Samoan concept. Melani Anae, Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics; Airini, Anae & Mila-Schaaf (2010), NZ Ministry of Education.

Western workplace thinking treats the space between two people as empty, something to cross on the way to the transaction. Teu le vā says the opposite: the space is the thing. It exists, it holds obligations both ways, and it can be tended or neglected. If it has been neglected, nothing you say across it lands properly, however well you say it.

flowchart LR
  A["Person"]
  V["THE VĀ<br/>the relational space<br/>real, shared, and<br/>somebody's responsibility"]
  B["Person"]
  A --- V --- B
  V -.->|teu le vā<br/>tend it before<br/>you need it| V

How to read it: the vā is not a gap between two people. It is a third thing, and both are responsible for its condition. The one with more power is responsible for more of it.

Worked example: a manager needs to tell a supervisor a shift pattern is changing. Untended: message on Friday afternoon, accurate and clear, received as a decision made about him. Teu le vā: she goes in person, asks about his mother who has been unwell, then says what is changing and why, and asks what it will cost him. Same decision, same words about the roster, entirely different outcome. The extra time was four minutes.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Anae, Teu Le Va: Samoan relational ethics (PDF)
  • 📄 Airini, Anae & Mila-Schaaf (2010), NZ Ministry of Education report (PDF)

→ Full framework page

FRM-033 Cultural Safety

Talanoa is how a leader finds out whether people actually feel safe, which is the only way to know, because safety is judged by the recipient. → Full framework page

6. Self-Assessment

Two options, and the listening one is the better fit for this topic.

ACT-021 How Well Do I Listen? from the Communication pillar. Talanoa is fundamentally a listening practice, and this instrument is already written and already in use.

ACT-063 Cultural Safety Leadership Self-Assessment if you are running this topic straight after TOP-LEA-008. Section 1, statement 3, and Section 3, statement 17, are both talanoa behaviours.

⚠️ Neither is validated. Teaching mirrors, not measures.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Think of a time someone gave you difficult news and it landed well. What had happened before

they said it?

  1. Whose vā have you left untended, and for how long?
  2. What is a protocol at your work that everyone follows and nobody has explained?
  3. When did you last change a decision because of something you heard?
  4. Who is never in the room when the decision about them is made?
  5. What have you consulted on and then never told anyone what changed?
  6. Where does your workplace have plenty of warp and almost no weft?
  7. What is one conversation you will open differently, with whom, and when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

(12-15 min). Values as warp, stories as weft. The moment the parallel strips fall apart is the whole topic in five seconds.

  • ACT-022 Tell It Back

(10-12 min). From the Communication pillar. Trains the mirroring that step 3 depends on.

Vaioleti, Anae and the Airini et al. report were added during this ingest, since the source names neither talanoa's nor teu le vā's scholarship. The story and the games were written fresh.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min if you run a real talanoa, and that is the version worth running. 120 at a

minimum

  • Say where the words come from, every time. Talanoa is Fijian, Tongan and Samoan. Teu le vā is

Samoan. The Māori relative of this territory is hui and whanaungatanga, which are their own things with their own literature. Do not treat any of them as translations of each other

  • What usually goes wrong: a talanoa gets run with a decision already made. People can tell, and

you will not get a second one

  • The gift back is not optional. Closing without saying what will change turns the session into

extraction. This is the single most important facilitator note on the page

  • If you are not Pacific, say so, name Vaioleti and Anae, and hold the practice with care. A room

respects that far more than a confident performance

here is Tongan and Samoan. Fijian-authored material on talanoa, and Sitiveni Halapua's work on talanoa in Pacific dialogue and conflict resolution, would ground this in the client's own context. Worth commissioning

PS-CUL-002Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

A diverse team that never gets asked has bought you a photograph

placeholder-storydiversityinclusionteamsevidencedecision-makingculture

Topic: TOP-CUL-002 What Diversity Actually Buys You · Pillar: Culture & Diversity

Point

Difference that is present and never asked does nothing at all. Hiring changes who is in the room. It does not change who gets listened to, and almost every organisation that has done the first one believes it has done the second.

Model

Three kinds, and only one of them is visible.

KindWhat differsVisible?
DemographicWho people areYes. It is what everybody means by "diverse"
InformationalWhat people knowNo, and rarely asked
Values-basedWhat people think the job is forNo, and it looks like a difficult colleague

Then the question the whole model exists for:

        difference in the room
                 │
      Does the team actually hear it?
         ┌───────┴───────┐
       YES               NO
         │                │
  better decisions   same decisions
  harder meetings     nicer photo

➜ The values row is the one rooms skip. It does not feel like diversity. It feels like somebody being awkward. It is the kind that produces the useful argument and the kind teams are least willing to name.

Metaphor

A toolbox where three drawers have never been opened.

You bought the full set. You are using the top drawer. And when a job goes wrong you conclude you need a bigger toolbox.

The sharper version, and the one that lands with employers: you are already paying for it. Every person on that team is on the payroll. The informational and values diversity is bought and sitting there. Not asking is not a saving, it is waste.

For a Māori or Pacific room: Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou, ka ora ai te iwi. Two half-empty food baskets make a meal, and only if both get opened.

Study

This is a Pink Sheet where the study section is the point of the talk.

The one that failed

**Hunt, V., Layton, D. & Prince, S. (2015). Why Diversity Matters. McKinsey.** Top-quartile gender diversity, 15% more likely to outperform. Racial and ethnic diversity, 35%. The two most quoted numbers in New Zealand diversity training.

**Green, J. & Hand, J. R. M. (2024). McKinsey's Diversity Matters/Delivers/Wins Results Revisited. Econ Journal Watch, 21(1).** McKinsey would not release its data, so they rebuilt the test on the S&P

  1. No statistically significant relationship with earnings margin, sales growth, gross margin,

return on assets, return on equity or total shareholder return.

⚠️ Do not use 15% and 35%. Not on a slide, not in a tender.

The ones that held

**Sommers, S. (2006). On racial diversity and group decision making. JPSP. Racially mixed mock juries deliberated longer, raised a wider range of facts, and made fewer factual errors. And the white jurors on mixed juries performed better before deliberation began**.

Phillips, K. W. (2014). Scientific American. The mechanism is not that the new person brings information. It is that the majority stops assuming everybody already agrees.

➜ The line for a stage: "The research does not say a diverse team is smarter because the new person knows more. It says everybody else stops coasting."

And the honest cost, which almost nobody says: diverse teams report feeling less comfortable and rate their own performance lower, while objectively doing better. Diversity buys a harder meeting and a better decision.

Story

The story on the page is the Ōtara health team and the ten-minute grace window: three people, three kinds of diversity, and a two-year-old problem that got fixed in one meeting once all three got heard.

Why it works: it is small, it is local, nobody is a villain, and the values disagreement at the bottom of it is left unresolved, which is honest.

The story to collect, and it is the most commercially valuable gap in this sheet: a Zeducation employer partner describing a decision that changed because somebody finally got asked. Auckland, Pacific or Māori workforce, named business, with permission.

And the confession story, which would be stronger: a leader describing the person on their team they never asked, and what that cost. Harder to get. Worth more.

⚠️ Placeholder. The Ōtara story is Zeducation's construction, not a collected case. Say so if asked from a stage. Never present it as a real client.

TOP-CUL-002Topic · Culture & Diversity

What Diversity Actually Buys You

✅ publishedCulture & DiversityIntermediate120 minLeadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 3 and 4diversityinclusionteamscultureevidencedecision-makingteam-roles

Pillar: Culture & Diversity · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 120 min · ID: TOP-CUL-002 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Leadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 3 and 4

Nā tō rourou, nā taku rourou, ka ora ai te iwi With your food basket and my food basket, the people will thrive

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A community health team in Ōtara is trying to work out why so many people miss their appointments. Five people in the room.

The Tongan health worker says families are turning up, and being turned away at ten minutes late. Ten minutes is nothing if you are getting three kids to school first.

The one who used to be a receptionist says the booking system can hold a fifteen-minute grace window, and nobody has ever switched it on.

And underneath both of those, unspoken: the clinician thinks the job is to protect clinic throughput, and the outreach worker thinks the job is to get people seen. They have never said this to each other. It is the actual disagreement, and it is why nobody fixed this two years ago.

Ask the room: which of those three people made the team smarter?

All of them, in different ways, and one of them by disagreeing.

Statement: Diversity that is present but never asked does nothing. A team can be completely mixed and completely silent, and the only thing it has bought is a better photo.

➜ Facilitator note: the third person, the values disagreement, is the one rooms skip. Come back to it in section 5. It does not feel like diversity, it feels like a difficult colleague, and that is precisely the point.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name the three kinds of diversity, and say which one your team is actually short of.
  2. Choose two accommodation moves and commit to a day for each.

3. About This Topic

When people say "a diverse team" they almost always mean demographic diversity: what the team looks like. That is one of three kinds, and it is the least interesting.

KindWhat differs
DemographicWho people are. Age, gender, ethnicity, disability, where they were born
InformationalWhat people know. Training, work history, trade, languages
Values-basedWhat people are for. What they think the job is actually for

Why it matters: the difference only helps if it gets heard. A team can be demographically diverse and informationally identical. A team can be diverse in every way and run by someone who only ever asks one person. Both of those buy you nothing.

⚠️ The evidence, and one claim in this field has fallen over

This section is the reason this topic exists, and it needs to be taught carefully.

The claim that failed. Everyone quotes McKinsey: companies in the top quartile for gender diversity are 15% more likely to outperform their industry median, and for racial and ethnic diversity, 35% more likely (Hunt, Layton & Prince, 2015). They are the two most quoted numbers in New Zealand diversity training, and they are usually stated as settled fact.

They did not replicate. In March 2024, Jeremiah Green (Texas A&M) and John R. M. Hand (University of North Carolina) published McKinsey's Diversity Matters/Delivers/Wins Results Revisited in Econ Journal Watch. McKinsey would not release its data, so they rebuilt the test on S&P 500 firms. They found no statistically significant relationship with earnings margin, sales growth, gross margin, return on assets, return on equity or total shareholder return.

➜ Do not use the 15% and 35% figures. Not in a workshop, not in a tender, not on a slide.

What that does not mean. It is not evidence that diversity harms performance and nobody should leave the room thinking so. It means that particular profit claim is unproven.

What held up, and it is better anyway. Samuel Sommers (2006) found racially mixed mock juries deliberated longer, raised more facts and made fewer factual errors than all-white juries. And the white jurors on mixed juries performed better before deliberation even began. Katherine Phillips (2014) summarised the wider literature: the mechanism is not that the new person brings information, it is that the majority stops assuming everyone already agrees.

➜ That is a process claim, not a profit claim, and it is more useful in a room full of people who do not own shares. "Your team will think harder" beats "your shareholders will do 35% better."

And say the cost. Diverse teams report feeling less comfortable and often rate their own performance lower while objectively doing better. Diversity buys you a harder meeting and a better decision. Learners are owed both halves.

Common mistakes: using the McKinsey numbers; making the whole case financial; stopping at demographic diversity; and selling it as comfortable.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Demographic diversityWho people are. The visible kind
Informational diversityWhat people know. Usually invisible and usually unasked
Values diversityWhat people think the work is for. The kind that produces the useful argument
ReplicationWhether an independent team gets the same result from the same test
AccommodationMaking room, practically, so people can actually take part

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-052 The Three Kinds of Diversity

Full page, with the evidence audit in full, at FRM-052.

The diagram that matters is the bottom of it: difference goes in, and the question is does the team actually hear it? Yes gives you better decisions and harder meetings. No gives you the same decisions and a nicer photo.

FRM-055 Accommodating Diversity — ten things a leader can actually do

Full page at FRM-055.

The four that matter most:

Move
1Learn to say everyone's name properly, and correct other people when they get it wrong
2Ask the quiet ones directly, by name, in advance
3Be flexible about time. Religious observance, school pickup, a tangi, a court date, a sick kid
4Check the meeting calendar against the actual calendar

Then six more, ending with: ask the team what would make this better, and then do one thing.

⚠️ Move 10 done badly is worse than not done at all. A team that gets asked and sees nothing happen will not answer honestly again.

FRM-053 Belbin's Nine Team Roles

Full page at FRM-053. One structured way to surface the informational and values diversity a team already has and has never named.

The half worth teaching is the allowable weakness: the weakness is the price of the strength, not a fault to train out.

FRM-054 Personality Tests At Work

Full page at FRM-054.

Include this whenever the room raises MBTI, and they will. Myers-Briggs still appears uncritically in a lot of leadership curricula. The library's position is that these instruments give people useful shared vocabulary and must never be used to decide who gets hired, promoted or trusted.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-091 The Ten Moves Audit is the assessment for this topic, and it assesses the workplace rather than the person. Ten moves, answered yes / sort of / no / not my call.

There is deliberately no score. The output is not a number, it is two commitments with a day on each.

Read the patternWhat it usually means
Lots of "sort of"The policy exists and nobody runs it
Lots of "not my call"Either true, and question 3 exists for them, or a way of not looking
Moves 6 and 4 done, moves 1 and 2 notThe visible, cheap ones are done and the ones that change something are not. Very common

Move 2 is the one nobody does. Asking the quiet ones directly, by name, in advance. Ask for the evidence on it and most rooms go quiet.

⚠️ Not validated, and not a compliance audit. If a client wants a real diversity audit, that is a different piece of work and probably a different provider.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Which of the three kinds of diversity is your team actually short of?
  2. What does someone on your team know that nobody ever asks them about?
  3. When did your team last have a genuinely useful disagreement? What made it useful?
  4. Statement 2 in the sorting game: what did you assume, and how fast?
  5. Who on your team disagrees with you about what the job is for? Have you ever said that out loud?
  6. Which of the ten moves would your team notice by Friday?
  7. Has a test or an assessment ever been used to decide something about you?
  8. What are your two moves, and what day are you doing them?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-092 Say My Name

(10-12 min). Names said properly, and the room says them back until they are right. Ten minutes, costs nothing, and something real happens in almost every room.

  • ACT-090 What Kind Of Difference Is This?

(12-15 min). Fourteen statements, three corners. Rigged, in the good way. Run it cold.

  • Both baskets (6 min). Put the whakataukī on the board and ask each person to name one thing

they bring that nobody else on their team does. Quick, warm, and it seeds the informational diversity idea before the model arrives.

TOP-LEA-008 Safe To Be Yourself HereDiversity is who is in the room. Cultural safety decides whether they can speak in it. Teach that one before this one if you have both
TOP-LEA-009 Weave Before You DecideTalanoa is a method for getting the difference heard, which is this topic's whole problem
TOP-LEA-005 One Team, Not Us And ThemWhat happens when values diversity is never named and hardens into two camps

PS-EMP-004Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Four stories, not twenty answers

placeholder-storycareer-readinessinterviewsstarstorytellingwork-readinessjob-search

Topic: TOP-EMP-004 Tell Them The Story · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

Point

People prepare for interviews by trying to guess the questions. That is why they freeze.

There are hundreds of possible questions and about four underlying stories. Prepare the four and they stretch to cover almost anything. Prepare twenty scripted answers and the first question worded differently takes the whole thing down.

Model

Four boxes, filled once, reused forever.

StoryA time you…Covers
1Dealt with a difficult personConflict · customers · teamwork · patience
2Had something go wrong, partly on youAccountability · honesty · learning · pressure
3Worked in a team and did a specific partTeamwork · communication · reliability
4Kept going when it was hardResilience · motivation · workload

Each one told in four parts, and the proportions are the teaching:

flowchart LR
  S["S · SITUATION<br/>set the scene<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"] --> T["T · TASK<br/>your job in it<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"]
  T --> A["A · ACTION<br/>what YOU did<br/><i>3-4 sentences</i>"]
  A --> R["R · RESULT<br/>what changed<br/><i>1-2 sentences</i>"]

Most people invert this. Ninety seconds of Situation, then nerve runs out, then "so yeah, it worked out." A is the answer. R is the part that gets forgotten and the part that gets remembered.

⚠️ Not FRM-003 STAR, which is Story · Tools · Apply · Reflect and is how Zeducation builds a session. Same four letters, different thing. Say which one you mean.

Metaphor

Four keys, not two hundred locks.

You cannot carry a key for every door you might walk up to. What you can carry is four that open most of them, because the locks are more similar than they look from the outside.

The person with two hundred keys is not better prepared. They are standing at the door going through their pockets.

Study

Behavioural interviewing rests on a premise that has held up: what somebody actually did before predicts what they will do next, better than what they say they would do in a hypothetical.

  • Structured interviews — same questions, same order, scored against set criteria — are among the

better-validated selection tools in the research literature, and clearly outperform unstructured "let's have a chat" interviews, which are close to useless as predictors

  • STAR itself is not the studied thing. No single author owns it. It is a memory aid the

recruitment industry built on top of the method

  • Tahatū's Job Hunters' Workbook teaches the same four letters, so a

learner who goes to the government careers service gets a consistent message

Honest limit: the evidence supports the interviewing method, not the acronym, and definitely not the claim that four stories is the right number. Four is a practitioner judgement about how much a nervous person can hold.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The two support worker answers in the topic — the one that talks about short-staffing for two minutes, and the one about the resident who would not let anyone near her — are written for teaching. They are composites, true to what tutors describe, not identified people.

The story to collect: a learner who did ACT-099, went to a real interview, and got asked one of the four. What lands is what they noticed themselves doing differently in the room, in their own words.

Second story worth collecting, and it is the higher-value one: a hiring manager describing two real candidates who were equally capable, where one got the job because they could tell you about it. Thirty seconds of that from an employer beats twenty minutes of facilitation.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any interview preparation, one-to-one or groupThe four boxes are the whole session if you only have an hour
The day before somebody's actual interview"Which four are you taking in with you?"
Employer and panel trainingStructured beats unstructured. It is the same evidence, pointed the other way
Staff developmentThe four boxes work for internal applications and performance conversations too

TOP-EMP-004Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

Tell Them The Story

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation150-180 minCareer Readiness, Part 3career-readinessinterviewsstarstorytellingjob-searchwork-readinessdisclosurequestions

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 150-180 min, or two sessions · ID: TOP-EMP-004 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Career Readiness, Part 3

⚠️ Name clash — read this before you introduce anything

Two different things in this library are called STAR.

Stands forWhat it is for
FRM-003 STARStory · Tools · Apply · ReflectZeducation's session shape. How a facilitator builds a session
FRM-059 STAR (this topic)Situation · Task · Action · ResultA learner's interview answer. How a candidate tells a story about themselves

Both are genuinely called STAR in the wild. In this topic, say "the STAR answer". Reserve "the STAR session shape" for FRM-003.

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two people are interviewed for the same support worker role, half an hour apart.

The first is asked "tell me about a time you dealt with someone difficult." She talks for two minutes about how the rest home was always short-staffed, and how management never listened, and how some of the families were hard work. Then she stops and says, "so yeah, it was pretty full on."

The second gets the same question. She says: "There was a resident who wouldn't let anyone near her in the mornings. I was on her wing for six weeks. I stopped trying to get her up on our schedule and started coming in fifteen minutes earlier just to sit. On the fourth day she told me she'd fallen in the shower two years ago and never told anyone. I told the RN, we got a shower chair and a second person on her, and after that she got herself up most mornings."

Same job. Same rest home, as it happens. Ask the room: which one has more experience?

The honest answer is that we have no idea. Only one of them told us anything.

Statement: An interview is not a test of your experience. It is a test of whether you can put your experience into a story that has a point.

➜ Facilitator note: read both answers out loud, in character. The first one gets nervous laughter because everybody recognises it, usually as themselves.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Build four STAR stories that stretch to cover almost any behavioural question.
  2. Answer out loud with the action as the longest part, and an actual result at the end.
  3. Say your own hardest question in three parts, finishing forward.
  4. Walk in with three questions of your own, and walk out knowing what happens next.

3. About This Topic

This is the third part of career readiness. TOP-EMP-002 worked out what you can do. TOP-EMP-003 got you in the door. This one is what happens when somebody asks you about it.

Four things happen in a session on interviews and they need holding apart.

What it isWhere it lives
The standard questions"Tell me about a time you…" Prepared for, practised, learnableFRM-059 and ACT-099
The one they are dreadingThe gap, the dismissal, the conviction, the visa, the reason somebody like them would not get this jobACT-100, and it needs care
The last five minutes"Do you have any questions for us?" Most people say noFRM-062 and ACT-102
Getting there at allTransport, childcare, clothes, a shift they cannot get out of, no quiet room for a video callACT-103, and it is not a confidence problem

Everybody in the room has one of the second kind. Most of the anxiety about interviews is attached to it, and a session that only teaches the first kind leaves it exactly where it was.

⚠️ Read the whole of ACT-100 before you run this topic. It handles disclosure, and it has rules that are not negotiable.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Behavioural question"Tell me about a time you…" The premise is that what you did before predicts what you will do next
STAR answerSituation, Task, Action, Result. The shape of a good answer to one
ResultWhat actually changed. A number if you have one, a lesson if you do not
PanelTwo or more interviewers together. Standard in government, health and education
Clean SlateNew Zealand law that lets many people, after seven clean years and other criteria, legally answer "no" about convictions

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-059 The STAR Interview Answer

What it is: a four-part shape that turns "tell me about a time you…" from a panic into a story with a point.

Origin: the behavioural interviewing tradition, from the 1970s on, built on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour better than hypothetical questions do. No single author owns STAR. Evidence: strong, for the underlying method rather than the acronym. Structured behavioural interviews are among the better-validated selection tools available and clearly beat unstructured "have a chat" interviews. The four letters are a memory aid sitting on top of that.

What goes in itHow long
SSituationWhere and when. Enough to picture it1 sentence
TTaskWhat you specifically had to do. Not the team1 sentence
AActionWhat you did, step by step. This is most of the answer3-4 sentences
RResultWhat happened. A number, or a lesson1-2 sentences
flowchart LR
  S["S · SITUATION<br/>set the scene<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"] --> T["T · TASK<br/>your job in it<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"]
  T --> A["A · ACTION<br/>what YOU did<br/><i>3-4 sentences</i>"]
  A --> R["R · RESULT<br/>what changed<br/><i>1-2 sentences</i>"]

How to read it: A is the answer. Most people spend ninety seconds on Situation, run out of nerve, and finish with "so yeah, it worked out." Flip the proportions.

Worked example, a warehouse interview. "Tell me about a time you dealt with pressure."

S: "Last Christmas we were two people down on the night shift for a fortnight." T: "I was the senior on nights, so getting the trucks loaded by six was on me." A: "I split the crew into two teams instead of four so nobody was working alone. I moved the pick order so the biggest customer's pallets got done first, in case we ran out of time. And I rang the day supervisor each morning to tell him exactly what was left, so he wasn't finding out at nine." R: "We got every truck out on time except one, which went an hour late. The day team said it was the first Christmas they hadn't inherited a mess."

➜ The result is not heroic. It contains a failure — one truck went late — and the answer is stronger for it. Perfect results sound rehearsed.

Four stories, not twenty answers. Trying to script every possible question is exactly why people freeze when one arrives worded differently. Build four and let them stretch.

StoryA time you…Covers
1Dealt with a difficult personConflict, customers, teamwork, patience
2Had something go wrong, partly on youAccountability, learning, honesty, pressure
3Worked in a team and did a specific partTeamwork, communication, reliability
4Kept going when it was hardResilience, motivation, workload

⚠️ "I" is genuinely hard for some learners, and it is not shyness. In many Pacific and Māori settings, taking individual credit is poor form. Do not tell anyone their upbringing is wrong. Name the clash and hand them the bridge: "our team did X, and my part was Y." Both true, and comfortable to say.

Learn more:

  • 🔗 Tahatū Job Hunters' Workbook teaches the same shape

→ Full framework page

The hard question (house content)

STAR does not cover the question people are actually dreading. That one has its own shape, three parts, and the third is where it turns.

Example
1. Say it plainlyOne sentence. No apology, no long story"I was out of work for two years."
2. What it wasBrief and factual"I was caring for my mum full time until she passed."
3. Turn forwardWhat you did about it, or what you can do now. Land here"I kept my first aid current, and I've just finished my Level 3. I'm ready to be back."
flowchart LR
  A["1 · SAY IT<br/>plainly, no apology"] --> B["2 · WHAT IT WAS<br/>brief, factual"]
  B --> C["3 · TURN FORWARD<br/>what you did, what you can do<br/><b>finish here</b>"]

How to read it: most people do 1 and 2 and then stop talking, leaving the silence for the interviewer to fill. Part 3 is the whole thing.

⚠️ On criminal convictions, do not improvise. New Zealand's Criminal Records (Clean Slate) Act 2004 means many people can legally answer "no" about convictions if they meet the criteria. It is specific and it is not guesswork. Send people to real advice: Community Law · Citizens Advice Bureau · their MSD case manager. A facilitator's job is the sentence, not the law.

⚠️ Open gap: the library has nothing on Clean Slate and it comes up constantly with MSD-referred learners. Worth building properly, with legal input, and it is logged as a priority-zero item on the Source Log.

FRM-062 The Questions You Ask Them (house model)

What it is: every interview ends with "do you have any questions for us?", most people say no, and it is the only moment in the whole hour where the power in the room is level.

Three things happen when somebody says no. Interest: you did not care enough to think of one. Judgement: you will take a job you know almost nothing about. The last impression: it is the final thing that happens, and it is what they say to each other afterwards.

Take three in, from at least two of these four kinds. Written on paper, and it is fine to read them.

flowchart TD
  Q["THREE QUESTIONS,<br/>WRITTEN DOWN"]
  Q --> A["1 · THE JOB<br/>what the work is actually like"]
  Q --> B["2 · THE PEOPLE<br/>who you'd be working with"]
  Q --> C["3 · THE FUTURE<br/>where this goes"]
  Q --> D["4 · THE PROCESS<br/>what happens next"]

How to read it: question 4 is not optional and it goes last. It is what gets you a date instead of a fortnight of refreshing your email.

KindExamples
The job"What does a normal day look like?" · "What's the hardest part of this job?"
The people"Who would I be working with day to day?" · "How does the team hand over?"
The future"Is there training or a ticket the company puts people through?"
The process"What are the next steps, and when will you be in touch?"

What to ask now, and what waits.

Ask it in the interviewWait until they offer you the job
The shift pattern and rosterWhether you can swap shifts
Whether the pay range in the ad is rightNegotiating the number
Whether there is training or a ticketWhether they will pay for a course you want
Start date and next stepsTime off you have booked, unless it is soon

➜ Pay is allowed. Learners are told constantly that asking about money looks greedy. "The ad said $26 to $28, is that right for this role?" is checking you can afford to take the job. The negotiation is a different conversation and it happens after the offer.

After the interview, two moves and five minutes: a three-line thank-you the same day, naming one thing from the conversation, and one follow-up if the date they gave you has passed. When there is silence it is usually the process, not you. Follow up once, then keep applying.

⚠️ In many Pacific and Māori settings, questioning somebody older or in authority is not straightforward. Do not treat that as a confidence gap to be fixed. Name it, and offer the framing that works: "Can I ask you something about the job?"

→ Full framework page

The day itself (house content, and it is not a confidence problem)

Most interview advice says "have an outfit ready." That sentence assumes a wardrobe, a car, a printer, a quiet room and nobody depending on you.

What actually stops our learners getting to an interview:
Getting thereNo transport, no fare, a bus that does not run on Saturdays
ChildcareAnd nobody asked until the night before
A shiftWhich they cannot get out of without saying why
ClothesNot "which outfit". Whether there is one at all
Online interviewsNo device, no data that holds 45 minutes, no room where nobody walks in

➜ None of that is fixed by wanting the job more, and none of it is a character flaw. It is logistics, it is solvable in a week, and it needs a facilitator who will act on what comes out of ACT-103.

⚠️ Never advise anybody to hide who they are. Cultural dress, taonga and moko are not problems to be managed. An employer who treats them as one has told you something useful early.

FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found — why the interview is not the start

What it is: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds.

It belongs in this topic for one reason. The best interview you will ever have is the one where somebody already vouched for you, because you are not a stranger being assessed, you are a known quantity being confirmed.

ChannelWhat the interview feels like
1. Applied coldYou are one of eight, and they are looking for reasons to cut
2. Someone inside handed your CV overYou arrive with credit already on the board
3. Never advertisedOften barely an interview. A conversation and a start date
4. Created for youThey have already decided. This is logistics

➜ So the practical move after this topic is not more interview practice. It is ACT-101 and the sentence: what I'm looking for, what I bring, would you let me know.

→ Full framework page

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-099 The STAR Answer LabRoleplay40-45 minFRM-059, FRM-057
ACT-102 Three QuestionsWorksheet25-30 minFRM-062
ACT-100 The Hardest QuestionRoleplay30-35 minThe three-part shape
ACT-103 The Day ItselfWorksheet, then one-to-one30-40 minThe barriers, not the nerves

Suggested flow, and it is now two sessions rather than one:
Session 1The two answers in section 1 read aloud → teach FRM-059 → ACT-099 in threes → teach FRM-062 → ACT-102 → close
Session 2Recap → the three-part shape → ACT-100 with the rules said out loud first → ACT-103 → ACT-101 to end forward rather than on the hard question → ACT-013

If it has to be one session: FRM-059 → ACT-099 → FRM-062 → ACT-102 → ACT-101. Give ACT-100 and ACT-103 their own time. Both surface hardship and neither survives being rushed.

⚠️ ACT-099 before ACT-100, always. The standard questions build the confidence that makes the hard one survivable. Reversing them is how a room shuts down.

⚠️ Do not end on ACT-100. Whatever your timing, put something forward-facing after it. ACT-101 is designed to be that.

6. Self-Assessment

The four ticks (house content, and it is an observer check, not a score).

Inside ACT-099, the observer has one job. Tick what they actually heard:

Heard it?
Situation kept to about a sentence☐
Said "I", not only "we"☐
Action was the longest part☐
There was an actual result at the end☐

Feedback is those four ticks and nothing else. No general opinions, no "that was good". Specific feedback is the only kind that changes anything.

For a written self-check after the session:

Yes / No
Do I have four stories written down, not just in my head?☐
Can I tell each one in under two minutes?☐
Does at least one of them include something going wrong?☐
Does every one finish with what changed?☐
Have I said my hardest answer out loud to another person?☐
Does my hardest answer finish on part 3?☐
Do I have three questions written down, and is one of them about next steps?☐
Do I know how I am getting there, and who is covering what I normally do?☐

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Which of the two answers in the opening story sounded more like you? Be honest.
  2. Which of the four story boxes was hardest to fill, and what does that tell you?
  3. Where do you catch yourself saying "we" when you mean "I"?
  4. Story 2 was a time something went wrong. How did it feel to tell it? What did telling it do?
  5. What is the question you have been dreading, and what would part 3 of your answer be?
  6. What have you been leaving off your CV entirely because of that question?
  7. What is the difference between explaining and apologising?
  8. When did you last say "no, I think you've covered everything"? What did you actually want to know?
  9. What would you need to sort out this week to get to an interview on Thursday?
  10. Who is the last person you told that you are looking for work? When will you tell three more?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • The two answers (6 min, low energy). Read both answers from section 1 in character, then ask

which one has more experience. Free, needs no materials, and it opens the whole topic.

  • "And then what happened?" (8 min, medium energy). The facilitator asks a question, takes any

answer, and replies only "and then what happened?" until there is a result. Usually three rounds. The single most useful drill in the topic, and it is part 3 of ACT-099.

  • ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?

(20-25 min, medium energy). Best used as the closer here, not the opener.

  • ACT-034 The Two Minute Introduction

(20-25 min). "Tell me about yourself" is the first question in almost every interview, and this is where it is practised.
