Built from SRC-010 Tahatū Career Navigator, ingested 2026-08-01. Tahatū's Job Hunters' Workbook teaches the same STAR shape and is where learners should go for the practice material. The three-part shape for the hard question is Zeducation house content, written because Tahatū does not cover gaps, dismissals or convictions and our learners arrive with them. Both worked examples and both roleplays were written fresh. The Clean Slate section is deliberately a signpost, not advice.

Enriched on 2026-08-01 from SRC-011 Indeed, "How To Prepare for an Interview in 11 Steps". ⚠️ That page could not be read — indeed.com is refused at the network gateway — so it was assessed from search results and not one sentence of it was ingested. Its value was in exposing what this topic was missing: the questions the candidate asks, and getting to the interview at all. Both are house content, written fresh. Where the source says "have an outfit ready", ACT-103 asks the question that has to come first.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: this topic is now genuinely two sessions. 180 min covers all of it; 150 is tight. Under

120, run FRM-059, ACT-099, FRM-062 and ACT-102, and give ACT-100 and ACT-103 their own time. Both are better as a whole session than as a rushed twenty minutes

  • ⚠️ ACT-103 produces a to-do list for you, not just for the learner. Do not run it unless you can

act on what comes out: bus fares, clothes, childcare, a room with wifi. Know your options before you walk in — the programme's own fund, their MSD case manager, a community clothing pool

  • ⚠️ Read ACT-100 in full before delivery. Nobody discloses to the room, pairs are chosen by the

learner, anyone can pass at any point with no reason given, and all of that is said out loud before it starts

  • ⚠️ Know your referral options before you walk in. Bereavement, illness, violence, prison and

deportation all surface here. Workplace EAP, their GP, 1737 call or text, and their MSD case manager

  • Say which STAR you mean, every single time. Facilitators trained on FRM-003 will use the word

by reflex and the room will follow them into the wrong model

  • The cheapest upgrade in this topic: make every ACT-099 roleplay finish with *"do you have any

questions for us?"* Nobody has an answer the first time. After a fortnight everybody does

  • Do not turn ACT-103 into a grooming lecture. No commentary on hair, jewellery, tattoos or how

somebody carries themselves. It is logistics, and barriers get named one-to-one, never to the room

  • What usually goes wrong: the twelve-minute Situation. Timebox it out loud during practice or it

will happen in the room

  • Push for a story where something went wrong. They are better answers and interviewers know it.

Learners will resist, because it feels like handing over ammunition

  • Never tell somebody to lie, and never tell them their honest answer is unsayable. If an answer

genuinely will not survive, that is a conversation about which employers to approach, not about becoming a better liar

  • The learner whose hard question is about their name, their age or their race is not describing

a gap. That is discrimination, and the answer is not a better sentence. It is FRM-061 and the Human Rights Commission

  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on this Pink Sheet yet, and no employer voice. **A

friendly hiring manager for the last twenty minutes beats any facilitator feedback**, and it is the easiest thing on this list to arrange

PS-EMP-003Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Your CV gets seconds, not minutes

placeholder-storycareer-readinesscvjob-searchwork-readinessatswriting

Topic: TOP-EMP-003 The CV That Gets Read · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

Point

You are writing for a reader who does not exist.

The reader you imagine has time, interest, and the whole page. The real one is software, then a tired person with a stack. The top third is your entire application. Everything below it only gets read if the top third worked.

Model

Two readers, in this order, wanting different things.

Reads firstWantsBreaks on
1. The softwareAn applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the adColumns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos, image-PDFs
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA fast answer to "can this person do the job?"A personal statement, hobbies, and the licence on page two
flowchart TD
  A["NAME · phone · email · suburb"] --> B["THE HEADLINE<br/>one line: what you are, for this job"]
  B --> C["THREE TO FIVE SKILL BULLETS<br/>each with evidence"]
  C --> D["WORK HISTORY<br/>achievements, not duties"]
  D --> E["TRAINING · LICENCES · TICKETS"]
  E --> F["REFEREES<br/>named, warned, willing"]
  B -.->|"the whole<br/>application"| C

B and C are above the fold. Everything else is the evidence file for a decision that has already been made.

And the test that carries the whole thing: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is a duty. Rewrite it as what changed because you were there.

Metaphor

A shop window, not a stockroom.

Nobody walks past a shop and reads the inventory list. They look at the window for about as long as it takes to walk past it, and that decides whether they come in.

Most CVs are a stockroom with the door open. Everything is in there somewhere, in no particular order, and the customer is expected to find it. The window is the top third, and you rearrange it for every person walking past.

Study

⚠️ This is the section where the popular numbers have to be refused.

Two figures circulate constantly and neither is usable:

The claimWhy it is not quoted here
"Recruiters spend six seconds on a CV"Traces to small eye-tracking studies published by a recruitment vendor as marketing. Sample and method are not independently checkable
"75% of CVs are never seen by a human"No traceable source. It is repeated by companies selling CV-optimisation services

What is defensible and enough to teach from:

  • Screening is fast, and at volume it is filtered by software before any person sees it. That is

not contested by anyone who hires

  • Tahatū, the Tertiary Education Commission's careers service, publishes

free New Zealand CV templates and a CV builder deliberately built plain enough to be machine-readable

Honest limit: the four-sentence letter and the two-readers model are practitioner models. There is no study saying four sentences beats five. What is defensible is that short and specific beats long and generic, and that a letter which gets written beats one that does not.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The forty-one applications, two automated replies, and the Class 2 licence on page two is composite and written for teaching. It is true to what tutors describe. It is not one identified person.

The story to collect: a learner who moved one thing to the top third — a licence, a ticket, a headline — and started getting calls. The shape that lands is the number before and the number after, because it is the same person and the same skills, only visible.

Second story worth collecting: a hiring manager, in their own words, on what they do with a stack of CVs on a Friday afternoon. Thirty seconds of that beats twenty minutes of facilitation, and it is the easiest story on this list to get.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any CV session, in the first five minutesBefore anyone opens a document. It reframes the whole task
One-to-one with somebody who has stopped applyingLook at their top third and nothing else
Employer engagementAsk them to confirm it. They will, and it is more powerful from them
Tutor trainingThe shop-window line is the one staff remember

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-EMP-002 You are not starting from nothingThat sheet fills the container. This one is the container. Always in that order
PS-EMP-004 Four stories, not twenty answersEverything in the top third has to survive being asked about
PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowThe honest counterweight. A perfect CV in channel 1 still has the worst odds

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on the four-sentence cover letter. The Point is already written: sentence 3 is the only one that proves you did not send this to forty employers.

TOP-EMP-003Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

The CV That Gets Read

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation120-150 minCareer Readiness, Part 2career-readinesscvcover-letterjob-searchwritingwork-readinesstahatuats

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-EMP-003 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Career Readiness, Part 2

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A man has applied for forty-one jobs in four months. He keeps a list. He has had two replies, both automated, and he has started to believe there is no work in Auckland.

His CV is two and a half pages. It is well laid out, in two columns, with a photo and a skills bar chart. Page one is his contact details, a personal statement about being a hardworking team player, and his hobbies. What he can actually do is on page two, under the third job down.

He has a Class 2 licence. It is on page two.

Ask the room: how long do you think somebody spends on a CV before they decide?

Then hand out four real CVs, face down, and give the room seven seconds each.

Statement: Your CV does not get read. It gets scanned by software, then glanced at by a tired person with a stack of them. The top third is your whole application.

➜ Facilitator note: run ACT-096 right here rather than talking about it. The point cannot be argued with once they have been the reader.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Rewrite the top third of your CV so a reader knows within seconds what job you are going for.
  2. Turn three duties into three achievements, each with evidence.
  3. Write a four-sentence cover letter for a real job, including one true, specific thing about

that employer.

3. About This Topic

This topic assumes you have already done TOP-EMP-002. That one worked out what you can do. This one is about the container it goes in.

Everybody leaves with a tailored CV and a cover letter for a real job they could apply for that night. Not an exercise. A finished thing, with a date against it. That is the design, and a session that ends with good intentions and no application has failed.

Use Tahatū's CV builder. It is free, it is New Zealand standard, and its templates are plain enough that screening software can read them. A blank Word document is where this work goes to die, and a beautiful Canva design is often worse than useless, because the software that reads it first cannot parse a text box.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ATSApplicant tracking system. Software that reads and filters CVs before any person sees them
The top thirdEverything visible without scrolling or turning the page. Name, headline, skill bullets
HeadlineOne line under your name saying what you are, for this job
DutyWhat you were told to do. Anyone in that role could write the same sentence
AchievementWhat changed because you were there
TailoringRewriting the top third for each job, using that ad's words. Fifteen minutes, not a rewrite

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-058 The CV That Gets Read (house model)

What it is: your CV gets a few seconds and a keyword scan before a person decides anything, so the top third has to do almost all the work.

Two readers, in this order. Most CV advice fails because it optimises for the wrong one.

Reads firstWants
1. The softwareIncreasingly, an applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the job ad
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA quick answer to "can this person do the job?"

⚠️ A beautiful CV the software cannot read is not a CV. Columns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos and PDFs-of-images all break parsers.

The shape:

flowchart TD
  A["NAME · phone · email · suburb"] --> B["THE HEADLINE<br/>one line: what you are, for this job"]
  B --> C["THREE TO FIVE SKILL BULLETS<br/>each with evidence"]
  C --> D["WORK HISTORY<br/>most recent first · achievements, not duties"]
  D --> E["TRAINING · LICENCES · TICKETS"]
  E --> F["REFEREES<br/>named, warned, willing"]

How to read it: everything above the fold is B and C. That is the whole strategy.

SectionThe rule
ContactPhone, email, suburb. No full street address, no date of birth, no photo. In New Zealand a photo invites discrimination and gives nothing back
HeadlineOne line, rewritten for every job. "Warehouse assistant with forklift F endorsement and four years on nights." Not "hardworking team player seeking opportunity"
Skill bulletsThree to five, in the job ad's words, each with evidence from FRM-057
Work historyWhat changed because you were there, not what you were told to do
TrainingLicences, tickets and endorsements go high if the job needs them. A Class 2 or a Site Safe card can be the entire reason you get called
RefereesNamed, asked first, and briefed on which job it is

Duties versus achievements. The single biggest lift available on most CVs.

Duty, which everyone writesAchievement, which gets read
"Responsible for stock""Cut stock discrepancies from weekly to almost none over six months"
"Customer service""Handled the complaints desk on Saturdays, the busiest shift"
"Cleaning duties""Held the kitchen at an A grade through two council inspections"
"Worked in a team""Trained four new starters, three of whom are still there"

➜ The test: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is still a duty.

Tailoring, which is not optional. One CV sent to forty jobs is why nobody called. Fifteen minutes:

  1. Print the job ad. Highlight every skill word
  2. Rewrite the headline for this job, in its words
  3. Reorder the skill bullets so what it asked for comes first
  4. Check the licence or ticket it names is visible without scrolling

⚠️ Use their words, not your synonyms. If the ad says "forklift licence", do not write "counterbalance certification". Software matches text, not meaning.

⚠️ On the "six seconds" figure. You will see it everywhere, along with "75% of CVs are never seen by a human". Both trace back to recruitment-vendor marketing, not to research anyone can check. Do not quote either as fact. What is not in dispute is that screening is fast and often filtered by software first, and that is enough to teach from.

Learn more:

  • 🔗 Tahatū CV templates and Job Hunters' Workbook

→ Full framework page

FRM-060 The Four-Sentence Cover Letter (house model)

What it is: four sentences that answer the only four questions a hiring manager has.

SentenceAnswers
1Which job, and one reason you want this one. Name the employer"Why are you writing?"
2The single strongest thing you bring, in the ad's words, with evidence"Can you do it?"
3One specific thing about them. A project, a value, a location, a customer"Do you actually want us?"
4What happens next. Availability, no fuss"What now?"
flowchart LR
  A["1 · WHICH JOB<br/>and why this one"] --> B["2 · WHAT YOU BRING<br/>their words + evidence"]
  B --> C["3 · WHY THEM<br/>one specific thing"]
  C --> D["4 · NEXT STEP<br/>availability, no fuss"]

How to read it: sentence 3 is the one almost nobody writes, and it is the one that proves this was not sent to forty employers. Write it first.

Worked example. Support worker, an Auckland disability provider.

Kia ora Sarah, [1] I'm applying for the support worker role at your Māngere site, because the shifts fit around my study and I've wanted to move into disability support since caring for my grandfather. [2] I've got two years of personal care experience, including medication support and working alongside district nurses, and I've just finished my Level 3 in Health and Wellbeing. [3] I noticed your team runs the community garden programme at that site. That's exactly the kind of support work I want to be part of, rather than only in-home. [4] I'm available from 12 August and can come in for a chat any weekday. My CV is attached. Ngā mihi, Losa

What to cut:

CutWhy
"I am writing to apply for the position advertised on Seek"They know. It wastes the best line on the page
"I am a hardworking team player with excellent communication skills"Everyone writes it, so it says nothing
Retelling the whole CVThe CV is attached. The letter is the reason to open it
An apology for anythingNever apologise for a gap, a career change, or being new

⚠️ Sentence 3 is where people invent. An invented detail is worse than no sentence, because it is checkable and it is a lie in writing.

→ Full framework page

FRM-057 Transferable Skills — where the content comes from

You cannot write skill bullets out of nothing. Every bullet in the top third comes from the skills work in TOP-EMP-002, and every one carries three parts:

Example
SkillThe employer's words"Cash handling and reconciliation"
WhereThe real setting, however informal"Two years on the till at a family takeaway"
ProofA number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it"Balanced the float nightly. Never short."

⚠️ A learner arriving without this work done cannot do the session properly. If they have not done TOP-EMP-002, run ACT-094 first and accept that you will only get the top third finished.

→ Full framework page

On using AI to write it (house content)

Learners will use it, and pretending otherwise wastes the chance to teach something.

Where AI helpsWhere it fails
Tidying grammar and shorteningSentence 3. It does not know the employer, so it invents something plausible and false
Turning a duty into a shorter sentenceInventing achievements you did not have
Suggesting the employer's word for a skill you haveMaking the whole thing sound like everyone else's

➜ The rule: AI can help you say what is true. It cannot decide what is true. See TOP-COM-006 and ACT-027.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-096 Seven SecondsGame / opener12-15 minFRM-058
ACT-097 The Tailoring LabWorksheet, then live editing40-50 minFRM-058, FRM-057
ACT-098 Four SentencesWorksheet25-30 minFRM-060
ACT-006 Two Things CommitmentReflection10 minCloses with a date

Suggested flow: ACT-096 cold, before any teaching → teach FRM-058 → ACT-097 on a real job ad → break → teach FRM-060 → ACT-098 on the same job ad → ACT-006 to close.

⚠️ The same job ad runs through both worksheets. One application, finished, in two activities. Splitting them across two different jobs halves the value and doubles the work.

6. Self-Assessment

The seven-second check (house content, and it is a partner check, not a score).

Swap CVs. Your partner gets seven seconds on the top third, then answers one question:

"What job is this person going for?"

If they cannot say, it is not tailored yet. That is the entire assessment, and it is harder to pass than any rating scale.

For a written self-check, tick honestly:

Yes / No
Is there a headline naming what I am, for this job?☐
Are three to five skill bullets visible without scrolling?☐
Does every bullet have evidence in it?☐
Are the ad's own words in my top third?☐
If the ad names a licence or ticket, is it above the fold?☐
Have I turned at least three duties into achievements?☐
Are my referees named, asked, and told which job?☐
Would a person who replaced me be able to write my bullets?☐ (this one should be no)

⚠️ Not validated, and not a score out of eight. A teaching mirror.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. What did you notice about your own CV when you had seven seconds on somebody else's?
  2. What was in the job ad that you have been doing for years and never written down?
  3. Which duty was hardest to turn into an achievement, and why?
  4. What did you find out about the employer that you did not know before?
  5. Did anything you found put you off the job? What does that tell you?
  6. What have you been leaving off your CV, and what is the honest reason?
  7. Who are your three referees, and when did you last ask them?
  8. Which job are you applying for, and when? Write the date.

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-096 Seven Seconds

(12-15 min, medium energy). Four real CVs, seven seconds each, and the room becomes the reader. Run it before any teaching, because it makes the argument for you.

  • Cut the waffle (10 min, high energy). Hand out one real, bad, five-paragraph cover letter.

Groups race to cut it to four sentences. Fast, funny, and it lands hard. Full version is a variation inside ACT-098.

  • Headline round (5 min). Everyone writes their headline on a sticky note. Read them out with no

names. The room guesses the job. Good after lunch.

Connections

Connects toHow it connects

TOP-EMP-004 Tell Them The StoryEverything claimed on the CV has to survive being asked about. That topic builds the stories
TOP-COM-003 Make Your Message LandThe headline and sentence 1 are BLUF. Same skill, different page

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable. 120 min works if ACT-096 is kept tight. Under 90, do ACT-096,

the employer up

PS-EMP-001Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

The job comes from the person you barely know

placeholder-storynetworkingweak-tiesrelationshipswork-readinessopportunity

Topic: TOP-EMP-001 The People You Work With · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

Point

The people who love you cannot help you find work. The people who barely know you can.

It is not about who cares about you most. It is about who knows something you do not.

Model

Strong tiesWeak ties
WhoFamily, close mates, the people you see every dayA former workmate, a tutor, someone from church, a cousin's friend
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you have never heard
Who they knowRoughly who you knowPeople you have never met
What they give youSupport, help, a place to stayInformation, opportunities, introductions
flowchart TD
  subgraph Y["Your close circle · everyone knows everyone"]
    A["You"] --- B["Best mate"]
    A --- C["Cousin"]
    B --- C
  end
  subgraph O["A different pocket of the world"]
    E["Their workmate"] --- F["Someone hiring"]
  end
  A -.->|the weak tie<br/>is the bridge| E

The closed triangle is your circle. Everybody in it hears the same news. The dotted line is the only one that reaches new information.

Metaphor

A closed circle and a bridge.

Your close friends are a circle. Warm, safe, and completely enclosed. Everyone inside hears the same news at the same time, so no matter how much they love you, they cannot tell you anything new.

A weak tie is a bridge out of the circle. You do not have to live on the bridge. You just have to have built one, and be willing to walk over it occasionally.

Study

**Mark Granovetter, "The Strength of Weak Ties", American Journal of Sociology 78(6), 1360-1380 (1973).** Granovetter surveyed 282 men in Massachusetts about how they had found their jobs. Casual acquaintances turned out to be more useful than close friends. It became one of the most cited papers in the social sciences.

📄 Full paper (PDF) · 📄 Stanford summary

Honest limit: 282 men, Massachusetts, early 1970s. The finding has held up broadly across fifty years of replication, but say what the original study was.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. This sheet needs a real one and it can only come from delivery.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who got work through a weak tie. The shape that lands is: applications that went nowhere, then one message to someone they had half-forgotten, and the job came from that. Ask tutors and coaches for it. Get permission and get the details right, including how long the gap was since they had last spoken.

Second story worth collecting: a learner who did not think they had a network, until someone walked them through church, sport, family and former workmates and counted it up. That one is more common and probably more useful.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any work-readiness sessionThe line that reframes "networking" for people who hate the word
CV and job search coachingBefore the CV. Most jobs are not found by applying
Employer conversationsWhy they should keep talking to past learners

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-COM-001 Assertive is clear, not loudBoth argue that a workplace skill people think needs confidence actually needs a small repeatable habit

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on the red flags, built on the contrast between building relationships and building them badly. The Point is already there: most damaged reputations started with telling one person, once.

TOP-EMP-001Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

The People You Work With

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 1relationshipsnetworkingprofessionalismwork-readinessgossipboundariesweak-ties

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-EMP-001 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 1

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two people start the same job on the same day. Both can do the work.

One of them says good morning to everyone, including the cleaner and the security guard. He asks the experienced guy how he sets out a job. When he is going to miss a deadline he says so early. When he gets pulled up he says "fair enough, I'll fix it."

The other is faster with the tools.

Twelve months later, one of them is being recommended for the next job. Ask the room: which one, and why?

Then the second question, which is the real one: think of someone at your last job who was good at the work but nobody wanted on their team. What was it about them?

Statement: Being good at the job gets you hired. How you are with people is what gets you kept, recommended, and told about the next opportunity.

➜ Facilitator note: the second question does the work. Every room has that person and the answers come fast. Collect three or four, then point out that not one of them was about competence.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Build a work relationship on purpose, starting with one short conversation with someone

outside your immediate team.

  1. Name the behaviours that protect a work relationship and the ones that quietly damage it.

3. About This Topic

Success at work is not just about doing your job well. It is also about deliberately building the right relationships, because the people around you can open doors, back you up, and speak well of you when you are not in the room. Or, if you choose badly, they can hold you back and make work harder than it needs to be.

This matters for four reasons. Support: the right relationships help you feel included and confident instead of isolated. Opportunity: strong connections lead to new work, honest feedback, and people who recommend you. Wellbeing: healthy relationships make work more enjoyable and give you people you can trust when things get hard. Influence: without them you have less say over decisions that affect you.

It is your job, not your employer's. Notice who is safe, respectful and growth-minded, and put your time into those people on purpose.

And you do not need to be loud. The shyest person in the room can do this, because it is built out of very small things repeated often.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Weak tieSomeone you know a bit but not well. A former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
SiloSticking to your own small group and not talking to anyone else
ProfessionalismBehaving the same way with everyone, no matter their job title
ConfidentialityKeeping to yourself what you were told in private

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits (house model)

What it is: the four habits that make people want to work with you, over time.

HabitWhat it looks like on a Tuesday
ProfessionalismYou speak to the cleaner the same way you speak to the manager
FeedbackSomeone says you cut people off, and you say thank you instead of explaining why they are wrong
Development mindsetYou ask the experienced person how they do it, and show the new person where things are
Conflict managementYou say something in week one, while it is still small
flowchart TD
  H["FOUR PROFESSIONAL HABITS"]
  H --> P["Professionalism<br/>same person to everyone"]
  H --> F["Feedback<br/>open to how you come across"]
  H --> D["Development mindset<br/>learn and share"]
  H --> C["Conflict management<br/>early, direct, respectful"]

How to read it: habits, not talents. Every one can be started this week by someone who has never done it.

Worked example: a new warehouse hand makes a point of learning the forklift driver's name and asking how he likes the pallets stacked. Six weeks later, when the new hand needs a favour on a bad day, he gets it. Nothing about that required confidence.

Learn more: house content, with no external reading matched to it yet. The gap and what would fill it are recorded on the framework page. → Full framework page

FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties

What it is: the job and the opportunity usually come from someone you barely know.

Origin: Mark Granovetter, American Journal of Sociology, 1973. He asked 282 men how they found their jobs. Casual acquaintances beat close friends, by a lot.

Strong tiesWeak ties
WhoFamily, close matesA former workmate, a tutor, someone from church
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you do not
What they give youSupport and helpInformation and opportunities
flowchart TD
  subgraph Y["Your close circle"]
    A["You"] --- B["Best mate"]
    A --- C["Cousin"]
    B --- C
  end
  subgraph O["Somewhere else"]
    E["Their workmate"] --- F["Someone hiring"]
  end
  A -.->|weak tie| E

How to read it: your close circle hears the same news you do. The dotted line is the valuable one.

Worked example: a woman sends forty online applications and gets two replies. Then she messages her tutor from four months ago, just to say what she has been up to. The tutor mentions a former student managing a distribution centre in Wiri who is short-staffed. One message beat forty applications.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties (PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — The strength of weak ties

→ Full framework page

The six red flags (house content)

Building relationships is powerful. How you build them decides whether they help you.

Red flagWhy it costs you
Oversharing personal informationBlurs boundaries and makes it harder to stay professional
Romantic entanglements and office dramaConflicts of interest, and hard for everyone involved
Being too close to a small groupOthers read it as favouritism or cliques
GossipingIf you talk about others, people assume you talk about them too
Using people only for personal gainShow up only when you want something and people pull away
No clear boundariesRelationships get unprofessional and distract from the work

→ Covered in full on FRM-021. For trust specifically, see FRM-022 The Trust Equation.

The shy starter (house content, and the most important paragraph in this topic)

You don't need to be loud or extroverted to build good relationships.

Three moves, and that is all:

  1. Brief eye contact when you walk past someone
  2. A nod or a small smile, as a simple sign of respect and openness
  3. A short human conversation. "How's your day going?" "How did that meeting go?"

These tiny actions help people feel seen and make the deeper conversations possible later.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Who at work would say something good about you if your name came up when you were not there?
  2. Think of a work relationship that has helped you. How did it actually start?
  3. Which of the six red flags have you seen damage someone? What did it cost them?
  4. When did you last talk to someone at work who is not in your usual group?
  5. Who is a weak tie you have not spoken to in six months, and what would it take to send one message?
  6. Are you someone people can tell things to in confidence? How do you know?
  7. Which of the four habits is your weakest right now?
  8. What is one thing you will do differently in the next week, with whom, and when?

  • ACT-036 Red Flag Or Green Flag?

Facilitator Notes

this topic is for extroverts and switches off. Say it early

costs you, not what you will be in trouble for

  • Do not push LinkedIn. For most Zeducation learners the live network is church, sport, family,

marae and former workmates. Naming what they already have beats teaching them to build something new

Career Readiness topics — TOP-EMP-002, TOP-EMP-003 and TOP-EMP-004 — are about getting it. Either order works, and a room that is currently out of work will engage with those three first

PS-EMP-002Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

You are not starting from nothing

placeholder-storycareer-readinesstransferable-skillsconfidencework-readinesscv

Topic: TOP-EMP-002 What You Can Already Do · Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness

Point

"I haven't really got any experience" is almost never true. It means nobody has ever helped you put it into words.

The skill is there. The vocabulary is missing. Those are completely different problems and only one of them is the person's fault, which is neither.

Model

Five sources, one set of skills, one translation.

WhereWhat people countWhat is actually there
Paid work✅ CountedUsually written as duties, not skills
Unpaid and family❌ Never countedBudgeting, logistics, personal care, advocacy
Church, marae, community❌ Never countedEvent organisation, handling money, speaking to a room
Sport and culture❌ Never countedReliability, coaching, being coached, losing well
Study and self-taught❌ Rarely countedAnything learned off YouTube is still learned
flowchart LR
  A["PAID WORK"] --> S(("YOUR<br/>SKILLS"))
  B["UNPAID<br/>AND FAMILY"] --> S
  C["CHURCH ·<br/>MARAE ·<br/>COMMUNITY"] --> S
  D["SPORT<br/>AND CULTURE"] --> S
  E["STUDY AND<br/>SELF-TAUGHT"] --> S
  S --> T["THE SAME SKILL,<br/>IN THE EMPLOYER'S WORDS"]

Four of the five arrows are ones people leave out. The box on the right is the whole job.

And the rule that stops it becoming a pep talk: every skill gets three parts — the skill in the employer's words, where you did it, and proof. A number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it. Without the third part it is a slogan.

Metaphor

A pantry you have never taken stock of.

You are standing in front of it saying there is nothing to cook. There are four shelves and you have only ever looked at the one at eye level. Everything on the other three is still food. It is just been sitting in packaging you do not recognise, with somebody else's labels on it.

Nobody is asking you to buy groceries. They are asking you to look on the bottom shelf.

Study

No single study proves this one, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. It is a practitioner model. What sits under it:

  • Tahatū, the Tertiary Education Commission's careers service, is built

on the premise that a career is not one ladder and that skills carry across a working life. Its 800-plus career profiles are organised so you can enter through skills rather than job titles

  • **O\*NET**, the US occupational database Tahatū's interest quiz

derives from, has spent thirty years describing jobs as bundles of skills instead of titles

Honest limit: neither of those is evidence that reframing changes employment outcomes. What this model is, is a translation tool. It should be taught as one, never as a proven intervention.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The section-1 story in the topic — the Māngere woman with the household budget, the school run, the interpreting and the fono catering — is composite and written for teaching. It is true to what tutors describe, and it is not one identified person.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who said "I haven't got any experience", did the skills work, and could then name eight things with evidence. What lands is the before and after sentence — what they said in the first ten minutes and what they said at the end. Get permission properly and get the detail right.

Second story worth collecting: a learner who got a job on the strength of a skill that came from church or family, not from paid work. That one closes the argument for good.

Where it goes

Use it inHow

One-to-one with somebody who has stopped applyingThe pantry metaphor does the work when a room is not available
Employer conversationsWhy a candidate with a thin CV is not a thin candidate
Tutor and coach inductionThe single sentence Zeducation staff should never let pass unchallenged

TOP-EMP-002Topic · Employment & Work Readiness

What You Can Already Do

✅ publishedEmployment & Work ReadinessFoundation120-150 minCareer Readiness, Part 1career-readinesstransferable-skillsriasecintereststahatujob-searchwork-readinessconfidence

Pillar: Employment & Work Readiness · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-EMP-002 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Career Readiness, Part 1

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A woman sits down for a work-readiness session in Māngere and says the sentence almost everybody says: "I haven't really got any experience."

Here is her actual week. She runs a household on a fixed budget and it balances. She gets three children to two different schools by 8:30 every day, and has done for six years. She translates for her parents at WINZ and at the doctor, which means she handles other people's most stressful conversations in two languages. She did the food for a fono of a hundred and forty people last month, to a budget, and there was enough.

Ask the room: which of those things did not count?

Then the second question, which is the real one: what have you been doing for years that you have never written down anywhere?

Statement: You are not starting from nothing. You are starting from a lot of experience that nobody has ever helped you put into words.

➜ Facilitator note: do not rush past the first question. Let the room answer it. Somebody will say "but that's just being a mum" and that sentence is the whole topic. Write it on the board.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name at least eight skills you already have, in the words an employer uses, each with a place

you did it and one piece of proof.

  1. Use Tahatū to turn your interests into a list of real New Zealand jobs, with pay and demand

attached.

  1. Say out loud, to a real person, what work you are looking for.

3. About This Topic

Most job-search teaching starts with the CV. That is the wrong end.

A CV is a container. If you sit down to write one before you know what goes in it, you produce half a page, feel worse about yourself, and stop. This topic is the part that comes first: working out what you can already do, what you are actually drawn to, and who already knows you.

Three questions, in this order.

The questionWhat answers it
1What can I do?FRM-057 Transferable Skills
2What am I drawn to, and what jobs is that?FRM-056 RIASEC, on Tahatū
3How do people actually get work?FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found

This topic uses somebody else's tool on purpose. Tahatū is the New Zealand government's careers site, run by the Tertiary Education Commission. It replaced careers.govt.nz in December 2025. It carries profiles for more than 800 careers with New Zealand pay ranges and job-demand ratings, an interest quiz, and a free CV builder. Zeducation does not have that data and never will. Our job is the teaching around it, not a copy of it.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Transferable skillSomething you can do that carries from one setting to another. Handling money, calming someone down, meeting a deadline
EvidenceThe proof underneath a claim. A number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it
Interest typeOne of six broad kinds of work people are drawn to. See FRM-056
Weak tieSomeone you know a bit, but not well. The person a job usually comes through
Job demandHow many of these jobs New Zealand actually needs right now. Tahatū rates it on every career profile

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-057 Transferable Skills (house model)

What it is: the skills you built somewhere nobody wrote down, which are the same skills the job ad is asking for, in different words.

Ask most people what they can do and they answer with job titles. Kitchenhand. Caregiver. Mum. Job ads do not ask for job titles. They ask for skills. The gap between those two sentences is where a lot of good people stop applying.

The five places skills come from. Most people count the first one and nothing else.

WhereWhat people miss
Paid workCounted, but usually described as duties rather than skills
Unpaid and familyRunning a household budget. Caring for a parent. Getting three kids somewhere on time
Church, marae, communityOrganising an event for 200 people. Handling money. Speaking in front of a room
Sport and cultureTurning up when you did not feel like it. Coaching. Being coached
Study and self-taughtAnything learned off YouTube counts. Welding, video editing, fixing a car
flowchart LR
  A["PAID WORK"] --> S(("YOUR<br/>SKILLS"))
  B["UNPAID<br/>AND FAMILY"] --> S
  C["CHURCH ·<br/>MARAE ·<br/>COMMUNITY"] --> S
  D["SPORT<br/>AND CULTURE"] --> S
  E["STUDY AND<br/>SELF-TAUGHT"] --> S
  S --> T["THE SAME SKILL,<br/>IN THE EMPLOYER'S WORDS"]

How to read it: one set of skills, five sources. The arrow on the right is the translation, and it is the actual work of this topic.

The translation. Left column is how a learner says it. Right column is how a job ad says it.

What they sayWhat it is called
"I just helped out at church"Volunteer coordination · event organisation
"I looked after my nana"Personal care · medication support · working with health professionals
"I did the food for the fono"Catering to budget and headcount · food safety
"I ran the till"Cash handling · reconciliation · customer service
"I translate for my parents"Bilingual · interpreting in high-stakes settings
"I got the kids to school every day"Reliability · logistics · time management

➜ Nothing in the right column is a lie. Say that out loud to a room worried about overselling. Naming a skill accurately is not exaggeration. Most people are doing the opposite, and it is costing them work.

The three-part evidence rule. A skill on a CV is a claim, and a claim without evidence is noise.

Example
SkillThe employer's words"Cash handling and reconciliation"
WhereThe real setting, however informal"Two years on the till at a family takeaway"
ProofA number, an outcome, or a person who would confirm it"Balanced the float nightly. Never short."

⚠️ The proof column is the one people skip, and it is the one that gets read.

Learn more: house model. The reframing comes from Tahatū's skills-not-jobs framing and the skills taxonomies underneath O\*NET. → Full framework page

FRM-056 RIASEC — Holland's six interest types

What it is: six broad kinds of work people are drawn to. It is the model behind Tahatū's interest quiz, and behind most careers tools in the world.

Nobody is one type. Everybody is a mix, usually described by their top two or three letters.

TypeDrawn toSounds like
RRealisticTools, machines, materials, outdoors, being physical"I like finishing the day and seeing what I built"
IInvestigativeWorking things out, data, diagnosis"I want to know why it broke"
AArtisticMaking, designing, performing, expressing"I'd rather it looked right than be quick"
SSocialTeaching, helping, caring, serving people"The best part of the job is the people"
EEnterprisingPersuading, selling, leading, running things"Put me in front of the customer"
CConventionalOrder, accuracy, systems, records"It should be right, and it should be filed"
flowchart LR
  R["R · REALISTIC<br/>things"] --- I["I · INVESTIGATIVE<br/>ideas"]
  I --- A["A · ARTISTIC<br/>expression"]
  A --- S["S · SOCIAL<br/>people"]
  S --- E["E · ENTERPRISING<br/>influence"]
  E --- C["C · CONVENTIONAL<br/>order"]
  C --- R

How to read it: the six sit in a circle, and neighbours are similar while opposites are not. Realistic and Conventional get on. Realistic and Social pull hard against each other.

⚠️ Be straight about what this is worth. The circular structure has held up across fifty years of studies. The promise attached to it has not. Matching your interests to your job is only weakly linked to being happy in it (r ≈ .17 across 53 studies), and a separate review of 27 studies found no significant link at all. The link to performance is stronger, around .32, which is not the direction most people assume.

➜ The honest line for a room: "This tells you what you're drawn to. It does not tell you what you'd be good at, and it is a weak predictor of whether you'd be happy. What it is genuinely good for is giving you words for something nobody has ever asked you about, and showing you jobs you had never heard of."

Learn more:

  • 🔗 Tahatū interest quiz and career profiles
  • 📄 O\*NET Interest Profiler

→ Full framework page

FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found (house model)

What it is: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds, and none into the one that works.

ChannelWhat it isCompetition
1. Advertised, applied coldSeek, Trade Me Jobs, the company siteHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering first
2. Advertised, with someone insideSame ad, but somebody hands your CV overMuch lower. You start as a known quantity
3. Not advertisedThe manager asks the team "know anyone?" firstLow, and most people never see these
4. Created for youSomebody meets you and finds work for youLowest, and rare
flowchart TD
  L(("A JOB<br/>SEEKER"))
  L -->|"most people<br/>spend 95% here"| C1["1 · APPLY COLD<br/>worst odds"]
  L -->|"almost nobody<br/>does this"| C2["2 · SOMEONE INSIDE"]
  L --> C3["3 · WORD OF MOUTH<br/>before it's advertised"]
  L --> C4["4 · CREATED FOR YOU"]
  C2 --> W["WEAK TIES<br/>people you barely know"]
  C3 --> W
  C4 --> W

How to read it: channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing, people who know you exist. That is what makes it teachable. One habit, not three.

And say why the job was never advertised, before any of the channels. Advertising costs money and about a fortnight of somebody's time: posting it, reading two hundred applications, interviewing. A manager who already has somebody in mind avoids all of that.

➜ "They are not hiding it from you. They are trying not to do two weeks of work." Without that sentence the room hears that the system is rigged. With it, they can see exactly where to stand.

The move is not "networking". That word closes people down. It is telling people what you are looking for, in one sentence with three parts:

  1. What you are looking for. Specific. "Warehouse or storeperson work" beats "anything going"
  2. What you bring. One thing. "I've got my F endorsement"
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"

➜ Said to a cousin, a neighbour, someone at church, a former supervisor, the parent at the school gate. Twenty of those beats sixty online applications, and it is less work.

And say this part. Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That is a real advantage and it usually goes completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that using it is allowed.

Learn more: built on FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties and Granovetter (1973). → Full framework page

Suggested flow: open with the story → teach FRM-057 → ACT-094 while the room is warm → break → teach FRM-056 honestly, including the evidence audit → ACT-095 on devices → teach FRM-061 → ACT-101 → ACT-013 to close with a date against a name.

With ACT-108 this becomes two sessions. The direct approach needs 45 minutes of its own and a real list of local employers. Put it at the start of session two, straight after a recap of FRM-061.

⚠️ ACT-095 needs devices and wifi. Check both the week before, and have a paper fallback. Half a room turning up without a phone that will hold a charge is a normal Tuesday.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-095 What's My Code? is the assessment for this topic, and it runs on Tahatū's interest quiz rather than anything Zeducation wrote.

The score is not the point. What the learner leaves with is:
Their top three lettersWords for something nobody has asked them about before
A list of jobsIncluding several they had never heard of
Pay and demand for eachReal New Zealand numbers, not a guess
One job to look into properlyWith a date against it

⚠️ Not a measure of ability. RIASEC describes what someone is drawn to now, and interests move. It should only ever widen a learner's list, never rule anything out. If it is being used to tell somebody what they cannot do, it is being used wrongly.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. What is something you have been doing for years that you had never counted as a skill?
  2. Which of the five places did you get the most from? Which one had you never thought about?
  3. Whose voice is it when you say "that doesn't really count"? Where did that come from?
  4. Which of your three letters surprised you, and which one did you already know?
  5. What job came up on Tahatū that you had never heard of? What made you look twice?
  6. Who is on your map that you had never thought of as a work contact?
  7. Who is the last person you told that you are looking for work?
  8. What is the one thing you will do in the next week, with whom, and when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?

(20-25 min, medium energy). Everyone maps their own network and counts it. Most people expect twenty names and write sixty. The count is the lesson, and it works as an opener or a closer.

  • The two-minute version: ask everyone to say one thing they can do that is not on any CV they

have ever written. Go round the room. It takes two minutes and it sets up the whole topic.

  • ACT-035 Six Degrees Of This Room

(10-12 min, high energy). If you have already run ACT-101 with this group, use this instead.

Source Trail

Built from SRC-010 Tahatū Career Navigator, ingested 2026-08-01, and enriched 2026-08-02 from SRC-013 Indeed, "What Is the Hidden Job Market?", which supplied the employer's-side explanation and the direct approach in ACT-108. Its vendor statistic and its US white-collar tactics were excluded on the record. The strategy is take the teaching, point at the tool: Tahatū holds the New Zealand career data, and Zeducation holds the facilitation around it. The story in section 1, the translation table, the three-part evidence rule and all four activities were written fresh. The RIASEC evidence audit was researched separately and is not Tahatū's framing.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. If you only have 90, run FRM-057, ACT-094 and

ACT-101, and set ACT-095 as homework with a due date

  • The first sentence of section 1 is the whole topic. "I haven't really got any experience."

Every room says it. Do not argue with it, and do not reassure. Count out loud instead

  • What usually goes wrong: the RIASEC quiz becomes the session, and everybody leaves with three

letters and no jobs list. Budget the second half of ACT-095 for the career profiles, because the profiles are the value and the letters are not

  • Do not let it become a personality-test session. Somebody will ask how it compares to MBTI or a

work-style quiz they did once. Answer it honestly using the evidence audit, then move on

  • Interests are shaped by exposure. A young person who has never met an engineer will not test

toward engineering. For learners whose working world has been retail, care and warehousing, treat a narrow result as a signal about their exposure, not about them

  • ⚠️ Never advise a learner to anglicise their name. If channel 1 bias comes up, the answer is to

spend the effort in channels 2, 3 and 4, not to change who they are

  • ⚠️ Open gap: we have no Zeducation learner story for the Pink Sheet yet. It can only come from

delivery. Ask your tutors and get permission properly

PS-LEA-003Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

The team that never argued is not a strong team

placeholder-storyteamsteam-developmentstormingconflictnormsleadership

Topic: TOP-LEA-003 Every Team Storms · Pillar: Leadership

Point

A team that has never had a disagreement is not a strong team. It is a new team, or a quiet one, and quiet is the more expensive of the two.

Storming is not the stage where a team is failing. It is the stage where a team stops pretending.

Model

flowchart LR
  F["FORMING<br/>polite and unsure"] --> S["STORMING<br/>differences surface"]
  S --> N["NORMING<br/>rhythm and trust"]
  N --> P["PERFORMING<br/>shared ownership"]
  P --> A["ADJOURNING<br/>close it well"]
  S -.->|new member,<br/>new boss| F
  P -.->|change| S

The solid arrows are what gets taught. The dotted arrows are what actually happens. A team does not climb the stages once and stay there.

StageYou know you are here when
FormingEveryone agrees with everything
StormingSomeone says "that's not my job"
NormingSomeone says "we usually do it like this"
PerformingThe leader can leave and the work still happens
AdjourningPride, relief, and nobody quite saying goodbye

Metaphor

Growing pains.

Nobody takes a teenager to the doctor because their legs ache after a growth spurt. The ache is not a symptom of something wrong, it is the thing itself, and the only alternative to it is not growing.

Storming is the same. It hurts, it is temporary, and a team that never feels it has usually just stopped growing.

Study

**Bruce W. Tuckman, "Developmental Sequence in Small Groups", Psychological Bulletin 63(6), 384-399 (1965). Tuckman reviewed fifty studies of groups, from therapy groups to training groups to work teams, and found the same four-stage pattern under all of them. In 1977, with Mary Ann Jensen, he reviewed the later research and added Adjourning**.

📄 1965 paper (PDF) · 📄 1977 paper

Honest limit: it is a review that found a pattern, not an experiment that predicts one. Tuckman and Jensen called for more empirical work themselves. It describes teams well and forecasts them poorly, and it is worth saying so rather than overselling a sixty year old model.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a Zeducation facilitator or client team that hit storming, was told it was normal, and stayed at the table because of that. The moment that makes the story is the sentence somebody said that kept them there.

The alternative, and probably the better one: a team that avoided storming for a year, and what that cost. Quiet dysfunction is harder to tell as a story and it is the more common experience in the rooms Zeducation teaches.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
New team formationGive them the map before they need it. It is worth far more in advance
A team currently in conflictThe reframe that lowers the temperature without dismissing the issue
Supervisor and team lead trainingPaired with the team charter as the practical response
Project close-outsAdjourning. Almost nobody teaches this and everyone has felt its absence

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-LEA-002 Nobody remembers breaking your trustTrust is what decides whether a team storms well or badly
PS-COM-001 Assertive is clear, not loudThe individual skill that storming requires

⚠️ This topic can carry a second sheet on Adjourning alone. The Point is there and unclaimed: most teams end without anyone saying so, and people carry that for years.

TOP-LEA-003Topic · Leadership

Every Team Storms

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 3teamsteam-developmentstormingconflictnormsleadershipcollaboration

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-003 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 3

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A new crew of six starts on a fit-out. Week one everyone is polite and the supervisor makes every call. Week three, two of them are arguing about who owns the site tidy-up, and the supervisor goes home thinking he has hired badly.

Ask the room: has he?

Then the second question:

Think of a team you were on that went through a rough patch and came out better. What actually happened in the rough patch?

Most people have one. And most people have never been told that the rough patch was not a failure, it was a stage with a name.

Statement: A team that has never argued is not a strong team. It is a new one, or a quiet one.

➜ Facilitator note: if the room is mostly people who have been in one workplace a long time, ask instead about what happened when a new manager arrived. Same stage, more familiar.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name which stage a team is in and choose one action that fits that stage.
  2. Run a disagreement so that it ends in an agreed rule rather than a truce.

3. About This Topic

Most teams move through the same stages as they learn to work together. Knowing the stages does two things: it takes the panic out of the uncomfortable one, and it tells you what the team needs from you right now.

The uncomfortable stage is Storming, when differences surface and people test roles, workload and authority. It feels like something is wrong. It is not. It is a normal part of a team learning to be honest with each other, and a team that skips it has usually just gone quiet instead.

Naming the stage changes the story a team tells about itself. Instead of "something is wrong with us", people can think "this is where we are, and here is what we need to move forward". That one shift lowers blame and raises empathy, because you can see the other person is reacting to the stage rather than being difficult.

It applies well beyond work: a new church committee, a sports team, a family after a big change, a group project at a course. Any group of people learning to work together goes through it.

Key words

WordWhat it means
NormsThe unwritten rules about how a team behaves. Every team has them, most never chose them
StormingThe stage where differences surface and get tested
Team charterThe norms, written down on purpose
AdjourningThe end of a team, and the stage most often skipped

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-018 Tuckman's Stages of Team Development

Origin: Bruce W. Tuckman, Developmental Sequence in Small Groups, Psychological Bulletin 63(6), 1965, from a review of fifty studies. Adjourning was added by Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen in 1977.

StageYou know you are here when
FormingEveryone agrees with everything. Nobody asks a hard question
StormingThe first real disagreement. Someone says "that's not my job"
NormingPeople start saying "we usually do it like this"
PerformingThe leader can step back and the work still gets done
AdjourningMixed feelings. Pride, relief, sometimes sadness
flowchart LR
  F["FORMING<br/>polite and unsure"] --> S["STORMING<br/>differences surface"]
  S --> N["NORMING<br/>rhythm and trust"]
  N --> P["PERFORMING<br/>shared ownership"]
  P --> A["ADJOURNING<br/>close it well"]
  S -.->|new member,<br/>new boss| F
  P -.->|change| S

How to read it: the dotted arrows matter most. Change a member, a manager or the work, and you drop back. That is not failure, that is the model working.

What the leader does at each stage: Forming needs direction · Storming needs presence, not absence and not suppression · Norming needs the rules written down · Performing needs you out of the way · Adjourning needs someone to say what people did.

Worked example: the fit-out crew from section 1. The supervisor runs a fifteen minute conversation about who does what by when, they agree the tidy-up rotates, and by week five they sort it between themselves. That conversation is what moved them to norming. Skipping it would have kept them storming for months.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Tuckman (1965), original paper (PDF)
  • 📄 MindTools — Forming, Storming, Norming and Performing
  • 🎬 Bruce Tuckman's model in just 2 minutes

→ Full framework page

FRM-027 The Team Charter (house tool)

What it is: a short written agreement about how a team will work together, made on purpose instead of by accident.

Why it is needed: every team already has norms and nobody decided them. They formed from whoever spoke loudest in week one and from what the last manager tolerated. That is how a team ends up with a rule like "we do not question Dave" that nobody would ever have agreed to out loud.

#QuestionWhat you are agreeing
1How do we make decisions?Who decides what, and how we know a decision has been made
2How do we disagree?Where, how it sounds, what is out of bounds
3How do we communicate?Which channel for what, and a reasonable reply time
4What if someone drops the ball?Agreed before it happens, while nobody is defensive
5How will we know this is working?The review date
flowchart TD
  A["1. How do we decide?"] --> B["2. How do we disagree?"]
  B --> C["3. How do we communicate?"]
  C --> D["4. What if someone<br/>drops the ball?"]
  D --> E["5. How will we know<br/>it is working?"]
  E -.->|review it| A

How to read it: behaviours, not values. "We respect each other" is unusable. "We do not talk about someone who is not in the room" can be checked.

Worked example: a team of nine keeps having the same argument about lunchtime phone cover. Forty minutes on a charter produces one line: "If you cannot cover your slot, find your own swap before the day. If you cannot, say so by Wednesday and we sort it together." The argument does not come back, because nine people agreed it while calm.

→ Full framework page

FRM-023 Psychological Safety

Storming without safety is just conflict. Safety is what lets a team disagree hard and eat lunch together afterwards. → Full framework page

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-044 Where Is My Team Right Now? Tick what is true across five blocks and count the columns. Unlike the other instruments in this library it is not scored on a scale, because there is no good or bad stage.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Which stage is your team in right now? What told you?
  2. Think of a team that came out of a rough patch better. What happened in the rough patch?
  3. What are your team's unwritten rules, and who set them?
  4. When did your team last drop back a stage? What caused it?
  5. What disagreement are you currently avoiding? What stage is that keeping you in?
  6. Think of a team that ended without anyone marking it. What did that feel like?
  7. If you wrote one line of a team charter tomorrow, what would it say?
  8. What is one thing you will do this week for the stage your team is actually in?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

(20-25 min, high energy). Build a tower in ten minutes, then debrief what happened in the first sixty seconds. Forming and Storming, lived rather than described.

  • ACT-039 The Silent Nod

(10-12 min). Shows the room what a team that never storms actually looks like from the inside.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min for the full flow. At 90, cut ACT-039 and shorten ACT-043 to two rounds
  • Ask "where are we now?", never "where should we be?" The value is the honest read, not the climb
  • What usually goes wrong: the model gets used to excuse behaviour. "We're just storming" is not

cover for bullying, and a facilitator should say so plainly

  • Do not skip Adjourning. It is the stage most often left out and the one Pacific and Māori

learners often value most. Ending well matters

from 1965 and 1977

PS-LEA-007Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

The most helpful person is the one about to leave

placeholder-storycollaborationworkloadburnoutboundariessaying-nowellbeing

Topic: TOP-LEA-007 Helpful Without Burning Out · Pillar: Leadership

Point

The person your workplace depends on most is the one most likely to be quietly looking for another job, and it is your best people this happens to, not your worst.

Nobody did anything wrong. That is precisely what makes it worth teaching.

Model

flowchart TD
  H["You are helpful<br/>and good at it"] --> R["More requests<br/>come your way"]
  R --> Y["You say yes<br/>desire to help ·<br/>need for accomplishment ·<br/>fear"]
  Y --> B["Your reputation<br/>as helpful grows"]
  B --> R
  Y -.-> O["Your own work slips.<br/>Engagement drops.<br/>You start looking."]

A loop powered by your best qualities. Willpower cannot break it, because willpower is not what is driving it. Only a decision rule can.

The rule, in two questions:

QuestionIf the answer is…
Does this really need me?No → delegate it to someone who will learn from it
Am I the best person, or just the most available?Most available → helpful no

Metaphor

The one path everyone walks on.

Cut across a field enough times and a track appears. Then everybody uses the track, because it is obviously the way through, and it gets deeper and muddier and harder to walk every season.

Nobody chose to ruin that strip of grass. Everyone was just taking the sensible route. The person who is everyone's shortcut is that path, and no amount of walking more carefully will fix it. Somebody has to build a second route.

Study

**Rob Cross, Reb Rebele and Adam Grant, "Collaborative Overload", Harvard Business Review, January-February 2016.** Network analysis across more than 300 organisations.

Finding
Most knowledge workers spend 85%+ of the week on email, meetings and callsAlmost nothing left for the actual work
20 to 35% of value-added collaboration comes from 3 to 5% of employeesA very small group carries it
Those most in-demand collaborators had the lowest engagement and career satisfactionThe finding that stops a room

📄 HBR · 📄 Full PDF

Provenance note worth keeping: the Zeducation source workbook says "researchers have found three common reasons people get overloaded by collaboration" and names none of them. This is who, and the workbook's three reasons map directly onto their drivers. Worth crediting in the next print run.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: the person everyone asked, who left, and the gap it left behind. Every organisation has one and nobody saw it coming, which is the whole point. Collect it carefully and anonymise it properly.

The better story, if it exists: someone who was that person, saw it, handed three things over, and stayed. That is the version with a way out in it, and this sheet needs one, because the finding on its own is bleak.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Leadership and supervisor trainingThe retention argument that has nothing to do with pay
Collaboration programmesThe mandatory counterweight. Teaching "collaborate more" without this produces the overload it describes
Wellbeing and workload conversationsThe reframe: this is a demand problem, not a time management problem
Client work on retentionAsk who their hubs are. They usually know within seconds, and have never done anything about it

Related sheets

SheetRelationship

PS-COM-004The Communication pillar's boundaries sheet. That is the script, this is the decision

⚠️ A second sheet is available here on habit 2, and it is a good one: the person who never delegates becomes the bottleneck, and a bottleneck is not a strength even when it feels like one.

TOP-LEA-007Topic · Leadership

Helpful Without Burning Out

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90-120 minCreating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Part 5collaborationboundariessaying-noworkloadburnoutdelegationwellbeing

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-007 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Creating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Part 5

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask the room one question:

"Who is the person everyone goes to when they're stuck?"

In most workplaces people name the same one or two within seconds. Often that person is sitting in the room and has never heard it said out loud.

Then ask the second question, gently:

"How do you reckon that person is doing?"

Then give them the finding. Across more than 300 organisations, researchers found that 20 to 35% of the valuable collaboration comes from just 3 to 5% of people. And those same in-demand people showed the lowest engagement and career satisfaction in the organisation.

Statement: The person everyone relies on is usually the one most likely to leave. Being helpful is not the problem. Having no way to say a helpful no is.

➜ Facilitator note: if the hub is in the room, frame this as a load problem the workplace created, never as "look how indispensable you are". That framing is the difference between relief and shame.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Say a helpful no that protects the work and the relationship.
  2. Decide which collaborations to accept, using your goals rather than your availability.

3. About This Topic

Modern work is built on collaboration. Meetings, messages, projects, shared documents, group chats. Working with others is powerful: better ideas, better solutions, stronger relationships. But if we say yes to everything, we end up overloaded, tired, and less effective for the people who need us most.

Being a great team player is not about saying yes to every request. It is about being helpful in a way that is sustainable for you and useful for the team.

Researchers have found three common reasons people take on too much:

  1. Desire to help. We want to be useful. People see us as reliable, so more requests come our

way, until we are so busy helping that our own work suffers.

  1. Need for accomplishment. It feels good to tick things off. But small wins for other people

crowd out the bigger work that needs deep focus.

  1. Fear. Fear of missing out on opportunities. Fear of losing control if someone else takes over.

Fear of what people will think if we say no.

This is not only a work problem. For many people the same pattern runs through family, church and community obligations at the same time, and the load is real in all of them.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Collaborative overloadBeing buried by the collaboration you are good at
Helpful noA counter-offer, not a refusal
BottleneckWhen you are the only one who can do something, so everything waits for you
HubThe person everyone goes to. Usually two or three people in any workplace

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-032 Collaborative Overload

Origin: Rob Cross, Reb Rebele and Adam Grant, Collaborative Overload, Harvard Business Review, January-February 2016. Built on network analysis across more than 300 organisations. Strongest evidence in this topic, and it is the research the source workbook refers to without naming.

FindingWhat it means
Most knowledge workers spend 85% or more of the week in email, meetings and callsVery little time left for the work itself
20 to 35% of value-added collaboration comes from 3 to 5% of employeesA tiny group carries most of it
Those in-demand collaborators show the lowest engagement and career satisfactionBeing the person everyone relies on is not a reward
flowchart TD
  H["You are helpful<br/>and good at it"] --> R["More requests<br/>come your way"]
  R --> Y["You say yes<br/>desire to help ·<br/>need for accomplishment ·<br/>fear"]
  Y --> B["Your reputation<br/>as helpful grows"]
  B --> R
  Y -.-> O["Your own work slips.<br/>Engagement drops."]

How to read it: a loop powered by your best qualities. That is why willpower does not break it and only a decision rule does.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Cross, Rebele & Grant (2016) — HBR
  • 📄 Full article PDF

→ Full framework page

FRM-031 The 3 Habits of a Healthy Team Player (house framework)

HabitThe question behind it
1Say a helpful no instead of an automatic yes"What can I actually give here?"
2Delegate and grow others"Does this really need me?"
3Be intentional with your time"Am I the best person, or just the most available?"
flowchart TD
  R["A request<br/>arrives"]
  R --> Q1{"Does this really<br/>need me?"}
  Q1 -->|no| D["DELEGATE<br/>guide, step back,<br/>let them learn"]
  Q1 -->|yes| Q2{"Am I the best person,<br/>or the most available?"}
  Q2 -->|most available| N["HELPFUL NO"]
  Q2 -->|best person| Y["YES, and be clear<br/>about what you can give"]

How to read it: the two questions in the diamonds are the framework. Most people never ask either one, which is how the automatic yes happens.

Habit 1, the helpful no, in three moves:

  • Explain what you already have on your plate. Information, not an excuse
  • Ask which task is the priority. The strongest move, because it hands the trade-off back to the

person allowed to make it. Often they did not know they were asking you to drop something

  • Offer a smaller way to help. "I can show you how to do it" instead of doing all of it
Every time you say yes, you are also saying no to something else, often your own goals or your wellbeing.

Habit 2: ask whether someone else could do it and learn from it. Give clear guidance, step back, and celebrate their win without jumping in to show you could have done it better. This stops you becoming the bottleneck.

Habit 3: before agreeing to another meeting or project, check it against your goals, the real hours it will take each week, and whether you are the best person or just the most available.

Worked example: a team leader is asked to join a fourth working group. Habit 3: is he the best person or the most available? Most available. Habit 2: his newest supervisor would learn a lot from it. Habit 1: "I can't take this on properly, and I'd rather say that than do it badly. Hemi would be good and he'd learn from it. I'll brief him and I'm happy to be the backstop." Thirty seconds, nobody let down, one person developed.

→ Full framework page

FRM-008 The Positive No — Yes, No, Yes

The full script for habit 1, already in the library from the Communication pillar. Yes to what you care about, No that is clear, Yes to a way forward. → Full framework page · Taught in full in TOP-COM-004 Boundaries Without Guilt

ACT-061 Am I Overloaded? Ten statements, scored 1 to 3, out of 30.

ScoreWhat it means
10-16Your load looks manageable and your yeses are mostly deliberate
17-23You are carrying more than your share, and it is probably invisible to everyone including you

In this instrument a high score is not a good result, and learners who have been praised for exactly these behaviours for years need that said plainly.

⚠️ Not validated, and not a wellbeing screen. If someone is genuinely struggling, this is a conversation, not a worksheet. Know your referral options first: workplace EAP, their GP, or 1737, the free national helpline, call or text.

  1. Who is the person everyone asks in your workplace? How do you think they are doing?
  2. Which of the three reasons puts you there most often: wanting to help, wanting the quick win, or fear?
  3. What have you said yes to for a reason that no longer exists?

  7. Who do you never say no to, and what does that cost you?

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min comfortable, 90 tight. Do not cut ACT-052
  • Research before habits, always. In the other order the habits sound like advice. With the 3 to

5% finding first, they sound like a response

  • What usually goes wrong: it gets heard as "say no more" and people reject it. The framing is

"stop saying yes without thinking", which is a different and much more acceptable instruction

  • This is partly a structural problem. If one person is carrying a team, the habits help them

survive it, they do not solve it. Say that rather than implying it is their failing

  • Cultural note: for many Pacific and Māori learners, saying no to someone senior or to family is

a relational act with real cost, not a workload decision. The helpful no works precisely because it keeps the relationship intact. Lead with that, or the topic reads as telling them to care less

  • Watch the room. This topic surfaces genuine distress more often than any other in this family.

PS-LEA-006Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Consultation that changes nothing is worse than no consultation

placeholder-storydecision-makingleadershipcollaborationtruststyles

Topic: TOP-LEA-006 How You Decide Is What They Learn · Pillar: Leadership

Point

Asking people what they think and then ignoring it costs more trust than never asking at all.

A straight decision is respected. Consultation theatre teaches people that their voice is decorative, and they only need to learn that once.

Model

flowchart TD
  L["THE LEADER<br/>same person, same day"]
  L --> A["AUTOCRATIC<br/>'My way'"]
  L --> D["DEMOCRATIC<br/>'Our way'"]
  L --> F["LAISSEZ-FAIRE<br/>'Your way'"]
StyleFitsTeaches the team
Autocratic "My way"Safety, urgency, complianceWait to be told
Democratic "Our way"Most decisions affecting people's daily workYour voice counts
Laissez-faire "Your way"Clear roles, skilled and motivated peopleYou are on your own, for better or worse

These are three options, not three kinds of person. The skill is choosing, not having a favourite.

And the fourth thing, which is not on Lewin's list and does the most damage:

flowchart LR
  A["ask for input"] --> B["decide what you<br/>were always going<br/>to decide"] --> C["never mention<br/>what anyone said"]
  C -.->|twice| D["nobody gives you<br/>a real answer again"]

Metaphor

A suggestion box that is nailed shut.

Everybody can see it. It has a slot. People post something in it once, maybe twice, and then they notice it has never been opened, and they stop.

The box is worse than no box, because a workplace with no suggestion box is honest about not asking. A nailed-shut one made a promise and broke it, in public, every day.

Study

Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939), University of Iowa. They ran after-school clubs for groups of eleven year old boys making models, and rotated adult leaders through them, each using a different style. Democratic leadership produced the most consistently productive, creative and cooperative groups. Under laissez-faire, productivity dropped sharply, the strongest personalities dominated, and frustration grew.

📄 MindTools summary · 📄 The study revisited (1994)

Honest limit, and say it: ten boys in Iowa in 1939. It was a real experiment with real findings, and the three styles have survived as a teaching model far better than that sample alone would justify. Teach it as a useful map, not as proof.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a leader who asked, listened, and visibly changed their decision because of what they heard, and what that did to how much people told them afterwards. The moment that makes it is the second decision, not the first, because that is when the team finds out whether the first was genuine.

The version most rooms already have: everybody has been on the receiving end of consultation theatre. The topic opener generates it live, and a collected story from a Zeducation client would be stronger.

Collaboration programmesThe mechanism. How a leader decides is what opens or closes a silo
