TOP-LEA-006Topic · Leadership

How You Decide Is What They Learn

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90 minCreating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Part 3decision-makingleadershipcollaborationstylesdelegationteams

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90 min · ID: TOP-LEA-006 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Creating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Part 3

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask the room to think about a time they were asked for their opinion at work, gave it honestly, and then watched the decision go exactly the way it was always going to go. No mention of what anyone said.

Then ask: what did you do the next time you were asked?

The answer is always some version of the same thing. Said less. Said what they wanted to hear. Or just stopped bothering.

Statement: Every decision you make teaches your team something about whether their voice counts. Consultation that changes nothing teaches them faster than no consultation at all.

➜ Facilitator note: this opener works on any group, because everyone has been on the receiving end of it, including people who have never led anything.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Name your default decision-making style and what it teaches the people around you.
  2. Choose the style that fits the decision, and plan a real consultation.

3. About This Topic

Leadership is not just about what decisions are made. It is about how they are made. The way a leader involves, or does not involve, others sends a clear message about trust, respect and whose voice counts. Over time that shapes whether people share information and speak up, or stay silent and stick to their own lane.

If decisions are always made alone and handed down, people learn to wait to be told, and collaboration dries up. If there is no clear direction at all, teams end up confused, working in silos and protecting their own area. But when leaders invite input, listen, explain their thinking and make people part of the process, it builds ownership, connection and shared responsibility.

In other words, leadership decision-making can either block collaboration or unlock it.

"Collaboration is not an event; it's the result of how leaders decide, listen, and respond."

This applies well outside work. The same three styles show up in a family, a church committee and a sports club, and the same lesson lands: people learn very quickly whether their view is wanted.

Key words

WordWhat it means
AutocraticThe leader decides alone and tells people. "My way"
DemocraticThe leader asks, listens, then decides. "Our way"
Laissez-faireThe leader stands back and lets people decide. "Your way"
Fake consultationAsking for input on something already decided

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-028 Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles

Origin: Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White, University of Iowa, 1939. They ran after-school clubs for eleven year old boys and rotated adult leaders through them, each using a different style. It is one of the founding studies of leadership research.

StyleThe lineWhat it isWhen it fits
Autocratic"My way"Decides alone and tells people. Fast and clear, limits buy-in if overusedSafety, urgency, compliance
Democratic"Our way"Asks for ideas, listens, then decides. Slower, builds ownershipMost team decisions, especially ones affecting daily work
Laissez-faire"Your way"Hands off. Works with skilled, motivated teams. Causes confusion and silos without guidanceWhen roles, goals and expectations are already clear
flowchart TD
  L["THE LEADER"]
  L --> A["AUTOCRATIC<br/>'My way'<br/>decides alone"]
  L --> D["DEMOCRATIC<br/>'Our way'<br/>asks, listens, decides"]
  L --> F["LAISSEZ-FAIRE<br/>'Your way'<br/>hands off"]

How to read it: not personality types. Three options available to the same leader on the same day. The skill is choosing, not having a favourite.

Lewin's finding: democratic leadership produced the most consistently productive and cooperative groups. The laissez-faire groups did worst, with productivity dropping and the strongest personalities taking over.

Using each one well:

StyleDo this, or it backfires
AutocraticStill explain the why. Ask for feedback afterwards so people feel respected
DemocraticSay how their input shaped the final call. Asking and never referring to it again is worse than not asking
Laissez-faireSet boundaries, check in, keep information flowing. Hands off is not absent

Worked example: a regional manager needs to change the weekend roster. Autocratic would be quickest, and it is also how you get four people quietly job hunting, because the roster is their family's weekend. She goes democratic: explains the constraint, asks what would work, and gets an option she had not thought of. When she confirms it, she says which part came from whom. The roster is only slightly better. The return is that nine people now believe saying something to her is worth the effort.

Learn more:

  • 📄 MindTools — Lewin's Leadership Styles Framework
  • 📄 Leadership Ahoy — The Kurt Lewin leadership experiments
  • 📄 The Lewin, Lippitt and White study revisited (1994)

→ Full framework page

FRM-029 The 3C Framework — Connect, Clarify, Commit (house model)

Democratic decision-making needs a conversation, and 3C is the shape of it. Clarify is the step that does the work: ask open questions and listen until you understand their view, not just your own.

flowchart LR
  A["CONNECT<br/>same side"] --> B["CLARIFY<br/>open questions,<br/>listen"] --> C["COMMIT<br/>who, what,<br/>by when"]

The test to teach: is that a real question, or your opinion with a question mark on it? "Don't you think it would be better if…" is a statement in disguise, and people hear it as one.

→ Full framework page

FRM-047 Likert's Four Systems (added 2026-08-01, optional extension)

Origin: Rensis Likert, The Human Organization, 1967. Full page at FRM-047.

Likert splits the middle of Lewin's ladder, and the split is where the useful teaching sits.

SystemNameWhat it feels like from the floor
1Exploitative authoritative"Do it or find another job." Nobody tells the boss anything true
2Benevolent authoritativeSame control, but there are rewards. People say what the boss wants to hear
3ConsultativeYou get asked. Your view is genuinely heard. The boss still decides
4ParticipativeYou are part of the decision. Information moves in every direction

➜ The line between 2 and 3 is the honesty line. Below it, people tell you what you want to hear. Above it, they tell you what is true.

And System 2 is the most common New Zealand workplace and the most misread. A System 2 manager is often warm, remembers birthdays, shouts the pizza, and has never once been told bad news early. They think they run a happy team. They run a quiet one.

The question that tests it: when did somebody last tell you something you did not want to hear, and what happened to them afterwards?

The trap worth naming out loud

There is one way to do this badly that costs more than never asking:

Ask for input, then make the decision you had already made, and never mention what anyone said.

Do that twice and nobody on your team will give you a real answer again. If a decision is already made, say so and explain the why. That is autocratic done well, and people respect it far more than consultation theatre.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises

ACT-039 The Silent NodGame10-12 minFRM-028
ACT-057 Three Leaders, One TaskRoleplay30-35 minFRM-028

Suggested flow: ACT-050 to open → teach FRM-028 → ACT-057 so they feel all three from the inside → ACT-058 quietly → ACT-056 with a real decision → close.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-058 What's My Default Style? Seven situations, three options each. Count A, B and C.

Question 7 is the real result. Questions 1 to 6 are what you do when things are calm. Question 7 is what you do under pressure, and that is the style your team actually experiences, because pressure is when leadership gets noticed. A democratic leader who goes hard autocratic under load is extremely common, and worth telling your team about so they can read you.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. When were you asked for your opinion and it clearly changed nothing? What did you do next time?
  2. What is your default style? What would your team say it is?
  3. Which recent decision did you make alone that should have been shared?
  4. Which one did you consult on that you should have just made?
  5. What happens to your style when you are under real time pressure?
  6. Who on your team has stopped offering ideas? When did that start?
  7. If you use laissez-faire, are roles and goals clear enough for it to work, or is it absence?
  8. What decision is coming up, who will you involve, and when will you ask them?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-050 Whose Call Is It?

(12-15 min). Ten decisions, three walls, fast. Establishes that all three styles are legitimate, which the room needs before it will rate itself honestly.

  • ACT-039 The Silent Nod

(10-12 min). What an autocratic default does to a team over time, demonstrated in four minutes.

  • What usually goes wrong: learners pick a decision for ACT-056 that is not theirs to make.

PS-LEA-011Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

A reason nobody can repeat is not a reason

placeholder-storyleadershipmanagementchangevisionmotivationtransformational

Topic: TOP-LEA-011 Leader Or Manager · Pillar: Leadership

Point

Booking the training is management. Giving people a reason they can say back to somebody else is leadership. Most changes fail because somebody did the first one thoroughly and never noticed the second one was missing.

And the test is embarrassingly simple. After you have explained it, ask the person to tell you why it is happening. If they cannot, you announced something.

Model

Two jobs, not two levels.

MANAGEMENT copes with complexityLEADERSHIP copes with change
Plan and budgetSet direction
Organise and staffAlign people
Control and problem-solveMotivate and inspire
Asks what and howAsks why and what if
Produces orderProduces movement

And the sequence rule, which is the part that matters in our rooms:

Transaction first, then transformation. Fix the roster, fix the pay, book the training. Then earn the right to talk about vision.

Bass's own finding was that transformational leadership augments transactional. It does not replace it. Nobody is inspired by a mission statement when their timesheet is wrong.

Metaphor

A car with a full tank and no destination.

Management is the fuel, the warrant, the tyres, the service history. Leadership is knowing where you are going. A perfectly maintained car in a car park is what an over-managed, under-led organisation looks like from the inside, and everybody in it is busy.

The metaphor's teeth: you cannot fix a car park problem by servicing the car harder. Which is exactly what most struggling organisations do.

The sharper version, for a room that has been through a bad restructure: a car with a destination and no fuel. Everybody knows where they are going and nothing moves, and after a while the vision itself becomes the thing people resent.

Study

**Kotter, J. P. (1990). What Leaders Really Do. Harvard Business Review, May–June. One of the most cited management articles ever written. Its opening claim is that leadership has nothing to do with charisma or special personality traits**, which is the sentence to quote, because it takes leadership away from people who were born magnetic and hands it back to everyone else.

**Judge, T. A. & Piccolo, R. F. (2004). Transformational and transactional leadership: a meta-analytic test of their relative validity. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(5), 755-768.** 626 correlations from 87 studies:

Correlation with effectiveness
Transformational leadership.44
Contingent reward (transactional).39
Laissez-faire–.37

Transformational also correlated .58 with follower job satisfaction.

➜ The number to use from a stage is –.37. Everyone expects hands-off to be neutral. It is the only negative figure in the set, and it makes the point that being absent is an active choice with an active cost.

⚠️ State the limitation. Most of this rests on followers rating their own leader on a questionnaire, and people who like their boss rate them high on everything. Real, and probably smaller than .44.

Story

The story on the page is the tablet rollout: training booked, deadline clear, tablets charged, and three weeks later half the jobs being logged at 4pm from memory on a tablet instead of on paper. Perfect management, zero leadership, and the reason the supervisor never gave was good enough to have worked.

Why it lands: every room has been on the receiving end of a system change nobody explained. It is the most reliably shared experience in New Zealand working life.

The story to collect: a Zeducation employer partner describing a change they rolled out twice. Once badly, once properly. The same change, the same team, two different outcomes, is worth more than any framework diagram.

The other story worth having, and it is Pasi's to tell or not: the change he explained badly. Nobody believes a leadership story where the teller is the hero.

⚠️ Placeholder. No collected Zeducation story yet.

TOP-LEA-011Topic · Leadership

Leader Or Manager

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90 minLeadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lesson 2leadershipmanagementchangevisionmotivationtransformationalteams

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90 min · ID: TOP-LEA-011 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Leadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lesson 2

"You can never be the king or queen on the mountain and say, 'We're going this way!' It doesn't work that way. You've got to involve people in your decision." — Dr Charles Royal, Director Ngā Manu Atarau, Te Papa

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A team gets told on a Tuesday that from the first of next month, every job goes on a tablet instead of the sheet at the end of the shift.

The supervisor does it properly. Training is booked. The tablets are charged. The deadline is clear and so is what happens if it does not get logged.

Three weeks later, half the jobs are being logged at 4pm from memory. On a tablet.

Ask the room: what did the supervisor not do?

He never told them why. And the why was good: the paper times were wrong about a third of the time, the company had lost two contracts in a year because it could not prove what it had done, and a third would mean redundancies.

He knew all of that. He just never said it, because it felt like management's business.

Statement: Managing a change is booking the training. Leading it is giving people a reason they can repeat to somebody else. Most changes fail because somebody did the first one and assumed it covered the second.

➜ Facilitator note: do not reveal the reason straight away. Let the room guess at what went wrong first. Half of them will say "he should have consulted them", which is a different answer and worth holding onto for section 5.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Sort your own work into the management job and the leadership job, and say which one your week

is actually made of.

  1. Give a real change a reason that somebody on your team can say back in their own words.

3. About This Topic

John Kotter's argument, from 1990, is that these are two different jobs and not two levels of the same one. A manager is not a junior leader. They are doing different work.

Management copes with complexity. Planning and budgeting, organising and staffing, controlling and problem solving. It produces predictability and order. Big organisations do not run without it, and neither does a five-person crew.

Leadership copes with change. Setting a direction, aligning people behind it, motivating and inspiring. It produces movement, sometimes uncomfortable movement.

Why it matters here: most of Zeducation's learners are supervisors, and the management half is what they are being paid for. The leadership half is what would make them promotable, and it is the half nobody has ever described to them as a skill. They think it is a personality they do not have.

Kotter's opening move is exactly that: leadership has nothing to do with charisma. It is a set of things you do.

Then the second framework, which puts numbers on it. Burns and Bass split how leaders get effort into transactional (you do the work, you get the reward) and transformational (you believe in where this is going, so you bring more than the job description). Judge and Piccolo's 2004 meta-analysis found transformational leadership correlated .44 with overall effectiveness and .58 with follower job satisfaction. It is the best-evidenced style model in this library.

⚠️ And the order matters more than the theory. Bass's own finding was that transformational leadership augments transactional, it does not replace it. For learners in low-wage, insecure work, being talked to about vision while their roster changes without notice and their last pay was short is not inspiring. Fix the transaction, then earn the right to the rest.

Common mistakes: teaching management as the boring one; treating vision as a personality trait; announcing a change and calling it leading one; and skipping the transaction because the vision is more fun to talk about.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ComplexityLots of moving parts that have to line up. The management problem
ChangeGoing somewhere the team is not currently going. The leadership problem
TransactionalEffort in exchange for reward. Necessary, and it stops at the standard
TransformationalEffort because the person cares about the outcome
The four I'sBass's four transformational behaviours. Idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration
Discretionary effortWhat somebody gives you that you could not have made them give you

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-049 Kotter on Leadership and Management

Origin: John P. Kotter, What Leaders Really Do, Harvard Business Review, May–June 1990. Full page at FRM-049.

MANAGEMENT copes with complexityLEADERSHIP copes with change
DirectionPlanning and budgetingSetting a vision
CapacityOrganising and staffingAligning people
ExecutionControlling and problem solvingMotivating and inspiring
AsksWhat, and howWhy, and what if
ProducesPredictability and orderMovement

➜ Kotter's actual claim is that most organisations are over-managed and under-led. That is a statement about the balance, not a statement that management is a lesser activity. Retellings of this framework often lose that distinction.

FRM-048 Transactional and Transformational Leadership

Origin: James MacGregor Burns, 1978; developed by Bernard Bass, 1985. Full page at FRM-048.

Bass's four I's, which are the practical half:

What the leader actually does
Idealised influenceWalks the talkDoes the thing they ask others to do, including when it costs them
Inspirational motivationGives the whySays where this is going in words people can repeat
Intellectual stimulationAsks, does not tell"How would you do it?" Treats a challenge as useful
Individualised considerationSees the personKnows what this particular person is working towards

The evidence: transformational .44 with effectiveness, .58 with follower satisfaction. Contingent reward .39. Laissez-faire –.37 (Judge & Piccolo, 2004).

⚠️ Be straight about the limits. Most of that rests on followers rating their own leader on a questionnaire, and people who like their boss rate them highly on everything. The effect is real and it is probably smaller than .44.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-085 Leader Or Manager? The SortGame12-15 minFRM-049
ACT-086 The Vision TestRoleplay25-30 minFRM-048
ACT-087 Your Leadership LegacyReflection15-20 minFRM-048, FRM-049
ACT-013 Start, Stop, ContinueReflection10-12 minCloses the topic

Suggested flow: ACT-085 cold, before any teaching → teach FRM-049 and let the room name what it just sorted → teach FRM-048 and the four I's → ACT-086 both rounds → ACT-087 to close.

⚠️ ACT-085 runs before the teaching. The arguments over which pile a card belongs in are the activity. If you teach first, there is nothing to argue about.

On the "he should have consulted them" answer from section 1: hold it until ACT-086 round two. The change is already decided. Intellectual stimulation means asking about how, not whether, and learners spot a fake consultation instantly. So do real teams.

6. Self-Assessment

There is no scored instrument for this topic, deliberately. The test is behavioural and it happens inside ACT-086:

After you have explained the change, can the other person say back why it is happening, in their own words?

That is the whole assessment. It is pass or fail, it takes ten seconds, and it is more honest than any questionnaire.

Run it twice. Once after a transactional-only explanation, once after adding the four I's. Most learners fail the first and pass the second, and the difference is what they take away.

➜ Learners who want a numbered self-assessment on their leadership style should use ACT-058 What's My Default Style? or ACT-083 from TOP-LEA-010. See FRM-054 for why this library is careful about instruments.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Of everything you did at work last week, how much was management and how much was leadership?
  2. If you disappeared for a month, which of those two would nobody pick up?
  3. What is the last change your workplace made? Do you know the real reason for it?
  4. Who is someone you worked harder for than you had to? What did they actually do?
  5. Which of the four I's is hardest for you, and why that one?
  6. Is there anything you are asking your team to do that you are not doing yourself?
  7. What is a transaction at your work that is broken, and is making the vision talk sound hollow?
  8. What change do you need to explain properly this month, to whom, and by when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-085 Leader Or Manager? The Sort

(12-15 min). Eighteen cards, two piles, no "both" pile allowed. The refusal is the engine. Run it as the opener, always.

  • The tablet story (5 min). Tell section 1 and take guesses before revealing the reason. Works

in any room where somebody has been through a system change, which is all of them.

  • Worked harder than you had to (8 min). Round the room: name one person you worked harder for

than you were paid to, and one thing they did. Every answer that comes back is one of the four I's, and the room derives Bass's model without being taught it. Slower than the sort and better if you have the time.

TOP-LEA-001Topic · Leadership

Leading With Your Strengths

✏️ draftedLeadershipFoundation60-90 minstrengthsself-leadershipconfidencedevelopmentteamsroles

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Foundation · ID: TOP-LEA-001 Status: ✍️ drafted — two frameworks and an activity now attached. Story, self-assessment and openers still open.

This topic came out of the STAR Teaching Framework document, which uses it as its worked example of Tools & Techniques. The tool and the technique are already named there, so the topic starts with real house content rather than a blank page.

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

⚠️ GAP: needs a story. Likely shape: someone who was told what they were bad at for years before anyone told them what they were good at.

2. Learning Outcomes

  1. Name your top strengths and where they show up at work.
  2. Use one technique to develop a strength on purpose rather than by accident.

3. About This Topic

⚠️ GAP: to be written. Core idea: most development conversations start with weaknesses. People grow faster, and lead better, when they build on what they already do well.

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

Already named in the house STAR document:

  • Tool: the "Discovering Your Strengths" mind map worksheet ⚠️ GAP: locate the original worksheet

and file it as a framework page

  • Technique: three tips for developing your strengths — 1. catch yourself doing good,
    • celebrate your successes, 3. education
  • ✅ Taught inside FRM-003 STAR

Added 2026-08-01, from SRC-009:

FRM-053 Belbin's Nine Team Roles

Full page at FRM-053. Nine roles a team needs, in three families: action (Shaper, Implementer, Completer-Finisher), people (Coordinator, Team Worker, Resource Investigator) and thought (Plant, Monitor-Evaluator, Specialist).

➜ Why it belongs on a strengths topic: it turns "what am I good at?" from a private question into a team one. And its best idea is the allowable weakness — the weakness is the price of the strength, not a fault to train out. The Completer-Finisher who will not hand anything over is why nothing shipped broken.

FRM-054 Personality Tests At Work

Full page at FRM-054.

Read this before teaching any strengths content. It is the library's position on MBTI, DISC, CliftonStrengths and the rest: useful as shared vocabulary, never as a basis for deciding who gets hired, promoted or trusted. It also settles the licensing question below.

⚠️ GAP: still no free, well-evidenced strengths instrument identified. VIA Character Strengths is the most likely candidate and it needs checking properly for licensing and for its evidence base before it goes near a room.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-093 Nine Roles, One TableWorksheet25-30 minFRM-053
ACT-006 Two ThingsReflection10-12 minCloses the topic

Use the peer-nomination variation of ACT-093. Instead of self-ticking, each person is told by two colleagues which roles they see. The difference between the self-assessment and what colleagues see is the most useful thing this topic produces.

⚠️ GAP: still needs a pure strengths-spotting activity, where peers name each other's strengths directly rather than through Belbin's nine roles.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-093 Nine Roles, One Table now serves as the interim self-assessment. Nine roles, self-ticked, then the matching weakness for each one you ticked.

⚠️ Not a validated instrument, and deliberately not the paid Belbin inventory, which is the part researchers have criticised since 1993. The roles are free and useful. The questionnaire is neither.

⚠️ GAP: a proper strengths instrument is still open. See FRM-054 above for the constraints.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. What are you good at that nobody has ever told you you were good at?
  2. Which of the nine roles do you fall into without thinking about it?
  3. What is the weakness that comes with your strongest role? Is it one your team can carry?
  4. Has anyone ever tried to fix something in you that was the price of what you are good at?
  5. Which role is missing from your team, and what has that cost you?
  6. Do you play the same roles at home as you do at work? What does that tell you?
  7. What is one strength you will use on purpose this month, rather than by accident?
  • ✅ Closer available: ACT-006 Two Things

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • Three families, three corners (8 min). Read the three Belbin families aloud. People move to the

corner that sounds most like them at work. Then ask each corner what they find hardest about the other two. Fast, and the answers are usually funny and true.

  • Catch yourself doing good (6 min). Round the room: one thing you did well last week that

nobody noticed. Awkward for about ninety seconds and then it opens up. It is technique one from the house STAR document, run as an opener.

⚠️ GAP: still needs a peer-nomination opener where people name each other's strengths out loud.

PS-LEA-005Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Every team is somebody else's "they"

placeholder-studycollaborationsilosteamscross-teamleadership

Topic: TOP-LEA-005 One Team, Not Us And Them · Pillar: Leadership

Point

Silos are not built by difficult people. They are built by decent, busy people who ran out of reasons to talk to each other, until the only contact left was the times something went wrong.

Which is why "be more collaborative" never works, and changing when two teams talk does.

Model

Four behaviours you could watch a team do on a Tuesday. Not four attitudes.

CollaborativeSiloed
InformationShared without being askedKept in the department
TimingTalk earlyTalk only when forced
ProblemsDiscussed openlyBlame "them"
Wins"Our result""My result"
flowchart LR
  subgraph S["SILOED"]
    S1["information held"] --- S2["talk only<br/>when forced"]
    S2 --- S3["blame 'them'"]
    S3 --- S4["my win"]
  end
  subgraph C["COLLABORATIVE"]
    C1["information<br/>shared unasked"] --- C2["talk early"]
    C2 --- C3["problems<br/>in the open"]
    C3 --- C4["our win"]
  end
  S -.->|four behaviours| C

The one-word diagnostic: listen for "they". Every "they" about another team is a small vote for the silo, and it is usually said by people who would describe themselves as collaborative.

Metaphor

Two houses on the same street with the curtains shut.

Neither family is hostile. Nobody has done anything. They just have no reason to knock, so the only time they ever speak is when a fence blows down, and by then the conversation is already about damage.

Collaboration is not a fence-repair conversation. It is knocking when nothing is wrong.

Study

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-study. The four signals and the seven leadership tips are Zeducation house content and are not matched to published research.

The nearest evidenced neighbour is Amy Edmondson's work on psychological safety, which covers the "problems discussed openly" row properly: 📄 Edmondson (1999).

What to look for: research on cross-functional collaboration and information hoarding, or NZ public sector work on agency silos. Until then, teach the four signals as a practitioner diagnostic and say so. It is a good tool and it does not need a study it does not have.

Honest counterweight, and it is evidenced: more collaboration is not automatically better. See Cross, Rebele & Grant (2016) on collaborative overload and PS-LEA-007.

Story

The board exercise from the topic opener is the story, and it is one the facilitator generates live in every room: six complaints, nine "theys", and the silence after "who is the 'they' in this room, for somebody else?"

⚠️ A collected story would still be better. What to look for: two Zeducation client teams who were each other's "they", and the specific thing that changed it. The moment worth capturing is usually small, and it is almost always a routine rather than a workshop.

TOP-LEA-005Topic · Leadership

One Team, Not Us And Them

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90-120 minCreating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Parts 1, 2 and 4collaborationsilosteamscross-teamleadershiptrustcommunication

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-005 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Creating a Collaborative Team Environment (SKILL UP), Parts 1, 2 and 4

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask the room one question and write the answers on the board in their own words:

"What is one thing that makes your job harder than it needs to be?"

Take five or six. Then go back and circle every "they", "them" and "that lot". In most rooms it is most of the board.

Then ask the question that does the work:

"Who is the 'they' in this room, for somebody else?"

Let the silence sit. Every team is somebody else's "they". Head office is the regions' "they". The regions are head office's. Night shift and day shift are each other's.

Statement: Silos are not built by difficult people. They are built by busy people who stopped having reasons to talk to each other, so all that was left was the times something went wrong.

➜ Facilitator note: nobody's name goes on that board. Teams and departments only.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Tell the difference between a collaborative and a siloed team using four observable signals.
  2. Run a cross-team conversation using Connect, Clarify, Commit.

3. About This Topic

A collaborative team environment is one where people work together instead of in isolation. Information, ideas and responsibility are shared, not protected. People feel safe to speak up, ask questions and offer ideas. Regional teams and head office see themselves as one team working towards the same purpose, not as "us and them".

Collaboration is not just about getting along. It directly affects performance. When people collaborate, communication is clearer, decisions are stronger, and problems get solved faster because more minds are involved. Trust grows because people know they are not carrying the load alone.

For the business it means better service, fewer mistakes, less rework, more innovation, and more consistency across sites. For staff it means feeling valued and heard, work that feels more manageable because support is shared, and better morale because people feel part of something bigger.

Leaders set the tone, by modelling respect, listening to different views, and making sure information is shared rather than hidden.

Key words

WordWhat it means
SiloA team that keeps information and problems inside its own group
Us and themTalking about another team as if they are the obstacle
Collaboration routineA regular check-in or joint plan, so collaboration survives a busy week
Shared purposeThe common goal, and who you are both actually serving

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-030 Collaborative vs Siloed Teams (house model)

The framing that makes it usable: a collaborative team is not just about people liking each other. You can see it in what they do each day.

Collaborative looks likeSiloed looks like
InformationShared without being askedKept to yourself or your department
TimingTeams talk early, not just when things go wrongTeams only talk when they have to
ProblemsDiscussed openly, not hiddenPeople blame "them"
WinsCelebrated as "our result"Claimed by one team
flowchart LR
  subgraph S["SILOED"]
    S1["information held"] --- S2["talk only<br/>when forced"]
    S2 --- S3["blame 'them'"]
    S3 --- S4["my win"]
  end
  subgraph C["COLLABORATIVE"]
    C1["information<br/>shared unasked"] --- C2["talk early"]
    C2 --- C3["problems<br/>in the open"]
    C3 --- C4["our win"]
  end
  S -.->|four behaviours<br/>to change| C

How to read it: four behaviours, not four attitudes. Every one is something you could watch a team do on a Tuesday.

The wins row predicts the rest. A team that says "our result" when it goes well will say "our problem" when it goes badly. A team that claims wins individually will find someone to blame individually, every time.

The seven leadership tips: model collaboration · clarify the shared purpose · connect people not just tasks · encourage questions and ideas · challenge "us vs them" thinking · build collaboration routines · celebrate shared wins.

The sixth is the one most often skipped and does the most work. Collaboration that depends on goodwill fails the first busy week. Collaboration built into a routine survives it.

Worked example: head office thinks the regions ignore process. The regions think head office invents work. Run the four signals and it is not close: information moves only when something breaks, nobody talks until a deadline is missed, both sides blame the other. Nobody is difficult. The structure taught them this, and "be more collaborative" will not change it. Changing when they talk will.

→ Full framework page

FRM-029 The 3C Framework — Connect, Clarify, Commit (house model)

StepWhat you doWhat it prevents
CConnectAcknowledge the person and their time. Show you are on the same sideThe conversation starting as a complaint
CClarifySay why you are talking, ask open questions, listen until you understand their viewSolving the wrong problem, confidently
CCommitAgree who does what, by whenA good conversation that changes nothing
flowchart LR
  A["CONNECT<br/>same side"] --> B["CLARIFY<br/>open questions,<br/>listen"] --> C["COMMIT<br/>who, what,<br/>by when"]

How to read it: in that order, always. Commit without Connect is a demand. Commit without Clarify is a guess.

Worked example: a regional site keeps sending reports late. Without 3C: "we need these on time, it's holding everything up", and nothing changes. With 3C, the Clarify step turns up the actual constraint: the figures the site needs do not arrive until Friday afternoon, so an on-time report was never possible. The Commit moves the deadline to Monday and gets finance sending Thursday. The problem was never the site.

→ Full framework page

FRM-018 Tuckman, read for collaboration

The same five stages, asking a different question: how do I encourage collaboration in this phase?

The idea this lens adds is worth the whole section: storming is when silos form. Leave a team alone through storming and people retreat to their own patch, and the "us and them" hardens into the way things are.

StageThe collaboration move
FormingConnect people across teams early, before there is a problem
StormingEncourage honest kōrero, clarify roles, reconnect to the shared goal so silos do not grow
NormingAgree how you will communicate, share information and decide. Write it down
PerformingProtect the cross-team routines. Do not coast
AdjourningCelebrate together and carry the habits into the next team

→ Full framework page · Taught in full in TOP-LEA-003 Every Team Storms

FRM-023 Psychological Safety

Why problems get hidden rather than discussed openly, which is the third row of the diagnostic. → Full framework page

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Who is the "they" in your workplace? What do you think they say about you?
  2. When did you last talk to that team about something that was not a problem?
  3. What information do you have that another team would find useful, that you have never sent?
  4. Think of a win your team claimed. Who else actually contributed?
  5. Which of the four signals is your team weakest on?
  6. What routine would keep two teams talking even in a busy month?
  7. What conversation have you been avoiding with another team, and what has that cost so far?
  8. Who will you have that conversation with, and when?

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 120 min for the full flow. At 90, cut ACT-042 and ACT-032
  • Running it with only one side in the room gives you a confident and partial picture. Say so out

loud, or the group concludes it has diagnosed the other team

  • What usually goes wrong: it becomes a complaint session about another department inside four

minutes. The redirect is always "what do we do that makes it worse?"

  • The strongest version puts both teams in the room in mixed groups. Much harder to arrange and

it is the only version that changes anything

  • Cultural note: "one team" language travels well where collective identity is already strong.

The harder row is information-sharing, where hierarchy can mean information genuinely is not yours to pass on. Ask rather than assume

PS-LEA-010Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Nice and effective are not opposite ends of one dial

placeholder-storyleadershipstylesresultspeopleassumptionsmanagement

Topic: TOP-LEA-010 People, Results, Or Both · Pillar: Leadership

Point

Most supervisors believe that caring about people and caring about results trade off against each other. That belief is the reason they are average at both.

The belief shows up as a choice between being the hard one and being the nice one. Both are real positions and both cost the team something. The third option is not a compromise between them, and it is harder than either.

Model

Two dials, not one. Concern for people on one axis, concern for results on the other, and the crucial claim is that they are independent.

HIGH  |  Country club                    TEAM
  P   |  lovely, nothing ships     high standards, full backing
  E   |
  O   |              Middle of the road
  P   |          average results, average commitment
  L   |
  E   |  Impoverished                Produce or perish
LOW   |  absent                      numbers hit, people gone
      +-------------------------------------------------
        LOW              RESULTS                    HIGH

And underneath the position sits a belief. Theory X, they do not want to be here. Theory Y, they want to do a good job. Both are self-fulfilling, and both generate their own evidence.

➜ The move: the position is a choice, the belief is a choice, and neither of them is a personality.

Metaphor

A hot tap and a cold tap.

People think leadership is one mixer tap. Turn it toward the people and you turn it away from the result. Turn it toward the result and somebody gets scalded.

It is two separate taps. You can run both hot.

The reason it feels like one tap is that turning both on takes more attention than most people are giving it. That is the honest constraint, and it is worth saying: the middle of the grid is not a failure of character, it is what happens when a supervisor is stretched across two sites and eleven staff and doing their best.

Alternative for a Māori or Pacific room, and probably the better one: Māku e whatu, mā koutou e tāniko. I will weave, all of you can fashion the ornamental border. The weaving and the pattern are not in competition. One holds, the other is why anybody wants it.

Study

**Blake, R. & Mouton, J. (1964). The Managerial Grid: The Key to Leadership Excellence. Houston: Gulf Publishing.** They observed managers at work and found nearly all of it reduced to two concerns. The grid has been in management training for sixty years.

Be honest about what it is. It is a thinking tool with light evidence, not a measured model. Do not claim otherwise from a stage. What it has is sixty years of practitioners recognising themselves in it.

The sharper study to pair with it: **Judge, T. A. & Piccolo, R. F. (2004). Transformational and transactional leadership: a meta-analytic test of their relative validity. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(5), 755-768. 626 correlations, 87 studies. Laissez-faire leadership correlated –.37 with effectiveness.** That is the number to use when somebody argues that hands-off is generous. Being absent is measurably worse than being merely transactional.

⚠️ Do not use the Blake-Mouton grid as evidence of anything. Use it as a picture. Use Judge and Piccolo when you need a number.

Story

The story on the page is the two warehouse supervisors and the four o'clock truck. It works and it is generic.

The story to collect is better, and it is a Zeducation one: a supervisor who was loved and got moved on. Everyone liked them. The team missed them. And the shifts they ran had been quietly costing the next shift for two years, and nobody said so until they left.

That story is more useful than the harsh-supervisor story, because the harsh one is easy to disown. Every room can point at a produce-or-perish boss and feel superior. Almost nobody can point at the country-club one, because that is the one they are trying to be.

The story that would be strongest, and hardest to get: somebody describing the moment they realised being liked and being good at the job were not the same thing. Ask Pasi. Ask the coaches.

⚠️ Placeholder. No collected Zeducation story yet. The warehouse version carries it for now.

TOP-LEA-010Topic · Leadership

People, Results, Or Both

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate120 minLeadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 1 and 2leadershipstylesresultspeopleassumptionsmotivationsituationalteams

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-010 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Leadership Kōnae Ako 1 (Te Wānanga o Aotearoa), Lessons 1 and 2

"You can't always be nice. You have to be able to tell it like it is." — Adrienne Whitewood, owner, Ahu Boutique

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Two supervisors, same warehouse, same problem. It is Thursday, the truck goes at four, and two of the crew have called in sick.

The first one says: "I don't care who's off. That truck leaves at four." The truck leaves at four. Three months later she has been through eleven staff and nobody will pick up a Sunday.

The second one says: "Don't stress about it team. Have a break, we'll sort it tomorrow." Everybody likes him. The truck is late, the next shift inherits it, and the crew on that shift are the ones who end up staying back.

Ask the room: which one is the better leader?

Let them argue. Then say the third thing.

"That truck has to leave at four and we're two down. What's the fastest way to do this, and who needs a hand?"

Statement: Caring about people and caring about the result are not opposite ends of one dial. Most leaders think they are, and that belief is what keeps them average.

➜ Facilitator note: do not resolve the argument early. The room needs to feel the pull of both wrong answers before the third one means anything.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Plot your own position on the people and results axes, and name one thing you would have to

stop doing to move.

  1. Match your style to the obstacle in front of one real person on your team, rather than using

your default on everyone.

3. About This Topic

Every leadership style model in this library answers a different question. This topic answers two of them, and they sit underneath the rest.

The first is what you are aiming at. Blake and Mouton found in the 1960s that almost everything managers did came down to two concerns: concern for people and concern for results. Draw them as two axes and you get five recognisable positions, from the leader who is absent to the leader who is high on both.

The second is what you believe. Underneath the position is an assumption. Douglas McGregor called them Theory X and Theory Y: either people basically do not want to work and have to be pushed, or work is as natural as rest and people commit when the conditions are right. You are running one of them right now, and your team can tell.

Why it matters: the belief comes before the technique. A supervisor who privately thinks their crew are lazy will run a textbook feedback conversation and it will still land as an accusation. The belief leaks through what gets checked, who gets asked, and what happens when someone brings bad news.

Then the third piece, which stops this being about personality at all. Robert House's Path-Goal theory says the leader's job is to clear the path to the goal, and which style you use depends on what is blocking it. The new starter and the fifteen-year veteran need different leaders, on the same Monday, from the same person.

Common mistakes: treating "high on both" as a personality type rather than a choice; assuming the middle of the grid is the safe compromise; picking one style and using it on everybody; and confusing being liked with being good to work for.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Concern for resultsHow much of your attention is on whether the work gets done, properly, on time
Concern for peopleHow much of your attention is on how the people are doing
Theory XThe belief that people avoid work and need pushing
Theory YThe belief that people want to do well when the conditions allow it
Allowable trade-offThe thing you give up when you choose a position. Every position costs something
The obstacleWhat is actually stopping this person. Not what is stopping the team

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-044 The Blake-Mouton Managerial Grid

Origin: Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton, The Managerial Grid, 1964.

Two dials, five positions. The full page, with the diagram and the warehouse worked example, is at FRM-044.

PositionPeopleResultsThe shorthand
ImpoverishedLowLowAbsent
Produce or perishLowHighNumbers hit, people gone
Middle of the roadMidMidAverage both
Country clubHighLowLovely, unproductive
TeamHighHighDemanding and backed

➜ Teach the middle hardest. Almost everybody plots themselves there and it is the position Blake and Mouton were arguing against.

FRM-045 Theory X and Theory Y

Origin: Douglas McGregor, The Human Side of Enterprise, 1960.

Both beliefs are self-fulfilling, and that is the entire teaching point. Full page at FRM-045.

The Theory X loop: you supervise closely → they do the minimum and stop offering → "see, I was right." The Theory Y loop: you set the goal and give room → they take responsibility and raise problems early → "see, I was right."

⚠️ Do not teach X as evil. A new crew on a dangerous site needs direction. The failure is choosing X permanently and never checking.

FRM-046 House's Path-Goal Theory

Origin: Robert J. House, 1971, revised 1996. Full page at FRM-046.

StyleUse it when the obstacle is
DirectiveThey do not know how
SupportiveThey are running on empty
ParticipativeThey know something you do not
Achievement-orientedThey are coasting, or they do not believe they are capable

FRM-047 Likert's Four Systems (optional extension)

Origin: Rensis Likert, 1967. Full page at FRM-047.

Use this only if the room is strong and you have time. Its one contribution is the line between System 2 and System 3: below it people tell you what you want to hear, above it they tell you what is true. Most New Zealand workplaces are System 2 and think they are System 3.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-083 What Do You Actually Believe About People?Assessment20 minFRM-045
ACT-082 The Grid Self-PlotWorksheet20-25 minFRM-044
ACT-084 Four Teams, One LeaderRoleplay30-35 minFRM-046

ACT-087 Your Leadership LegacyReflection15-20 minCloses the topic

Suggested flow: ACT-083 cold, before any teaching → teach FRM-045 and let the room recognise what they scored → teach FRM-044 → ACT-082 → teach FRM-046 → ACT-084 as the live practice → ACT-087 to close.

⚠️ ACT-083 must run before the framework is taught. Once learners know which answers are the approved ones, the assessment measures nothing.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-083 What Do You Actually Believe About People? Ten statements, agree or disagree, scored out of 10 toward Theory X.

ScoreWhat it suggests
0-3Leans strongly Theory Y. Watch that trust is not standing in for standards
4-6Mixed. Where most working supervisors land
7-10Leans Theory X. Not a character flaw, and possibly an accurate read of your workplace

Statement 6 is the one to spend time on. "You have to earn trust before you get it." Nearly every room agrees. Then ask whether a new starter begins on zero and earns their way up, or begins with a full tank and spends it. Both are defensible and they produce very different workplaces.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. It is a set of statements written for a classroom, not a psychometric instrument. See FRM-054 for why that distinction is worth being strict about.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Think of the best leader you ever had. Where would you plot them, and where would you plot

yourself?

  1. Which axis is easier for you to raise, and what would raising it cost you?
  2. What does your team do because you are watching, rather than because they think it matters?
  3. Which of your team is currently getting the wrong style from you?
  4. When did somebody last tell you something you did not want to hear? What happened to them

afterwards?

  1. Is there a situation where being lower on the people axis would be the right call for a week?
  2. Which statement in the self-assessment would you most like to be wrong about?
  3. What is the one thing you will change, with which person, and by when?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • The two supervisors (5 min). Tell the warehouse story from section 1 and take a vote before any

teaching. Cheap, fast, and it sets up everything that follows.

  • Floor grid (10 min). Masking-tape two axes on the floor and have people physically stand where

they think they sit. More honest than paper, and the clustering in the middle is visible to everyone at once. This is the physical variation of ACT-082.

  • ACT-050 Whose Call Is It?

(12-15 min). Sorts real decisions by who should make them. A good warm-up if the room already knows Lewin.

PS-LEA-004Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

You cannot copy an adjective

placeholder-storyrespectrole-modelsleadershiphabitscommitmenthouse-content

Topic: TOP-LEA-004 Respect In Motion · Pillar: Leadership

Point

"Be more respectful" has never changed anyone's behaviour. "Ask the apprentice before you give your own view" changes it on Monday.

Admiration is common and useless. It only becomes useful at the moment you can name the exact thing the person does.

Model

flowchart LR
  W["W — WHO<br/>name one person<br/>you respect, and why"]
  H["H — HOW<br/>name one behaviour<br/>you can actually watch"]
  O["O — OUTCOME<br/>time, place, person,<br/>impact"]
  W --> H --> O

Each step narrows the last. Stop at W and you have a feeling. Stop at H and you have an intention. The O is the only step that produces behaviour.

The stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."
FromTo
"She's a great leader""She asks the quietest person what they think, by name, before she gives her own view"
"I'll be more respectful""I will open Tuesday's meeting by checking everyone's name and pronunciation"

Metaphor

Tracing paper.

You do not learn to draw by admiring a picture. You learn by laying tracing paper over it and following one line at a time.

W-H-O is tracing paper for behaviour. You are not trying to become the person. You are following one line of theirs until your hand knows it.

Study

Two, and together they cover the whole framework.

**Albert Bandura, Social Learning Theory (1977).** Most human behaviour is learned by watching others and copying them. Bandura's own words: "most human behavior is learned observationally through modeling." The W and H steps are that process, made deliberate. 📄 Simply Psychology summary

**Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38, 69-119. A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests and over 8,000 participants found implementation intentions ("when X happens, I will do Y") produced a medium to large effect on goal attainment, d = 0.65**, with a similar effect on the specific failure of never getting started. That is the O step. 📄 Gollwitzer (1999) (PDF)

Worth saying out loud: W-H-O is house content wrapped around two of the better evidenced findings in behaviour change. When someone asks whether it is just a nice exercise, that is the answer.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a learner who named a role model, converted it to a behaviour, did it, and something changed. The aged care example on the topic page is illustrative, not real, and should not be told as though it happened.

The story most likely to be the best one: a learner who told the person they had named. The source's whole premise is that the aunties, coaches and elders who showed us respect become quiet mentors we can call on. Someone going back and saying so is the story this sheet is waiting for.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any leadership session, at the endThe strongest closer Zeducation has. It ends in a dated commitment
Youth and rangatahi programmesThe W step honours family and church role models rather than corporate ones
Values or culture work with a clientThe answer to "how do we make our values real?" You cannot. You can make one behaviour real

Related sheets

SheetRelationship

PS-COM-003 The flight is judged on the landingBoth are about the final step being the one that counts

TOP-LEA-004Topic · Leadership

Respect In Motion

✅ publishedLeadershipFoundation90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 4respectrole-modelsleadershiphabitscommitmenthouse-contentculture

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-004 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 4

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask everyone to think of one person who taught them what respect looks like. Not told them. Showed them.

Give it a moment. It is rarely a manager. It is an aunty, a coach, a supervisor from years ago, a church leader, a grandparent.

Then ask: what did they actually do?

The room will start with adjectives. Kind. Humble. Fair. Push once more and the real answers arrive, and they are always tiny and specific. She learned how to say my name properly. He asked the apprentice first. He never talked about anyone who wasn't there.

Statement: You cannot copy "respectful". You can copy "asks the apprentice first". Respect is not a value, it is a set of small things somebody does on purpose.

➜ Facilitator note: this opener is warm and it can go deep quickly, especially where the person has died. That is not a problem to manage away. Give it room.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Turn a person you respect into one specific behaviour you can copy this week.
  2. Commit to that behaviour with a time, a place and a person attached.

3. About This Topic

Respect is not just something we give or earn. It is something we learn and practise. We learn it by watching people who carry themselves with dignity, keep their word, and lift others even when it is inconvenient. Then we turn what we saw into repeatable actions: greet people by name, listen without interrupting, follow through, give clear feedback, protect people's focus time.

Real leadership is respect in motion.

One of the most effective ways to build a behaviour is to name a role model, pull out the specific thing you admire, and commit to doing it yourself. Keep it specific: who, when, where, and why it matters. Over time those choices become your repetition, and your repetition becomes your reputation.

This matters more under pressure than in calm. As the source puts it: when we are under pressure, we do not rise to the level of our intentions, we fall to the level of our habits.

And it works anywhere. The behaviours that earn respect on a building site are the same ones that earn it at home, at church and on the sports field.

"Respect yourself and others will respect you." — Confucius

Key words

WordWhat it means
ModellingLearning a behaviour by watching someone do it
Observable behaviourSomething someone could watch you do. Not a feeling or a quality
Implementation intentionA plan in the form "when X happens, I will do Y"
Role modelSomeone whose behaviour you deliberately copy

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-019 W-H-O — Who, How, Outcome (house framework)

What it is: pick someone you respect, name one thing they actually do, and commit to doing it yourself this week.

StepThe questionWhat you write
WWHOWho will I mirror?One role model, and why
HHOWHow will I act like them?One observable behaviour
OOUTCOMEWhat outcome will I create?Time, place, person, impact
flowchart LR
  W["W — WHO<br/>name one person<br/>you respect, and why"]
  H["H — HOW<br/>name one behaviour<br/>you can actually see"]
  O["O — OUTCOME<br/>time, place, person,<br/>impact"]
  W --> H --> O

How to read it: each step narrows the last. Stop at W and you have a nice feeling. Stop at H and you have a good intention. The O is what makes it happen.

The commitment stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."

The house examples:

Example 1Example 2
WMy older brotherChurch youth leader
HGreets people by name and checks pronunciationArrives early and sets the room up for success
OI will open tomorrow's team meeting by confirming everyone's name and pronunciation so that people feel seen and respectedI will arrive 10 minutes early to Thursday's workshop to set up chairs, slides and materials so we start on time and keep momentum

Worked example: a team leader in aged care names her late grandmother as her W. The H is that her grandmother never talked about anyone who was not in the room. Her O: "I will change the subject when the afternoon shift starts talking about Mere, on Tuesday, in the staff room, so that people know this team does not do that." That is a leadership act, on a date, that anyone can picture.

→ Full framework page

FRM-026 Modelling and Social Learning

Why W-H-O works. Albert Bandura found that most human behaviour is learned by watching other people and copying them. Four conditions have to be present:

ConditionWhere it breaks
1AttentionYou admire someone but have never watched what they specifically do
2RetentionYou noticed once and never put it into words, so it faded
3ReproductionThe behaviour is beyond you today. Pick a smaller one
4MotivationYou do not believe it will work for you
flowchart LR
  A["ATTENTION"] --> R["RETENTION"] --> P["REPRODUCTION"] --> M["MOTIVATION"] --> B["The behaviour<br/>becomes yours"]

How to read it: a chain, so it breaks at the weakest link. Most people break at Retention, which is exactly what the H step fixes.

The uncomfortable half: you are a model whether you want to be or not. Anyone junior to you is learning how to behave by watching you, including how you talk about people who are not there and what you do when you are wrong.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Simply Psychology — Bandura's Social Learning Theory
  • 📄 Albert Bandura — Modeling and Observational Learning

→ Full framework page

FRM-025 Implementation Intentions

Why the O step is shaped the way it is. Peter Gollwitzer found that plans in the form "when X happens, I will do Y" dramatically outperform general good intentions. The Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis pooled 94 tests and over 8,000 participants and found a medium to large effect on goal attainment (d = 0.65), with a similar effect on the specific problem of never getting started.

That is why the commitment stem demands a day, a place and a person. Say the number out loud in the room. Learners take the commitment more seriously when they hear it was tested on 8,000 people.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Gollwitzer (1999) (PDF)

→ Full framework page

The instrument's last statement is the whole thing in one line: if someone copied how I behave at work this week, would I be happy with that? If it is the lowest number on the page, ignore the total and work on whatever made you circle it.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Who taught you what respect looks like? What did they actually do?
  2. What would it mean to that person to know you named them today?
  3. Somebody junior to you is already copying something you do. What is it?
  4. What have you picked up from someone you did not admire?
  5. Are you the same person under pressure as you are on a good day? Who would notice the difference?
  6. When did someone last get your name, or something else about you, wrong for a long time? What did

that feel like?

  1. Which one behaviour, copied for a month, would change how people experience you?
  2. What is your O? Day, place, person, impact.

  • ACT-046 Behaviour, Not Adjective

(8-10 min). Shout adjectives, the room converts them into behaviours, and the facilitator rejects anything that is still an adjective.

PS-LEA-002Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

Nobody remembers breaking your trust

placeholder-storytrustteamspsychological-safetyreliabilityleadership

Topic: TOP-LEA-002 Trust Is Built In Small Promises · Pillar: Leadership

Point

Trust is not broken by betrayal. It is broken by twenty small things the other person has already forgotten doing.

Which is also the good news, because that is exactly how it gets rebuilt. No grand gesture is available to you, and none is required.

Model

The ladder, read from the bottom. Each layer rests on the one below, so the weak one at the bottom brings down everything above it.

flowchart TD
  R["5. Inattention to Results<br/>my win beats our win"]
  A["4. Avoidance of Accountability<br/>nobody says anything"]
  C["3. Lack of Commitment<br/>unclear decisions"]
  F["2. Fear of Conflict<br/>fake yes"]
  T["1. Absence of Trust<br/>people hide"]
  T --> F --> C --> A --> R

Most teams try to fix the top. They set better goals and add another meeting, and none of it holds, because the reason nobody speaks up in the meeting is at the bottom.

The repair loop, at the bottom rung:

flowchart LR
  S["SAY"] --> D["DO"] --> C["CLOSE"] -.-> S

Metaphor

A bank account nobody tells you the balance of.

Every kept promise is a small deposit. Every missed one is a small withdrawal. Nobody reads you the statement, and you only find out you are overdrawn when you ask for something and the answer is a polite version of no.

The person who overdrew the account is usually the last to know, because from where they stand every single withdrawal was reasonable at the time.

Study

**Amy C. Edmondson, "Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams", Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 350-383 (1999).**

Edmondson set out to study hospital nursing teams and found something that looked wrong: the teams with the best relationships reported the most errors. They were not making more mistakes. They were the only ones willing to report them.

Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 of its own teams between 2012 and 2016 and found psychological safety was the strongest single predictor of team effectiveness.

📄 The paper · 🎬 Edmondson's TEDx talk

Why this study and not Lencioni: the 5 Dysfunctions is the better teaching model and the weaker evidence. When someone in the room wants proof, use Edmondson.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. Needs a real one from delivery.

The story to collect: a supervisor who rebuilt a team's trust with small kept promises rather than a big change. The shape: a team that had stopped bringing them things, three or four weeks of boring reliability, and the specific moment they noticed it had turned. That moment is the story.

The alternative shape, which is often stronger: someone who was on the receiving end. A person who stopped telling their manager things, and what the manager did that changed it back.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any leadership sessionThe opener. It gets past "trust is important" in ninety seconds
Supervisor trainingPaired with Say-Do-Close as the practical week
Client work on cultureThe honest answer to "how long will this take?"

Related sheets

SheetRelationship
PS-COM-001 Assertive is clear, not loudFear of conflict is the second rung of this ladder. That sheet is the skill that gets you past it
PS-EMP-001 The job comes from the person you barely knowSame source workbook. Build the relationship, then make it trustworthy

TOP-LEA-002Topic · Leadership

Trust Is Built In Small Promises

✅ publishedLeadershipIntermediate90-120 minBuilding Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 2trustteamspsychological-safetyaccountabilityreliabilityconflictleadership

Pillar: Leadership · Level: Intermediate · Suggested time: 90-120 min · ID: TOP-LEA-002 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Effective Work Relationships (SKILL UP), Part 2

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: Ask the room to think of someone at work they do not fully trust. Not a villain. Just someone whose word they have learned to discount.

Then ask: what did they actually do?

The answers are never dramatic. They said they would send it and did not. They agreed in the meeting and something different happened. They told you something in confidence and it came back to you from somewhere else. They were fine with you and different with someone else.

Then the second question, which is the one that lands:

How many of those would that person even remember doing?

Almost none. That is the whole topic.

Statement: Nobody breaks trust in one big moment. They break it in twenty small ones they have already forgotten about, and they rebuild it the same way.

➜ Facilitator note: do not let anyone name a real person out loud. The thinking is private, the answers are general.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Rebuild trust using a small promise, kept on time and closed off with proof.
  2. Respond to bad news in a way that makes the person bring you the next one.

3. About This Topic

Trust is the foundation of every effective work relationship. When people trust each other they feel safe to speak honestly, share ideas, ask for help and admit mistakes without fear of being judged. Work becomes less about protecting yourself and more about solving the problem together.

Teams with high trust move faster, communicate better and handle conflict without damage. When trust is low, people hold back, misunderstandings grow, and simple tasks become stressful.

Building trust is not about being perfect. It is about being consistent, honest and human.

Five things trust gets you: people feel safe to speak up; there is less stress and drama; work gets done faster because there is less second-guessing; people admit mistakes and learn; and good people want to stay.

This matters everywhere, not only at work. The same behaviours build or break trust in a family, a church group, a sports team and a marae committee.

Key words

WordWhat it means
Psychological safetyThe shared belief that it is safe here to ask a question, admit a mistake or disagree
ReliabilityDoing what you said you would do, by when you said it
Self-orientationBeing in it for yourself. The thing that cancels out everything else
Fake yesAgreeing in the room and doing something different afterwards

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-017 The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team

What it is: five problems that stack, so if the bottom one is weak everything above falls over. Origin: Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (2002).

flowchart TD
  R["5. Inattention to Results<br/>my win beats our win"]
  A["4. Avoidance of Accountability<br/>nobody says anything"]
  C["3. Lack of Commitment<br/>unclear decisions"]
  F["2. Fear of Conflict<br/>fake yes"]
  T["1. Absence of Trust<br/>people hide"]
  T --> F --> C --> A --> R

How to read it: the arrows are causes, not steps. Fix the bottom first. Working on results while trust is broken is wasted effort.

Worked example: a kitchen keeps missing Friday orders. The manager adds a checklist and it does not help. The real cause is that the newest chef cannot read the handwriting on the tickets and has never said so, because the first time he asked a question he got laughed at. A results problem, four layers above its actual cause.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Table Group overview (PDF)
  • 🎬 Patrick Lencioni presenting the model

→ Full framework page

FRM-020 Say-Do-Close (house technique)

What it is: make a small promise, deliver on time, confirm it is done with proof.

flowchart LR
  S["SAY<br/>a small promise<br/>with a time on it"] --> D["DO<br/>deliver it<br/>on the day"]
  D --> C["CLOSE<br/>confirm it,<br/>with proof"]
  C -.->|trust goes up<br/>a small amount| S

How to read it: one trip round changes nothing. Twenty trips round is a reputation.

The step everyone skips is Close. From the outside, silent delivery and no delivery look identical until somebody checks.

Worked example: a supervisor known for saying "I'll sort it" and not sorting it picks one thing. "I'll get you the roster by Thursday lunchtime." He writes it Wednesday night. Thursday 11am it goes in the group chat: "roster's up, as promised, tell me if I've got your Saturday wrong." Nobody praises him. Three weeks later people start asking him for things again.

The other five house trust tips: Share the Why · Make it Safe · Set Clear Rules · Repair Fast (within 24 hours) · Be Fair and Private. → Full framework page

FRM-023 Psychological Safety

What it is: a shared belief that this team is safe for interpersonal risk, so you can ask, admit or disagree without being punished for it. Origin: Amy Edmondson, Harvard, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999. Strongest evidence in this topic.

Her study of hospital nursing teams found the teams with the best relationships reported the most errors. They were not making more. They were willing to report them. Google's Project Aristotle later found the same factor was the strongest predictor of team effectiveness across 180 of its own teams.

Low standardsHigh standards
High safetyComfort zoneLearning zone
Low safetyApathy zoneAnxiety zone

Safety is not softness. It is what makes high standards achievable, because a team that can talk about failure can fix it.

The three leader moves: frame the work as a learning problem · admit your own limits out loud · respond productively to bad news. The third one decides it. People are not testing what you say about openness, they are watching what happened to the last person who was open.

Learn more:

  • 📄 Edmondson (1999)
  • 🎬 TEDxHGSE — Amy Edmondson, Building a psychologically safe workplace (about 11 min)

→ Full framework page

FRM-022 The Trust Equation

                Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy
Trustworthiness = ───────────────────────────────────
                        Self-orientation

The top three add up, the bottom one divides. It explains the person who is expert, reliable and warm and still not trusted: everyone can tell they are mainly in it for themselves. → Full framework page

How trust gets broken (house content)

Mixed messages · missed promises · hidden information · blame and gossip · favouritism · poor listening · breach of confidence.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

6. Self-Assessment

Step 1 of ACT-031 Fix Your Lowest Pillar is the instrument: rate yourself 1 to 5 on Trust, Conflict, Commitment, Accountability and Results, and circle the lowest. House content, taken as written from the source workbook.

There is no scored band here on purpose. The lowest pillar is the result, and the worksheet turns it straight into a daily action with a trigger.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. Think of someone whose word you have learned to discount. What did they actually do?
  2. When did someone last bring you bad news? What did your face do in the first two seconds?
  3. Which of the five pillars is weakest for you personally? For your team?
  4. What is something you agreed to in a meeting and then quietly did differently?
  5. Who on your team has stopped telling you things? When did that start?
  6. Where have you dropped the ball and not repaired it? What would repairing it take?
  7. Whose trust would change your working life most if you rebuilt it?
  8. What is the one small promise you will make, keep and close this week, and to whom?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-039 The Silent Nod

(10-12 min). Three briefed people agree with a mildly bad proposal and the room stays silent. Fake yes, experienced live. The best opener in this topic.

  • ACT-036 Red Flag Or Green Flag?

(12-15 min). Use the trust variation: trust-breaking behaviours, asked as "have you seen this?"

PIL-WELPillar · 01-Pillars

Wellbeing & Identity

Hauora, resilience, values and culture. The foundation the other five pillars stand on, and the pillar that decides whether learning sticks.

Who it serves: everyone, and especially learners carrying pressure from work, family and money at the same time.

The boundary: if it is about the learner's own identity and wellbeing, it belongs here. If it is about working across difference, or what a leader builds, it belongs in Culture & Diversity.
