PS-WEL-001Pink Sheet · 01-Pillars

You only need the next rock

placeholder-storywellbeingresiliencehauoraabc-modelactionsetbackshouse-content

Topic: TOP-WEL-001 Building Resilience · Pillar: Wellbeing & Identity

Point

Clarity comes from action, not the other way around.

People wait to start until they can see how it ends. That wait is not caution, it is the thing keeping them stuck. You do not need to see every step. You need the next one, and the one after it only becomes visible once you are standing on the first.

Model

ABC. Three steps, and the third is the whole thing.

flowchart LR
  A["A · ACCEPT<br/>What are the facts?<br/>What can I control?"] --> B["B · BELIEVE<br/>My past wins?<br/>My support group?"]
  B --> C["C · COMMIT<br/>My next rock?<br/>What will I do?"]
StepWhat it doesThe failure mode
AAcceptSplits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannotHeard as "get over it"
BBelieveReplaces doubt with evidence, not encouragementSkipped, and it is the step with the research behind it
CCommitOne action, fifteen minutes, with a time and a definition of doneBecomes a project instead of a step

⚠️ Not Ellis's ABC (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), which is a therapy model with the same three letters. Say "the ABC of resilience".

And the frame that has to come first: resilience is ordinary. It is common, it runs on ordinary systems, and it is not a personality trait some people were issued with. Without that framing the tool lands as "try harder", which is worse than teaching nothing.

Metaphor

Crossing a river on stepping stones.

Some people can see the whole line of rocks to the other side. They know each step and they just follow it.

Others can only see the rock right in front of them. That is fine. Step onto it, and the next one shows up.

Different views, same goal. Keep moving.

➜ This is Zeducation's own, straight from the SKILL UP guide, and it is the strongest thing in the resource. It also runs as an activity — ACT-107 puts a paper river on the floor and it takes fifteen minutes.

Study

Two anchors, and it matters which part of the model each one holds up.

1. Resilience is ordinary. Ann S. Masten, University of Minnesota, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development (Guilford, 2nd ed. 2024). Decades of longitudinal work with children exposed to serious adversity. Her finding: resilience is common, and it runs on ordinary adaptive systems — relationships, routines, a functioning body, culture, belief — rather than on rare personal strength. Evidence: strong.

2. Why step B works. "Remember your past wins" is Bandura's mastery experiences, which the self-efficacy literature consistently finds to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief. Direct personal evidence of having done a hard thing beats encouragement from anybody else.

➜ The line: being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can. Remembering that you already did is the strongest.

And the part worth saying in a Zeducation room: Masten's list of ordinary systems is the same list as Te Whare Tapa Whā (Durie, 1984) and Fonofale (Pulotu-Endemann). Three traditions, arrived at separately, one answer. Durie got there forty years earlier.

⚠️ Honest limit: the ABC model itself has no study behind it. Step B does. The other two steps are craft, and they should be presented as craft.

Story

⚠️ GAP: placeholder-story. The man on the stepping stones is the resource's own metaphor, told as a teaching story. It is not a real person.

The story to collect: a Zeducation learner who was stuck waiting to see the whole path, took one small step, and found the next one. What lands is what the step actually was — small enough to sound unimpressive, which is the point — and what became visible afterwards.

Second story worth collecting, and it is the higher-value one: somebody whose confidence moved on the ABC worksheet while nothing about their situation changed. The before and after number, in their own words. That is the proof of the whole model in about fifteen seconds.

Where it goes

Use it inHow
Any wellbeing or resilience sessionThe full topic, 120-150 min
One-to-one after a knockbackA job rejection, a failed assessment, a fallout at home. Fifteen minutes and a sheet
Team debriefsA lost tender, a bad audit, a restructure. One sheet, whole team
Talks and keynotesThe river stones is the strongest metaphor Zeducation owns. It carries a whole talk
Funder and employer conversationsThe "resilience is ordinary" framing is why Zeducation does not treat circumstances as a motivation problem

⚠️ Where it does not go: grief, trauma, depression, anxiety. This is a tool for a setback. Know the difference, and know the referrals: their GP, 1737 free call or text, workplace EAP.

TOP-WEL-001Topic · Wellbeing & Identity

Building Resilience

✅ publishedWellbeing & IdentityFoundation120-150 minBuilding Resilience (SKILL UP)wellbeingresiliencehauorate-whare-tapa-whafonofaleabc-modelidentitysetbacks

Pillar: Wellbeing & Identity · Level: Foundation · Suggested time: 120-150 min · ID: TOP-WEL-001 · 🩷 Pink Sheet Module: Building Resilience (SKILL UP)

1. Open With This (Story & Statement)

Story: A man is crossing a river on stepping stones. He knows the far bank is there, but standing where he is, he can see exactly one rock. The rest is under the glare of the water.

Next to him is somebody who can see the whole line of stones, all the way across. She steps out and walks it in eight seconds.

He waits. He waits because it feels obvious that you should be able to see where you are going before you go. Then eventually he puts one foot on the one rock he can see, and stands on it, and from there the next one is visible.

He crosses. Slower than her, and he still gets to the other side.

Ask the room: which one of them needed the whole plan?

Then the second question, which is the real one: what have you not started, because you cannot see how it ends?

Statement: Clarity comes from action, not the other way around. You do not need to see every step. You need the next one.

➜ Facilitator note: the room will have an answer to the second question and most of them will not say it out loud. That is fine. Let the silence sit for a moment, then move.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this topic you will be able to:

  1. Explain what resilience actually is, and name the ordinary systems it runs on.
  2. Name one thing that needs care in each part of your whare or your fale.
  3. Apply the ABC model to a real setback and leave with one small step, with a time on it.

3. About This Topic

Everyone gets knocked around. A deadline slips, the bills stack up, a relationship strains, a health scare turns up, or somebody dies. The details differ. The feeling is the same: pressure, uncertainty, and the question "what now?"

Resilience is the answer to that moment. It is not about being unbreakable. It is about adapting: steadying yourself, learning from what happened, and taking the next small step.

This topic runs in three moves.

The moveWhy it is in this order
1What resilience actually isBecause half the room has already decided it is a personality trait they do not have
2The whole personTe Whare Tapa Whā and Fonofale. Because "be more resilient" aims at the mind and ignores the four things holding it up
3The toolThe ABC model, on a real setback, leaving with one step

⚠️ Do not skip move 1. A resilience session taught without it becomes a session about trying harder, and for a learner already carrying a heavy load that is worse than teaching nothing.

Key words

WordWhat it means
ResilienceAdapting after a knock. Steadying, learning, taking the next step. Not being unbreakable
HauoraWellbeing, in the whole-person sense. Body, mind, family, spirit, place
PouA post or a pillar. One of the parts holding the house up
AigaFamily, including extended family and anyone you are linked to
SetbackSomething that knocks you off course and that you can do something about. Not the same as a crisis
Self-efficacyYour belief that you can do a particular thing. Built mostly out of having done hard things before

4. Frameworks, Tools & Techniques

FRM-066 Resilience Is Ordinary

What it is: resilience is common, not rare, and it runs on ordinary systems around a person rather than on exceptional personal strength.

Origin: Ann S. Masten, University of Minnesota, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development. Decades of work with children exposed to serious adversity. Evidence: strong, and built on longitudinal research rather than one study.

Most people arrive with one of two beliefs and both are wrong.

The beliefWhere it leads
"Resilient people are made differently"Nothing you teach applies to them, because they have decided it is a trait they lack
"Resilience means taking anything"The word becomes a weapon, used to explain why the problem is you and not the load
flowchart TD
  M["RESILIENCE IS ORDINARY"]
  M --> A["It is COMMON,<br/>not rare"]
  M --> B["It runs on ORDINARY SYSTEMS,<br/>not exceptional people"]
  M --> C["So it can be BUILT,<br/>and it can be DAMAGED"]
  A --> D["'I'm not that kind of person'<br/>is not true"]
  B --> E["relationships · routines · a body<br/>that works · culture · belief"]
  C --> F["Protect the systems<br/>and you protect the person"]

How to read it: the question is never "are you strong enough?" It is "which of your systems is missing, and can we put it back?"

⚠️ The sentence this framework exists to refuse: "you just need to be more resilient." Said to somebody working two jobs whose car has died, that is not support. It moves a structural problem into a personal failing. The honest version: resilience is real and it can be built, and it is not a substitute for enough hours, a safe house, or somebody to ring.

Learn more:

  • 📕 Ann S. Masten, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development, 2nd ed.

→ Full framework page

FRM-063 Te Whare Tapa Whā · FRM-065 Fonofale

Teach these two together. Never one alone. A room offered a single model has been told which half of itself counts.

Te Whare Tapa Whā is Sir Mason Durie's, developed at Hui Taumata in 1984 in response to Rapuora, research carried out 1978 to 1980 by the Māori Women's Welfare League into the health barriers Māori were experiencing. It is the framework that got wairua acknowledged in health practice in this country.

flowchart TD
  W["TE WHARE TAPA WHĀ"]
  W --- A["TAHA WAIRUA<br/>spirit, purpose"]
  W --- B["TAHA HINENGARO<br/>mind and emotions"]
  W --- C["TAHA TINANA<br/>the body"]
  W --- D["TAHA WHĀNAU<br/>family and belonging"]
  A --- E["TAHA WHENUA<br/>connection to land and roots"]
  B --- E
  C --- E
  D --- E

How to read it: four walls on one foundation. A whare with three walls does not stand.

Fonofale is Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann's, built across Cook Islands, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Niuean and Tokelauan values. Culture is the roof. Aiga is the floor. Four pou between them, and the whole fale sits inside its environment, its time and its context.

Te Whare Tapa WhāFonofale
FamilyTaha whānau, one of four wallsAiga is the floor. Everything stands on it
CultureCarried through whenua and wairuaThe roof. Named on its own
The fourth elementTaha wairua"Other" — age, gender, sexuality, money
What surrounds itWhenua as the foundationEnvironment, time and context

➜ The "other" pou does something no other wellbeing model here does. It puts money, age, gender and sexuality inside the picture of health instead of outside it.

Why this matters for resilience specifically:

What it gives you when things go wrong
BodySteadies the stress. Sleep and food change what a problem feels like before they change anything else
MindLets you think straight enough to make a decision you will not regret
Family, aigaThe backup. Somebody to ring, somebody who turns up
Spirit, cultureThe reason to keep going when there is no short-term reason
Whenua, contextKnowing who and where you are from, when a setback is telling you that you are nothing

⚠️ Aiga cuts both ways and the room knows it. Family is the strongest support most Pacific learners have, and sometimes also the obligation grinding them down. Do not teach the floor as though it is only a resource.

⚠️ Say whose these models are. Durie by name, 1984. Pulotu-Endemann by name, and he is a living person. Teaching a Māori or Pacific model without attribution is the exact habit this library exists to break.

Learn more:

  • 🔗 Mental Health Foundation — Te Whare Tapa Whā
  • 📄 Fonofale Model of Health — Pulotu-Endemann (PDF)

→ Te Whare Tapa Whā · Fonofale

FRM-064 The ABC Model of Resilience (house model)

⚠️ Name clash. This is not Ellis's ABC (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), which is what a counsellor or a psychology student will mean. Say "the ABC of resilience" when you introduce it. And it is not Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which shares two of its words and is a clinical therapy delivered by clinicians. This is a workshop tool.

What it is: three steps from spinning your wheels to having one small thing you are going to do.

flowchart LR
  A["A · ACCEPT<br/>What are the facts?<br/>What can I control?"] --> B["B · BELIEVE<br/>My past wins?<br/>My support group?"]
  B --> C["C · COMMIT<br/>My next rock?<br/>What will I do?"]

How to read it: in order, and C is the point. A and B without C is a nice conversation that changes nothing by Friday.

StepWhat it does
AAcceptStops the spinning. Splits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannot
BBelieveReplaces doubt with evidence. Evidence, not a pep talk
CCommitTurns insight into momentum. Fifteen minutes, with a time on it

Worked example. You have been turned down for a job you thought you had.
Accept"They said no. I can't change that. I can control whether I ring and ask why, and whether I apply for the other two this week."
Believe"I got the warehouse job in March and I had less experience then. I've got Mere, who knows people at the DC."
Commit"Tomorrow at 10, I'll ring and ask what would have made the difference. Done means I've asked one question and written the answer down."

➜ Notice what the commitment is not. Not "be more positive", not "get back out there". One action, a time, and a definition of done.

Where the evidence actually sits. Be honest about which part is backed and which is craft.

StepWhat holds it up
AcceptThe control / no-control split. A useful distinction, not a research finding
BelieveThe strongest part. "Remember your past wins" is Bandura's mastery experiences, consistently found to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief
CommitSmall, specific, time-boxed action. The specificity does the work, not the size

➜ The line worth saying out loud: "Being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can do it. Remembering that you already did is the strongest. That is why step B asks for a past win and not a compliment."

Learn more:

  • 🔗 Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy

→ Full framework page

⚠️ Where to send someone (house content, and it is not optional)

The ABC model is for a setback. It is not a treatment for depression, anxiety, grief or trauma, and somebody in the room will be carrying one of those.
1737Free call or text, any time, to a trained counsellor
Their GPThe first door for anything that has lasted more than a couple of weeks
Workplace EAPFree, confidential, and most learners in work do not know they have it
Their MSD case managerFor the practical load: money, housing, transport
Healthline 0800 611 11624/7

Say these out loud at the start, not the end. Somebody who needs them will have stopped listening by the end.

5. Apply — Suggested Activities

ActivityTypeTimePractises
ACT-104 Three QuotesWorksheet, opener25-30 minFRM-066
ACT-105 One Thing Per WallAssessment25-30 minFRM-063, FRM-065
ACT-107 The River StonesGame15-20 minFRM-064, FRM-066

Suggested flow: the river story in section 1 → ACT-104 while the room is settling → teach FRM-066 → teach both wellbeing models → ACT-105 → break, because they have been sitting → ACT-107 to get them up → straight into ACT-106 while they are standing → ACT-006 to close.

⚠️ ACT-107 goes immediately before step C of ACT-106. That is what it is for. Running the game early and the worksheet after lunch loses most of its value.

6. Self-Assessment

ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall is the assessment, and both models are on the sheet so the learner picks.

⚠️ There is no score. No total, no rating out of ten, nothing to hand in. One thing per wall that needs care. That is the entire instrument, and somebody will ask what a good result looks like. There is not one.

What the learner leaves with:
One thing per wallNamed, in their own words
The wall holding everything up on its ownUsually obvious once the model gives them the word
The wall they have been letting goUsually tinana. Sometimes wairua
One step on one wallFifteen minutes, with a time and somebody who will know

The ABC worksheet also carries a confidence check, 1 to 10, before and after planning. Also not validated, also not recorded. The movement is the lesson — people routinely go up two or three points in fifteen minutes while nothing about the situation has changed.

⚠️ Never fill either in about a learner. A hauora model used to assess somebody else is doing the opposite of what it was built for.

7. Reflection Questions

  1. What have you not started, because you cannot see how it ends?
  2. Which quote landed fastest, and what does that say about what you already carry?
  3. Which wall or pou has been holding everything up on its own?
  4. Which one have you been letting go, and how long has that been going on?
  5. What have you been spending energy on that belongs in the "cannot control" column?
  6. What is a past win you had stopped counting?
  7. Who is the one person who would turn up for you at 2am? Do they know that is what they are?
  8. What is your next rock, when will you step on it, and who will know that you did?

8. Fun Openers — Games & Energisers

  • ACT-107 The River Stones

(15-20 min, 🔥 high energy). Two volunteers cross a paper river, one seeing every stone and one seeing only the next. The best fifteen minutes in this topic, and it works as an opener too if the room arrives full of energy.

  • ACT-104 Three Quotes

(25-30 min, low energy). The quiet opener. Use this one when the room arrives flat or wary.

  • Two-minute version: ask everyone to say one thing they have got through that they did not think

they would. Round the room, no detail required. Two minutes, and it sets up FRM-066 for free.

Source Trail

Built from SRC-012 Building Resilience (SKILL UP Participant Guide), Zeducation house content by Pasitaua Haufano, ingested 2026-08-02. This is the topic that opens the Wellbeing & Identity pillar.

From the resource: the two learning outcomes, the framing on page 2, Te Whare Tapa Whā, the ABC model and its worked example, the ABC worksheet including the confidence check, the three-quotes activity and its note, and the river stones metaphor.

Added: Fonofale, because a Māori model alone does not serve a Pacific room. FRM-066, because the research corrects the myth the resource is already arguing against. ACT-107, which turns the metaphor into fifteen minutes on the floor. The referral list, which the resource does not carry. The Durie origin story, the Bandura anchor under step B, and both name-clash warnings were researched separately.

Facilitator Notes

  • Timing: 150 min comfortable, 120 min tight. Under 90, run FRM-066, one wellbeing model, ACT-107

and ACT-106. Never drop the referral list to save time

  • ⚠️ Read the referral list out at the start of the session, not the end. Somebody who needs it

will have stopped listening by the end

  • Teach both wellbeing models, always. Ten minutes each. A Pacific room given only Te Whare Tapa

Whā, or a Māori room given only Fonofale, has been told something you did not mean to say

  • Do not comment on which model anybody picks. Some Māori learners will pick Fonofale. Some

Pacific learners will pick the whare. It is not a test of identity

  • The ABC worksheet needs a real setback. Not hypothetical. Say at the start that it is fine to

pick something small, and that nobody will be asked to share the situation

  • What usually goes wrong: "Accept" is heard as "get over it" or "it was your fault". Say what it

means before they write, not after. It is the single most common misfire in the topic

  • Step C will be too big. "Sort my life out" is not a step. Be strict, because this is where the

session is won or lost

  • ⚠️ Somebody's setback will turn out to be a crisis. Bereavement, a diagnosis, violence, a

relationship ending, losing the house. ABC is not for those. Have the referrals ready before you walk in

  • Come back to the sheets a fortnight later and ask whether the step happened. This is where the

tool either becomes real or dies in the room it was taught in

  • ⚠️ Open gap: no Zeducation learner story on the Pink Sheet yet. It can only come from delivery.

Ask your tutors and get permission properly

  • ⚠️ Open gap: FRM-066 rests on

US developmental research. New Zealand longitudinal evidence would strengthen it, and the Dunedin and Christchurch studies are the obvious places to look

FRM-001Framework · 02-Frameworks

The 4 Communication Styles

modelpractitionerassertivenesscommunication-stylesconflictself-awareness

What it is in one line: the four ways people communicate under pressure, and what each one costs.

Origin: a long-standing assertiveness training model (passive / aggressive / passive-aggressive / assertive), taught in this form in Zeducation's Effective Communication workbook. Evidence: practitioner. Widely taught in assertiveness training and clinical psychology; the four-style split is a teaching device rather than a validated instrument, so teach it as a mirror, not a diagnosis. Best for: self-awareness at the start of any communication, conflict or leadership module.

The model

Two questions decide the style: am I open to communication? and am I considerate of others?

Considerate of othersNot considerate of others
Open to communicationASSERTIVE — I win, you winAGGRESSIVE — I win, you lose
Not open to communicationPASSIVE — I lose, you winPASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE — I lose, you lose
flowchart TD
  Q{Under pressure,<br/>what do you do?}
  Q -->|Say nothing,<br/>keep the peace| P[PASSIVE<br/>I lose, you win]
  Q -->|Push, blame,<br/>talk over| A[AGGRESSIVE<br/>I win, you lose]
  Q -->|Say it is fine<br/>when it is not| PA[PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE<br/>I lose, you lose]
  Q -->|Say what you mean,<br/>kindly, and listen| AS[ASSERTIVE<br/>I win, you win]

How to read it: the four styles are the four exits people take when the pressure comes on. Only one of them protects the result and the relationship at the same time.

The steps

StyleWhat it looks likeSounds likeThe risk
PassiveQuiet, avoids conflict, rarely shares needs, struggles to say no, apologises a lot"It's okay, I guess… I'll manage."People take advantage. Your ideas never get heard
Passive-aggressiveAgreeable on the surface, upset underneath. Sarcasm, silent treatment, fake smiles"Sure, I'll do it. Just like last time when no one helped me."Hidden feelings damage relationships and build stress
AggressiveDominates, forces opinions, interrupts, invades space, reacts without thinking"You're hopeless at this job."Wins the moment, loses trust. Struggles to build strong relationships
AssertiveSpeaks confidently and respectfully, says no when needed, protects boundaries, listens"I understand you're busy, but I need this report by 3pm."The healthiest style. The goal

Why it works

It gives people a mirror before it gives them a method. Most learners can name their own default within a minute of seeing the four, and naming it is what makes change possible. The win/lose framing does the rest of the work: nobody argues for the "I lose, you lose" box once they can see it.

Teach it as a situation style, not a personality. Most people are assertive in some rooms and passive in others. The useful question is "where do you drop out of assertive, and with who?"

Worked examples

Workplace: A supervisor asks a team member to stay late for the third time this week. Passive: "…okay." Aggressive: "You always dump this on me." Passive-aggressive: "Fine. Whatever." Assertive: "I can't stay tonight, I have my kids. I can start early tomorrow if that helps."

Home / community: Someone volunteers you for a church duty without asking. Assertive: "I want to help, but I can't take that on this month. I can do it in November."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10-15 minutes
  • Demonstrate first: say the same sentence four ways and let the room name each one. It gets a

laugh and it lands the model faster than any slide

  • Common mistakes: learners label each other ("you're so aggressive"). Set the rule early that

the model is for looking at yourself. Also watch for "assertive equals blunt" — pair it immediately with FRM-002

  • Adaptations: for youth, use group chat and social media scenarios. For Pacific and Māori

groups, talk about the difference between respect for elders and staying silent when something is unsafe. Both can be true

Learn more

  • 📄 Positive Psychology — Assertive communication, styles and techniques
  • 📄 University of Iowa — I-statements and conflict management
  • 🎬 TED — Adam Galinsky: How to speak up for yourself (15 min) — the low-power double bind. Best used after the styles, to explain why people go passive
  • 🎬 Assertiveness scenarios in the workplace — short worked scenarios, good as a discussion trigger

FRM-002Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Assert Approach & "I" Statements

techniquemoderateassertivenessi-statementsboundariesconflictfeedback

What it is in one line: three sentences that let you raise something hard without putting the other person on the defensive.

Origin: the Assert Approach is Zeducation's own, from the Effective Communication workbook. The underlying "I message" was coined by American psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s in his work with parents and children (background). Evidence: moderate, and worth being honest about. Research finds I-language is less likely to provoke negative emotion and more likely to evoke compassion and cooperation (Rogers et al., 2018), but outside romantic relationships some studies find no difference between "I" and "you" phrasing (IEEE ProComm review). Teach it as a strong habit that lowers defensiveness, not a magic sentence. Best for: raising an issue, saying no, setting a boundary, giving feedback.

The model

flowchart LR
  N["1. NAME<br/>the situation<br/><i>facts only</i>"] --> S["2. SAY<br/>how it affects you<br/><i>I feel / I need</i>"]
  S --> A["3. ASK<br/>what you need<br/><i>clear and specific</i>"]
  A --> C(["Calm voice.<br/>Steady eyes.<br/>Same message."])

How to read it: three steps, said calmly. The calm is not decoration, it is the fourth step.

The steps

StepWhat you doSounds like
1. Name the situationState the facts. No blame, no history, no "always" or "never""The report came through after 3pm today."
2. Say how it affects youOwn it with "I". Effect, not accusation"I feel stuck, because I can't finish my part without it."
3. Say what you needBe specific and reasonable. Make it a request, not a demand"I need it by 1pm on Fridays. Can we do that?"

The "I" statement formula: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. What I need is ___.

Instead of…Say…
"You never listen.""I feel unheard when I'm interrupted."
"You're always late.""When the shift starts late, I'm the one covering. I need us to start at 7."
"You dumped this on me.""I've got three jobs on today. I can do this one tomorrow morning."

Why it works

A "you" sentence puts the other person on trial, and people defend themselves before they listen. An "I" sentence describes your own experience, which nobody can argue with, and then makes a request they can actually say yes to. It also forces you to work out what you actually want before you open your mouth, which is where most difficult conversations fall over.

Four rights it rests on (taught with it in the workbook): you have the right to share your opinion, the right to say no without feeling guilty, the right to be treated with respect, and the right to set clear boundaries.

Worked examples

Workplace: Manager sets a deadline that is not realistic. "The install is booked for Thursday and we've still got two rooms to do. I'm worried we'll cut corners on the safety checks. Can we either move it to Monday or put a second person on Wednesday?"

Home / community: Family asks for money you do not have. "I want to help with the fundraising. Money is tight for us this month, so I can't put in cash. I can do the cooking and the setup."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then practise. It does not stick without practice
  • Demonstrate first: ask the room for a real "you" statement, then rewrite it live together
  • Common mistakes:
    • "I feel that you are being unfair" is a "you" statement wearing a hat. If "that" follows "I feel",

rewrite it

    • Over-apologising in front of it ("sorry, sorry, it's probably just me…") deletes the message
    • Tone. The same words said sharply are still aggressive. Practise the voice, not just the script
  • Adaptations: for low literacy, teach the three prompts as *what happened / how it lands / what I

need*. For groups where directness with elders is uncomfortable, keep the words and slow the pace, and open with respect before the ask

Learn more

  • 📄 University of Iowa — I-statements
  • 📄 Psychology Today — Are "I" statements better than "you" statements? — the honest counter-view
  • 📄 Rogers et al. (2018) — the benefits of I-language during conflict
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen (10 min, one of TED's most-watched talks) — HAIL: honesty, authenticity, integrity, love. Excellent closer for this framework
  • 🎬 How to be assertive at work without being rude — practical, workplace-focused

FRM-003Framework · 02-Frameworks

STAR Teaching Framework

facilitationpractitionerstarfacilitationteaching-methodhouse-content

⚠️ Name clash, read this first

This is not FRM-059 STAR.

Stands forWhat it is for
FRM-003 STAR (this page)Story · Tools and techniques · Apply · ReflectZeducation's teaching recipe. How a facilitator builds a session
FRM-059 STARSituation · Task · Action · ResultA learner's interview answer. How a candidate tells a story about themselves

Two different things, same four letters, both in this library and both genuinely called STAR in the wild. Say which one you mean, every time. In any session where both could come up — most of Employment & Work Readiness — call this one "the STAR session shape" and FRM-059 "the STAR answer".

⚠️ Facilitators trained on this page will use the word by reflex in a job-search session, and the room will follow them into the wrong model. It happens. Name it before it does.

What it is in one line: the house recipe for teaching anything at Zeducation — Story, Tools & Techniques, Apply, Reflect.

Origin: Zeducation Limited. Source document. Its purpose is to help Zeducators teach more effectively, and to let Zeducation scale quality facilitation across every programme. Evidence: practitioner. It maps closely to experiential learning practice: concrete experience → concept → active experimentation → reflection. Best for: every topic, every module, every session. This is the structural rule of the whole Content Library.

The model

flowchart LR
  S["S — STORY<br/>& Statement<br/><i>why this matters</i>"] --> T["T — TOOLS<br/>& Techniques<br/><i>what and how</i>"]
  T --> A["A — APPLY<br/>& Action<br/><i>practise it</i>"]
  A --> R["R — REVIEW<br/>& Reflect<br/><i>what changes now</i>"]
  R -.-> S

How to read it: run it in order, every topic. The dotted line is the next session — reflection from one topic becomes the story that opens the next.

The steps

StageWhat the facilitator doesWhy it matters
SStory & StatementShare a relevant story that introduces the topic and shows why it matters. Summarise it in a StatementStories make an idea visual and memorable, and make the topic relevant
TTools & TechniquesIntroduce the tools (what you use) and techniques (how you do it) and show how to apply themThis is where knowledge becomes practical
AApply & ActionRun an activity so learners use the tool, then discuss what they foundLearners need time to apply. This is where learning becomes real
RReview & ReflectReview the outcomes, help learners reflect and set a goal for what they will do nextLearning that is not committed to is learning that is lost

Why it works

It puts relevance before content. Most teaching opens with the model and hopes people care by the end. STAR opens with the story, so learners know why they should listen before anything technical arrives, and closes with a written commitment, so the session ends in an action rather than a feeling.

Worked examples

Story example from the framework document: a facilitator describes making up bedtime stories for his two-year-old daughter using her soft toys as characters, and noticing how closely she listens and processes the ideas even knowing the toys are not really speaking. Statement: "Stories have a way of making an idea more visual and tangible within someone's mind. When people can see something, they are more likely to believe it or understand it."

Tools & Techniques example: topic Leading with your strengths. Tool: the "Discovering Your Strengths" mind map worksheet. Techniques: catch yourself doing good; celebrate your successes; education.

Facilitating it

  • Story: use visual aids, images, video or physical props. Stories can be made up or factual;

personal is better. No story? Ask a question so learners share theirs, then build on it

  • Tools & Techniques: show a video or image of the tool in action, or demonstrate it yourself

before learners try. Test any tool you found online before you use it

  • Apply: roleplays, worksheets, video plus discussion, group activities, fun games. Roleplay

followed by reflective discussion is the strongest option. Add fun. Give enough time. Keep improving the activity

  • Reflect: a bullet summary talked through; learners explain the purpose in their own words;

journal it; set a goal and write it down; share it with a peer; challenge them to action it

How the library uses it

Every topic page is written to STAR:

Topic page sectionSTAR stage
1. Open with this (story & statement) · 3. About this topicS
4. Frameworks, tools & techniquesT
5. Apply — suggested activities · 8. Fun openersA
6. Self-assessment · 7. Reflection questionsR

Learn more

  • 📄 Internal: source note and the

original PDF

FRM-004Framework · 02-Frameworks

The DESC Script

modelmoderateassertivenessconflictdifficult-conversationsfeedbackboundaries

What it is in one line: a four-line script you write before a hard conversation so you say what you mean without losing your temper or your nerve.

Origin: created by Sharon and Gordon Bower in their book Asserting Yourself (1976). Still the most widely taught assertiveness script in workplace and clinical training (overview). Evidence: moderate. Long-standing practitioner model, adopted into healthcare communication training and organisational change programmes (National Collaborating Centre for Methods and Tools). Best for: prepared conversations — a performance issue, a repeated behaviour, pushback from someone senior, a boundary that keeps getting crossed.

The model

flowchart LR
  D["D — DESCRIBE<br/>the behaviour<br/><i>facts, no labels</i>"] --> E["E — EXPRESS<br/>how it affects you<br/><i>own it with I</i>"]
  E --> S["S — SPECIFY<br/>what you want instead<br/><i>one clear change</i>"]
  S --> C["C — CONSEQUENCES<br/>what happens then<br/><i>positive first</i>"]

How to read it: four sentences, written down before you speak. Most people can do D and E. The conversation only changes when you do S and C as well.

The steps

StepWhat you doSounds like
D — DescribeDescribe the specific behaviour affecting you. Facts only, no judgement, no "always""The last three toolbox talks started ten minutes late."
E — ExpressSay how it affects you. Use "I" so you own the feeling"I'm concerned, because we end up rushing the safety part."
S — SpecifySay exactly what you want changed. One thing, clearly"I'd like us to start at 7 sharp, with the checks done first."
C — ConsequencesSay what happens if it changes. Lead with the positive"That way we're on the tools by 7:15 and nobody gets pulled up on site."

Write it before you say it. DESC is a preparation tool. Four lines on a phone or a notepad, then have the conversation.

Why it works

Difficult conversations fail in two ways: people go in hot and blame, or they go in soft and never say what they want. DESC removes both. Describe keeps the facts separate from the story you have built about the person, and Specify forces you to decide what change you are actually asking for. Naming the consequence turns a complaint into an agreement.

Worked examples

Workplace (peer): "The last two Fridays the van's come back without being restocked. I end up doing it on Monday before I can start my run. I need it restocked before it's parked up. Then we both start Monday clean and nobody's chasing anybody."

Home / community: "The last few weeks I've been the only one at pack-up. I'm tired and I've been getting short with people. I need two others rostered on for pack-up each week. Then we're all out by nine and it stays enjoyable."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes, plus 20 to write and practise one
  • Demonstrate first: take a real situation from the room and build the four lines on the

whiteboard together

  • Common mistakes:
    • Describe becomes a label. "You're unreliable" is not a description. "The last three times…" is
    • Specify is vague. "I need you to lift your game" gives the person nothing to do
    • Consequences become a threat. Lead with what good looks like. Keep any negative consequence

factual and only if it is genuinely within your control

    • Running it in one breath. Pause after each part and let them respond
  • Adaptations: for youth, run it on friendship and social media scenarios first, work second. For

frontline and low-literacy groups, use a printed four-box card they fill in

Learn more

  • 📄 In Equilibrium — the DESC model for assertiveness
  • 📄 NCCMT — the DESC model for assertive communication
  • 📄 Sylvia Larrass — DESC for assertive communication and effective feedback
  • 🎬 Indeed — Assertive communication: speak up for yourself — short, career-framed, good pre-work
  • 🎬 Assertiveness training: 7 tips for confident and assertive communication — part 1 of 4, useful as a homework series

FRM-005Framework · 02-Frameworks

BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front

techniquemoderateclear-messagingblufwritten-communicationemailbriefing

What it is in one line: put your main point in the first line, then explain.

Origin: the US military. The Army formalised it in AR 25-50 (1988) so commanders did not have to wade through background paragraphs to find the one thing that mattered. An Army writing pamphlet put the reason plainly: the greatest weakness in ineffective writing is that it does not quickly transmit a focused message. It has since spread into business, legal and government writing (BLUF on Wikipedia)). Evidence: moderate. Decades of institutional adoption and strong practitioner consensus, and it lines up with what is known about readers scanning rather than reading. Not a laboratory-tested model. Best for: emails, chat messages, requests, updates, reports, and any message to a busy person.

The model

flowchart TD
  A["THE BOTTOM LINE<br/>your point, decision or request<br/><i>first line, always</i>"]
  A --> B["THE SUPPORTING DETAIL<br/>the why, the how, the background<br/><i>everything else, underneath</i>"]

How to read it: one line up top, everything else below it. If the reader stops after line one, they still know what you need.

The steps

StepWhat you doExample
1. Decide the bottom lineWhat is the one thing you need them to know or do?I need 4 more labourers on Monday
2. Say it in the first lineNo warm-up, no "hope you're well", no history"I need 4 more labourers on site Monday to hit the concrete pour deadline."
3. Add the supporting detailThe why, the how, the background"We're a day behind from the rain."
4. Close with the actionWho does what, by when"Can you confirm by Friday so I can book them?"

The quick fix for existing writing: write the message however it comes out, then look at your last paragraph. Your conclusion is usually sitting there. Move it to the top and delete the run-up.

Why it works

Busy people scan. They read the first line, decide whether this needs them, and act or move on. If your point is in the last paragraph, you are gambling that a supervisor with 60 unread messages will get there. Putting it first is not blunt, it is respectful of their time, and the opening line is the part people remember.

Worked examples

Before: "Hi team, hope you all had a good weekend. There's been a bit going on with the schedule. I need everyone to submit their timesheets by Wednesday at 3pm. Payroll closes early this month, so anything late won't be paid until next cycle. Let me know if you have questions."

After (BLUF): "Timesheets are due Wednesday 3pm. Payroll closes early this month, so anything late goes into the next cycle. Questions, come see me."

Home / community: "I can't make the meeting on Thursday. I've got the kids that night. I can send my notes through beforehand if that helps."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8-10 minutes
  • Demonstrate first: put a real rambling message on the screen and rewrite it live with the room
  • Common mistakes:
    • Confusing BLUF with rude. A greeting is fine. Burying the point for three lines is not
    • More than one bottom line. If there are two asks, that is two messages
    • Vague bottom lines. "We need to talk about timesheets" is not a bottom line. "Timesheets are

due Wednesday 3pm" is

    • Cultural fit: in some settings opening cold reads as abrupt. Keep the greeting, then go straight

to the point on line two

  • Adaptations: for low literacy, teach it as "say the ask first, then the story". For frontline

crews, run it on radio calls and text messages rather than email

Learn more

  • 📄 BLUF (communication) — Wikipedia)
  • 📄 Animalz — BLUF: the military standard that can make your writing more powerful
  • 📄 Aspiration Marketing — what is BLUF and how do I use it
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen (10 min, one of TED's most-watched talks) — the seven deadly sins of speaking, and HAIL. Good closer for the whole topic

FRM-006Framework · 02-Frameworks

PREP — Point, Reason, Example, Point

modelpractitionerclear-messagingpreppresentingpersuasionimpromptu-speaking

What it is in one line: four sentences that turn a rambling explanation into a convincing case in under a minute.

Origin: a long-standing public speaking structure, best known through Toastmasters International, which recommends it as the easiest structure to learn and use, and where it is the standard tool for impromptu Table Topics speaking (Toastmasters). Evidence: practitioner. Decades of use in speaking training rather than formal research. It earns its place by being usable on the spot under pressure. Best for: taking a position — a recommendation, a piece of feedback, a proposed solution, or answering a question you were not expecting.

The model

flowchart LR
  P1["P — POINT<br/>what you think"] --> R["R — REASON<br/>why you think it"]
  R --> E["E — EXAMPLE<br/>proof it is true"]
  E --> P2["P — POINT<br/>say it again, as the ask"]

How to read it: you start at the conclusion and end at the conclusion. The middle is the evidence.

The steps

StepWhat you sayExample
PointYour main point, in one sentence"We should hold a short safety briefing every morning."
ReasonWhy it matters"Most accidents happen in the first hour of work, when people aren't switched on yet."
ExampleA real or likely case that proves it"Last month a two-minute briefing caught a forklift parked in a walkway before anyone got hurt."
PointRestate it, as the ask"So let's make the morning briefing part of every shift."

Why it works

Starting with the conclusion means the listener has somewhere to put everything that follows. They are not guessing where you are heading, so they can weigh your reasoning instead of decoding it. The example is what moves people: a reason is an argument, an example is a picture. And closing on the point again turns an explanation into a request, which is what makes something actually happen.

It also makes you sound organised and credible, because it shows you have thought your position through.

When not to use it. PREP is for taking a position. It is the wrong shape for brainstorming, for open exploratory conversations, or for a moment when someone needs to be heard rather than answered. Reaching for PREP in those moments makes you sound like you are closing the conversation down.

Worked examples

Workplace: "We should give new starters a buddy for their first week (Point). New people don't ask questions when they don't know anyone (Reason). The last three who left early all said they felt lost in week one (Example). So let's pair every new starter with a buddy from day one (Point)."

Home / community: "We should start the fundraiser meeting at 6 instead of 7 (Point). Half the committee has kids to get to bed (Reason). Last month four people left before we voted (Example). So let's move it to 6 and finish by 7:30 (Point)."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then practise on the spot
  • Demonstrate first: ask the room for any opinion, then build it into PREP live
  • Common mistakes:
    • Starting with the reason. Most people naturally build up to the point. That is exactly the

habit PREP is fixing

    • A weak example. "For example, it could cause problems" is not an example. It needs to be a

specific thing that happened, or a specific thing that would

    • Forgetting the final P. Without it the message trails off and nobody acts
  • Adaptations: for youth, practise it on things they actually care about — a rule they disagree

with, a change they want. For frontline crews, run it as a 60-second toolbox pitch

Learn more

  • 📄 Toastmasters International — 90 tips, including PREP
  • 📄 Beverly Landais — tips to PREP for effective communication
  • 📄 Anecdote — a variation that puts the example before the reason (PERP) — worth knowing when the room needs convincing before it will listen to logic
  • 🎬 TED — Julian Treasure: How to speak so that people want to listen (10 min)

FRM-007Framework · 02-Frameworks

The What-Why-How Briefing Framework

toolpractitionerbriefinginstructionstoolbox-talksafetyclear-messagingteams

What it is in one line: three questions that turn instructions into a briefing the team actually understands and can question.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Effective Communication workbook, Module 2. Evidence: practitioner, but it sits on solid ground. WorkSafe NZ guidance treats pre-work briefings (toolbox or tailgate talks) as a standard way to check in with workers at the start of a shift: what will happen on site, what the specific risks are, and whether people are ready for work (WorkSafe NZ). Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, a PCBU must ensure workers are informed about the risks in their workplace, so a briefing structure is not just good practice, it is part of meeting a duty. Best for: toolbox talks, shift starts, handing out a task, briefing a change, any moment where someone has to go and do something.

The model

flowchart TD
  W["WHAT<br/>is the task or focus?<br/><i>clear direction</i>"] --> Y["WHY<br/>is it important?<br/><i>purpose and buy-in</i>"]
  Y --> H["HOW<br/>do we do it safely and correctly?<br/><i>steps, risks, expectations</i>"]
  H --> T["TEAM INPUT<br/>questions, concerns, suggestions<br/><i>this is what makes it a briefing</i>"]
  T --> C{"Does everyone<br/>understand the plan?"}

How to read it: the first three are the leader talking. The fourth is the one most people skip, and it is the one that turns a presentation into a briefing.

The steps

StepThe questionWhy it is there
WhatWhat are we doing today?Clear direction, so everyone knows what they are doing
WhyWhy is this important?Purpose. It could be safety, customers, timelines or teamwork. When people understand the why, they are more engaged
HowHow do we do it safely and correctly?The steps, safety requirements, risks and expectations
RisksWhat do we need to watch out for?Names the hazards before the job, not after
Team inputQuestions, concerns, suggestions?Where the crew's real knowledge comes out
ConfirmDoes everyone understand the plan?Yes / needs clarification. Never assume

The key note from the workbook: a strong briefing is a team conversation, not a leader presentation.

Why it works

Most instructions fail on the Why. People given a task without a reason do it to the letter and no further, and the moment reality differs from the instruction they stop or guess. People who understand the purpose adapt correctly. Adding team input on top surfaces what the leader does not know, which on a work site is usually the thing that was going to hurt someone.

Worked examples

Workplace (site): "What: we're pouring the slab on the east side today. Why: the weather's clear this morning and we lose the window if it rains Thursday, and the framers can't start until it's cured. How: pump arrives 7:30, Sione and Tama on the screed, everyone else clearing the run first. Hi-vis and boots, nobody walks behind the pump truck. Risks: wet surface at the gate, and the truck reversing across the walkway. Anything I've missed?"

Home / community: the same shape works for a church working bee or a whānau event. What we're doing, why it matters, how we'll do it safely, and what have I missed.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes with the template in front of them
  • Demonstrate first: deliver a bad briefing (What only, no Why, no questions), then the same one

properly. The difference lands instantly

  • Common mistakes:
    • Skipping Why, because the leader already knows it
    • Asking "any questions?" while packing up. Nobody speaks. Ask it standing still, and wait
    • Talking through the whole thing. If nobody else spoke, it was not a briefing
    • Confirming as a group. "Everyone good?" gets nods. Ask individuals on anything that matters
  • Adaptations: for low literacy, use the template as spoken prompts rather than a form to fill.

For crews with English as a second language, slow down on How and confirm individually

The briefing plan template

FocusNotes
What? What are we doing today?
Why? Why is this important?
How? How do we do this safely and correctly?
Risks / safety checks. What do we watch out for?
Team input. Questions, concerns, suggestions
Confirmation. Does everyone understand the plan?☐ Yes ☐ Need clarification

FRM-008Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Positive No (Yes – No – Yes)

modelpractitionerboundariessaying-noassertivenessworkloadnegotiation

What it is in one line: a three-part way to turn down a request so the other person hears a clear no and still feels respected.

Origin: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No: How to Say No and Still Get to Yes (2007). Ury co-founded the Harvard Program on Negotiation and co-wrote Getting to Yes (author's page). Evidence: practitioner. Widely taught in negotiation and leadership training, grounded in negotiation practice rather than controlled trials. Best for: turning down extra work, declining a shift, refusing a request from someone senior, protecting family or study time.

The model

flowchart LR
  Y1["YES<br/>to what you value<br/><i>name the priority</i>"] --> N["NO<br/>to the request<br/><i>short and clear</i>"]
  N --> Y2["YES<br/>to a way forward<br/><i>offer an option</i>"]

How to read it: the no in the middle is the easy part to write and the hard part to say. The two yeses are what make it possible to say out loud.

The steps

StepWhat you doSounds like
YesName the value, priority or person you are protecting. Not an apology, a reason"I really value getting this project right."
NoSay no to the request, not the person. Keep it short. Do not pad it"I can't take on the extra report this week."
YesOffer a way forward so the door stays open. It must be something you can actually do"I can help you find someone, or look at it Monday."

The order matters. Leading with the no makes people defensive. Leading with the first yes tells them what you are protecting, so the no reads as a priority rather than a rejection.

Why it works

Ury's argument is that behind every no there is a deeper yes: to your time, your standards, your family, your team's safety. A bare no hides that yes, so it sounds like rejection. A soft yes hides your limit, so you end up overloaded and resentful. Naming the yes first makes the no honest and survivable. As Ury puts it, yes without no is appeasement, and no without yes is war.

The third part is what protects the relationship. You are not closing the conversation, you are changing what is on the table.

Worked examples

Site: "I want our crew to hit the standard on this (Yes). I can't sign this off as it is (No). Fix these two points and I'll sign it today (Yes)."

Aged care / shift work: "Sunday is the one day I've got with my kids (Yes). So I can't cover this weekend (No). I can take the Tuesday night if that helps the roster (Yes)."

Home and church: "I want to be useful to this group for the long haul (Yes). I can't run the fundraiser again this year (No). I'll train whoever takes it on and stay on the roster (Yes)."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, plus 20 to build and practise one
  • Demonstrate first: take a real request from the room and build the three parts on the whiteboard
  • Common mistakes:
    • The no goes missing. People write two yeses and a maybe. Make them read the middle line on its

own and check it is actually a no

    • The first yes becomes an apology. "Sorry, I'm just so busy" is not a value, it is a hedge
    • The third yes overpromises. If you cannot really do Monday, do not offer Monday. A broken

alternative costs more than the original no

    • Over-explaining. One reason is enough. Three reasons sound like you are negotiating with yourself
  • Adaptations: for youth, run it on friends asking for money, lifts and homework before work

scenarios. For learners who find a flat no culturally uncomfortable, spend the time on the third part, because the offer is what makes the no feel respectful

Cultural note

In many Pacific, Māori and migrant families, a direct no to an elder, a minister or an employer can read as disrespect, and the cost of refusing is carried by more than one person. The Positive No works well here precisely because the refusal is wrapped in a stated value and an offer. Teach it as a way to be clear and respectful, not as permission to be blunt. Let learners choose their own words for the middle line.

Learn more

  • 📄 William Ury — The Power of a Positive No
  • 📄 Harvard Program on Negotiation — The Power of a Positive No

  • 🎬 TED — Nedra Glover Tawwab: Your 3-step guide to setting better boundaries at work — short, practical, good opener
  • 🎬 TED — William Ury: The walk from "no" to "yes" — Ury on conflict and the "third side". Broader than the Positive No, better as pre-work than in-session

FRM-009Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Broken Record (Acknowledge – Appreciate – Explain Priorities)

techniquepractitionerboundariessaying-noassertivenesspressurede-escalationcustomer-service

What it is in one line: a calm way to hold your answer when someone keeps pushing, by repeating the same clear line while showing them you heard them.

Origin: the underlying skill is persistence, published by psychologist Manuel J. Smith in When I Say No, I Feel Guilty (1975) as part of systematic assertive therapy, where it is nicknamed the "broken record". The three-step wrapper taught here, Acknowledge, Appreciate, Explain priorities, is the Zeducation house version. Smith's original is closer to bare repetition; the house version adds the two steps that keep the relationship intact. Evidence: practitioner. The repetition-plus-validation pattern also appears in clinical de-escalation guidance, where it is described as a "verbal loop" of listening, validating and restating (Project BETA consensus statement, Richmond et al., 2012). Best for: a customer pushing for a discount, a manager pushing for a deadline you cannot safely meet, anyone who keeps asking after you have already answered.

The model

flowchart TD
  A["1 — ACKNOWLEDGE<br/>show you heard them<br/><i>I hear that you need it today</i>"] --> B["2 — APPRECIATE<br/>value their position<br/><i>I know this deadline matters to you</i>"]
  B --> C["3 — EXPLAIN PRIORITIES<br/>your reason, then your answer<br/><i>Safety checks come first, so it's tomorrow</i>"]
  C --> D{"Do they<br/>push again?"}
  D -->|"Yes"| A
  D -->|"No"| E["Done. Answer unchanged."]

How to read it: it is a loop, not a line. Every time round, the words change slightly and the answer does not change at all.

The steps

StepWhat you doSounds like
1 — AcknowledgeSay back what they asked for, so they know you heard it"I hear that you need it today."
2 — AppreciateValue their point or their position. Genuine, not sarcastic"I know this deadline is important to you."
3 — Explain prioritiesGive your reason once, then repeat your answer in the same words"Safety checks come first, so it'll be ready tomorrow morning."

The repeat line is the whole technique. Decide your one sentence before the conversation and do not improve it under pressure. Change the wrapper, keep the line.

Why it works

When someone keeps pushing, the trap is arguing new points. Every new reason you offer is a new thing for them to attack, and ten minutes later you are defending an argument instead of holding a decision. Repetition takes the argument off the table.

Repetition on its own reads as stonewalling, which is why the first two steps matter. Acknowledging and appreciating tell the other person they are being heard, so the sameness reads as steadiness rather than stubbornness. That is the same pattern clinical de-escalation guidance describes: listen, validate, restate, and expect to go round several times before it lands.

Worked examples

Customer: "I get that you'd like a discount (Acknowledge). I appreciate you choosing us (Appreciate). Our price reflects the quality we promise, so the rate stays the same. I'm confident you'll be happy with the result."

Site, pushed three times: "I hear you need it today. I know the deadline matters. My crew's safety checks come first, so it'll be with you tomorrow morning." → "I understand the pressure you're under, I really do want to help. The checks come first, so it'll be tomorrow morning." → "I know this is frustrating. Tomorrow morning."

Home: "I hear you want to stay out later. I know your mates are all going. School night, so it's still 9 o'clock."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, plus 20 to practise. It only works once they have felt the pressure
  • Demonstrate first: have a learner push you three times while you hold one line. They need to see

a calm third repetition before they believe it

  • Common mistakes:
    • The line drifts. Round three becomes "well, maybe by lunchtime". Once the line moves, pushing

has worked and they will push every time from now on

    • Acknowledge turns sarcastic. "I hear you" with an edge undoes the whole thing
    • Explaining more each round. Give the reason once. After that, just the answer
    • Using it on someone who has a fair point. This is a technique for holding a decision you have

already thought through, not for winning

  • Adaptations: for customer-facing roles, script the repeat line as a team so everyone holds the

same one. For youth, run it on peer pressure scenarios

When not to use it

If the person is raising something you have not actually considered, stop and listen. The Broken Record is for pressure, not for new information. Holding a line you should have changed is not assertive, it is just wrong at volume.

FRM-010Framework · 02-Frameworks

Active Listening and SOLER

techniquemoderatelisteningactive-listeningbody-languageempathyde-escalation

What it is in one line: giving someone your full attention, and showing it with your body, so they know they are being heard.

Origin: SOLER was created by Gerard Egan in The Skilled Helper (1975) as a teaching aid for the first stage of his counselling model, where the helper's job is to let the person tell their story (overview). It is now taught across counselling, nursing and social work. Evidence: moderate. Very widely taught for fifty years, but see the honest critique below. Best for: one-to-one conversations that matter. A worker who seems off, a complaint, a performance chat, anyone who is upset.

The model

LetterStands forWhat you actually do
SSquareFace the personTurn your body towards them, so they have your attention
OOpenOpen postureNo crossed arms, no turning away, no barrier between you
LLeanLean in slightlyA small lean forward reads as interest
EEye contactComfortable eye contactSteady, not a stare. See the cultural note
RRelaxStay calm and unhurriedIf you look rushed, they will keep it short
flowchart TD
  A["ACTIVE LISTENING<br/>full attention, reply held back"]
  A --> B["S — Square<br/>face them"]
  A --> C["O — Open<br/>uncrossed"]
  A --> D["L — Lean<br/>slight lean in"]
  A --> E["E — Eye contact<br/>comfortable, not a stare"]
  A --> F["R — Relax<br/>calm and unhurried"]

How to read it: SOLER is the body half of listening. It is what the other person can see. On its own it is posture, not listening, so it always runs with holding your reply back.

Why it works

Most people listen to reply. They hear the first sentence, decide what they think, and spend the rest of the time waiting for a gap. People can tell, and it changes what they tell you. Active listening flips it: you focus fully on the person, hold your own reply back, and let them finish.

SOLER matters because listening is invisible. You can be listening hard while looking at your phone, and the speaker will not believe you. The five signals make attention visible, which is what actually changes how much people say.

Worked example

A supervisor notices a worker has gone quiet since a near-miss on site. Instead of asking across the yard, they sit down at the smoko table, turn their chair to face them, put the phone away, and say "you've been quiet this week, how are you going?" Then they say nothing for ten seconds. The worker starts talking.

Cultural note, and an honest critique

The workbook already flags this and it is worth taking seriously. In many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, direct eye contact can read as disrespectful, especially with elders. The "E" is the part of SOLER most likely to work against you.

There is published criticism of SOLER on exactly this ground. Stickley (2011) argued the model had been taught for thirty years with almost no critical appraisal, and that it produces mechanistic behaviour rather than genuine empathy. He proposed SURETY instead: Sit at an angle, Uncross legs and arms, Relax, Eye contact, Touch, Your intuition (From SOLER to SURETY for effective non-verbal communication, Nurse Education in Practice, 11(6), 395-398).

Two things worth teaching from that:

  • Sitting at an angle rather than squarely is often more comfortable, and side-by-side is how a

lot of real conversations happen — in the ute, at the bench, walking to the car

  • Your intuition matters more than the checklist. Read the person in front of you and adjust

Teach SOLER as a starting checklist for people who have never thought about it, and say plainly that a good listener adapts it.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. It lands far better after the bad-listening experience than before it
  • Always run the contrast first: two minutes of deliberately bad listening, then SOLER. The

feeling of being ignored is the lesson; SOLER is just the fix

  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning it into a performance. Learners exaggerate the lean and the eye contact and look

unhinged. Say "slightly" and mean it

    • Treating it as the whole of listening. SOLER is the outside. Holding your reply back is the

inside

    • Forcing eye contact on learners it does not fit. Offer the angle-and-presence alternative
  • Adaptations: for phone-based roles, translate each letter into voice: don't multitask, don't

interrupt, slow down, use small sounds so they know you are there

FRM-011Framework · 02-Frameworks

The 3 Levels of Listening

modelpractitionerlisteningactive-listeningempathycoachingself-awareness

What it is in one line: a ladder that names three depths of listening, so you can notice which one you are on and climb.

Origin: the Co-Active Coaching model, developed by Laura Whitworth, Henry Kimsey-House, Karen Kimsey-House and Phil Sandahl, and taught by the Co-Active Training Institute (their explanation). It has spread well beyond coaching into leadership and management training. Evidence: practitioner. A well-documented and widely taught coaching model rather than a research finding. Best for: building self-awareness. It gives people language for something they already do, which is why it changes behaviour faster than most listening models.

The model

flowchart TD
  L3["LEVEL 3 — GLOBAL<br/>the room, the energy,<br/>what is not being said"]
  L2["LEVEL 2 — FOCUSED<br/>their words, their tone,<br/>their meaning"]
  L1["LEVEL 1 — INTERNAL<br/>your own thoughts<br/><i>what does this mean for me?</i>"]
  L1 --> L2 --> L3

How to read it: bottom to top. Level 1 is not bad, it is just where everyone starts. Leading happens at 2 and 3.

LevelWhere your attention isYou know you are here when
1 — InternalOn yourselfYou are working out what to say next, or what this means for you
2 — FocusedOn the other personYou forget about yourself for a moment. Their words, their tone, their meaning
3 — GlobalOn everything around itYou notice the feelings, the body language, the energy in the room, the thing not being said

Why it works

Most listening advice tells people to listen better without telling them what better means. This model gives them three things to notice, and the noticing is the skill.

Level 1 is normal and unavoidable. You need it to plan, to decide, to protect yourself. The problem is staying there in the moments that matter, when someone is upset, unsure, or trying to tell you something hard. Once a leader can hear themselves at Level 1, they can choose to move.

Worked examples

Same conversation, three levels. A worker says they are "fine".

LevelWhat happens
1You take the word and move on, already thinking about your next task
2You hear how they said it, flat and quiet, and you stay with them
3You notice they will not meet your eye, their shoulders are tense, the room has gone quiet. You gently ask if they are really okay

Site meeting, Level 3: the leader asks for questions, gets none, and notices two people glance at each other. "I saw that. What's the thing nobody wants to say?"

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The sorting activity does the real work
  • Start with a confession: name a time you were at Level 1 while someone was telling you something

important. Learners will not admit to Level 1 until you do

  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating Level 1 as a failure. It is not a moral ranking. Say so early, or people get defensive

and stop being honest about where they are

    • Faking Level 3. Guessing at a feeling and announcing it confidently is worse than not trying.

Level 3 is noticing and asking, not diagnosing

    • Confusing Level 3 with being intuitive about people. It is attention, not talent
  • Adaptations: for teams, ask them to spot the levels in a meeting they were all in. For youth,

run it on a conversation with a parent

  • 📄 MindTools — Co-Active Coaching

FRM-012Framework · 02-Frameworks

Paraphrasing and Reflecting

techniquemoderatelisteningparaphrasingreflectingde-escalationempathycustomer-service

What it is in one line: saying back what you heard, in your own words, so the other person can confirm it or correct it.

Origin: reflective listening comes out of Carl Rogers' person-centred counselling and is now standard in counselling, mediation, motivational interviewing and customer service training. The reflect-before-you-fix sequence taught here matches clinical de-escalation guidance (Project BETA consensus statement, Richmond et al., 2012, Western Journal of Emergency Medicine). Evidence: moderate. Reflective listening is well documented across several professional fields, and the de-escalation guidance is an expert consensus statement rather than a trial. Best for: anything with a risk of misunderstanding or heat. Instructions, complaints, upset customers, a teammate who has had enough.

Two close cousins

flowchart LR
  H["YOU HEAR<br/>words + feeling"]
  H --> P["PARAPHRASE<br/>say back the <b>content</b><br/><i>So the order's delayed and you<br/>need a new date by Friday?</i>"]
  H --> R["REFLECT<br/>name the <b>feeling</b><br/><i>It sounds like that<br/>really frustrated you.</i>"]
  P --> C["THEY CONFIRM<br/>or correct you"]
  R --> C

How to read it: two moves off the same listening. Paraphrase checks the facts. Reflect checks the feeling. Most people only ever do the first one.

ParaphrasingReflecting
What you say backThe content, in your own wordsThe feeling you are picking up
What it checksThat you understood the factsThat you understood the emotion
Sounds like"So what you're saying is…" / "Let me check I've got this…""It sounds like you felt…" / "That must have been…"
When it matters mostInstructions, handovers, deadlines, numbersComplaints, conflict, someone who is upset

This is sometimes called mirroring. The skill under it is noticing the feeling beneath the words, in tone, face and body.

The de-escalation rule

Reflect the feeling before you try to fix anything.

People cannot hear solutions until they feel heard. Jumping to the fix, even a good fix, tells an upset person you were not listening, and they start again louder. The clinical de-escalation guidance describes the same loop: listen, find something you can genuinely validate, then say what you need to say, and expect to repeat it.

"I can see you're really annoyed about this. Let's sort it out together."

Worked examples

Worker: "I've asked three times and nothing's changed."

  • Paraphrase: "So you've raised this a few times and still nothing's moved."
  • Reflect: "I can hear how frustrating that is."

Customer: "This is the second time it's broken."

  • Reflect first: "That's really disappointing, especially twice." Then fix.

Handover, paraphrase only: "Let me check I've got this. The pump's booked for 7:30, not 8, and Level 1 is clear. Yes?"

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then practise. This one is all reps
  • Common mistakes:
    • Parroting. Repeating their exact words back sounds like a call centre script. Paraphrasing

means your own words

    • Naming the wrong feeling confidently. "You're angry" when they are embarrassed makes it worse.

Offer it tentatively: "it sounds like…", "am I right that…". Being corrected is a good outcome, it means they are engaged

    • Reflecting then immediately fixing in the same breath. "That sounds frustrating, anyway what

I'll do is…" is not reflecting, it is a speed bump. Let it land

    • Overusing it. Not every sentence needs a mirror. Use it at the turns
  • Adaptations: for phone and contact centre roles, drill the opening reflect line until it is

automatic. For learners with English as a second language, give sentence starters on a card

Learn more

FRM-013Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Channel-Fit Matrix

modelmoderatedigital-communicationemailchannelhybridwritten-communicationteams

What it is in one line: a 2×2 that tells you in seconds whether a message belongs in a chat, an email, a call, or face to face.

Origin: Zeducation house framework. It is a plain-language version of Media Richness Theory, introduced by Richard L. Daft and Robert H. Lengel in 1986 in Management Science (overview). Their argument: match how rich the channel is to how ambiguous the message is. Evidence: moderate. Media richness theory is a classic and heavily cited organisational theory, though it has been extended and challenged since, notably by channel expansion theory, which argues experience with a channel changes how rich it feels. Best for: the thirty seconds before you send something. Especially bad news, feedback and anything with feelings in it.

The model

Two questions decide it:

  1. How complex is it? One fact, or many?
  2. How emotional or sensitive is it? Routine, or will it stir feelings?
Simple messageComplex or sensitive message
Low emotionChatEmail
High emotionQuick callVideo or in person
The golden rule: the harder or more personal the message, the richer the channel. Never deliver bad news, criticism or conflict by text message.

What each channel actually carries

ChannelCarriesGood forCosts you
ChatWords onlyFast, small, factualNo tone. Easy to misread. No record anyone can find later
EmailWords, structure, a recordDetail, decisions, anything you may need to proveSlow. Very easy to misread. People skim
CallWords and tone of voiceQuick sensitive things, checking inNo record. No face
VideoWords, tone, faceComplex and sensitive together, remote teamsEffort. Scheduling. Screen fatigue
In personEverything, including the roomThe hardest conversationsTime and travel
flowchart TD
  Q1{"Is it complex?<br/>more than one fact"}
  Q1 -->|"No"| Q2{"Any feelings<br/>in it?"}
  Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"Any feelings<br/>in it?"}
  Q2 -->|"No"| C["CHAT"]
  Q2 -->|"Yes"| P["QUICK CALL"]
  Q3 -->|"No"| E["EMAIL"]
  Q3 -->|"Yes"| V["VIDEO OR IN PERSON"]

How to read it: two questions, four answers. When you are unsure between two boxes, go richer.

Why it works

The same message can land well or badly depending on where you send it. A great message in the wrong channel still fails.

Daft and Lengel's insight was that channels differ in how much they carry: how fast you get feedback, how many cues come through, whether it feels personal. When a message is ambiguous, open to more than one reading, you need a rich channel so both people can trade cues and check they agree. When a message just lacks a fact, a lean channel delivers it faster and cheaper. Sending a layoff by email is not rude because email is rude, it is wrong because the message needed cues the channel cannot carry.

Worked examples

MessageChannelWhy
"Start time moved 30 minutes"ChatOne fact, no feelings
"Here's the signed variation order"EmailSimple, but you need the record
"Your hours are being cut"In personComplex and personal. Never a message
"A workmate has had a family loss"In person, then a written follow-upHighest emotion in the matrix
"What time's the concrete truck booked?"ChatOne fact
"Explaining a new safety procedure"Video or in personComplex, and you need to see they got it

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The sorting activity is where it lands
  • Common mistakes:
    • Arguing the edge cases forever. Some messages genuinely sit on a line. Say so, and use the

"when unsure, go richer" rule to move on

    • Reading the matrix as a rule against email. Email is the right answer for a lot of work
    • Forgetting the record question. Sometimes the channel is chosen by what you will need in six

months, not by the conversation

  • Adaptations: for teams that live in one tool, run the sort against their actual channels

(Teams, WhatsApp group, the whiteboard in the smoko room). The two questions do not change

  • 📄 Media Richness Theory — AURA Lab, SIUE
  • 📄 Channel expansion theory — the main challenge to it
