FRM-014Framework · 02-Frameworks

Tone-in-Text

techniquestrongdigital-communicationemailtone-in-textwritten-communicationhybrid

What it is in one line: five moves that stop a message you meant kindly from reading as cold or angry.

Origin: Zeducation house framework. The evidence under it is Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng (2005), "Egocentrism over e-mail: can we communicate as well as we think?", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (paper · PubMed record). Evidence: strong. Five experiments, published in a leading peer-reviewed journal, replicated in the popular literature ever since. Best for: every written message, and especially the ones you write when you are annoyed or in a hurry.

The evidence, plainly

Kruger and colleagues found that people overestimate how well their tone comes across in email, both their ability to send tone and their ability to read it. The cause they identify is egocentrism: you "hear" your own message in the tone you meant it, and you cannot easily un-hear it, so you assume the reader hears it too. They do not. They bring their own mood instead.

That is the whole problem in one sentence: you are the worst judge of how your message reads.

The model

flowchart LR
  W["WHAT YOU MEANT<br/>warm, quick, helpful"] --> S["THE CHANNEL<br/>strips voice, face,<br/>timing, warmth"]
  S --> R["WHAT THEY READ<br/><i>they supply the missing tone,<br/>and when unsure, people<br/>assume the worst</i>"]

How to read it: the middle box is doing the damage, and you cannot see it from where you are standing.

What goes wrong

The moveHow it reads
A short replyAnnoyed
A missing "thanks"Rude
A full stop after a one-word answer ("Fine.")Sharp
ALL CAPSShouting
A neutral message to someone already stressedCold

The five moves

#MoveExample
1Open with something human before the ask"Thanks for flagging this."
2Soften instructions"Could you…" or "When you get a chance…" instead of "Do this."
3Say the positive out loud. They cannot see your friendly face"This is good work, one change:"
4Re-read it as your most stressed teammate. Could it be misread? Reword it—
5Use a name and a sign-off. It makes a message feel personal"Hi Sam… Cheers, Pasi"

Move 4 is the one that matters most, because it is the direct counter to the egocentrism in the research. You cannot judge your own tone from inside your own head, so deliberately read it from somewhere else.

Cold and warm, side by side

Reads coldReads warm
"No.""I can't do that one this time, sorry. Could we look at [option] instead?"
"Quick call""Hi Sam, I noticed this isn't done yet, is everything okay? Let me know if you need a hand."
"Fine.""Yep, that works for me, thanks!"
"We need to talk.""Have you got 10 minutes today? Want to go over the roster with you, nothing to worry about."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Open with the research finding, it gets attention because everyone

believes they are the exception

  • Common mistakes:
    • Warm becoming waffly. Warm is not longer. "Thanks for flagging this" is four words. Watch for

learners padding a clear message into a soft one

    • Emoji as the whole answer. A 👍 does not fix a cold message, and it reads differently across

ages and cultures. Use words

    • Softening a message that needed to be firm. Tone-in-text is about warmth, not about hedging.

A clear no can be warm

  • Adaptations: for teams, agree a couple of shared norms (do we use "no worries"? do we sign off?)

and the guesswork drops. For learners writing in a second language, give the five moves as a printed card of sentence starters

⚠️ A correction to the source workbook

The Module 5 page says "In person, 90% of your warmth comes from voice and face." That number is a version of the Mehrabian 7-38-55 rule, which is one of the most misquoted findings in communication training. Mehrabian's experiments were about communicating feelings and attitudes from single spoken words where the words and the tone conflicted. He has stated publicly that the ratios do not apply to communication generally (background).

The teaching point survives without the number: text strips out voice, face and timing, and readers fill the gap themselves. Say that instead, and use Kruger et al. for the evidence. Recommend the number is dropped in the next print run.

  • 📄 Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng (2005) — Egocentrism over e-mail (PDF)
  • 📄 American Psychological Association — E-mails and egos — a short readable write-up of the study
  • 📄 British Psychological Society — how sarcastic emails fall flat
  • 📄 Big Think — debunking the 7-38-55 rule

FRM-015Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Video Presence Checklist

toolmoderatedigital-communicationvideo-presencehybridmeetingscredibility

What it is in one line: an eight-point setup check that makes you look calm and capable on camera, run once before any call that matters.

Origin: Zeducation house framework. The reasoning behind it draws on Jeremy Bailenson (Stanford Virtual Human Interaction Lab), Nonverbal Overload: A Theoretical Argument for the Causes of Zoom Fatigue, Technology, Mind and Behavior (2021) (paper PDF · Stanford summary with fixes). Evidence: moderate. Bailenson's paper is peer-reviewed but explicitly a theoretical argument rather than a trial; several of the checklist items are practical craft with no study behind them. Best for: interviews, client calls, all-staff updates, anything where people are meeting you for the first time through a screen.

Why setup beats talent

People judge your credibility on a video call in the first few seconds, before you have said anything worth hearing. The good news is that most of what they are judging is setup, not personality. A shadowy face, a camera below your chin, a messy background, talking over a lag: none of it is about how smart you are, and all of it shapes how seriously people take you. Fix the basics once and they are sorted for every call after that.

Bailenson's work adds the other half. Video calls are tiring for specific, fixable reasons: seeing yourself constantly, faces at unnatural close range, being stuck in one spot, and the extra effort of producing and reading nonverbal cues through a screen. Several checklist items below are as much about protecting your energy as your image.

The checklist

flowchart TD
  A["BEFORE THE CALL<br/>setup, once"] --> A1["Camera at eye level"]
  A --> A2["Light in front, not behind"]
  A --> A3["Quiet, tidy background"]
  A --> A4["Head and shoulders in frame"]
  B["DURING THE CALL<br/>habits"] --> B1["Look at the lens when you speak"]
  B --> B2["Mute when not talking"]
  B --> B3["Use names to bring quiet people in"]
  B --> B4["Slow down and pause"]

How to read it: the left branch you fix once. The right branch you practise.

☐ItemWhy
☐Camera at eye level. Raise the laptop on a few booksLooking down at people feels like looking down on them
☐Look at the lens when you speak, not at your own faceThat is how you make eye contact on video
☐Light in front of you, not behind. Face the windowA window behind you turns you into a shadow
☐Quiet, tidy background. Clear the clutter, shut the doorThe background is part of the message
☐Frame head and shoulders, a little space above your headToo close reads as intense, too far reads as absent
☐Mute when not talkingKills the background noise everyone else is straining past
☐Use people's names to bring quiet people in: "Mere, what's your take?"On video, quiet people stay quiet unless invited
☐Slow down and pauseRushing reads as nervous. Pauses read as confident, and they cover the lag

Two additions from the research

  • Hide your own video once the call starts. Bailenson's team point out that no one would work with

a mirror held up beside them all day. Most platforms have a "hide self view" option

  • Give yourself permission to look away. Constant close-range eye contact from a grid of faces is

the unnatural part, not looking away from it

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run the dry run. Reading the list changes nothing; seeing your own

frame on a projector changes everything

  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating it as vanity. Frame it as respect for the people on the call and as credibility, not

as looking good

    • Buying gear. Books under a laptop and turning a desk to face a window costs nothing. Do not let

the conversation become about ring lights

    • The checklist becoming stiffness. Slowing down does not mean speaking in a newsreader voice
  • Adaptations: many learners join calls from a phone, a ute or a shared room. The rules still work:

prop the phone, put the light in front, find a wall. Teach it for the setup they actually have. Where learners share a home with several people, do not make a tidy background a standard anyone can fail; the point is to control what you reasonably can

Learn more

  • 📄 Bailenson (2021) — Nonverbal Overload: causes of Zoom fatigue (PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — four causes of Zoom fatigue and their solutions
  • 📄 Zoom Exhaustion and Fatigue Scale (ZEF), Fauville et al. — a measure, if you want to track it
  • 🎬 TED — Tsedal Neeley: 4 ways to make hybrid work better for everyone

FRM-016Framework · 02-Frameworks

Leading Communication in the AI Era (Voice, Truth, Honesty, Judgment)

modelmoderatedigital-communicationaiethicstrustwritten-communicationdigital-capability

What it is in one line: four checks that let AI help you write without costing you the trust you write for.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Module 5 page of the Effective Communication workbook. The evidence under it is Hohenstein, Kizilcec, DiFranzo, Aghajari, Mieczkowski, Levy, Naaman, Hancock & Jung (2023), "Artificial intelligence in communication impacts language and social relationships", Scientific Reports 13:5487 (open access). Evidence: moderate. One well-designed peer-reviewed study plus a growing literature; the field is young and moving. Best for: anyone whose team now drafts with AI, which is most teams.

The rule

Let AI help you think and draft. You stay the leader.

The evidence, plainly

The Scientific Reports study found both halves of this, which is why it is worth teaching rather than just asserting:

  • Using AI helped. It increased communication speed, increased positive emotional language, and

conversation partners rated each other as closer and more cooperative

  • **Being suspected of using AI hurt. People were evaluated more negatively when their partner

suspected AI involvement**, whether or not that suspicion was correct

So the risk is not the tool. The risk is the gap between what people think you wrote and what you actually wrote. That is a trust problem, and trust is a leadership problem.

The model

flowchart TD
  D["AI DRAFTS"] --> V["VOICE<br/>does it sound like me?"]
  V --> T["TRUTH<br/>have I checked the facts?"]
  T --> H["HONESTY<br/>should this have come<br/>from my own hand?"]
  H --> J["JUDGMENT<br/>have I read the room?"]
  J --> S["YOU SEND"]

How to read it: four gates between the draft and the send. Skipping any one of them is where the trust goes.

CheckThe riskWhat you do
VoiceAI writing sounds generic and stiff. If every message sounds like a machine, people stop sensing a real personEdit the draft until it sounds like you. Cut the stiff bits
TruthAI can be confidently wrong, or invent factsCheck anything important before you send. Your name is on it, so you own it
HonestyPassing off an AI message as heartfelt breaks trust fastBe open about routine help. Never use it for a condolence, an apology or a personal thank you
JudgmentAI can draft words. It cannot read the room, weigh someone's feelings, or make the callThat part is your job as a leader

Where the line sits

TaskAI can helpDo it yourself
Tidying a long update email✅
Summarising a long safety report✅ (then read it)
Drafting a routine roster notice✅
Translating a notice for a worker whose first language is not English✅ (then have it checked by a speaker)
Sympathy to a worker who lost a family member✅
A personal thank you to someone who went above and beyond✅
Apologising to a customer after a serious mistake✅

The pattern: **AI is fine for the routine and the structural. The moment the message is the relationship, write it yourself.**

Worked examples

Good use: "AI, tidy up this long email." Then you cut the stiff bits, add your own voice, check the facts, and send.

Good use: using AI to summarise a long meeting, then reading it to make sure it is accurate before sharing.

Poor use: copy-pasting an AI-written message of sympathy to a grieving teammate. It feels hollow and damages trust.

Poor use: forwarding an AI summary you never checked, which contains a wrong figure that misleads the team.

The Truth check in action: an AI drafts the line "Our safety record shows zero incidents across all 14 sites this year." Nobody has verified it. If it is wrong, you have put a false safety claim in writing under your own name, and every real incident it overlooks becomes a bigger problem than the email was ever worth.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Lead with the study, because the "suspected of using AI" finding lands

with people who assume the risk is only about getting caught

  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning it into an anti-AI session. The study found real benefits. A blanket ban is not a

leadership position, it is an avoidance of one

    • Turning it into an AI training session. This is about trust, not prompting
    • Making learners feel judged for using it. Most already do. The question is where their line is
  • Adaptations: for workplaces with an actual AI policy, run Part B against their policy. For

learners with low digital confidence, the Voice exercise still works with any stiff formal letter

A note on where this belongs

This sits in Module 5 because that is where the workbook teaches it, and the running order matters for rebuilding the workbook. But it reaches past communication into Digital Capability, and when that pillar gets built out this framework should be linked from there too rather than copied.

Learn more

  • 📄 Hohenstein et al. (2023) — Artificial intelligence in communication impacts language and social relationships, Scientific Reports
  • 📄 ScienceDaily — social consequences of using AI in conversations — the plain-language summary
  • 📄 Hohenstein & Jung (2020) — AI as a moral crumple zone, Computers in Human Behavior — on who gets blamed when an AI-mediated conversation goes wrong

FRM-017Framework · 02-Frameworks

The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team

modelpractitionertrustteamsconflictaccountabilityleadershippsychological-safety

What it is in one line: five problems that stack on top of each other, so if the bottom one is weak everything above it falls over.

Origin: Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (Jossey-Bass, 2002). Lencioni runs the consulting firm The Table Group and built the model from years of working with executive teams. The book is written as a business fable about a fictional company called DecisionTech (Table Group overview PDF · Wikipedia). Evidence: practitioner. It is one of the best known team models in the world and it is built on consulting experience, not controlled research. Teach it as a shared language, not as a diagnosis. Best for: naming what is actually wrong with a team when everyone can feel it but nobody can say it.

The model

Read it from the bottom up. Each layer rests on the one below.

#DysfunctionWhat it looks likeWhat it should be
5Inattention to resultsPeople protect their own patch, their own numbers, their own reputationThe team result comes first
4Avoidance of accountabilityEveryone can see someone is slipping. Nobody says itPeople call each other on it, early and kindly
3Lack of commitmentThe meeting ends and nobody is sure what was decidedClear decisions, everyone knows their part
2Fear of conflictFake yes. Polite meetings, then the real meeting in the car parkHonest debate about the work
1Absence of trustPeople hide mistakes, needs and questionsPeople admit "I got that wrong" and "I need help"
flowchart TD
  R["5. Inattention to Results<br/>my win beats our win"]
  A["4. Avoidance of Accountability<br/>nobody says anything"]
  C["3. Lack of Commitment<br/>unclear decisions"]
  F["2. Fear of Conflict<br/>fake yes"]
  T["1. Absence of Trust<br/>people hide"]
  T --> F --> C --> A --> R

How to read it: the arrow is a cause, not a sequence. Absence of trust causes fear of conflict, which causes weak commitment, and so on up. Fix the bottom one first. Working on results while trust is broken is wasted effort.

Why it works

Because it puts the problem in the right order. Most teams try to fix the top of the ladder. They set better goals, tighten the reporting, add another meeting. None of it holds, because the reason nobody speaks up in the meeting is that they do not feel safe enough to be wrong in front of each other.

It also gives people words for something they could already feel. "We are not storming, we just do not trust each other yet" is a sentence a team can act on. "Something feels off" is not.

Worked example

A kitchen team keeps missing orders on Friday nights. The manager adds a checklist. It does not work. When she asks properly, it turns out the newest chef has never told anyone he cannot read the handwriting on the tickets, because the first time he asked a question he got laughed at.

That is dysfunction one, showing up as a results problem four levels higher. The checklist was never going to fix it. Printing the tickets and saying "ask me anything, any time" did.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 to 15 minutes. Draw the pyramid, name the five, then go straight to

ACT-031 Fix Your Lowest Pillar

  • Always work bottom up. If a group rates trust low and results low, only trust is worth working

on this month

  • Common mistakes:
    • Using it to label a person. It describes a team, not an individual. "You are a dysfunction

two" is not a thing

    • Skipping to conflict. Groups love talking about healthy conflict. If trust is not there,

encouraging debate just produces a fight

    • Treating fear of conflict as a personality problem. It is usually a safety problem, and the

leader usually caused it

  • Cultural note: in many Pacific and Māori settings, open disagreement with someone senior is not

a comfort issue, it is a respect issue. Healthy conflict may need to happen in a different shape, such as one to one first, or through a trusted third person. Ask the group how honest debate actually works in their world before prescribing the Western meeting-room version

Learn more

  • 📄 The Table Group — The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (overview PDF)
  • 📄 MindTools — Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions of a Team
  • 📄 BiteSize Learning — summary, pyramid and manager tactics

  • 🎬 Five Dysfunctions of a Team, Lencioni talk (2013) — longer conference version, better as pre-work than in-session

FRM-018Framework · 02-Frameworks

Tuckman's Stages of Team Development

modelmoderateteamsteam-developmentconflictleadershipnormscollaboration

What it is in one line: every team goes through the same five stages, and the awkward one in the middle is normal.

Origin: Bruce W. Tuckman, an American educational psychologist, published Developmental Sequence in Small Groups in Psychological Bulletin 63(6), 384-399 in 1965. He reviewed fifty studies of groups and found the same four stages under all of them: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen reviewed the later research and added a fifth stage, Adjourning, in Stages of Small-Group Development Revisited, Group & Organization Studies 2(4), 419-427 (1965 paper, reprint · 1977 paper). Evidence: moderate. It came from a genuine literature review and it is taught everywhere, but it describes a pattern rather than predicting one. Tuckman and Jensen themselves called for more empirical work. Best for: taking the panic out of a team that has started arguing.

The model

StageWhat the team is going throughYou know you are here when
FormingJust come together. Polite, guarded, unsure of roles. Leaning on the leader for directionEveryone agrees with everything. Nobody asks a hard question
StormingDifferences surface. People test roles, workload and authority. Cliques can appearThe first real disagreement. Someone says "that is not my job"
NormingThe team settles. Norms form about how meetings run and how people treat each other. Trust growsPeople start saying "we usually do it like this"
PerformingHigh functioning. Roles clear, people disagree without damage, shared ownershipThe leader can step back and the work still gets done
AdjourningThe work ends. People hand over, reflect and move onMixed feelings. Pride, relief, sometimes sadness
flowchart LR
  F["FORMING<br/>polite and unsure"] --> S["STORMING<br/>differences surface"]
  S --> N["NORMING<br/>rhythm and trust"]
  N --> P["PERFORMING<br/>shared ownership"]
  P --> A["ADJOURNING<br/>close it well"]
  S -.->|new member,<br/>new job,<br/>new boss| F
  P -.->|change| S

How to read it: the solid arrows are the normal path. The dotted arrows are the important part. A team does not climb the stages once and stay there. Change a member, change the manager, change the work, and you drop back. That is not failure, it is the model working.

Why it works

Because it changes the story a team tells about its own discomfort. Without the model, storming feels like proof that the team is broken or that someone is difficult. With it, storming is a stage with a name and an exit.

That reframe does real work. It lowers blame, because people can see the other person is reacting to the stage rather than being a pain. It builds shared language, so someone can say "I think we are storming, can we sort the roles out?" and be understood. And it sets honest expectations, because teams stop waiting for instant harmony.

Worked example

A new crew of six starts on a fit-out job. Week one everyone is polite and the supervisor makes every call. Week three two of them argue about who owns the site tidy-up, and the supervisor thinks he has hired badly.

He has not. That is storming, on schedule. He runs a fifteen minute conversation on who does what by when, they agree the tidy-up rotates, and by week five they are sorting it between themselves without him. That conversation is what moved them to norming. Skipping it would have kept them storming for months.

What the leader does at each stage

StageWhat the team needs from you
FormingDirection. Be clear about the goal, the roles and the standards. Do not mistake the quiet for agreement
StormingPresence. Do not disappear and do not crush it. Surface the disagreement and make it about the work
NormingLet go a bit. Write the norms down while they are forming, so they survive the next new person
PerformingGet out of the way. Protect the trust and keep the goal in front of them
AdjourningClose it properly. Name what people did, thank them, and let them mark the end

Reading the stages for collaboration

Tuckman appears in two Zeducation SKILL UP resources, with the same five stages framed for different outcomes. Worth knowing which lens you are teaching.

LensSourceThe question it answers
RelationshipsSRC-004What do I do to build relationships in this stage?
CollaborationSRC-005How do I encourage collaboration in this stage?

The collaboration lens adds one genuinely useful idea: storming is when silos form. If a team is left alone through storming, people retreat to their own patch and the "us and them" hardens into the way things are. Naming the stage keeps people at the table long enough to get to norming.

StageThe collaboration move
FormingConnect people across teams and sites early, before there is a problem to solve
StormingEncourage honest kōrero, clarify roles, and reconnect everyone to the shared goal so silos do not grow
NormingAgree how you will communicate, share information and make decisions. Write it down
PerformingProtect the trust and the cross-team routines. Do not coast on them
AdjourningCelebrate what was achieved together and carry the habits into the next team

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes for the five stages, 20 more with

ACT-041 Name The Stage

  • Ask "where are we now?" not "where should we be?" The value is in the honest read, not the

climb

  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating it as a ladder you climb once. Any change drops a team back. Teach the dotted arrows
    • Using it to excuse bad behaviour. "We are just storming" is not cover for bullying, and

facilitators should say so plainly

    • Skipping Adjourning. It is the stage most often left out and the one Pacific and Māori

learners often value most. Ending well matters

  • Where it is thin: the model does not tell you how long a stage lasts or how to get out of one.

That is why it pairs with a team charter

Learn more

  • 📄 Tuckman (1965), Developmental Sequence in Small Groups (reprint PDF)
  • 📄 Tuckman & Jensen (1977), Stages of Small-Group Development Revisited
  • 📄 MindTools — Forming, Storming, Norming and Performing
  • 📄 West Chester University — Tuckman's Stages of Group Development
  • 🎬 Bruce Tuckman's Model in Just 2 Minutes — short and light. Good as the opener
  • 🎬 The Tuckman Model Explained — a fuller walkthrough of the five stages

FRM-019Framework · 02-Frameworks

W-H-O — Who, How, Outcome

techniquepractitionerrespectrole-modelsleadershiphabitshouse-contentcommitment

What it is in one line: pick someone you respect, name one thing they actually do, and commit to doing it yourself this week.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004). It is one of the clearest pieces of original Zeducation IP in the library. Evidence: practitioner as a named framework, but each of its three steps rests on well evidenced research. See "Why it works" below. Best for: turning respect from a value on a poster into a behaviour someone does on Thursday.

The model

StepThe questionWhat you write
WWHOWho will I mirror?Name one role model you respect, and why
HHOWHow will I act like them?Choose one observable behaviour to copy
OOUTCOMEWhat outcome will I create?State the time, the place, the person and the impact
flowchart LR
  W["W — WHO<br/>name one person<br/>you respect, and why"]
  H["H — HOW<br/>name one behaviour<br/>you can actually see"]
  O["O — OUTCOME<br/>time, place, person,<br/>impact"]
  W --> H --> O

How to read it: each step narrows the last. Admiration becomes a behaviour, and a behaviour becomes a promise with a time on it. If you stop at W you have a nice feeling. If you stop at H you have a good intention. The O is what makes it happen.

The commitment stem:

"I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person or team] so that [impact]."

The house examples

Straight from the source, and they are good ones. Keep them.

Example 1Example 2
WMy older brotherChurch youth leader
HGreets people by name and checks pronunciationArrives early and sets the room up for success
OI will open tomorrow's team meeting by confirming everyone's name and pronunciation so that people feel seen and respectedI will arrive 10 minutes early to Thursday's workshop to set up chairs, slides and materials so we start on time and keep momentum

Why it works

The framework's own line is the best explanation of it: "When we are under pressure, we do not rise to the level of our intentions, we fall to the level of our habits."

Two well evidenced ideas sit underneath it.

The W and the H are observational learning. Albert Bandura showed that most human behaviour is learned by watching other people and copying them, not by being told or rewarded. W-H-O just makes that deliberate. Instead of absorbing whoever happens to be around you, you choose your model on purpose and name the exact behaviour worth copying. See FRM-026 Modelling and Social Learning.

The O is an implementation intention. Peter Gollwitzer's research found that plans in the form "when situation X happens, I will do Y" dramatically outperform general good intentions. The meta-analysis with Paschal Sheeran across 94 studies and more than 8,000 people found a medium to large effect on actually reaching the goal. The commitment stem is exactly that structure. See FRM-025 Implementation Intentions.

So W-H-O is a house wrapper around two of the better evidenced findings in behaviour change, in language a room can use in ten minutes. That is worth saying out loud when someone asks whether it is "just a nice exercise".

It also travels culturally. The source names "the aunties, coaches, supervisors and elders who kept their word, listened first, and lifted others". For Pacific and Māori learners the role model is often a family or church figure rather than a manager, and the framework works better for it, not worse. Do not steer people towards workplace examples.

Worked example

A team leader in aged care names her late grandmother as her W. The behaviour she picks, the H, is that her grandmother never talked about anyone who was not in the room.

Her O: "I will change the subject when the afternoon shift starts talking about Mere, on Tuesday, in the staff room, so that people know this team does not do that."

That is a leadership act, on a date, that anyone can picture. Compare it with "I will be more respectful", which nobody can picture and nobody can follow up.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run

ACT-033 Who Is Someone You Respect?

  • Do the W out loud first. Naming the person warms the room up and it is often the most moving

part of the session. Give it time

  • Common mistakes:
    • Choosing an adjective instead of a behaviour. "He is humble" is not an H. "He asks the

apprentice's opinion before his own" is

    • An O with no time in it. If there is no day and no person, it is a wish. Push until there is
    • Picking a famous person. It works far better with someone the learner has actually watched.

If someone names a celebrity, ask who in their own life is a bit like that

  • Follow up. The O is a promise with a date, so it can be checked. Ask the group the following

week. A framework nobody follows up teaches people that commitments are optional, which is the opposite of the point

Learn more

  • 📄 Simply Psychology — Bandura's Social Learning Theory
  • 📄 Gollwitzer (1999), Implementation intentions: strong effects of simple plans (PDF)
  • 📄 Albert Bandura — Modeling and Observational Learning

⚠️ GAP: no video yet that teaches W-H-O itself, because it is house content. Film one. A two minute clip of a Zeducation facilitator doing their own W, H and O would be the most useful asset on this page.

Say-Do-Close

techniquepractitionertrustreliabilityhouse-contentaccountabilityteams

What it is in one line: make a small promise, deliver it on time, and tell the person it is done.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, the first of the six trust tips in the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004). The source line is "Say-Do-Close: Make small promises, deliver on time, and confirm completion with proof." Evidence: practitioner. The middle step maps onto the Reliability term in the Trust Equation, which is the closest thing to external support. Best for: rebuilding trust when there is no big gesture available, which is nearly always.

The model

StepWhat you doWhat it proves
SAYMake a small promiseSomething specific, with a time on it. Small enough that you will definitely do itYou are willing to be held to something
DODeliver it, on timeNot early, not "nearly". On the day you saidYour word matches your actions
CLOSEConfirm it is doneTell the person, with the proof. "Sent, here it is"They do not have to chase you or wonder
flowchart LR
  S["SAY<br/>a small promise<br/>with a time on it"] --> D["DO<br/>deliver it<br/>on the day"]
  D --> C["CLOSE<br/>confirm it,<br/>with proof"]
  C -.->|trust goes up<br/>a small amount| S

How to read it: the loop is the point. One trip round changes almost nothing. Twenty trips round is what a reputation is made of.

Why it works

Most people think trust is built in big moments. It is not. It is built in a hundred small ones, and it is broken the same way, by a series of things that were "only small".

The step people skip is Close. They do the work and say nothing, so the other person is left wondering, chasing, or assuming it did not happen. From the outside, silent delivery and no delivery look identical until someone checks. Closing costs ten seconds and it is the difference between being reliable and being seen to be reliable.

The other reason it works is that it is deliberately small. Someone who has broken trust cannot fix it with a promise to change, because their promises are exactly what is not trusted. They can fix it with three small promises kept in a row.

Worked example

A supervisor has a habit of saying "I'll sort it" and then not sorting it. His team has stopped asking.

He picks one thing. Say: "I'll get you the new roster by Thursday lunchtime." Do: he writes it Wednesday night. Close: Thursday 11am he puts it in the group chat and says "roster's up, as promised, have a look and tell me if I've got your Saturday wrong."

Nobody praises him for it. That is fine. Three weeks of that and people start asking him for things again, which is the only measure that counts.

The other five house trust tips

Say-Do-Close is the first of six in the source. The rest are worth teaching alongside it:

#TipThe line
2Share the WhyExplain the reason and risks behind decisions, then invite two questions
3Make it SafeThank people for dissent or bad news and protect them from blame
4Set Clear RulesEnd meetings with who does what by when and the first proof you expect
5Repair FastIf you drop the ball, own it, apologise and fix it within 24 hours
6Be Fair and PrivateSame standard for everyone. Praise in public, coach in private

Tip 3 is psychological safety in one sentence. Tip 5 is the one learners find hardest and the one that moves trust fastest.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 5 minutes. It is three words. Spend the rest of the time on the practice
  • Run it as a week, not a discussion. Everyone makes one small promise in the room, delivers it

during the week, and reports back. See ACT-037 Say It, Do It, Close It

  • Common mistakes:
    • Promising too big. "I'll fix the roster system" fails. "I'll send you the roster by Thursday"

works. Make them shrink it until it is boring

    • Skipping Close because it feels like showing off. It is not. It is saving the other person a

follow-up

    • Using it only downwards. It works upwards too, and a supervisor who closes the loop with

their own manager gets noticed fast

  • Cultural note: in many workplaces the closing step happens face to face, not in writing. A word

at smoko counts. Do not teach it as an email habit

Learn more

  • 📄 Trusted Advisor — Understanding the Trust Equation — the Reliability term is Say-Do-Close by another name
  • 📄 MindTools — Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions of a Team — why the bottom layer is the one worth working on

⚠️ GAP: no study specific to promise-keeping and workplace trust yet. The Trust Equation is practitioner work too. Worth finding a real one, because this framework is taught as fact.

The Four Professional Habits

modelpractitionerprofessionalismwork-readinessfeedbackconflicthouse-contentrelationships

What it is in one line: the four habits that make people want to work with you, over time.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004), where it appears as "Professional habits that support healthy relationships". Evidence: practitioner. It is house practice wisdom, and it holds up well against what employers actually say they want. Best for: work readiness. The gap between "can do the job" and "people want you on the team".

The model

HabitWhat it meansWhat it looks like on a Tuesday
ProfessionalismKeep your communication, behaviour and follow-through consistent and respectful, no matter who you are talking toYou speak to the cleaner the same way you speak to the manager
FeedbackBe open to feedback about how you come across, and be willing to adjustSomeone tells you that you cut people off in meetings, and you say thank you instead of explaining why they are wrong
Development mindsetSee each relationship as a chance to learn. Look for mentors, share what you know, support other people's growthYou ask the experienced person how they do it, and you show the new person where things are
Conflict managementDeal with disagreements early, directly and respectfullyYou say something in week one, while it is still small
flowchart TD
  H["FOUR PROFESSIONAL HABITS<br/>what makes people want<br/>to work with you"]
  H --> P["Professionalism<br/>same person to everyone"]
  H --> F["Feedback<br/>open to how you come across"]
  H --> D["Development mindset<br/>learn and share"]
  H --> C["Conflict management<br/>early, direct, respectful"]

How to read it: these are habits, not talents. Every one of them is something you do repeatedly, which means every one of them can be started this week by someone who has never done it.

Why it works

Because it separates the two things people confuse. Being good at the job gets you hired. These four get you kept, recommended and promoted, and their absence is what turns a technically competent person into someone nobody wants on their crew.

The one that does the most work is Professionalism, because of the "no matter who you are talking to" clause. People are watching how you treat the person who cannot do anything for you. That is the one they use to decide what you are actually like.

The one people most often lack is Feedback. Not receiving it, hearing it. The person who argues with every piece of feedback trains everyone around them to stop giving it, and then wonders why nobody warned them.

Worked example

Two apprentices start on the same day. Both are competent.

One of them says good morning to everyone including the security guard, asks the leading hand how he sets out a job, tells the foreman early when he is not going to make a deadline, and says "fair enough, I'll fix it" when he gets pulled up.

The other is faster with the tools.

Twelve months later the first one is being recommended for the next job. Not because he is nicer, but because four habits, repeated daily, made him someone people wanted to keep.

The red flags that undo it

The same source pairs the habits with six risks. Teach both halves. Building relationships badly is worse than not building them.

Red flagWhy it costs you
Oversharing personal informationSharing too much too soon blurs boundaries and makes it harder to stay professional
Romantic entanglements and office dramaCreates conflicts of interest and makes it difficult for everyone involved
Being too close to a small groupOthers read it as favouritism or cliques, which damages team morale
GossipingIf you talk about others, people assume you talk about them too
Using people only for personal gainShow up only when you want something and people will feel used and pull away
No clear boundariesWithout limits on time, topics and behaviour, relationships get unprofessional and distract from the work

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes for the habits, 10 more for the red flags. Run them together
  • Start with the red flags if the group is young. They are more concrete, they get a laugh, and

they open the door to the habits

  • Common mistakes:
    • Teaching it as a rules list. It reads as being told off. Anchor every habit in what it gets

you, not what you will be in trouble for

    • Skipping the shy-starter practice. Half a room will believe this topic is for extroverts. It

is not, and the source is good on this. Say so early

  • The shy starter, from the source. *"You don't need to be loud or extroverted to build good

relationships."* Three moves: brief eye contact when you walk past someone, a nod or a small smile, and being willing to have a short human conversation such as "how's your day going?". Small things that make the bigger conversations possible later

Learn more

⚠️ GAP: no external reading linked yet. This is house content and it has not been matched to published work on workplace professionalism or employability skills. Worth pairing with NZ evidence, for example employer surveys from MBIE or careers material from Tahatū, so the topic can cite what NZ employers actually ask for.

The Trust Equation

modelpractitionertrustreliabilitycredibilityleadershipteamsrelationships

What it is in one line: trust has four parts, and one of them sits on the bottom of the fraction and can cancel out the other three.

Origin: David H. Maister, Charles H. Green and Robert M. Galford, The Trusted Advisor (Free Press, 2000). Green's firm still publishes the model (Trusted Advisor — Understanding the Trust Equation). Evidence: practitioner. It comes from professional services consulting, not research. It earns its place because it is the clearest answer to "yes, but what is trust?" that a room can hold onto. Best for: the moment someone says "I just don't trust him" and cannot say why.

The model

                Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy
Trustworthiness = ───────────────────────────────────
                        Self-orientation
TermIt is aboutThe question in the other person's headFails when
CredibilityYour words"Does she know what she is talking about?"You bluff instead of saying you do not know
ReliabilityYour actions"Does he do what he said?"You are "nearly" on time, most of the time
IntimacySafety"Can I tell her the real problem?"People edit themselves around you
Self-orientationYour motives"Is he in this for me, or for him?"Every conversation comes back to you
flowchart TD
  C["CREDIBILITY<br/>your words"] --> T
  R["RELIABILITY<br/>your actions"] --> T
  I["INTIMACY<br/>safety to be honest"] --> T
  T["TRUSTWORTHINESS"]
  S["SELF-ORIENTATION<br/>whose interest are you in it for?"] -->|divides everything above| T

How to read it: the top three add up. The bottom one divides. That is the whole insight. A person can be expert, reliable and warm, and still not be trusted, if everyone can tell they are mainly in it for themselves.

Why it works

Because it explains the person everyone has met: highly competent, always delivers, and somehow nobody trusts them. The equation says why. Their self-orientation is high, so it divides everything else down.

It is also useful in the other direction. Most people trying to build trust work on Credibility, because it is the one that feels like the job. They collect qualifications and get better at answering. Meanwhile the two that move faster, Reliability and Intimacy, get no attention at all. Reliability is free. It is just doing what you said.

Worked example

A new team leader in a call centre wants to be trusted, so she works on knowing the systems better than anyone. Credibility, high.

Her team still routes problems around her. Why? Because she reschedules one-to-ones when she gets busy, which is low Reliability, and every conversation ends up being about her targets, which is high Self-orientation.

She fixes it with two changes that have nothing to do with expertise. She stops moving one-to-ones, ever. And she starts asking "what do you need from me?" and then actually doing that thing. Six weeks later people bring her problems while they are still small.

Rating yourself honestly

Score each from 1 to 10. Most people find the shape more useful than the number.

  • If Reliability is your lowest, go straight to

Say-Do-Close. It is the fastest fix in this library

  • If Intimacy is your lowest, the work is

psychological safety and listening, not warmth

  • If Self-orientation is your highest, ask a person who will tell you the truth. It is the term

nobody rates accurately by themselves

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Draw the fraction. The division line is the whole lesson
  • Do not make people share their scores. Self-orientation is a confronting thing to say out loud

in front of colleagues. Let people keep it private

  • Common mistakes:
    • Reading intimacy as personal closeness. It is not about being friends. It is about whether

people can say the real thing to you

    • Treating self-orientation as selfishness. Often it is anxiety. Someone worried about their

own performance listens for how things affect them, and it reads identically from the outside

    • Presenting it as maths. There is no research behind the numbers. It is a way of thinking,

and saying so protects your credibility while you teach credibility

  • Cultural note: high self-orientation is judged hard in collective cultures. In many Pacific and

Māori settings, a leader visibly in it for themselves loses standing faster than one who is simply not very good at the job yet

Learn more

  • 📄 ModelThinkers — Trust Equation
  • 📄 The Trusted Advisor (Maister, Green & Galford) — book details

Psychological Safety

modelstrongtrustteamspsychological-safetyleadershiplearningconflict

What it is in one line: a shared belief that this team is safe for taking interpersonal risks, so you can ask a question, admit a mistake or disagree without being punished for it.

Origin: Amy C. Edmondson, Novartis Professor of Leadership and Management at Harvard Business School. Her 1999 paper Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams appeared in Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 350-383 (paper · HBS record). Evidence: strong, and the strongest in this part of the library. It began with a genuinely odd finding: the hospital nursing teams that reported the best relationships also reported the most errors. They were not making more mistakes. They were willing to report them. Google's Project Aristotle, which studied 180 of its own teams between 2012 and 2016, later found psychological safety was the strongest predictor of team effectiveness. Best for: the evidence-backed answer when someone asks why "soft stuff" matters.

The model

Edmondson's simplest version is a 2×2 of safety against standards. Both matter, and the trap is thinking they trade off.

Low standardsHigh standards
High psychological safetyComfort zone — pleasant, not much gets doneLearning zone — people stretch, admit mistakes, improve
Low psychological safetyApathy zone — people turn up and switch offAnxiety zone — people are pushed hard and hide everything
flowchart TD
  A["Is it safe to say<br/>the awkward thing here?"]
  A -->|yes| B["People ask questions,<br/>admit mistakes,<br/>raise concerns early"]
  A -->|no| C["People stay silent,<br/>hide errors,<br/>agree in the room<br/>and complain outside"]
  B --> D["The team learns<br/>and performs"]
  C --> E["The team looks fine<br/>until it does not"]

How to read it: the top path and the bottom path look identical in a meeting. The difference only shows up when something goes wrong.

Why it matters more than being nice

This is the point most often lost. Psychological safety is not comfort, niceness or lowered standards. Edmondson's argument is that safety is what makes high standards achievable, because a team that can talk about failure is a team that can fix it. The mechanism is learning, not comfort.

The anxiety zone is where a lot of workplaces sit: real pressure to perform, no safety to admit a problem. That combination produces hidden errors, and hidden errors are the expensive kind.

Worked example

On a build site, an apprentice notices the scaffold does not look right. He is fairly sure he is wrong, and the last person who queried something got told to get on with it.

In a low-safety crew he says nothing, because the cost of looking stupid is certain and the cost of staying quiet is only possible. In a high-safety crew he says "this is probably me being thick, but should that be tied off?" and it takes eleven seconds.

The safety of the site rests on whether an eighteen year old feels able to look stupid in front of people he wants to impress. That is not soft.

What a leader actually does

Edmondson's practical guidance comes down to three moves:

MoveWhat it sounds like
Frame the work as a learning problem"This is new for all of us and we will get some of it wrong" rather than "just execute it properly"
Model curiosity, admit your own limits"I don't know" and "I got that wrong" said out loud, by the most senior person in the room
Respond productively to bad newsThank the person who brought it, every time, especially when it is inconvenient. This is the one that actually decides it

The third move is where safety is won or lost. People are not testing what you say about openness. They are watching what happened to the last person who was open.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The nurse study is the hook, so lead with it
  • Common mistakes:
    • Confusing it with being nice. Say plainly that it is not about agreement or comfort
    • Making it a policy. You cannot declare safety. It is inferred from what happens to people
    • Asking a group to rate their own safety in front of their manager. The irony is real and the

data will be useless. Do it anonymously or not at all

  • Cultural note: speaking up to someone senior carries different weight across cultures, and a

Western "just say it" instruction can put a Pacific or Māori learner in an impossible position between honesty and respect. Ask how it works in their setting. Often the safe route is one to one, or through someone trusted, and that is a legitimate answer

Learn more

  • 📄 Edmondson (1999), Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
  • 📄 Harvard Business School — the paper's record
  • 📄 Psych Safety — the history of psychological safety
  • 🎬 TEDxHGSE — Amy Edmondson, Building a psychologically safe workplace (about 11 min) — the nurse study told by the person who ran it. The best single video in this part of the library
  • 🎬 Amy Edmondson — Creating Psychological Safety at Work — longer, better as facilitator pre-work

The Strength of Weak Ties

modelstrongnetworkingrelationshipswork-readinessopportunitycareer

What it is in one line: the job, the opportunity and the tip-off usually come from someone you barely know, not from your close friends.

Origin: Mark S. Granovetter, then a sociology PhD student, published The Strength of Weak Ties in the American Journal of Sociology 78(6), 1360-1380 in 1973 (full paper PDF). It is one of the most cited papers in the social sciences. He surveyed 282 men in Massachusetts about how they found their jobs and found that casual acquaintances were more useful than close friends. Evidence: strong. Fifty years of replication across sociology, economics and network science. Best for: the learner who says "I don't know anyone" or "networking isn't really me".

The model

Strong tiesWeak ties
Who they areFamily, close mates, the people you see dailyPeople you know a bit. A former workmate, a tutor, someone from church, a cousin's friend
What they knowRoughly what you knowThings you do not know
Who they knowRoughly who you knowPeople you have never met
What they give youSupport, help, a place to stayInformation, opportunities, introductions
flowchart TD
  subgraph Y["Your close circle"]
    A["You"] --- B["Best mate"]
    A --- C["Cousin"]
    B --- C
  end
  subgraph O["Somewhere else entirely"]
    E["Their workmate"] --- F["A hiring manager"]
  end
  A -.->|weak tie:<br/>old tutor,<br/>someone from church| E

How to read it: your close circle all know each other and mostly hear the same news. The dotted line is the valuable one. A weak tie is a bridge to a pocket of information your circle does not have.

Why it works

Because your close friends' knowledge overlaps almost entirely with your own. You go to the same places, hear about the same jobs, know the same people. They love you, and they cannot tell you anything new.

A weak tie lives in a different pocket of the world. That is exactly why they know about the vacancy that was never advertised, the course that is free this year, the boss who is hiring.

This is the finding that makes the whole idea usable for shy learners, and it should be said plainly in the room: weak ties work because they are weak. You do not need close friendships with a hundred people. You need to be on decent terms with a lot of people you rarely see, and to stay faintly on their radar.

Worked example

A woman finishes a six week programme and applies for warehouse work online. Forty applications, two replies, no job.

Then she messages the tutor from her course, who she liked but has not spoken to in four months, just to say what she has been up to. The tutor mentions that a previous student manages a distribution centre in Wiri and is short-staffed.

That is one message to a weak tie, and it did more than forty applications. Nothing about it required confidence, only being remembered warmly enough to be worth a mention.

What to actually do

The practical version, in three moves:

MoveWhat it means
WidenTalk to people outside your immediate team. Different department, different shift, different site
Stay warmA message every few months keeps a tie alive. "Saw this and thought of you" is enough
Give firstSend something useful before you need anything. The person who only appears when they want something is a red flag, not a network

The third one links straight back to the red flags in FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits: using people only for personal gain. Weak ties are only strong if they are real.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run

ACT-035 Six Degrees Of This Room, which makes the group's own weak ties visible in about eight minutes

  • Lead with the research, not the word "networking". Networking is a word a lot of learners

already dislike. "Most jobs come from someone you barely know" is the same idea and it lands

  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning it into LinkedIn homework. For many Zeducation learners the live network is church,

sports club, marae, family and former workmates. Start there

    • Implying quantity is the goal. Collecting contacts is not the point. Being genuinely known by

a wide range of people is

    • Overstating the study. It was 282 men in Massachusetts in the early 1970s. The finding has

held up broadly, but say what it was

  • Cultural note: Pacific and Māori learners often already have very large networks through

family, church and iwi, and do not recognise them as networks because the word sounds corporate. Naming what they already have is usually more useful than teaching them to build something new

Learn more

  • 📄 Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties (full paper PDF)
  • 📄 Stanford — The strength of weak ties
  • 📄 Semantic Scholar — the paper and its citations

Implementation Intentions — if-then plans

techniquestrongcommitmenthabitsgoal-settingbehaviour-changereflection

What it is in one line: decide in advance exactly when, where and how you will do the thing, and you are far more likely to actually do it.

Origin: Peter M. Gollwitzer, Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans, American Psychologist 54, 493-503 (1999) (PDF). The form is "When situation X arises, I will do Y." Evidence: strong. The Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 38, 69-119 pooled 94 independent tests and over 8,000 participants and found a medium to large effect on goal attainment (d = 0.65), and a similar effect specifically on the problem of never getting started (d = 0.61) (reference). Best for: the last five minutes of any session, when good intentions are about to walk out the door and evaporate.

The model

A goal intention says what you want. An implementation intention says when and where it happens.

Goal intentionImplementation intention
Shape"I intend to do X""When X happens, I will do Y"
Example"I'll be better at giving feedback""When someone finishes a shift well, I will tell them one specific thing they did, before they leave"
Why it fails or worksRelies on remembering and deciding in the momentThe situation itself triggers the action
flowchart LR
  G["GOAL<br/>what you want<br/>'be more respectful'"] --> P["PLAN<br/>if-then<br/>'when I walk in Monday,<br/>I will greet everyone by name'"]
  P --> C["CUE<br/>the situation<br/>arrives on its own"]
  C --> A["ACTION<br/>happens without<br/>a fresh decision"]

How to read it: the work moves from your willpower to the situation. You decide once, in a calm moment, and the cue does the remembering for you.

Why it works

Two reasons, both in Gollwitzer's research.

The cue does the remembering. Once you have linked a specific situation to a specific action, the situation grabs your attention when it turns up. You are not relying on thinking of it at the right moment, which is exactly when you are busiest.

The decision is already made. Most good intentions die at the point of choosing, usually when you are tired or under pressure. An if-then plan moved that choice to earlier, when you had the capacity to make it well.

This is why the meta-analysis found the biggest effect on getting started. Getting started is almost always the problem.

Where it already lives in this library

This framework explains why several existing pages are shaped the way they are. Point at it whenever someone asks why the commitment step matters.

PageThe if-then in it
FRM-019 W-H-OThe O step: "I will [behaviour] on [day and time] with [person] so that [impact]"
ACT-031 Fix Your Lowest PillarThe "Trigger" step: "when will you do it? Link it to a routine, such as the start of stand-up"
ACT-006 Two ThingsThe standard STAR closer. Two commitments, and they work far better with a time attached
ACT-013 Start, Stop, ContinueSame. "Start" is a goal intention until someone adds a when

➜ Facilitator tip: the single highest-value change you can make to any Zeducation session is to stop accepting commitments without a when and a where. It costs thirty seconds and it is the best-evidenced thing on the page.

Worked example

Two people leave the same workshop having decided to give more recognition.

The first writes "be more encouraging". Nothing happens. There is no moment that reminds him.

The second writes "when I do the Friday handover, I will name one thing each person did well that week." Friday arrives whether he remembers or not, and the handover is already in his day. He does it eleven Fridays in a row.

Same intention. One had a cue attached.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 5 minutes, or teach it invisibly by simply insisting on the format
  • The three questions that turn a wish into a plan: When exactly? Where exactly? With whom?
  • Common mistakes:
    • A cue that never arrives. "When I get a chance" is not a cue. Anchor it to something already

in the week: stand-up, smoko, Friday handover, Sunday after church

    • Too many at once. One or two if-then plans work. Six do not
    • Quoting the effect size without the caveat. d = 0.65 is across a broad set of goals, many of

them health related. It is strong evidence that plans beat intentions, not a promise about any one person

  • Say the number out loud. Learners take a commitment exercise more seriously when they hear it

was tested on 8,000 people rather than invented by a trainer

Learn more

  • 📄 Gollwitzer (1999), Implementation intentions: strong effects of simple plans (PDF)
  • 📄 Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis — reference
  • 📄 Gollwitzer, Implementation Intentions (chapter PDF, US National Cancer Institute)

Modelling and Social Learning

modelstrongrole-modelsleadershiplearningrespectbehaviour-changeculture

What it is in one line: people learn most of what they do by watching other people do it, which means whoever they watch is teaching them, on purpose or not.

Origin: Albert Bandura, Stanford University. Formalised in Social Learning Theory (1977) after his experiments through the 1960s, including the well known Bobo doll studies (Bandura's own page on modelling · Simply Psychology summary). Bandura's line is that "most human behavior is learned observationally through modeling." Evidence: strong. One of the most influential and most replicated theories in psychology. Best for: explaining why a leader's actual behaviour matters more than anything they say, and why W-H-O works.

The model

Bandura's four conditions. Watching alone is not enough. All four have to be present for a behaviour to transfer.

ConditionWhat it meansWhere it breaks
1AttentionYou have to actually notice the behaviourYou admire someone but have never watched what they specifically do
2RetentionYou have to remember itYou noticed it once and never named it, so it faded
3ReproductionYou have to be able to do itThe behaviour is beyond you right now, so pick a smaller one
4MotivationYou have to want to, and expect it to be worth itYou saw it work for them but do not believe it will work for you
flowchart LR
  A["ATTENTION<br/>notice it"] --> R["RETENTION<br/>remember it"]
  R --> P["REPRODUCTION<br/>be able to do it"]
  P --> M["MOTIVATION<br/>want to, and<br/>expect it to pay off"]
  M --> B["The behaviour<br/>becomes yours"]

How to read it: it is a chain, so it breaks at the weakest link. Most people's chain breaks at Retention, because they admired something without ever putting it into words.

Why this matters for leadership

Two consequences, and both are worth saying in the room.

You are a model whether you want to be or not. Anyone junior to you is learning how to behave from watching you. That includes how you talk about people who are not there, how you take bad news and what you do when you are wrong. You cannot opt out of this, you can only be deliberate about it.

Naming the behaviour is the whole trick. Admiration is common and useless on its own. It becomes useful when you can say the exact observable thing the person does. "She is a good leader" transfers nothing. "She writes down what she promised in the meeting and reads it back at the end" transfers immediately, because now it is at step 2.

That is precisely what the H in W-H-O forces.

Worked example

A trainee supervisor says she wants to be like her old team leader, who "just had a way with people". That is Attention with no Retention, so nothing transfers.

The facilitator pushes: what did she actually do? After a minute the trainee remembers: she always asked the quietest person in the room what they thought, by name, before she gave her own view.

Now it is a behaviour. It can be remembered, it can be copied on Monday, and it costs nothing. That one question moved it from admiration to something teachable.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 5 to 8 minutes, as the "why" behind W-H-O. It is rarely a topic on its own
  • Use it to push for specifics. Whenever a learner names an adjective, ask "what do they actually

do that makes you say that?" That question is this framework in practice

  • Common mistakes:
    • Only using famous role models. Bandura found models we identify with are far more powerful.

Someone the learner has actually stood next to beats someone off the internet

    • Ignoring the negative version. People model badly-behaved leaders just as efficiently. A

useful and uncomfortable question is "what have you already picked up from someone you did not admire?"

    • Skipping Reproduction. If the behaviour is out of reach today, the chain breaks and the

learner concludes they are just not that kind of person

  • Cultural note: this framework sits naturally with Pacific and Māori ways of learning, where

watching, doing alongside and copying an elder is often the normal way skill is passed on. The research is Western; the practice is not new to most of the room. Say that

Learn more

  • 📄 Albert Bandura — Modeling and Observational Learning
  • 📄 Simply Psychology — Bandura's Social Learning Theory
  • 📄 UC Berkeley HR — How Social Learning Theory Works
  • 📄 Positive Psychology — What is Bandura's Social Learning Theory? 3 examples

The Team Charter — agreeing how you will work together

toolpractitionerteamsnormsteam-developmentleadershipconflictagreements

What it is in one line: a short written agreement about how a team will treat each other, made on purpose instead of by accident.

Origin: team charters and working agreements are standard practice across project management, agile teams and organisational development, with no single originator. The five question version on this page is Zeducation's, written to give Tuckman's Norming stage something a facilitator can actually run. Evidence: practitioner. Best for: a new team, a team that has just stormed, or any team that has never said out loud how it works.

Why a team needs one

Every team already has norms. Nobody decided them.

They formed from whoever spoke loudest in week one, from what the last manager tolerated, and from a hundred small moments nobody noticed. That is how a team ends up with a rule like "we do not question Dave" that nobody would ever have agreed to on purpose.

A charter is just the decision to choose them instead. It is the difference between Norming happening to you and Norming being something you did.

The five questions

#QuestionWhat you are actually agreeing
1How do we make decisions?Who decides what, and how we know a decision has been made
2How do we disagree?Where it happens, how it sounds, and what is out of bounds
3How do we communicate?Which channel for what, and what counts as a reasonable reply time
4What do we do when someone drops the ball?Agreed before it happens, while nobody is defensive
5How will we know this is working?The check-in date. A charter with no review date is a poster
flowchart TD
  A["1. How do we decide?"] --> B["2. How do we disagree?"]
  B --> C["3. How do we communicate?"]
  C --> D["4. What if someone<br/>drops the ball?"]
  D --> E["5. How will we know<br/>it is working?"]
  E -.->|review it,<br/>and after every<br/>change to the team| A

How to read it: the dotted line matters most. A charter written once and never looked at again is worth nothing. Review it when it is calm, and always when someone joins or leaves.

The rules that make it work

  • Short. Five to eight statements. If it needs a folder, nobody will use it
  • Behaviours, not values. "We respect each other" is unusable. "We do not talk about someone who

is not in the room" can be checked

  • Written by the team, not for them. A charter handed down by a manager is a policy, and people

follow policies exactly as far as they are watched

  • Visible. On the wall, in the group chat, at the top of the shared doc
  • Reviewed. Question 5 is not optional

Worked example

A community services team of nine keeps having the same argument about who answers the phone at lunchtime. It flares up every few weeks and dies down without resolving.

They spend forty minutes on a charter. The line they land on for question 4 is: "If you cannot cover your slot, you find your own swap before the day, in the group chat. If you cannot find one, you say so by Wednesday and we sort it together."

The argument does not come back. Not because the rule is clever, but because nine people agreed it while calm, so applying it is no longer a confrontation between two people at 12:30.

Facilitating it

  • Run it in: 40 to 60 minutes for a real team. 25 minutes as a training exercise
  • Do not run it during a storm. In the middle of a live conflict, a charter session becomes a

proxy for the argument. Deal with the conflict, then charter

  • Common mistakes:
    • Writing values. Push every line until it names something a stranger could watch you do
    • The manager writing it. Let them contribute one voice among many, and say that out loud at

the start

    • No review date. Set it in the room, before people leave
    • Too long. If you have fifteen statements, ask which five actually change behaviour
  • Cultural note: in Pacific and Māori settings a kaupapa or set of tikanga for how a group works

together is often already understood, and may be better established than anything a Western team charter produces. Ask what already exists before importing a template over the top of it

Learn more

⚠️ GAP: no external reading linked yet. Team charters are widely practised and thinly researched, and the good published material tends to sit behind project management paywalls. If a solid open source turns up, add it here. The nearest evidenced neighbour is psychological safety, which is what a charter is trying to manufacture.

Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles

modelmoderateleadershipdecision-makingcollaborationdelegationteamsstyles

What it is in one line: three ways a leader can make a decision, and each one teaches the team something different about whether their voice counts.

Origin: Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939), in a study at the University of Iowa. They put groups of eleven year old boys into after-school clubs making models and rotated adult leaders through them, each using a different style. It is one of the founding studies of leadership research (MindTools summary · a revisit of the original study). Evidence: moderate. It was a real experiment with real findings, and it was ten boys in Iowa in

  1. The three styles have held up as a teaching model far better than the study alone would

justify. Best for: the leader who makes every decision alone and cannot work out why nobody brings them anything.

The model

StyleThe lineWhat it isWhen it fits
Autocratic"My way"The leader decides alone and tells people what to do. Fast and clear, but limits input and buy-in if overusedSafety, urgency, compliance
Democratic"Our way"The leader asks for ideas, listens, then decides. Slower, but builds trust and ownershipMost team decisions, especially ones affecting people's daily work
Laissez-faire"Your way"The leader stays hands-off and lets people decide. Works with skilled, motivated teams. Causes confusion and silos without enough guidanceWhen roles, goals and expectations are already very clear
flowchart TD
  L["THE LEADER"]
  L --> A["AUTOCRATIC<br/>'My way'<br/>decides alone"]
  L --> D["DEMOCRATIC<br/>'Our way'<br/>asks, listens, decides"]
  L --> F["LAISSEZ-FAIRE<br/>'Your way'<br/>hands off"]

How to read it: these are not personality types. They are three options available to the same leader on the same day. The skill is choosing, not having a favourite.

Why it matters for collaboration

The point the source makes well: leadership is not just what decisions are made, but how they are made. Every decision teaches the team something about whose voice counts, and people adjust their behaviour to what they learn.

  • Decide alone every time, and people learn to wait to be told. Collaboration dries up because there

is no reason to offer anything

  • Give no direction at all, and people work in silos and protect their own patch, because nobody has

said what "together" means

  • Invite input, listen, explain your thinking, and people take shared ownership, because they have

seen their contribution change something

Lewin's own finding was that democratic leadership produced the most consistently productive and cooperative groups, and that the laissez-faire groups did worst, with productivity dropping and the strongest personalities taking over.

Using each style well

StyleDo this, or it backfires
AutocraticStill explain the why. Ask for feedback afterwards so people feel respected even when they were not consulted
DemocraticBe clear about how their input shaped the final call. Asking for ideas and then never referring to them again is worse than not asking
Laissez-faireSet boundaries, check in regularly, and make sure people still share information. Hands-off is not the same as absent

The middle row is where most leaders lose trust. Consultation that visibly changes nothing teaches people that being asked is theatre.

Worked example

A regional manager needs to change the weekend roster.

Autocratic would be quickest: post the new roster. It is also how you get four people quietly looking for other jobs, because the roster is their family's weekend.

She goes democratic. She explains the constraint, asks the team what would work, and gets an option she had not thought of, splitting the Saturday shift. When she confirms it she says which part came from whom.

The roster is only slightly better than the one she would have written. The difference is that nine people now believe that saying something to her is worth the effort. That is the actual return.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then run

ACT-050 Whose Call Is It?

  • Ask "what is your default?" and then "what does your team think it is?" The gap between those

two answers is the lesson

  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating democratic as always right. It is not. Democratic decision-making in an emergency

gets someone hurt, and a leader who consults on everything reads as unable to decide

    • Confusing democratic with consensus. Lewin's democratic leader still decides. They ask,

listen, then call it

    • Calling laissez-faire "empowerment". Empowerment has clear boundaries and check-ins. If those

are missing it is just absence with a nicer name

  • Cultural note: in many Pacific and Māori settings, decisions are already made collectively

through discussion until the group settles, which is closer to democratic than most Western workplaces manage. Learners from those settings often find the autocratic default of their workplace, not the democratic option, is the thing that needs explaining

Learn more

  • 📄 MindTools — Lewin's Leadership Styles Framework
  • 📄 Leadership Ahoy — The Kurt Lewin leadership experiments
  • 📄 The Lewin, Lippitt and White study revisited (1994)
  • 📄 TSW Training — Kurt Lewin's leadership theory

The 3C Framework — Connect, Clarify, Commit

modelpractitionercollaborationhouse-contentconversationsteamscross-teamclear-messaging

What it is in one line: three moves that turn a conversation with another team from a request into an agreement.

Origin: Zeducation house framework, from the Creating a Collaborative Team Environment SKILL UP resource (SRC-005). Evidence: practitioner. It is house content, and its three steps line up with well established practice: relationship before task, understand before responding, and end on who does what by when. Best for: the cross-team conversation. Head office to region, department to department, the people who only talk to each other when something has gone wrong.

The model

StepWhat you doWhat it prevents
CConnectStart with the relationship. Acknowledge the person and their time. Show you are on the same sideThe conversation starting as a complaint
CClarifySay why you are talking, ask open questions, and listen until you understand their view, not just your ownSolving the wrong problem, confidently
CCommitAgree what happens next. Who will do what, by whenA good conversation that changes nothing
flowchart LR
  A["CONNECT<br/>same side,<br/>acknowledge them"] --> B["CLARIFY<br/>purpose, open questions,<br/>listen to their view"]
  B --> C["COMMIT<br/>who does what,<br/>by when"]

How to read it: in that order, always. Commit without Connect is a demand. Commit without Clarify is a guess. Most failed cross-team conversations skipped one of the first two.

Why it works

Because the usual cross-team conversation opens at step three. Someone arrives with the problem already diagnosed and the solution already chosen, and the other team hears an accusation, so they defend rather than think.

Connect costs about fifteen seconds and it changes what the other person is listening for. "Thanks for making time, I know you're flat out, I think we're both trying to fix the same thing" is enough. It is not a nicety. It is the sentence that decides whether the next two steps land.

Clarify is where the real information is. The other team almost always knows something you do not, and it is usually the reason they are doing the thing that annoys you.

Commit is the step that gets skipped when the conversation goes well. Everyone leaves feeling positive and nothing changes, and three weeks later the same conversation happens again.

Worked example

A regional site keeps sending its reports late. Head office is frustrated.

Without 3C: "We need these on time, it's holding everything up." The site hears blame, explains why it is not their fault, and nothing changes.

With 3C. Connect: "Thanks for the time, I know Fridays are your busiest day. We're both trying to get the regional numbers right." Clarify: "Help me understand what your Friday actually looks like. When does the data you need land?" It turns out the figures the site needs do not arrive until Friday afternoon, so an on-time report was never possible. Commit: "So we move the deadline to Monday midday, and I'll ask finance to send the figures Thursday. I'll confirm by Wednesday."

The problem was never the site. Two minutes of Clarify found that, and Commit made it real.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. Then plan a real conversation with

ACT-051 Plan A Real 3C Conversation

  • Always use a real conversation the learner actually needs to have. The framework is thin as

theory and strong as a plan for Thursday

  • Common mistakes:
    • Fake Connect. A warm opener followed by an ambush is worse than no opener. If the person

senses the sequence is a technique, you have lost more than you gained

    • Clarify that is really a lecture. If your "open question" has the answer in it, it is not

Clarify. "Don't you think it would be better if…" is a statement wearing a question mark

    • Vague Commit. "We'll keep in touch" is not a commitment. A name, an action and a date, or it

did not happen

  • Cultural note: Connect is not optional in Pacific and Māori settings, and the version taught in

most workplaces is far too thin. Time spent on the relationship before the business is the business

Learn more

  • 📄 FRM-007 What-Why-How Briefing — the house sibling for briefing a team rather than negotiating with one

⚠️ GAP: no external reading or video linked yet. 3C is house content and has not been matched to published work on cross-functional collaboration. The nearest evidenced neighbour is collaborative overload.
