The CV That Gets Read

techniquepractitionercareer-readinesscvjob-searchwork-readinesswritingats

What it is in one line: your CV gets a few seconds and a keyword scan before a human decides anything, so the top third has to do almost all the work.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written to sit alongside Tahatū's CV templates and Job Hunters' Workbook, which are free, NZ standard, and should be what learners actually type into. Evidence: practitioner. The "six seconds" figure you see everywhere comes from small eye-tracking studies by a recruitment vendor and should not be quoted as fact. What is not in dispute is that screening is fast and often filtered by software first. Best for: the learner who has applied for forty jobs and heard nothing.

Two readers, in this order

Most CV advice fails because it optimises for the wrong one.

Reads firstWants
1. The softwareIncreasingly, an applicant tracking systemPlain text it can parse, and the words from the job ad
2. The humanA few seconds on the top thirdA quick answer to "can this person do the job?"

⚠️ A beautiful CV that the software cannot read is not a CV. Columns, text boxes, headers, graphics, photos and PDFs-of-images all break parsers. Tahatū's templates are safe. A Canva design often is not.

The shape

flowchart TD
  A["NAME · phone · email · suburb"] --> B["THE HEADLINE<br/>one line: what you are, for this job"]
  B --> C["THREE TO FIVE SKILL BULLETS<br/>each with evidence"]
  C --> D["WORK HISTORY<br/>most recent first · achievements, not duties"]
  D --> E["TRAINING · LICENCES · TICKETS"]
  E --> F["REFEREES<br/>named, warned, willing"]

Everything above the fold is B and C. That is the whole strategy.

SectionThe rule
ContactPhone, email, suburb. No full street address, no date of birth, no photo. In New Zealand a photo invites discrimination and gives nothing back
HeadlineOne line, rewritten for every job. "Warehouse assistant with forklift F endorsement and four years on nights." Not "hardworking team player seeking opportunity"
Skill bulletsThree to five, in the job ad's words, each with the evidence from FRM-057
Work historyWhat changed because you were there, not what you were told to do
TrainingLicences, tickets and endorsements go high if the job needs them. A Class 2 or a Site Safe card can be the whole reason you get called
RefereesNamed, asked first, and briefed on which job it is

Duties versus achievements

The single biggest lift available on most CVs.

Duty, which everyone writesAchievement, which gets read
"Responsible for stock""Cut stock discrepancies from weekly to almost none over six months"
"Customer service""Handled the complaints desk on Saturdays, the busiest shift"
"Cleaning duties""Held the kitchen at an A grade through two council inspections"
"Worked in a team""Trained four new starters, three of whom are still there"

➜ The test: could the person who replaced you write the same sentence? If yes, it is a duty. Make it specific to you.

Tailoring, which is non-negotiable

One CV sent to forty jobs is why nobody called. Tailoring is not a rewrite. It is fifteen minutes:

  1. Print the job ad. Highlight every skill word.
  2. Rewrite the headline for this job, using its words
  3. Reorder the skill bullets so the ones it asked for are first
  4. Check the licence or ticket it names is visible without scrolling

⚠️ Use their words, not your synonyms. If the ad says "forklift licence" do not write "counterbalance certification". Software matches text, not meaning.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 15 minutes. Then get them into

Tahatū's builder rather than a blank Word document

  • Run ACT-096 Seven Seconds to open

and ACT-097 The Tailoring Lab to apply

  • Common mistakes:
    • Design over parsing. See the warning above
    • An objective statement. "Seeking a challenging role in a dynamic company" says nothing. Replace

it with the headline

    • Listing every job since 2004. Ten to fifteen years is plenty. Anything older is one line
    • Referees "available on request". Just name them. It reads as delay
    • No numbers anywhere. One number changes the whole page
  • ⚠️ Gaps are normal and they are not a scandal. Illness, caring, redundancy, prison, raising

kids, a visa. Teach a one-line honest account and move on. The gap is rarely the problem; the panic about it is. See ACT-100

  • ⚠️ Names and discrimination are real. New Zealand research has found candidates with non-Pākehā

names get fewer callbacks. Never advise a learner to anglicise their name. Do tell them why networks and referrals matter so much, which is FRM-061

Learn more

  • 📄 Tahatū — CV templates and the Job Hunters' Workbook
  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — applying for a job
  • 📄 Human Rights Commission — discrimination in employment

⚠️ GAP: the "six seconds" and "75% of CVs are rejected by software" figures circulate everywhere and both trace back to vendor marketing rather than independent research. This page deliberately does not use them, and neither should a facilitator.

The STAR Interview Answer — Situation, Task, Action, Result

techniquestrongcareer-readinessinterviewsstarjob-searchwork-readinessstorytelling

⚠️ Name clash, read this first

This is not FRM-003 STAR.

Stands forWhat it is for
FRM-003 STARStory · Tools and techniques · Apply · ReflectZeducation's teaching recipe. How a facilitator builds a session
FRM-059 STAR (this page)Situation · Task · Action · ResultA learner's interview answer. How a candidate tells a story about themselves

Two different things, same four letters, both in this library and both genuinely called STAR in the wild. Say which one you mean, every time. In any session where both could come up, call this one "the STAR answer" and FRM-003 "the STAR session shape".

What it is in one line: a four-part shape that turns "tell me about a time you…" from a panic into a story with a point.

Origin: the behavioural interviewing tradition, which took hold from the 1970s on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour better than hypothetical questions do. No single author owns STAR; it is the standard teaching shape across the recruitment industry, and Tahatū's Job Hunters' Workbook teaches it too. Evidence: strong, for the underlying method rather than the acronym. Structured behavioural interviews are among the better-validated selection tools available, and clearly outperform unstructured "have a chat" interviews. The four letters are a memory aid on top of that. Best for: anyone who freezes, rambles, or answers in the abstract.

The model

What goes in itHow long
SSituationWhere and when. Enough to picture it1 sentence
TTaskWhat you specifically had to do. Not the team. You1 sentence
AActionWhat you did, step by step. This is most of the answer3-4 sentences
RResultWhat happened. A number if you have one, a lesson if you do not1-2 sentences
flowchart LR
  S["S · SITUATION<br/>set the scene<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"] --> T["T · TASK<br/>your job in it<br/><i>1 sentence</i>"]
  T --> A["A · ACTION<br/>what YOU did<br/><i>3-4 sentences</i>"]
  A --> R["R · RESULT<br/>what changed<br/><i>1-2 sentences</i>"]
  A -.->|"the half<br/>people skip"| A

How to read it: A is the answer. Most people spend ninety seconds on Situation, run out of nerve, and finish with "so yeah, it worked out." Flip the proportions.

Worked example, a warehouse interview

Question: "Tell me about a time you dealt with pressure."

Weak answer: "Yeah I'm pretty good under pressure, we were busy heaps, especially Christmas, and you just get on with it aye."

STAR answer:

S: "Last Christmas we were two people down on the night shift for a fortnight." T: "I was the senior on nights, so getting the trucks loaded by six was on me." A: "I split the crew into two teams instead of four so nobody was working alone. I moved the pick order so the biggest customer's pallets got done first, in case we ran out of time. And I rang the day supervisor each morning to tell him exactly what was left, so he wasn't finding out at nine." R: "We got every truck out on time except one, which went an hour late. The day team said it was the first Christmas they hadn't inherited a mess."

➜ The result is not heroic. It contains a failure — one truck went late — and the answer is stronger for it. Perfect results sound rehearsed.

The three questions everyone gets

Prepare these and most interviews are covered:

  1. Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult person. → the answer lives in

TOP-COM-002

  1. Tell me about a time something went wrong. → they want to know if you own it. Never blame the

absent

  1. Tell me about a time you worked in a team. → make sure "I" appears, not only "we"

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, then straight into practice. This one dies on a slide
  • Run ACT-099 The STAR Answer Lab
  • Prepare four stories, not twenty answers. Four good STAR stories flex to cover most questions.

Trying to script every question is why people freeze when one is worded differently

  • Common mistakes:
    • "We" all the way through. The panel cannot hire the team. Make them say "I"
    • No result. The story just stops. Ask "and then what happened?" every single time
    • A twelve-minute Situation. One sentence. Timebox it in practice
    • Only glorious stories. A story where something went wrong and they fixed it is usually better
  • ⚠️ Culturally, "I" is genuinely hard for some learners. In many Pacific and Māori settings,

claiming individual credit is poor form and the group comes first. That instinct is right at home and costly in a Pākehā interview room. Do not tell them their upbringing is wrong. Name the clash, and give them the bridge: "our team did X, and my part was Y." Both true, both comfortable. Same territory as FRM-042's culture barrier

Learn more

  • 📄 Tahatū — Job Hunters' Workbook, including interview preparation
  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — interviews
  • 📄 Public Service Commission — behavioural interviewing in NZ government recruitment

The Four-Sentence Cover Letter

techniquepractitionercareer-readinesscover-letterjob-searchwritingwork-readiness

What it is in one line: four sentences that answer the only four questions a hiring manager has, which is three paragraphs shorter than what most people send and considerably more likely to be read.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written because cover letters are where learners stall hardest. Sits alongside Tahatū's cover letter templates. Evidence: practitioner. There is no research saying four sentences beats five. What is defensible is that short and specific beats long and generic, and that a letter which never gets written beats nothing at all. Best for: the learner who has been staring at a blank page for two days and has now decided not to apply.

The four sentences

SentenceAnswers
1Which job, and one reason you want this one. Name the employer"Why are you writing?"
2The single strongest thing you bring, in the ad's own words, with evidence"Can you do it?"
3One specific thing about them. A project, a value, a location, a customer"Do you actually want us?"
4What happens next. "I'm available from the 12th and happy to come in any time""What now?"
flowchart LR
  A["1 · WHICH JOB<br/>and why this one"] --> B["2 · WHAT YOU BRING<br/>their words + evidence"]
  B --> C["3 · WHY THEM<br/>one specific thing"]
  C --> D["4 · NEXT STEP<br/>availability, no fuss"]

Worked example

Job: Support worker, an Auckland disability provider.

Kia ora Sarah, [1] I'm applying for the support worker role at your Māngere site, because the shifts fit around my study and I've wanted to move into disability support since caring for my grandfather. [2] I've got two years of personal care experience, including medication support and working alongside district nurses, and I've just finished my Level 3 in Health and Wellbeing. [3] I noticed your team runs the community garden programme at that site. That's exactly the kind of support work I want to be part of, rather than only in-home. [4] I'm available from 12 August and can come in for a chat any weekday. My CV is attached. Ngā mihi, Losa

Ninety seconds of a manager's time. Every sentence earns its place. Sentence 3 is the one almost nobody writes, and it is the one that shows this was not sent to forty employers.

What to cut

CutWhy
"I am writing to apply for the position advertised on Seek"They know. It wastes the best line on the page
"I am a hardworking team player with excellent communication skills"Everyone writes it, so it says nothing. Replace with evidence
Retelling the whole CVThe CV is attached. The letter is the reason to open it
"Thank you for taking the time to consider my application"Harmless, and it is not a sentence that gets you an interview
An apology for anythingNever apologise for a gap, a career change, or being new

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 8 minutes. The example does most of the work
  • Run ACT-098 Four Sentences
  • The best move: have them write sentence 3 first. It is the hardest and it forces them to

actually look the employer up, which is the real skill hiding inside this exercise

  • Common mistakes:
    • No name. "Dear Sir/Madam" on an ad that lists a contact person is a tell. Ring and ask if it

is not there

    • Sentence 3 invented. "I've always admired your commitment to excellence" is worse than

leaving it out. It must be something real they found

    • Writing it before the CV. Sentence 2 comes straight out of

FRM-057. Do the skills work first

  • ⚠️ On using AI to write it: learners will, and Tahatū's own workbook covers it. The honest

position is that AI is fine for tidying and terrible at sentence 3, because it does not know the employer and will invent something. Anything it writes must be checked against the truth, and sentence 3 should always be theirs

Learn more

  • 📄 Tahatū — cover letter templates and the Job Hunters' Workbook
  • 📄 Employment New Zealand — applying for a job

How Jobs Are Actually Found — the four channels

modelmoderatecareer-readinessjob-searchnetworkingweak-tieswork-readinesshidden-job-marketdirect-approachvolunteering

What it is in one line: most people put all their effort into the channel with the worst odds, and none into the one that actually works.

Origin: Zeducation house model. The evidence underneath it is FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties — Mark Granovetter's finding that people hear about jobs far more often through acquaintances than through close friends, because close friends know the same openings you already know about. Evidence: moderate. Granovetter's core finding has held up over fifty years and across countries. The specific percentages people quote for "the hidden job market" are not reliable and this page deliberately gives none. Best for: the learner who has sent sixty online applications, heard nothing, and concluded there are no jobs.

The four channels

ChannelWhat it isCompetitionEffort per application
1. Advertised, applied coldSeek, Trade Me Jobs, the company websiteHighest. Hundreds of applicants, software filtering firstLow per application, terrible odds
2. Advertised, with someone insideSame ad, but somebody hands your CV over or mentions your nameMuch lower. You start as a known quantityMedium
3. Not advertised, filled by word of mouthThe manager asks the team "know anyone?" before it is ever written upLow, and most people never see theseMedium
4. Created for youSomebody meets you and finds work for youLowest of all, and rareHigh, and slow
flowchart TD
  L(("A JOB<br/>SEEKER"))
  L -->|"most people<br/>spend 95% here"| C1["1 · APPLY COLD<br/>worst odds"]
  L -->|"almost nobody<br/>does this"| C2["2 · SOMEONE INSIDE"]
  L --> C3["3 · WORD OF MOUTH<br/>before it's advertised"]
  L --> C4["4 · CREATED FOR YOU"]
  C2 --> W["WEAK TIES<br/>people you barely know"]
  C3 --> W
  C4 --> W

How to read it: channels 2, 3 and 4 all run on the same thing — people who know you exist. That is what makes this teachable. It is one habit, not three.

Why the job was never advertised

This is the part that stops it sounding like a conspiracy, and it is the question every room asks. Teach it before the channels, not after.

The employer's reasonWhat it actually means
Advertising costs money and timePosting the ad, then reading two hundred applications, then interviewing. That is a fortnight of somebody's work
There is already an internal candidateSomeone in the building who knows how the place runs
Referral programmesEmployers ask their own staff first, because a workmate's recommendation is a known quantity

➜ Say this out loud: "They are not hiding it from you. They are trying not to do two weeks of work."

That reframe does more than any tactic on this page. A learner who thinks the hidden job market is a closed club stays out of it. A learner who understands it is a tired manager taking the easy option can see exactly where to stand.

⚠️ And the flip side, which follows from the same logic. If the manager is avoiding the work, then a person who turns up already vouched for is doing them a favour, not asking for one. That is the whole psychology of channels 2, 3 and 4 in one sentence.

The move

Not "network", which is a word that makes most people close down. Tell people what you are looking for.

Most people do not know what their cousin's boss does, and their cousin's boss does not know they are looking. Both problems are fixed by one sentence, said out loud, to twenty people.

The sentence has three parts:

  1. What you are looking for. Specific. "Warehouse or storeperson work" beats "anything going"
  2. What you bring. One thing. "I've got my F endorsement"
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"

➜ Said to a cousin, a neighbour, the person at church, a former supervisor, the parent at the school gate. Twenty of those beats sixty online applications, and it is less work.

Four ways into channels 2, 3 and 4

The sentence is the main one. These four are how you create chances to say it.

The way inWhat it looks like here
1Tell the people you already knowThe list from ACT-101. Cousin, neighbour, church, former supervisor, the parent at the school gate
2Ask inside where you already workA large share of unadvertised jobs are internal. If you are in work and want a change, ask around other departments before you look outside. Do it discreetly, and be straight with your supervisor once you are actually applying
3Go straight to the employerA walk-in, a phone call, or a short written message to a real named person. Not asking for a job in the first sentence. Practised in ACT-108
4VolunteerUnpaid work in a place you would like to be paid. It produces referees, referrals and somebody who has seen you turn up on time. Most of our learners are already doing this at church, at a club, or on a marae and have never counted it

And one signal worth watching. A company announcing a new site, a new contract or a new shift is a company about to need people. A new distribution centre in Drury, a supermarket fit-out, a rest home wing, a roading contract awarded. That is the moment to ring, not three months later when the ad goes up.

⚠️ Channels 2, 3 and 4 all still run on a name. Direct approaches and online profiles are places where a non-Pākehā name gets fewer callbacks, the same as cold applications. The answer is never to change the name. It is that a person who has met you, or been told about you by somebody they trust, is no longer a name on a screen.

Why this matters more for Zeducation's learners, not less

Two things are true at once and both should be said in the room.

The good news: Pacific and Māori communities often have denser networks than the people writing careers advice — church, marae, sports club, extended family. That is a real advantage and it is usually going completely unused, because nobody has said out loud that it is allowed.

The hard part: New Zealand research has found candidates with non-Pākehā names get fewer callbacks from cold applications. Channel 1 is where that bias bites hardest, because a name on a screen is all there is. Channels 2, 3 and 4 route around it, because somebody has already vouched for you.

⚠️ That is not a reason to hide a name. It is a reason to spend the effort where it pays. Never advise a learner to anglicise their name.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes
  • Run ACT-101 Who Do You Already Know?
  • The best question: "who is the last person you told that you're looking?" Most rooms go quiet
  • Common mistakes:
    • Quoting a percentage for the hidden job market. The figures circulating are unsourced. Say

"most", say "often", do not say "80%"

    • Making it sound like schmoozing. It is one honest sentence to people who already know you
    • Skipping channel 1 entirely. Advertised jobs are real jobs. The point is proportion, not

abandonment

    • Teaching the tactics before the reason. The employer's-side explanation is what makes the rest

land. Without it the room hears "the system is rigged"

    • Importing advice written for somebody else. Alumni associations, professional bodies,

conferences, business cards and informational interviews all assume a white-collar career. The New Zealand equivalents are careers expos, open days, industry training organisations, unions, and the person you already know who works there. See SRC-013

  • ⚠️ Do not let this become "it's who you know, so why bother". For a learner who feels shut out,

this framework can land as confirmation the system is rigged. Turn it the other way: you already have a network, you just have not used it, and using it is free

Learn more

  • 📄 FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties — Granovetter's research,

in full

  • 📄 Tahatū — career profiles and job-hunting guidance
  • 📄 Work and Income — help finding work
  • 📄 Volunteering New Zealand — for way in number 4

⚠️ GAP: the New Zealand name-discrimination research is referred to here in general terms because the specific studies were not verified during this ingest. Find and cite them properly, or reword to "international and New Zealand research has found", before this is used in a tender.

FRM-062Framework · 02-Frameworks

The Questions You Ask Them

techniquepractitionercareer-readinessinterviewsquestionsjob-searchwork-readinessfollow-up

What it is in one line: every interview ends with "do you have any questions for us?", most people say no, and it is the only moment in the whole hour where the power in the room is level.

Origin: Zeducation house model, written after SRC-011 showed the library taught how to answer and stopped there. Evidence: practitioner. There is no study saying three questions beats two. What is defensible is that "no, I think you've covered everything" reads as no interest, and that an interview is a two-way decision whether or not the candidate is treating it as one. Best for: the learner who prepares hard for the questions coming at them and has nothing for the last five minutes.

Why "no" costs you

Three separate things happen when somebody says they have no questions.

What the interviewer takes from it
InterestYou did not care enough to think of one
JudgementYou are willing to take a job you know almost nothing about
The last impressionIt is the final thing that happens. It is what they remember at the table afterwards

➜ And a fourth thing, which matters more than all of them: you have just agreed to spend forty hours a week somewhere without asking a single thing about it.

The four kinds of question

Take three in, from at least two different rows. Written down, on paper, and it is fine to read them.

flowchart TD
  Q["THREE QUESTIONS,<br/>WRITTEN DOWN"]
  Q --> A["1 · THE JOB<br/>what the work is actually like"]
  Q --> B["2 · THE PEOPLE<br/>who you'd be working with"]
  Q --> C["3 · THE FUTURE<br/>where this goes"]
  Q --> D["4 · THE PROCESS<br/>what happens next"]
  D -.->|"always ask<br/>this one"| D
KindExamples
1The job"What does a normal day look like in this role?" · "What would you want me to have got on top of in the first month?" · "What's the hardest part of this job?"
2The people"Who would I be working with day to day?" · "How does the team hand over between shifts?" · "How long has the person doing this job been here?"
3The future"Is there training or a ticket the company puts people through?" · "Where have people gone from this role?"
4The process"What are the next steps, and when will you be in touch?"

⚠️ Question 4 is not optional and it goes last. It is the one that gets you a date instead of a fortnight of refreshing your email.

The questions that are fine to ask, and the ones that wait

This is where learners get bad advice from everywhere at once.

Ask it in the interviewWait until they offer you the job
The shift pattern and the rosterWhether you can swap shifts
Whether the pay range in the ad is rightNegotiating the number
Whether there is training or a ticketWhether they will pay for a course you want
Start date and next stepsTime off you have already booked, unless it is soon

➜ Pay is allowed. Learners are told constantly that asking about money looks greedy. Asking "the ad said $26 to $28, is that right for this role?" is not greed, it is checking you can afford to take the job. The negotiation is a different conversation and it happens after the offer.

⚠️ If you have something already booked in the next few weeks — a funeral, a wedding, a court date, a tangi, a trip home — say it at the end of the interview, not after you start. It is almost always fine, and it is very much not fine as a surprise in week one.

Three that do not work

QuestionWhy it lands badly
"How did I do?"Puts them on the spot and reads as anxious. Ask about the process instead
Anything answered on their websiteIt says you did not look. This is the risk of a memorised list
"What does the company do?"Same problem, larger

After the interview

Two moves, and the whole thing takes five minutes.

WhenWhat
Same dayA short thank-you email or text to whoever arranged it. Three lines. Name one thing from the conversation so it is obviously not a template
After the date they gave youIf the day they named has passed, follow up once. Politely, and once

And when there is silence: it is usually the process, not you. Restructures, an internal candidate, the manager on leave. Follow up once, then put it down and keep applying. The learner who stops applying while waiting on one answer is the one this framework is really for.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. The four rows are the whole model
  • Run ACT-102 Three Questions
  • The best move: at the end of every roleplay in

ACT-099, make the interviewer finish with "do you have any questions for us?" Nobody has an answer the first time. After a fortnight everybody does

  • Common mistakes:
    • A memorised list, asked regardless. If they answered it during the interview, say so and ask

a different one. That is why you take three

    • Questions that are really complaints. "How much overtime is there?" asked in a certain tone

is heard as "I don't want to do any"

    • Not writing them down. Under pressure the questions evaporate. Paper is allowed and it looks

prepared, not weak

  • ⚠️ **In many Pacific and Māori settings, questioning someone older or in authority is not

straightforward.** Do not treat that as a confidence gap to be fixed. Name it, and offer the framing that works: "Can I ask you something about the job?" Asking permission first makes it comfortable and it costs nothing

Where it goes

Use it inHow
TOP-EMP-004The last five minutes of the interview, taught with the first fifty-five
The day before a real interviewThree written questions is the single highest-value ten minutes available
Employer engagementAsk employers what candidates never ask them. The list is worth having

FRM-063Framework · 02-Frameworks

Te Whare Tapa Whā

modelstrong adoption, practitioner outcomeswellbeinghauorate-whare-tapa-wharesiliencemaoriidentityholistic

What it is in one line: wellbeing as a wharenui with four walls and a foundation, where letting any one wall go weakens the whole house.

Origin: Sir Mason Durie, developed at Hui Taumata in 1984. It was a response to Rapuora, research carried out between 1978 and 1980 by the Māori Women's Welfare League into the health barriers Māori were actually experiencing. Evidence: it is a model, not an intervention, so the honest word is not "proven". What is true is that it is the standard wellbeing framework across New Zealand health, education and social services, and that it is the framework that got wairua acknowledged in health practice in this country. See the audit below. Best for: any room where wellbeing is being taught, and especially the learner who thinks wellbeing means going to the gym.

The whare

flowchart TD
  W["TE WHARE TAPA WHĀ"]
  W --- A["TAHA WAIRUA<br/>spirit, purpose, meaning"]
  W --- B["TAHA HINENGARO<br/>mind and emotions"]
  W --- C["TAHA TINANA<br/>the body"]
  W --- D["TAHA WHĀNAU<br/>family and belonging"]
  A --- E["TAHA WHENUA<br/>connection to land and roots"]
  B --- E
  C --- E
  D --- E

How to read it: four walls on one foundation. A whare with three walls does not stand, and that is the whole argument.

PouWhat it holdsWhat "needs care" looks like on a Tuesday
Taha wairuaSpirit, purpose, faith, what makes life mean somethingYou have not been to church, to the moana, or anywhere quiet, in a month
Taha hinengaroMind, emotions, how you think and feelYou are snapping at people and cannot say why
Taha tinanaThe body. Sleep, food, movement, healthFour hours a night and takeaways since Tuesday
Taha whānauFamily, relationships, the people you belong toYou have not rung your mum in three weeks
Taha whenuaConnection to place, land, roots, where you are fromYou have been in Auckland eight years and never been home

⚠️ Whenua is the foundation, not a fifth wall. It sits underneath the other four, which is the point. Somebody disconnected from where they are from is standing on a floor that moves.

Why it matters for resilience specifically

Each pou does a different job when you get knocked around.

PouWhat it gives you when things go wrong
TinanaSteadies the stress. Sleep and food change what a problem feels like before they change anything else
HinengaroLets you think straight enough to make a decision you will not regret
WhānauThe backup. Somebody to ring, somebody who turns up
WairuaThe reason to keep going when there is no short-term reason
WhenuaKnowing who you are and where you are from, when a setback is telling you that you are nothing

➜ This is why "just be more resilient" is bad advice. It aims at hinengaro alone and ignores the four things holding it up.

⚠️ The evidence audit

Facilitators get asked whether this is evidence-based. Answer it straight.

What is true: it is the most widely adopted wellbeing framework in Aotearoa. It is used by the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand, the Mental Health Foundation, schools under the New Zealand Curriculum's hauora concept, ACC and most social services. It has been in continuous use for over forty years.

What is not the claim: nobody has run a randomised trial on "using Te Whare Tapa Whā". It is a way of organising what wellbeing consists of, not a treatment. Asking whether it is proven is a category error, in the same way you would not ask for a trial on the food pyramid's shape.

What it genuinely did: before it, spiritual wellbeing was not something a New Zealand health practitioner was expected to ask about. After it, it was. That is a real change and it is traceable.

➜ The honest line for a room: "This is not a therapy. It is a picture of what a whole person is made of, built out of Māori women's research into their own communities, and it has held up for forty years because it describes something true."

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes. Draw the whare on the board as you talk. Do not use a slide
  • Run ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall
  • The best question: "which wall have you been letting go?" Most rooms answer honestly and fast,

because the model gives them a word for something they already knew

  • Pair it with FRM-065 Fonofale. Offering only one model to a mixed room

tells half of it which half counts. Teach both, let people choose

  • Common mistakes:
    • Scoring the walls out of ten. It turns a picture into a test. One thing per wall that needs

care is all it is for

    • Treating wairua as religion. For some people it is. For others it is the moana, music, a

garden, or their kids. Do not narrow it

    • Skipping whenua because it is awkward for migrants. It is not awkward, it is often the most

important pou in the room. Ask about where they are from, not where they live

    • Using it as a checklist for someone else. It is a self-check. Never fill one in about a

learner

  • ⚠️ Say whose it is. Durie's name, 1984, Hui Taumata, and the Māori Women's Welfare League

research underneath it. Teaching a Māori model without attribution is exactly the habit this library exists to break

Learn more

  • 🔗 Mental Health Foundation — Te Whare Tapa Whā
  • 🔗 Healthify — Te whare tapa whā and wellbeing
  • 🔗 Te Ara — Māori health: te whare tapa whā model
  • 📄 Health Quality & Safety Commission — Te Whare Tapa Whā resource (PDF)

Use it inHow

Any programme inductionTen minutes on day one changes what learners will tell you in week three
One-to-one when somebody is strugglingIt gives them language for a thing they cannot otherwise name

FRM-064 The ABC Model of ResilienceThis is the picture, that is the tool. This one tells you which wall to work on

FRM-050 Tikanga Māori in BusinessSame whakaaro, applied to an organisation rather than a person
FRM-064Framework · 02-Frameworks

The ABC Model of Resilience — Accept, Believe, Commit

techniquepractitioner, with a strong anchor under step Bwellbeingresilienceabc-modelsetbacksself-efficacyhouse-contentaction

⚠️ Name clash, read this first

This is not Ellis's ABC, which is the one a counsellor, a psychology student or a Google search will mean.

Stands forWhat it is
FRM-064 ABC (this page)Accept · Believe · CommitZeducation's house tool for getting moving after a setback
Ellis's ABC (1950s, REBT)Activating event · Belief · ConsequenceA therapy model about how beliefs, not events, produce feelings

Same three letters, different models. Say "the ABC of resilience" when you introduce it, and if somebody in the room names Ellis, they are right and it is a good moment rather than an awkward one.

⚠️ And a second one to know about. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) shares "accept" and "commit" as its two anchors. It is a clinical therapy delivered by clinicians. This is a workshop tool. Do not let the resemblance turn a facilitator into a therapist.

What it is in one line: three steps that take you from spinning your wheels after a setback to having one small thing you are actually going to do.

Origin: Zeducation house model, from the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide. Evidence: practitioner overall, but step B has a genuinely strong anchor and it is worth knowing which part of this is doing the work. See below. Best for: the moment after something goes wrong, when somebody has been going over it for three days and nothing has moved.

The model

flowchart LR
  A["A · ACCEPT<br/>What are the facts?<br/>What can I control?"] --> B["B · BELIEVE<br/>My past wins?<br/>My support group?"]
  B --> C["C · COMMIT<br/>My next rock?<br/>What will I do?"]

How to read it: in order, and C is the point. A and B without C is a nice conversation that changes nothing by Friday.

StepThe questionWhat it does
AAcceptWhat actually happened, and what can I control?Stops the spinning. Splits the problem into the part you can move and the part you cannot
BBelieveWhen have I got through something like this before?Replaces doubt with evidence. Evidence, not a pep talk
CCommitWhat is one small thing I will do, and when?Turns insight into momentum. Fifteen minutes, with a time on it

Worked example

Situation: you have been turned down for a job you thought you had.
Accept"They said no. I can't change that. I can control whether I ring and ask why, and whether I apply for the other two this week."
Believe"I got the warehouse job in March and I had less experience then. I've got Mere, who knows people at the DC."
Commit"Tomorrow at 10, I'll ring and ask what would have made the difference. Done means I've asked one question and written the answer down."

➜ Notice what the commitment is not. It is not "be more positive" or "get back out there". It is one action, with a time, and a definition of done. That is what makes it a commitment instead of an intention.

Where the evidence actually is

Be honest about which part of this is backed and which part is craft.

StepWhat holds it up
A · AcceptThe control / no-control split is old, practical and uncontroversial. Not a research finding, a useful distinction
B · BelieveThe strongest part. "Remember your past wins" is exactly Bandura's mastery experiences, which the self-efficacy literature consistently finds to be the most influential of the four sources of self-belief. Direct personal evidence of having done a hard thing beats encouragement from anyone else, every time
C · CommitSmall, specific, time-boxed action is standard behavioural practice. The specificity is what does the work, not the size

➜ The line worth saying out loud: "Being told you can do it is the weakest way to believe you can do it. Remembering that you already did is the strongest. That is why step B asks for a past win and not a compliment."

⚠️ What this is not. It is not a treatment for depression, anxiety, grief or trauma. It is a tool for a setback. Know the difference and know where to send somebody: their GP, 1737 to call or text free, or a workplace EAP.

The confidence check

The house worksheet asks for confidence out of 10 before planning and after. Keep it.

  • It is a teaching mirror, not a measure. Nothing is validated and nothing should be recorded

against anyone

  • The movement is the lesson. People routinely go from a 3 to a 6 in fifteen minutes without

anything about the situation changing, which is the most persuasive demonstration of the model available

  • If it does not move, that is information too, and it usually means step C is still too big

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 12 minutes with one worked example
  • Run ACT-106 The ABC Worksheet
  • The best move: do the whole thing on a real, current, small setback from the room rather than a

hypothetical. It has to be somebody's actual week or it stays theoretical

  • Common mistakes:
    • Accept heard as "get over it". It is not. It is naming the facts so you can stop arguing with

them and start on the part that moves. Say that explicitly, because the word does real damage otherwise

    • A step C that is a whole project. "Sort out my CV" is not a step. "Open the file and rewrite

the top three lines, Tuesday 7pm" is

    • Skipping B. It is the step that gets rushed and it is the one with the research behind it
    • Using it on something too big. A bereavement is not a setback to ABC your way through
  • ⚠️ Somebody's "setback" will turn out to be much bigger than a setback. Have your referrals

ready before you run it, and never push a learner to share the situation itself

Where it goes

Use it inHow

One-to-one after a knockbackA job rejection, a failed assessment, a fallout at home
Team debriefsWorks on a group setback with the whole team filling in one sheet
CoachingFaster than a full coaching conversation, and it lands with a room that has been knocked around

FrameworkRelationship

FRM-066 Resilience Is OrdinaryWhy the tool works at all. Resilience runs on ordinary systems, and this is one of them written down

FRM-065Framework · 02-Frameworks

Fonofale — the Pacific model of health

modelstrong adoption, practitioner outcomeswellbeinghauorafonofalepacificresilienceidentityholisticaiga

What it is in one line: wellbeing as a fale, where culture is the roof, aiga is the floor, four pou hold it up, and the whole house sits inside its environment, its time and its context.

Origin: Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann, developed in the New Zealand context and drawing on Cook Islands, Samoan, Tongan, Fijian, Niuean and Tokelauan values. It has been accepted by the Mental Health Commission as a standard for Pacific mental health. Evidence: a model, not an intervention, so the same honesty applies as with FRM-063. What is true is that it is the standard Pacific wellbeing framework in this country and has been for decades. Best for: any Zeducation room, and non-negotiable in a Pacific one.

Why this page exists

The SKILL UP Building Resilience guide teaches Te Whare Tapa Whā and stops there. It is a good model and it is not the only one.

➜ A room that is offered only one model is being told which half of itself counts. Teach both, side by side, and let people work in the one that is theirs.

The fale

flowchart TD
  R["ROOF · CULTURE<br/>beliefs and values<br/><i>the shelter</i>"]
  R --- P1["POU<br/>SPIRITUAL"]
  R --- P2["POU<br/>PHYSICAL"]
  R --- P3["POU<br/>MENTAL"]
  R --- P4["POU<br/>OTHER<br/><i>age, gender, sexuality,<br/>money, status</i>"]
  P1 --- F["FLOOR · AIGA<br/>family, immediate and extended"]
  P2 --- F
  P3 --- F
  P4 --- F
  F --- E(("ENVIRONMENT · TIME · CONTEXT<br/><i>the fale sits inside all three</i>"))

How to read it: the roof and the floor are not optional extras. Culture shelters the whole house, and aiga is what everything stands on. That is a different claim from a Western model that starts with the individual.

PartWhat it holds
Roof · cultureYour beliefs and value system. What protects and shelters the rest
Floor · aigaFamily. Not only immediate. Extended, and anyone you are linked to by partnership or agreement
Pou · spiritualFaith, religious belief, connection with the sacred. Self-awareness, identity and purpose
Pou · physicalThe body. Healthy behaviours, managing illness
Pou · mentalEmotions, thinking, communication, the motivation to get somewhere. Not only mental illness
Pou · otherAge, gender, sexuality, socioeconomic status. The things that shape your wellbeing whether anyone names them or not
Environment, time, contextWhere you are, when this is, and what is going on around it

⚠️ The pou are continuous and interactive. They connect the roof to the floor and each other. Working on one moves the others, which is the same argument Te Whare Tapa Whā makes.

Fonofale and Te Whare Tapa Whā side by side

Not the same model, and the differences are the interesting part.

Te Whare Tapa WhāFonofale
ShapeWharenui, four wallsFale, roof and floor and four pou
FamilyTaha whānau, one of four wallsAiga is the floor. Everything stands on it
CultureCarried through whenua and wairuaCulture is the roof. Named on its own
The fourth elementTaha wairua"Other" — age, gender, sexuality, money
What surrounds itWhenua as the foundationEnvironment, time and context as a circle around the whole fale

➜ The "other" pou is the one that does something no other wellbeing model here does. It puts money, age, gender and sexuality inside the picture of health instead of outside it. For a learner who is broke, or young, or takatāpui, that is the difference between a model that describes them and one that does not.

Why it matters for resilience

PartWhat it gives you when things go wrong
AigaThe floor. In practice this is who feeds you, who has your kids, who lends you the money
CultureThe roof. What tells you who you are when a setback is telling you that you are nothing
The four pouThe same four jobs the whare's walls do
ContextPermission to say "this is hard because of what is going on around me", which is often the truest thing in the room

⚠️ Aiga cuts both ways and the room knows it. Family is the strongest support most Pacific learners have, and it is sometimes also the obligation that is grinding them down. Do not teach the floor as though it is only a resource. Ask the honest question.

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 10 minutes, alongside Te Whare Tapa Whā, not instead of it
  • Run ACT-105 One Thing Per Wall,

which carries both models on one sheet and lets people choose

  • The best question: "which part of your fale has been holding everything up on its own?"
  • Common mistakes:
    • Treating it as the Samoan version of Te Whare Tapa Whā. It is not a translation. It was built

across six Pacific nations and it makes different claims

    • Skipping the "other" pou because it raises money and sexuality. It is the most useful pou for

the learners who need the model most

    • Assuming every Pacific learner will pick Fonofale. Some will not, and some Māori learners will

pick it. Let people choose and do not comment on the choice

    • Getting the words wrong. If you are not confident with pronunciation, say so and ask the room.

They will help, and asking is better than avoiding

  • ⚠️ Say whose it is. Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann, by name. He is a living person and this is

his work

Learn more

  • 📄 Fonofale Model of Health — Fuimaono Karl Pulotu-Endemann (PDF, Health Promotion Forum)
  • 🔗 Health Promotion Forum — Pacific health models
  • 🔗 Mental Health Foundation — the Fonofale model
  • 📄 Ministry for Pacific Peoples — Fonofale presentation (PDF)
  • 🔗 Karl Pulotu-Endemann: "You can only be yourself" — E-Tangata

Resilience Is Ordinary

modelstrongwellbeingresilienceevidencemythshauorasystemshouse-content

What it is in one line: resilience is common, not rare, and it runs on ordinary systems around a person rather than on exceptional personal strength.

Origin: Ann S. Masten, Regents Professor of Child Development at the University of Minnesota, in Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development (Guilford Press; second edition 2024). Her central finding, across decades of work with children exposed to serious adversity, is that resilience depends on ordinary adaptive systems inside and around a person: relationships, routines, a functioning body, culture, community, belief. Evidence: strong. This is one of the better-supported findings in developmental psychology and it is built on longitudinal work rather than a single study. Best for: the ten minutes before you teach any resilience tool, because it decides how the tool gets heard.

Why the framing matters more than the tool

Most people arrive at a resilience session with one of two beliefs, and both are wrong.

The beliefWhere it leads
"Resilient people are made differently." They are tougher, and I am notNothing you teach will apply to them, because they have already decided it is about a trait they do not have
"Resilience means being able to take anything." Keep absorbing, keep goingThe word becomes a weapon. It is used to explain why the problem is you and not the load

Masten's finding takes both apart at once.

flowchart TD
  M["RESILIENCE IS ORDINARY"]
  M --> A["It is COMMON,<br/>not rare"]
  M --> B["It runs on ORDINARY SYSTEMS,<br/>not exceptional people"]
  M --> C["So it can be BUILT,<br/>and it can be DAMAGED"]
  A --> D["'I'm not that kind of person'<br/>is not true"]
  B --> E["Relationships · routines · a body<br/>that works · culture · belief"]
  C --> F["Protect the systems<br/>and you protect the person"]

How to read it: if resilience runs on ordinary systems, then the question is never "are you strong enough?" It is "which of your systems is missing, and can we put it back?"

What "ordinary adaptive systems" actually means

The systemWhat it looks like for a Zeducation learner
Close relationshipsOne adult who has your back. A partner, an aunty, a coach, a tutor
Routines and structureSomewhere to be at 9am. This is a large part of why a programme itself works
A body that functionsSleep, food, health. Nothing else works well underneath a body that does not
Belief and meaningFaith, culture, purpose. A reason that outlasts a bad week
Community and cultureChurch, marae, club, aiga. Belonging that does not depend on performing
A sense of agencyHaving done a hard thing before, and knowing you did it

➜ Read that list against Te Whare Tapa Whā and Fonofale. It is the same list. Durie in 1984 and Pulotu-Endemann named these systems from within Māori and Pacific knowledge; Masten's research arrived at them from the outside. Three traditions, one answer, and that is worth saying out loud in a room that has been taught to treat Western research as the real version.

The sentence this framework exists to refuse

⚠️ "You just need to be more resilient."

Said to somebody working two jobs, whose car has died and whose landlord has given notice, it is not support. It relocates a structural problem into a personal failing.

The honest version: "Resilience is real and it can be built. It is also not a substitute for enough hours, a safe house, or someone to ring. If the load is the problem, the answer is not more strength."

⚠️ A facilitator who cannot say that sentence should not teach resilience. It is the difference between a wellbeing session and a compliance one.

What this does to how you teach the ABC model

Without this framingWith it
"Here is a tool for bouncing back""Here is one of the ordinary systems, written down so you can use it on purpose"
The learner who fails to bounce back has failedThe learner who cannot use it is telling you a system is missing, and that is the useful information
Resilience is a personal qualityResilience is a set of things that can be protected, and some of them are not in the learner's control

Facilitating it

  • Teach it in: 6 minutes, before FRM-064. It is framing,

not a session of its own

  • The best question: "who is the one person who would turn up for you at 2am?" Then: *"that is

not luck. That is the biggest single predictor in the research."*

  • Run ACT-107 The River Stones

after it, so the room moves before it thinks too hard

  • Common mistakes:
    • Turning "resilience is common" into "so this should be easy for you". It means the opposite:

it is common because the systems are common, and somebody without them is not weak

    • Quoting a number. There is no clean percentage and this page deliberately gives none
    • Treating it as a licence to skip the tool. The framing is not the session. It is the ten

minutes that make the session land

  • ⚠️ Somebody in the room will not have the systems. No safe adult, no routine, no house. Notice

it, do not name it publicly, and know where to send them

Learn more

  • 📕 Ann S. Masten, Ordinary Magic: Resilience in Development, 2nd ed. (Guilford Press)

⚠️ GAP: no New Zealand replication is cited on this page. Masten's work is US-based and developmental. What would strengthen it: New Zealand longitudinal evidence, and the Dunedin and Christchurch studies are the obvious places to look. Worth a proper research pass.

Use it inHow

ACT-002Activity · 03-Activities

How Assertive Am I?

10-15 minassessmentassertivenessself-assessmentself-awareness

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it practises: self-awareness against FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles

Materials: the printed assessment, a pen. Nobody collects it. Say that clearly before they start.

The instrument

Read each statement and answer honestly. Score each one: 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I do not feel guilty when I ask others to do something
2If I do not want to do something someone has asked me to do, I can say "no" without feeling guilty
3I have no problem speaking to large groups of people or audiences
4I am able to express myself openly and honestly to my superiors
5I am able to verbally express my feelings of anger, tension, stress and frustration openly
6When sitting in a large group, I am able to speak up confidently
7If I disagree with a decision in a meeting, which goes against the majority, I am able to stay focused and stick to my opinion
8I openly acknowledge my mistakes
9If somebody's behaviour bothers me, I tell them
10I do not use a blaming tone of voice when I express my anger
11I am able to meet new people in different environments confidently and at ease
12I do not label other people's opinions as senseless, stupid or irrational when we disagree
13I believe in myself and feel confident when doing something for the first time
14I believe in live and let live. My needs are just as important as everyone else's
15I assume people are honest, reliable and trustworthy, and I am not hesitant about delegating to others
Total

Scoring

ScoreWhat it meansYour next step
60+Your beliefs, opinions and actions are those of a very assertive person. You handle most situations well, respecting your own rights and the rights of people around youPick the situation where you still hold back, and go there next
45-59You are fairly assertive, depending on the situation. Remember that respect is a key part of assertiveness: respecting yourself and expecting respect from othersNotice which rooms and which people you drop out of assertive with
30-44You are in the middle of the road. Neither aggressive nor assertiveSpeak up for yourself and take the tools from this course into your next conversation
15-29The first positive step towards being more assertive is being hereListen, learn and apply. Start with one "I" statement this week

Debrief

  • Which statements did you score lowest on? Is there a pattern?
  • Is your score different at work than it is at home?
  • Which one statement, if it moved from a 2 to a 4, would change the most for you?

The point to land: this is a snapshot, not a label. Assertiveness is situational and it is trainable. The lowest scores are the training plan.

Variations

  • Youth: reword items 4 and 15 to school, coach and part-time work settings
  • Low literacy: read each statement aloud and have learners hold up fingers 1-5
  • Online: a form with auto-scoring, results shown only to the learner
  • Repeat measure: run it again at the end of the programme and compare. Good evidence for

funders and for the learner

Watch out for

  • Never have learners read their score out. Ask what they noticed, not what they scored
  • Some people score themselves harshly. Reframe: a low score means the tools have somewhere to work
  • Do not turn this into a diagnosis. It is a mirror

Used by

TopicPillarLink

Source: Zeducation Effective Communication workbook.

How Clear Am I?

10-12 minassessmentself-assessmentclear-messagingself-awarenessblufbriefing

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it practises: self-awareness against BLUF, PREP and What-Why-How.

⚠️ Note: Module 2 of the workbook has no self-assessment. This one was written to match the house instrument in ACT-002 — same 1-5 scale, same band structure, same tone. It is Zeducation's, not from an external source, and has not been validated. Treat it as a teaching mirror, not a measure.

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this. 5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I say the main point in the first line of a message
2People do the thing I asked for without needing a follow-up message
3I know what I want to say before I start saying it
4I use plain words instead of jargon my team may not know
5I back up my recommendations with a real example
6When I give instructions, I explain why the task matters, not just what to do
7I check understanding rather than assuming people got it
8I choose the channel to fit the message (a call for something sensitive, a message for something simple)
9My messages are short enough that people read all of them
10When I brief a team, other people talk too
11I ask for the specific action I want, with a deadline
12People rarely misunderstand what I meant
Total

Scoring

ScoreWhat it meansYour next step
50-60Your messages land. People know what you mean and what to do, and you check rather than assumeTeach it. Fix one team member's briefing habit this month
38-49You are clear most of the time, and it slips when you are busy or under pressureNotice which situations cost you clarity. Rushed messages are usually the culprit
25-37Middle of the road. Your point is in there, but people have to dig for itStart with BLUF. First line, main point, every message for two weeks
12-24Being here is the first step. This is a skill, not a talent, and it moves fast with practicePick one message a day. Write it, then move your last line to the top

Debrief

  • Which statements did you score lowest on? Is the pattern in your writing, your speaking, or your

briefings?

  • Is your score different for messages up the chain versus down the chain?
  • Which single one, if it moved from a 2 to a 4, would save you the most time in a week?

The point to land: clear communication is a habit stack, not a personality. Every low score on this page has a tool attached to it that you learned today.

Variations

  • Repeat measure: run it again at the end of the programme and compare. Useful evidence for

funders and for the learner

  • 360 version: ask a team member to score the same 12 statements about you. The gap is the real

conversation

  • Low literacy: read each statement aloud, learners hold up 1-5 fingers
  • Online: a form with auto-scoring, results visible only to the learner

Watch out for

  • Never have learners read scores aloud. Ask what they noticed, not what they scored
  • Item 12 depends on other people, so some learners will not know. Tell them to answer on their best

guess and talk about that uncertainty in the debrief

  • This is a mirror, not a diagnosis

How Well Do I Hold My Limits?

10-15 minassessmentboundariessaying-noself-assessmentworkloadwellbeing

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: the behaviours taught in FRM-008 The Positive No, FRM-009 The Broken Record and FRM-004 DESC.

⚠️ This instrument was written by Zeducation to match the house style of ACT-002 How Assertive Am I?. Module 3 of the Effective Communication workbook has no self-assessment of its own. It is a teaching mirror, not a validated measure. Do not use it for selection, performance management or reporting.

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this.

5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I can say no to extra work without apologising three times
2When I turn something down, I say what I am protecting, not just that I am busy
3I offer an alternative when I say no, instead of just closing the door
4⟲ I say yes to things I know I do not have room for
5When someone keeps pushing, my answer stays the same
6I can stay calm when someone is pressuring me
7⟲ I avoid the person rather than have the conversation
8I raise a problem early, before it builds up into resentment
9When I raise a problem, I describe what happened rather than labelling the person
10I ask for one specific change, so people know what to do differently
11⟲ I feel guilty for days after saying no
12People know where my limits are without having to test them
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 4, 7 and 11, flip your answer before adding it up: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60You hold your limits and keep your relationships. That combination is rareTeach it. Someone on your team is drowning in yeses right now, and you know who
38-49You hold most of the time. It slips with certain people, or when you are tiredWork out who you cannot say no to. It is usually one or two people, not everyone. Build one Positive No for that person this week
25-37The limit is there, but people have to find it by accidentStart with the middle line. Write one clear no, one sentence, and say it out loud before you need it
12-24Being honest here is the first step, and it is the hard onePick one small, low-risk request this week and use all three parts: Yes, No, Yes. One. Not a new personality, one sentence

Facilitating it

  • Run it before teaching the frameworks, so learners have a reason to listen, or after, as the

reflection. Both work. Before is stronger for groups who think this is not their problem

  • Say clearly that nobody hands it in
  • The reverse-scored items catch the people-pleaser pattern. If you have a group that scores high on

everything except 4, 7 and 11, that is your teaching point for the day

  • Do not read scores out. Ask instead: "which single statement did you least want to be honest

about?"

Watch out for

  • Some learners genuinely cannot say no at work: probation, a visa, an insecure contract, or being the

only earner. A low score here is a circumstance, not a character flaw. Say that out loud before people score themselves, or the instrument does harm

  • Item 11 can surface real distress. Know your referral path before the session

Used by

How Well Do I Listen?

10-15 minassessmentlisteningactive-listeningself-assessmentempathy

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: the behaviours taught in FRM-010 SOLER, FRM-011 The 3 Levels of Listening and FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting.

⚠️ This instrument was written by Zeducation to match the house style of ACT-002 How Assertive Am I?. Module 4 of the Effective Communication workbook has no self-assessment of its own. It is a teaching mirror, not a validated measure. Do not use it for selection, performance management or reporting.

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this.

5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I let people finish before I respond
2⟲ While someone is talking, I am working out what I will say next
3I put my phone down and face the person when it matters
4I say back what I heard, to check I got it right
5I notice when someone's tone does not match their words
6⟲ I jump to solving the problem before the person has finished describing it
7When someone is upset, I name the feeling before I offer a fix
8I ask questions to understand, not to make a point
9⟲ I finish other people's sentences for them
10People tell me things they have not told other people
11I notice what is not being said in a meeting
12I can repeat back what someone told me yesterday
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 2, 6 and 9, flip your answer before adding it up: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60People feel heard around you, and it is why they tell you thingsNotice which conversations you still rush. It is usually the ones with people you find hard
38-49You listen well when you are calm and unhurried, which is not when it is most neededPick your worst listening moment of the day, usually mid-afternoon or mid-crisis, and do one paraphrase in it
25-37You are hearing the words and missing the restStart with one move: before you reply, say back what you heard. Just that, for two weeks
12-24Honest scoring here takes more self-awareness than most people havePut the phone face down for one conversation a day and let the person finish without interrupting once. That is the whole task

Facilitating it

  • Best run after ACT-018 Bad Listening, Then SOLER.

People score themselves far more honestly once they have felt what bad listening does

  • Item 10 is the useful one. It is the only item that measures the result rather than the

behaviour, and it is the one that changes people's minds about their score

  • Say clearly that nobody hands it in
  • Optional and powerful: ask learners to also guess how the person they work most closely with

would score them. The gap is the conversation

Watch out for

  • Overconfidence. Nearly everyone rates themselves a good listener. If the whole room scores 50+,

do not argue with them, go back to item 10 and to the round-one experience instead

  • Learners in noisy, fast, high-interruption jobs (kitchens, sites, wards, contact centres) will score

low on items 1 and 9 for reasons that are about the job, not about them. Name that

How Do I Land On A Screen?

10-15 minassessmentdigital-communicationself-assessmentemailvideo-presencehybrid

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: the behaviours taught in FRM-013 Channel-Fit, FRM-014 Tone-in-Text, FRM-015 Video Presence and FRM-016 the AI era.

⚠️ This instrument was written by Zeducation to match the house style of ACT-002 How Assertive Am I?. Module 5 of the Effective Communication workbook has no self-assessment of its own. It is a teaching mirror, not a validated measure. Do not use it for selection, performance management or reporting.

The instrument

Answer honestly. Nobody collects this.

5 = always · 4 = often · 3 = sometimes · 2 = rarely · 1 = never

#StatementScore
1I think about which channel a message belongs in before I send it
2⟲ I have delivered bad news or criticism by text or chat
3My subject lines tell the reader the topic and what I need
4My first line contains the main point or the ask
5I re-read a message as the person receiving it before I send
6⟲ People reply to my messages asking what I meant
7I open with something human before the ask
8My camera is at eye level on video calls
9I look at the lens when I speak, not at my own face
10I use people's names on calls to bring quiet people in
11⟲ I have sent an AI-drafted message without editing it into my own voice
12I check the facts in anything AI drafts for me before it goes out
Total

⟲ = reverse-scored. For items 2, 6 and 11, flip your answer before adding it up: 5→1, 4→2, 3→3, 2→4, 1→5.

Your score

RangeWhat it meansYour next step
50-60People get a clear, warm, credible version of you through a screen. That is rarer than it soundsFix it for your team next. Agree two channel norms with them this month
38-49Strong on some channels, weaker on others. Usually good at email and rough on video, or the reverseFind your weak channel from the item numbers and pick one habit from it
25-37Your messages get there, but they cost the reader effort and sometimes a follow-upStart with item 4. First line, main point, every message, for two weeks
12-24The screen is doing your talking for you and you have not had a say in itPick one thing: put your camera at eye level today. It takes two minutes and a couple of books, and it changes every call you make from now on

Facilitating it

  • Best run at the end of the module, as the reflection. The items double as a summary of everything

taught

  • Item 8 is the one that gets fixed fastest. Point it out: it is the cheapest score improvement on the

sheet

  • Items 11 and 12 will make some learners uncomfortable. Say early that most people in the room use

AI, that the study found real benefits, and that the question is only about what you do with the draft

  • Do not read scores out. Ask: "which item are you fixing before your next call?"

Watch out for

  • Learners who do not use video at work will score low on 8, 9 and 10 for reasons that are not about

them. Tell them to skip those three and score out of 45, with bands adjusted by three quarters, or just treat it as a checklist

  • Item 2 is a confession. Do not push anyone to share it
  • Learners who do not use AI at all should score 5 on item 11 (reverse-scored to 5) and 5 on item 12

by default, or skip both

10-15 minassessmentself-assessmentrelationshipsnetworkingwork-readinessprofessionalismhouse-content

Type: self-assessment · Time: 10-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: the habits in FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits and the reach described by FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties.

This is house content. The ten statements and the score bands are taken exactly as written from the Building Effective Work Relationships SKILL UP resource (SRC-004). Do not reword them without a reason.

How to run it

  1. Circle the number for each statement that best describes you.
  2. Total the ten numbers.
  3. Find your total on the score chart.

The instrument

Circle the number for each question which best describes you.

#StatementNot really meSometimes meUsually me
1I actively look for chances to get to know people beyond my immediate team123
2I can usually tell if someone feels safe, respectful and positive to be around123
3I start small conversations with new people at work, events or in class123
4I treat everyone with respect, no matter their role or status123
5People can trust me to keep private or sensitive information confidential123
6I avoid gossip and try not to talk about others behind their backs123
7I don't only contact people when I need something. I also check in or offer help123
8I follow up with people (messages, emails, LinkedIn) to keep relationships warm123
9I am willing to receive feedback about how I work with others and use it to improve123
10I am involved, or taking steps to get involved, in at least one network beyond my immediate workplace or class (alumni, professional group, community, online)123

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move
24-30You are actively and consistently building healthy professional relationshipsPick the one statement you scored lowest on. That is the growth edge
18-23You have a good base, with a few areas to strengthenChoose two statements to work on this month. Two, not five
10-17You are still developing these habitsStart with one simple change from this topic. The easiest place to begin is the shy starter: eye contact, a nod, and one short conversation a day

What the questions are really asking

Worth naming after people have scored, because it turns a number into a map.

QuestionsWhat they measureWhere to go next
1, 3, 10Reach. Do you have ties beyond your immediate circle?FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties
4, 5, 6Trustworthiness. Are you safe to be around?FRM-022 The Trust Equation
7, 8Warmth over time. Do you keep ties alive, or only use them?FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits
2, 9Self-awareness. Can you read a room and take feedback on yourself?FRM-021, the Feedback habit

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody reads out their score. Say so before they start
  • Watch for the shy learner reading a low score as a personality verdict. It is not. Every one of

the ten is a behaviour, and behaviours can be started on Monday. The lowest band deliberately names the smallest possible first step

  • Question 8 lands badly with some groups. Learners who are not on LinkedIn and do not email can

feel the instrument is not for them. Say clearly that a text, a message on the way past, or a word after church all count

  • The most useful debrief question is question 7. "Do you only contact people when you want

something?" is the one that tends to go quiet, and it is the one most worth sitting with

  • ⚠️ This instrument is not validated. It is a teaching mirror, not a measure. Fine for the room,

not for reporting

Circle the number for each question which best describes you.

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move
24-30You are actively and consistently leading in a collaborative wayKeep modelling it and share what works. Then pick your lowest single statement
18-23A good foundation, with a few habits to strengthenChoose one or two areas to focus on. One is better than two

What the questions map to

QuestionsWhat they measureWhere to go next

Where Is My Team Right Now?

12-15 minassessmentteamsteam-developmentself-assessmentleadershipdiagnosis

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: which stage of FRM-018 Tuckman your team is actually in. Unlike most instruments here it is not scored on a scale. You tick what is true and count the columns.

⚠️ Not validated. It is a teaching mirror, not a measure. Fine for the room, not for reporting.

How to run it

Tick every statement that is true of your team right now. Be honest rather than hopeful. Then count the ticks in each block.

Block F

  • ☐ People are still polite and careful with each other
  • ☐ Most decisions come from the person in charge
  • ☐ I am not completely sure what some people's jobs are
  • ☐ Nobody has really disagreed with anyone yet

Block S

  • ☐ There is tension about who does what
  • ☐ People agree in the meeting and complain afterwards
  • ☐ Small groups have formed and they do not mix much
  • ☐ Someone has said, or nearly said, "that's not my job"

Block N

  • ☐ People say "we usually do it like this"
  • ☐ New people get shown how things work here without being told to
  • ☐ Someone can raise a problem without it becoming an argument
  • ☐ We have sorted out most of who does what

Block P

  • ☐ People disagree openly and it does not damage anything
  • ☐ Work gets done when the boss is away
  • ☐ People step in for each other without being asked
  • ☐ We talk about the result, not about whose fault it is

Block A

  • ☐ This work is ending or the team is changing soon
  • ☐ People are talking about what comes next
  • ☐ Nobody has said anything about what we achieved together

Ticks: F ___ S ___ N ___ P ___ A ___

Reading it

ResultWhat it meansYour first move
One block clearly highestThat is your stageGo to that row in ACT-032 Stage Moves and pick one action
F and S both highVery common, and usually means the team is storming quietlyThe work is making it safe to disagree out loud. Start with psychological safety
N and P both highGood position. The risk is coastingWrite the norms down before the next person joins or leaves
Spread evenly across allUsually means different parts of the team are in different placesAsk who is in which. It is often the newest people in Forming while everyone else has moved on
A ticked at allSomething is ending, and it is probably not being handledSay something out loud about what the team did. It costs nothing and people remember it for years

Facilitator notes

  • There is no good or bad stage. Say that before people start, or Forming and Storming get read

as failure and the answers stop being honest

  • The most useful follow-up question: "would your team give the same answers?" Most learners are

rating the team they wish they had

  • Watch for the person rating a team they have just left. Let them. It is often the most honest

reading in the room, and it usually explains why they left

  • Use it twice. Once now, once in three months. The movement is more informative than the reading

Circle the number that best describes you.

1I say people's names correctly, and I ask if I am not sure123
2I speak to people the same way regardless of their role or status123

4I do not talk about people who are not in the room123
5I do what I said I would do, by when I said it123
6I let people finish before I reply123
7I give credit to the person who actually did the work123
8I ask the quieter people what they think, by name123
9I am the same person under pressure as I am on a good day123
10If someone copied how I behave at work this week, I would be happy with that123

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move
24-30People around you are learning good habits by watching you, which is the strongest kind of leadership there isPick your lowest single statement. That is the one someone has already noticed
18-23A solid base, with a few habits that slip when you are busyLook at statement 9. Most people in this band score well on a good day and badly under pressure. That gap is the work
10-17These habits are still forming, and every one of them can be started this weekChoose statement 1 or 5. They are the two easiest to change and the two people notice fastest

The question that matters

Statement 10 is the whole instrument in one line. If it is the lowest number on your page, ignore the total and work on whatever made you circle it.

Ask it the other way round too: somebody junior to you is already copying something you do. What is it? Most people can answer that, and the answer is not always comfortable. That is the honest start of this topic.

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statements 4 and 9 are confronting and people will not answer

honestly if they think it is going to be read out

  • Link straight into W-H-O. The lowest-scoring statement becomes the H for

ACT-033. That turns a score into a commitment inside ten minutes, which is the point of running it

  • Statement 9 is the one to discuss as a group, in general terms. Everybody is respectful when

things are calm. Respect under pressure is the only kind that counts, and the framework's own line covers it: under pressure we do not rise to the level of our intentions, we fall to the level of our habits

  • Do not use it with a team to rate each other. It is self-report only. A peer version would need

far more care than a workshop allows
