What's My Default Style?

12-15 minassessmentdecision-makingleadershipself-assessmentstylescollaboration

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: which of Lewin's three styles you fall back on, especially under pressure.

⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. Written in house to match the other Zeducation instruments.

The instrument

For each situation, tick the response closest to what you actually do, not what you would like to do.

#When…ABC
1A decision needs making and time is shortI decide and tell peopleI grab two people for a quick viewI let whoever is closest to it decide
2Someone asks "what do you reckon we should do?"I tell themI ask what they reckon firstI say "up to you"
3The team disagrees with a call I madeI explain why it standsI ask what I have missedI let them change it
4A new person is unsure how to do a taskI show them the way we do itI show them, then ask what they would changeI let them work it out
5Something has gone wrongI sort it, then tell peopleI get the people involved togetherI leave it with the people involved
6I am planning next month's workI plan it and share the planI draft it and ask for input before finalisingI ask the team to plan it
7Under real pressure, my instinct istake controlpull people inget out of the way

Count your ticks: A ___ B ___ C ___

Reading it

MostlyYour defaultWhat it gets youYour risk
AAutocratic, "my way"Speed and clarity. People always know where they standPeople stop bringing you things. You end up the only one thinking
BDemocratic, "our way"Ownership and better decisionsSlower. If overused you can read as unable to decide alone
CLaissez-faire, "your way"Space for capable people to growConfusion and silos if roles and goals are not already clear
Even spreadYou are already choosing per situationThis is the goalCheck question 7. Under pressure most people still have one default

Question 7 is the real result

Everything above question 7 is what you do when things are calm. Question 7 is what you do when they are not, and that is the style your team actually experiences, because pressure is when leadership gets noticed.

If your answers to 1 to 6 are spread and question 7 is a hard A, you are a democratic leader who becomes autocratic under load. That is extremely common, it is not a character flaw, and it is worth telling your team so they can read you.

Facilitator notes

  • There is no winning column. Say it before people start. Lewin found democratic produced the

best outcomes overall, and question 1 has a right answer that is not democratic

  • The most useful follow-up: "what would your team say your default is?" Ask people to guess,

then to actually go and ask someone. The reports back are the best material in this topic

  • Do not have people share their letters in front of their manager. Column A is easy to read as a

criticism

  • Pair it with ACT-050 Whose Call Is It?, run

first. People assess themselves more honestly once they have seen that all three styles are legitimate

Circle the number that best describes you.

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move

The top band is deliberately worded that way. In this instrument a high score is not a good result, and learners who are used to being praised for exactly these behaviours need that said plainly.

StatementsDriverWhat helps
2, 8Desire to helpHabit 1, the helpful no. Offer something smaller instead of everything
3, 4Need for accomplishmentHabit 3. Check it against your goals before you answer
6, 9FearName it. Fear of missing out, of losing control, of what people will think
5, 7, 10You have become the bottleneckHabit 2. Delegate and grow others. This is the most urgent one

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statements 6 and 8 are personal
  • The 3 to 5% statistic first. Give people the research before the instrument, or a high score

reads as a personal weakness rather than a predictable outcome of being good and willing

  • Statement 10 is the leader's question. If a whole team scores high on it, the organisation has

a design problem, not ten individual problems

  • If someone is clearly not coping, this is a conversation, not a worksheet. Know your referral

options before you run it: EAP if the workplace has one, their GP, or 1737, the free national helpline, call or text

This is house content, taken as written from the Cultural Safety in the Workplace SKILL UP resource (SRC-006). It is the longest instrument in the library, 18 items on a 1 to 5 scale.

Scale: 1 = Never · 2 = Rarely · 3 = Sometimes · 4 = Often · 5 = Always

Section 1 — Cultural Awareness

Safety subtotal (max 30): ______

Your profile

Score
Cultural Awareness____ / 30

Cultural Safety____ / 30

Interpreting each section:

ScoreWhat it means
24-30Strong and consistent
18-23Developing, with clear progress
12-17Early stage. Choose two habits to build now
0-11Starting out. Begin with simple daily practices

Reading the shape, not the total

Do not add the three sections together. The pattern is the result.

PatternWhat it usually meansWhere to go
Awareness high, Competence and Safety lowThe most common profile. You can see it and you have not built anythingFRM-034 S.A.F.E, the S and E steps
Competence high, Safety lowYou know the protocols and people still do not feel safe. This is the important one, and it is a power question rather than a knowledge oneFRM-033, the Curtis et al. section

Facilitator notes

  • Statement 16 is the trap, and it is deliberate. *"Team members say they can be themselves here

without penalty."* You cannot answer that. Only they can. Ramsden's whole point is that cultural safety is judged by the recipient. Say this out loud when people reach it, and treat any high score on 16 that is not based on someone actually saying so as a guess

  • Nobody shares scores. Especially not in front of their own team
  • The best follow-up is a real one: run statement 17 for a week. "Did you feel respected today?"

Then compare what you hear with what you scored

  • ⚠️ Not validated. A teaching mirror, not a measure. Fine for the room, not for reporting, and

definitely not for assessing whether an organisation is culturally safe

  • Watch the room. In a mixed group, people who have been on the receiving end of the failures in

this instrument are doing unpaid emotional work while their manager fills it in. Do not ask anyone to help their manager score it

How Do I Handle Conflict?

12-15 minassessmentconflictconflict-resolutionself-assessmentde-escalationlisteningcommunication

Type: self-assessment · Time: 12-15 min · Group: individual · Energy: low

What it measures: what you actually do when conflict turns up, across the four things this programme teaches: noticing, listening, responding and resolving.

⚠️ Not validated, and written fresh. The Future Ready: Conflict Resolution guide (SRC-007) contains no self-assessment, which was the largest gap in it. This instrument was written in house to match the Zeducation shape. It is a teaching mirror, not a measure.

The instrument

Circle the number that best describes you.

#StatementNot really meSometimes meUsually me
1I deal with disagreements early, while they are still small123
2I can tell the difference between a problem with the work and a problem with the person123
3When someone is upset with me, I let them finish before I explain123
4I ask what matters to the other person, not just what happened123
5I say something out loud about how the other person is feeling123
6I notice what my own face and body are doing in a tense conversation123
7I stay calm when someone raises their voice at me123
8I ask the other person how they would like it resolved, before I suggest anything123
9I can take a break in a conversation without it feeling like giving up123
10I go back and check whether a resolution actually held123

My total: _______ / 30

Score chart

ScoreWhat it meansYour first move
24-30You handle conflict deliberately rather than by reflexPick your lowest single statement. It is probably 5, 8 or 10
18-23A good base, and some of it disappears when the pressure goes upLook at statements 3, 6 and 7 together. That cluster is what goes first
10-17Conflict is mostly happening to you rather than being handledStart with statement 1. Dealing with one small thing early is the cheapest change on this page

What the questions map to

QuestionsWhat they measureWhere to go
1, 2Noticing and naming. Do you know what kind of conflict you are in?FRM-037 The Three Types
3, 4, 5Listening past the words. Content, values, feelingsFRM-038 Powerful Listening
5, 6, 7, 9Staying steady and respondingFRM-039, FRM-041 De-escalation
8, 10Resolving, and checking it heldFRM-040 Moving to Resolution

The two statements worth talking about

Statement 1 is the highest-leverage item in the instrument. Nearly every conflict in this programme's case studies became difficult because it was left. It is also the one people score themselves generously on, so ask the follow-up: what is the thing you are currently not dealing with?

Statement 10 is the one almost nobody scores well on, and it is invisible. Most people treat a resolved conflict as finished. Going back a fortnight later and asking "did that actually work?" is rare, cheap, and the reason some resolutions hold and others quietly do not.

Facilitator notes

  • Nobody shares their score. Statement 7 in particular is personal
  • Run it early, not late. It works better as a map at the start of the programme than as a

verdict at the end. If you have time, run it twice and let people see the movement

  • Watch for the low scorer reading it as a character verdict. Every item is a behaviour, and the

lowest band names the smallest possible first step on purpose

  • Statement 7 can be heavy for anyone who has faced real aggression at work. It is a skill

question, not a courage question, and the answer for genuine aggression is to leave and get help. See the safety note on FRM-041

  • This is not part of the micro-credential. It carries no assessment weight and should not be

uploaded as evidence

What Do You Actually Believe About People?

20 minassessmentleadershipassumptionstrustmotivationself-assessmentmindset

Type: self-assessment · Time: 20 min · Group: individual, then whole room · Energy: low

What it practises: FRM-045 McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y.

⚠️ Run it before you teach the framework, not after. If people know which answers are the "right" ones, they will give you those and learn nothing.

The statements

Tick agree or disagree. First reaction. Do not think about it.

StatementAgreeDisagree
1Most people would rather be told what to do than take responsibility☐☐
2If you don't check, it doesn't get done☐☐
3People are mostly here for the money☐☐
4Most people want to do a good job☐☐
5Given the chance, people will take on more than you asked☐☐
6You have to earn trust before you get it☐☐
7If someone is underperforming, they usually know why☐☐
8Most problems at work are people problems☐☐
9If you give people freedom, most will use it well☐☐
10The best way to get performance is clear consequences☐☐

Scoring. Give yourself one point for each agree on 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 10. Give yourself one point for each disagree on 4, 5, 7, 9.

Your score: ____ out of 10

ScoreWhat it suggests
0-3You lean strongly Theory Y. Watch that you are not confusing trust with an absence of standards
4-6Mixed, which is where most working supervisors land. Worth knowing which statements pushed you which way
7-10You lean Theory X. That is not a character flaw and it may be an accurate read of your workplace. It is worth knowing you are running it

How to run it

  1. Statements first, cold (5 min). No framing, no theory, no context. "Just tick"
  2. Score it (2 min). Do not reveal what the scale is yet
  3. Now teach Theory X and Theory Y (7 min).

The room works out what they just scored, and the recognition is the moment the session works

  1. The two questions (6 min). Individually, in writing:
    • Which single statement would you most like to be wrong about?
    • What would you have to see to change your mind on it?

Statement 6 is the interesting one

"You have to earn trust before you get it."

Most rooms agree with it almost unanimously, and it sounds like plain common sense. Then ask:

Your new starter walks in on day one. Do they start on zero and earn their way up, or do they start with a full tank and spend it?

Both are defensible. But a leader who starts everyone on zero has to be told everything twice before they believe it, and their team learns that fast. This one statement usually generates more discussion than the other nine combined.

Debrief

Ask these to the room, not to individuals.

  • Which statement did the room split on most?
  • Think of a workplace where Theory X was the correct read. What made it correct?
  • Has anyone ever had a manager decide you were a Theory X employee? What did that do?
  • The real one: does your team think you are running X or Y? Would they be right?

Variations

  • Two-corners version: read each statement aloud and have people physically move to the agree

wall or the disagree wall. Faster, more honest, and you can see the splits

  • Team version: the whole team fills it in anonymously about the workplace, not about

themselves: "around here, it is assumed that…". The result is a culture reading

  • Manager and team version: the leader predicts their team's average score, then the team scores

it. The gap is the finding, and it is usually a big one

  • Low literacy: read the statements aloud, thumbs up or thumbs down, eyes closed

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ This is not a test with a right answer, and learners will assume it is. Say so before and

after. McGregor leaned Theory Y, and a high X score is information, not a verdict

  • ⚠️ Some learners supervise people they genuinely cannot trust. Sometimes for good reasons,

sometimes because of the workplace rather than the people. Do not push them to recant in the room

  • The socially acceptable score. Once anyone works out which way the scale runs, the answers get

nicer. This is why the statements come first

  • Do not let it become a diagnosis of an absent manager. Fun, useless. Bring it back to *"and

which one am I running?"*

What's My Code?

30-40 minassessmentcareer-readinessriasecintereststahatujob-searchwork-readiness

Type: assessment, on the real tool · Time: 30-40 min · Group: individual, with devices · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-056 RIASEC, using Tahatū's interest quiz.

⚠️ This activity uses somebody else's tool on purpose. Zeducation does not have 800 career profiles with New Zealand pay and demand data, and never will. Tahatū does, it is free, and it is kept current. Our job is the twenty minutes either side of the quiz, which is where the value is.

Before the session

  • [ ] Check the devices and the wifi. This activity dies without them
  • [ ] Run the quiz yourself and know your own code, so you can go first
  • [ ] Have a plan for anyone without a device: pair them up, no comment
  • [ ] Read FRM-056's evidence audit so you can answer "is

this like those Facebook quizzes?" honestly

How to run it

1. Frame it before anyone opens a laptop (5 min). This sentence decides whether the activity helps or harms:

"This tells you what you're drawn to. It does not tell you what you'd be good at, and it's only a weak guide to whether you'd be happy. What it's actually good for is giving you words, and showing you jobs you've never heard of. Nobody in here is going to be defined by four letters."

2. Take the quiz (10 min). tahatu.govt.nz · Everyone works alone. Quiet room.

3. Write down three things (5 min):
My top letters______
One job on my list I had never heard of______________________
One job on my list that surprised me______________________

4. Go to the career profiles (10 min). This is the part that matters. Pick one job from the list and find:

  • What it actually pays in New Zealand
  • What you need to get in — a ticket, a licence, a qualification, or nothing
  • Whether anyone is hiring

5. Pairs (5 min). Tell your partner the job you looked up and one thing that surprised you.

6. Close (5 min). "What do you want to look up tonight?"

Step 4 is the whole activity

The quiz is a doorway. The career profiles are the room.

A learner who leaves knowing their code has got a souvenir. A learner who leaves knowing that a diesel mechanic apprenticeship pays what it pays, and takes what it takes, has got something they can act on.

➜ If time is short, cut the quiz, not step 4. Have them search a job they are already curious about.

Debrief

  • Who got a result that felt wrong? What did it miss?
  • What is one job on the list nobody in here had heard of?
  • Did anyone's list have something they have always wanted to do and never said?
  • The important one: what would you have to find out to take that seriously?

Variations

  • No devices: print six type descriptions, put them in six corners, have people stand in the one

that sounds most like them, then second-most. Crude, fast, and it still opens the conversation

  • Whānau version: homework is to have a family member guess your code before you tell them. The

gap is usually interesting

  • Employer version: with a group already in work, run it as "what part of your current job do you

actually like?" rather than as career change

  • Youth version: the surprise job is the hook. Run step 4 as a race to find the strangest real job

with a real salary

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never let a code become a verdict. "I'm not a Social so I shouldn't do support work" is the

failure mode, and it can steer somebody away from a career they would be good at. Interests are not ability

  • ⚠️ Interests are limited by exposure. A learner who has never met an engineer will not test

toward engineering. For people whose exposure has been narrow, the quiz partly measures what they have been shown. Say so

  • ⚠️ Watch the gendered pull. Realistic skews male, Social skews female, mostly because of how

people are raised. Do not let a result quietly move a young woman away from a trade or a young man away from care work

  • ⚠️ Somebody's result will land badly, especially anyone who has been out of work a long time,

or whose list is full of jobs needing study they cannot afford. Have the next step ready: what is on the list that needs a ticket rather than a degree?

  • The learner who says "it's rubbish". Sometimes they are right and the quiz missed them. Agree,

and go to step 4 with a job they choose themselves

Statement Sort — Four Corners

12-15 mingameicebreakerenergisercommunication-stylesassertiveness

Type: game / energiser · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class · Energy: high

What it practises: recognising FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles in real language

Materials: four A4 signs — PASSIVE, AGGRESSIVE, PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE, ASSERTIVE — one in each corner of the room. The statement list below.

Set up

Put the four signs up before the session starts. People will read them on the way in, which is half the teaching done already.

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in the middle.
  2. Read a statement out loud, in character.
  3. Learners walk to the corner they think it belongs to. No talking on the way.
  4. Once they are in corners, ask one person from the biggest corner and one from the smallest: what

made you pick that?

  1. Give the answer, then read the next one. Twelve statements takes about ten minutes.

The statements

#StatementStyle
1"It's fine… I'll just do it myself."Passive-aggressive
2"You never do this right, I have to fix it every time."Aggressive
3"I can't take on extra work today, but I can help tomorrow."Assertive
4"Whatever you think… it doesn't matter to me."Passive
5"We need to follow the safety checks before starting."Assertive
6"Hurry up! You're slowing everyone down."Aggressive
7"I'd like to finish what I'm saying before we move on."Assertive
8"It's okay, I guess… I'll manage."Passive
9"You're hopeless at this job."Aggressive
10"I understand you're busy, but I need this report by 3pm."Assertive
11"Sure, I'll do it. Just like last time when no one helped me."Passive-aggressive
12"Oh, don't worry about me… I'm used to picking up the slack."Passive-aggressive

Facilitator: read them with the tone. Number 1 said flatly is passive-aggressive; said with genuine warmth it is not. That is the whole lesson and it lands better if they hear it than if you say it.

Debrief

  • Which ones split the room? Why?
  • How much of your decision was the words, and how much was my tone?
  • Which of these have you heard this week? Which have you said?

The point to land: the same words can be three different styles depending on how they are said. Assertive is not a script you memorise, it is words plus tone plus intent lining up.

Variations

  • Small room / online: four zoom reactions, or hold up 1-4 fingers instead of moving
  • Youth: swap in text messages and group chat lines
  • Competitive version: teams score a point per correct corner, best of twelve
  • Closer, not opener: run it again at the end of the session and see how much faster the room is

Watch out for

  • Do not let it become "which corner is the smart one". Every corner is a real thing people do
  • Nobody gets singled out for standing in the wrong corner. Ask for reasoning, not defence
  • Watch mobility. Offer the fingers version to anyone who would rather stay seated

Used by

ACT-005Activity · 03-Activities

The No Game

8-10 mingameicebreakerenergiserboundariessaying-noassertiveness

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: pairs · Energy: high Materials: none. Nothing to print, nothing to set up.

What it practises: the second assertive right — saying no without guilt. Warms up FRM-002 The Assert Approach.

How to run it

  1. Pairs. Person A asks Person B for anything at all: a lift home, their phone, their lunch, a

weekend shift, their car.

  1. Person B's only job is to say no. Every time. Sixty seconds, as many asks as A can fire out.
  2. Swap. Sixty seconds the other way.
  3. Round two: same thing, but B has to say no and stay friendly. No apologising, no long excuse,

no "maybe". Just a warm, clear no. Sixty seconds each.

Expect noise and laughter. That is the point.

Debrief

  • Which round was harder? Almost everyone says round two.
  • What did you notice yourself doing to soften it? (Apologising, explaining, going quiet, laughing.)
  • What did a good no sound like when you heard it?
  • Who in your real life do you find it hardest to say no to? Why that person?

The point to land: most of us do not struggle with the word. We struggle with the guilt that comes after it. Saying no to a request is not saying no to a person, and a clear no now saves an apology, a rushed job or a resentment later.

Variations

  • Youth: the asks get funnier and more outrageous, which is fine. It works better that way
  • Frontline: use real workplace asks — cover my shift, sign this off, come in Saturday
  • Online: breakout rooms in pairs, same timing
  • Extension: round three, B says "no, and here is what I can do instead". This is the bridge

straight into the Assert Approach

  • Cultural adaptation: in groups where a direct no to an elder is not appropriate, run round

three only and focus on the "no to the request, yes to the relationship" wording

Watch out for

  • Keep it fast. It dies if pairs start negotiating
  • Some learners genuinely cannot get the word out in round one. That is useful information for them,

not a failure. Name it gently and move on

  • Do not let asks get personal or target something someone actually needs

ACT-010Activity · 03-Activities

Whisper Chain — The Message That Didn't Land

10-12 mingameicebreakerenergiserclear-messaginglistening

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: lines of 6-8 · Energy: high

What it practises: why a message has to be built to survive the trip. Sets up FRM-005 BLUF.

Materials: two message cards, written out beforehand.

How to run it

  1. Two lines of 6-8 people. Everyone faces forward.
  2. Give the person at the front of each line the same message card, written down. They read it,

then whisper it once to the next person. No repeats, no questions.

  1. Last person says out loud what they received.
  2. Read out the original.

Round 1 message (the rambler):

"Hey, so the boss reckons the delivery might come Thursday instead of Wednesday, but only if the weather holds, and if it doesn't, we'll need someone to stay back Friday, probably Sione, but check with him first."

Round 2 message (BLUF):

"Delivery moved to Thursday. If it rains, Sione stays back Friday. Confirm with Sione today."

Round 1 comes out mangled. Round 2 usually survives almost intact. That contrast is the entire teaching point and you do not have to explain it, they will see it.

Debrief

  • Which round survived? Why?
  • What got lost first in round one? (Usually the action, which is buried at the end.)
  • Where does this happen for real at your work?
  • Whose job is it to make sure the message lands, the sender or the receiver?

The point to land: a message is not finished when you have said it. It is finished when it has landed. Short, ordered and specific messages survive the trip. Rambling ones do not, and they were never going to.

Variations

  • Small group: one line, run both messages through the same line
  • Online: private chat one person to the next, same rules, no copy and paste
  • Harder: add background noise, which is closer to a real site anyway
  • Extension: groups rewrite round one's message so it would have survived, then test it on the

other line

Watch out for

  • Someone will try to repeat or clarify. That is the game working, not a rule break. Note it and

hold the rule, then raise it in the debrief: asking for a repeat is exactly what people do not do at work

  • Keep the messages work-relevant, not silly sentences. The point is a real message failing
  • Do not single out whoever "broke" the chain. Nobody broke it. The message did

ACT-011Activity · 03-Activities

Bury the Lede Race

8-10 mingameicebreakerenergiserblufclear-messaging

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: teams of 3-4 · Energy: high

What it practises: spotting the bottom line fast. Warms up FRM-005 BLUF.

Materials: four to six long, rambling messages printed on cards. Real ones from your own inbox work best, with names removed.

How to run it

  1. Teams of 3-4. Each team gets the same card face down.
  2. On "go", they turn it over, find the one sentence that is the real bottom line, and one person

stands up and reads only that sentence.

  1. First team standing with the correct sentence wins the round.
  2. Five rounds, keep score.
  3. Final round, reversed: give every team the same bare bottom line and 60 seconds to write the

most buried, waffliest version of it they can. Read them out. This one gets the biggest laugh and makes the point harder than any of the serious rounds.

Debrief

  • What were you scanning for? (Most people say a verb, a deadline or a name.)
  • How long did it take you to find it? Now imagine 60 unread messages
  • In the reverse round, what were the tricks you used to bury it? Do you do any of those for real?

The point to land: you just did in ten seconds what your reader does in two. If your point is not findable that fast, it is not landing. And notice how easy it was to bury it on purpose. Most buried messages are not written to confuse, they are written by someone thinking out loud.

Variations

  • Youth: use group chat messages and captions
  • Frontline: use real site emails, notices and text messages
  • Online: messages in chat, teams race in breakout rooms, first to post the sentence
  • Quiet groups: teams write the sentence on a card and hold it up instead of standing

Watch out for

  • Use real messages, but scrub names, companies and anything identifiable. Never use a message from

someone in the room

  • Keep rounds short. It dies if teams start debating
  • The reverse round can tip into mocking a particular writing style. Keep it about the message

ACT-017Activity · 03-Activities

The Yes Pile

10-12 mingameboundariessaying-noworkloadicebreakeropener

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, works from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-008 The Positive No and the whole of TOP-COM-004.

Materials: a stack of sticky notes or scrap paper per person, pens.

How to run it

  1. Write the yeses (3 min). Everyone writes down one thing per note that they have said yes to

in the last two weeks. Work, home, church, sport, family, friends. Anything they agreed to do. Push for volume: "keep going, one per note, don't think too hard."

  1. Build the pile (2 min). Everyone puts their notes in a single pile in the middle of the table,

or up on the wall. It gets big fast, and that is the point.

  1. Take back three (3 min). Everyone retrieves three of their own notes: the three they would

still say yes to if they could start the fortnight again.

  1. Look at what is left (2 min). Point at the pile still on the table. "That is the stuff you did

anyway."

The link back

Every one of those was a yes you gave to something, which means it was a no you gave to something else. You just did not get to choose what.

Saying yes to everything is not generous. It is a decision made by whoever asked first. The rest of this module is about making that decision on purpose.

Then go straight into the module opener: every leader has limits, the skill is holding them without damage.

Debrief

  • What kind of thing ended up in the leftover pile? (Watch for the pattern: the leftovers are usually

the things asked for in person, at short notice, by someone hard to refuse.)

  • Who was asking, for the ones you would take back?
  • Did anyone struggle to pick only three?

Variations

  • Small groups (under 6): skip the pile, just lay the notes out and count them
  • Online: a shared whiteboard with sticky notes, or everyone types their list in the chat but does

not send until you say go, then the wall of text lands all at once. That works surprisingly well

  • Low literacy: run it spoken. Go round the room, each person names one thing they said yes to,

keep going round until people run out. The count is the point, not the writing

  • Teams from one workplace: run it on work commitments only. The leftover pile becomes a real

conversation about workload that a manager can act on

Watch out for

  • It can get heavy. Some people will look at that pile and see their whole life. Keep the pace up

and land the point quickly rather than sitting in it

  • Do not let it become a moan about the boss. The point is that a yes is a choice, including the

ones that felt like they were not

  • Nobody reads out anyone else's note. Say so before you build the pile

ACT-022Activity · 03-Activities

Tell It Back

10-12 mingamelisteningparaphrasingicebreakeropenerempathy

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, works from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting and the whole of TOP-COM-005.

Materials: none.

How to run it

  1. Pair up (30 sec). Everyone pairs with someone they do not know well.
  2. Ninety seconds each (3 min). Person A tells Person B something true about themselves: how they

got into this work, the best thing about their weekend, who taught them something that stuck. Then swap. No note-taking. No questions. Just listening.

  1. Introduce your partner (5 min). Go round the room. Everyone introduces their partner to the

group, in the first person: "I'm Mere, and I got into this work because…" Speaking as them, not about them.

  1. One correction each. After each introduction, the person being introduced gets one sentence

to correct anything that was wrong.

The link back

Notice what happened. You did not need a notepad. You needed to actually be there for ninety seconds.

Then the two points that open the module:

  • The corrections were mostly small. Because when you actually listen, you get it right. Most

workplace misunderstandings are not hard problems, they are ninety seconds nobody gave

  • Being introduced accurately feels good. That feeling is what people mean when they say a leader

makes them feel heard. It is not a personality trait, it is a thing you just did

Then go into the module opener: we think leading is about talking, but the best leaders are the best listeners.

Debrief

  • How did it feel to hear yourself described by someone else?
  • Who got a detail right that they were not told directly? (Someone always picks up a feeling or an

emphasis rather than a fact. That is Level 3 listening, and you can name it later.)

  • What did you notice yourself doing while your partner was talking? Were you listening, or getting

ready to remember?

Variations

  • Groups who already know each other: the topic becomes "something about you that most people here

do not know", which is a better icebreaker anyway

  • Online: works well in breakout rooms, then introductions in the main room. Ask people to turn

cameras on for the introduction of their partner

  • Very shy groups or low literacy: drop the first-person framing, which is the part that raises

the stakes. "Tell us about your partner" is enough

  • Large rooms (over 20): do introductions in groups of six rather than to the whole room, or it

takes twenty minutes

Watch out for

  • The remembering trap. Some learners will concentrate so hard on memorising that they stop

listening. That is a gift for the debrief. Ask who did it, and connect it to Level 1 listening: your attention was on your own performance

  • Nobody shares anything real if the room is cold. Model it first with your own ninety seconds,

and make it specific

  • Consent. Say before you start that they should only share what they are happy to have repeated

to the room. Then hold that line

ACT-029Activity · 03-Activities

Read The Room Cold

8-10 mingamedigital-communicationtone-in-texticebreakeropenerhybrid

Type: game / opener · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, works from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-014 Tone-in-Text and the whole of TOP-COM-006.

Materials: eight short messages on cards, or written up on the whiteboard one at a time.

The messages

Short, ordinary, and genuinely ambiguous. These work:

#Message
1"Fine."
2"Can you come see me when you get in."
3"Interesting."
4"Thanks."
5"Noted."
6"K"
7"We should talk about the report."
8"Sure, whatever works."

How to run it

  1. Show one message (10 sec). One at a time, on the board or held up.
  2. Everyone votes with their hands. Three options, called out fast:
    • One hand up = they are happy or neutral
    • Two hands up = they are annoyed
    • Arms crossed = something is wrong and I would be worried
  3. Look around the room. Do not discuss. Just look at the split, then move to the next one.
  4. Run all eight in about four minutes. Pace matters. It should feel like a quiz, not a seminar.

The room will split badly on almost every message, and the splits are the whole game.

The link back

Same words. Same eight messages. And this room could not agree on a single one of them.

Then the point that opens the module:

  • The sender knew exactly what they meant every time. They always do. What they did not know is

that half of you would read it the other way

  • Kruger and colleagues (2005) tested this properly: people overestimate both their ability to

send tone in writing and their ability to read it. You hear your own message in the tone you meant, and you cannot un-hear it

  • When people are unsure, they assume the worst. Watch how many hands went up for "annoyed" on

perfectly innocent messages

Then go into the module opener: screens strip out a lot, and a quick message can land far harder than you meant.

Debrief

  • Which message had the biggest split?
  • Item 6, "K": ask who reads that as rude. Then ask them how old they are. The age split on this one is

usually visible across the room and it is a good, light way into the point that the reader brings their own rules

  • Has anyone here misread a message from their boss and worried about it for a day? (Someone always

has. Item 2 is the one that does it.)

  • What extra information would have settled it? (Tone of voice. Their face. Knowing what kind of day

they were having. All the things text removes.)

Variations

  • Real messages: ask three learners to volunteer a genuinely ambiguous message they have received.

More powerful, but check they are comfortable before it goes on the board

  • Online: run the vote through the reactions or a poll. The split shows as a number, which is even

clearer than hands

  • Team version: use messages in the team's actual style, from their actual channel. The splits get

uncomfortable in a productive way

  • Youth: group chat messages, read receipts and one-word replies. They will have strong opinions

and a lot of evidence

Watch out for

  • It turning into a session about one person's boss. Keep it on the cards
  • Do not let anyone identify who sent a real message if you run that variation
  • Pace. Ten seconds per message. If you discuss each one as you go, the cumulative effect is lost,

and the cumulative effect is the point

ACT-035Activity · 03-Activities

Six Degrees Of This Room

10-12 mingamenetworkingweak-tiesicebreakeropenerrelationshipswork-readiness

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: high

What it sets up: FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties. It makes the group's own hidden network visible, which is far more convincing than the research.

Materials: a ball of string or wool if you want the picture. It works without.

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in a circle (1 min).
  2. First person holds the end of the string and names something specific about themselves: a

suburb they grew up in, a job they have had, a sport, a church, a school, a country their family is from.

  1. Anyone who shares it puts a hand up. The first person throws the ball to one of them, keeping

hold of their end. The catcher now names something new about themselves.

  1. Keep going for six or seven minutes. The web builds across the circle. Do not let people only

throw to their mates. If nobody puts a hand up, they name something else.

  1. Stop and look at it. Everyone holds their string tight so the web is visible.

The link back

Ask two questions, in this order.

"Put your hand up if you learned something about someone you already knew."

Most hands go up.

"Now look at the string. How many of those lines go to someone you would call a close friend?"

Almost none of them.

Then land it:

Those lines are weak ties, and they are the most useful thing in this room. Not because they are deep, but because each one goes somewhere you cannot get to on your own. Somebody here knows somebody who is hiring. You just do not know which one yet.

Then go into the research: Granovetter, 1973, 282 men, and the finding that the job came from the acquaintance far more often than the close friend.

Debrief

  • What surprised you about who you had something in common with?
  • Which connection in this room could actually be useful to you, and for what?
  • Who in your life is a weak tie you have not spoken to in six months?

That last question is the one to close on, because it leads straight into a real action.

Variations

  • No string: run it as "stand up if". Same effect, less picture, and it works with 30 people
  • Small groups (under 8): each person names three things, and the group counts the overlaps
  • Online: use the chat. Each person types one thing, others react with an emoji if they share it.

The overlap is visible in the reaction counts

  • Low literacy: it is spoken already. No change needed
  • Work teams: restrict it to work history and previous employers. The web that appears is

effectively the team's real professional network, and it is usually much bigger than anyone thought

Watch out for

  • Do not let it get personal. Keep prompts to places, jobs, sports, schools, food. Not family

circumstances, not health, not money

  • The person nobody connects to. It happens, and it stings. Have a couple of broad prompts ready

("who has ever worked a weekend shift?") so everyone is in the web before you stop

  • Untangling the string takes longer than you think. Budget two minutes or take a photo and drop

it

ACT-036Activity · 03-Activities

Red Flag Or Green Flag?

12-15 mingamerelationshipsboundariesprofessionalismgossipicebreakeropenertrust

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: high

What it sets up: the red flags half of FRM-021 The Four Professional Habits, and it works just as well as a trust opener for FRM-022 The Trust Equation.

Materials: a RED FLAG sign on one wall and a GREEN FLAG sign on the other. Or just point.

How to run it

  1. Explain it (1 min). You read out a situation. Everyone walks to the wall that matches what

they think. No standing in the middle.

  1. Read a situation. Everyone moves.
  2. Ask two people why, one from each wall. Never argue with an answer. Just get the reasoning out.
  3. Move on quickly. Ten situations in ten minutes. Pace is what keeps the energy up.

The situations

The good ones are the ones the room splits on. Six of these are designed to split.

#SituationWhere it usually lands
1A workmate tells you something personal about another workmateRed, and fast
2You add your new supervisor on InstagramSplits. This is the best one in the list
3You only ever eat lunch with the same three peopleSplits. Most people say green until someone names cliques
4Someone messages you out of the blue asking for a job reference, and you have not heard from them in two yearsSplits
5You tell your team leader you are struggling with the workloadGreen, though shy learners often say red
6A senior person tells you about their divorce on your second dayRed, but people find it hard to say why
7You say yes to every after-work drink because you want to fit inSplits
8You share something a colleague told you in confidence, with one other person you trustRed. The "just one person" is the whole lesson
9You ask the most experienced person on the crew to show you how they do itGreen
10You vent about your manager in the group chatSplits, and it usually splits by age

The link back

After the last one:

Nearly every red flag in that list started as something normal. Nobody sets out to be the gossip. They just told one person, once.

Then go to the six red flags in the topic: oversharing, romantic entanglements and drama, being too close to a small group, gossip, using people, and no clear boundaries. Most of the room has just argued their way to all six on their own, which is a far better way to arrive at them than a slide.

Debrief

  • Which one did the room split on hardest? Why do you think that is?
  • Has anyone been on the wrong end of number 8?
  • Where is the line between being friendly and oversharing? (There is no clean answer. The

disagreement is the value)

  • Number 3 is the interesting one. When does a close group become a clique?

Variations

  • Seated version: thumbs up or thumbs down. Lower energy, works with limited mobility, and

nobody is exposed by standing alone

  • Online: poll per situation, then ask one person from each side to unmute
  • Trust version (TOP-LEA-002): swap the list for trust-breaking behaviours from the topic. Mixed

messages, missed promises, hidden information, blame, favouritism, poor listening, breach of confidence. Ask "have you seen this happen?" instead of "is this a red flag?"

  • Team version: run it with an intact team and the conversation afterwards becomes a de facto

team charter

Watch out for

  • Never let it become about a real person. If someone starts describing an actual colleague, thank

them and move to the next situation

  • The lone person at a wall. Go to them second, not first, and be warm about it. Then move on

quickly

  • Do not correct people. There is no answer key. Situation 2 genuinely does not have one
  • Number 6 can be raw for someone going through it. It is in the list because oversharing is

usually well-meant, not malicious. Keep it light

The Silent Nod

10-12 mingametrustpsychological-safetyconflicticebreakeropenerteamsstorming

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: fear of conflict, the second layer of FRM-017 The 5 Dysfunctions, and FRM-023 Psychological Safety. It also works as the storming opener for FRM-018 Tuckman.

The point: the group experiences fake yes happening to them, live, in about four minutes.

How to run it

  1. Brief three people quietly before the session, or in the corridor at the break. Their job:

whatever the facilitator proposes, agree with it enthusiastically and quickly. Nobody else knows.

  1. Propose something mildly bad (3 min). A plan with an obvious flaw. Suggestions below. Present

it confidently, as though it is already decided.

  1. The three plants agree fast. "Yeah, that makes sense." "Sounds good."
  2. Ask the room: "Anyone got any concerns?" and then wait. Do not fill the silence. Count to ten

in your head. It will feel very long.

  1. Usually nobody says anything. Occasionally one person does, and that is even better material.
  2. Stop the game. Explain what you did.

Proposals that work

  • "We'll finish forty minutes late today so we can get through everything. That's fine with everyone?"
  • "New rule: the team WhatsApp gets checked before 7am so we can start on time."
  • "We'll do the presentations in alphabetical order, and everyone presents alone, no notes."

Pick something with a real flaw that affects them, not an absurd one. Absurd gets laughed at. Mildly unreasonable gets nodded at, which is the lesson.

The link back

Three people in this room were told to agree with me. That was enough. Nobody else said anything, and most of you had a concern.

Then the point:

That is fake yes. It is not that you are cowards, it is that agreement looked like the consensus and disagreeing would have cost something. Now imagine that happening in a real meeting, about a real decision, with your actual manager in the room.

Then land it on the model: this is why Lencioni puts fear of conflict directly on top of absence of trust. And it is why a leader asking "any concerns?" and getting silence should never read that as agreement.

Debrief

  • Who had a concern and did not say it? (Hands go up. Lots of them)
  • What stopped you? Collect the reasons: did not want to be first, thought it was decided, thought it

was just me, did not want to hold everyone up

  • What would have made it easier to speak?
  • What does this mean about the last meeting you sat in?

Variations

  • No plants: it often works without them, just from the facilitator's confidence and the framing

"so that's decided". Slightly less reliable, and completely honest

  • Small groups: brief one plant instead of three
  • Online: it works better online, not worse. Silence on a call is heavier, and the plants can

agree in the chat where everyone sees it

  • Intact teams: be careful. It exposes something real about that team and you need time to deal

with what surfaces

  • The fix version: rerun the proposal afterwards, with the facilitator explicitly saying "I want

two problems with this before anyone agrees." Watch how fast the room changes

Watch out for

  • Do not humiliate the plants. Name them as helpers and thank them
  • Do not let it become "you all failed". They behaved exactly like everyone does. That is the

finding, not a fault

  • The one person who did speak up should be acknowledged carefully, not held up as a hero, or the

rest of the room feels judged

  • Never run this with a proposal that touches something genuinely sensitive such as pay, rosters

people actually depend on, or anything that could be believed for the rest of the day. Debrief quickly so nobody leaves thinking it was real

ACT-042Activity · 03-Activities

Build It Fast, Then Talk

20-25 mingameteamsteam-developmenticebreakeropenerstormingnormscollaboration

Type: game / opener · Time: 20-25 min · Group: teams of 4-6 · Energy: high

What it sets up: FRM-018 Tuckman's Stages. A team cannot discuss Forming and Storming honestly from memory. This makes them do both in ten minutes, in front of each other, and then debrief what just happened.

Materials per team: 20 sticks of spaghetti, a metre of tape, string, and one marshmallow. Or a cheaper version: a stack of newspaper and a roll of tape.

How to run it

  1. The task (1 min). Build the tallest free-standing tower you can in ten minutes. The

marshmallow must be on top. It must stand on its own for ten seconds.

  1. No talking about process. Do not tell them to plan. Do not tell them to assign roles. The

whole value is in what they do without being told.

  1. Ten minutes. Call the time at 5, 2 and 1 minutes.
  2. Measure. Brief celebration.
  3. Now the real activity: the debrief (10 min).

The debrief, which is the actual lesson

Ask these in order. Do not rush them.

  1. "What happened in the first sixty seconds?" Nearly every team describes Forming: polite,

nobody wanted to take charge, a lot of looking at the materials and not much doing.

  1. "When did someone take over? How did that happen?" This is Storming, and it usually happened

without a word being said.

  1. "Did anyone have an idea they didn't say?" Hands go up in most teams. Ask why not.
  2. **"Which team talked about how they'd work before they started building?"** Usually none. Ask

what that cost them.

  1. "What rule would you set if you did this again?" Their answers are a

team charter, invented by them, in ninety seconds.

The link back

You just did Forming and Storming in ten minutes, with people you already know, on a task with no real consequences. Now think about a team that has to do it over six months, with people they did not choose, on work that pays their rent.

Then name the finding: teams that skip the "how will we work?" conversation do not save time. They spend it later, in the Storming stage, and usually with more damage.

Debrief extras

  • Who ended up leading? Was that decided or did it just happen?
  • What would have been different if you had spent two of your ten minutes planning?
  • Did anyone get quieter as it went on? What made that happen?

Variations

  • The planning contrast: give half the teams two extra minutes with a rule that they may only

talk, not touch the materials. Compare results. This is the strongest version

  • Cheap version: newspaper and tape. Works just as well and costs almost nothing
  • Seated / accessible version: build the tallest tower flat on the table as a structure, or use a

paper chain for length rather than height

  • Online: each person builds separately from what is in their room, and the team has to agree a

shared design first over video. The forming and storming happens in the design conversation

  • Low literacy: no reading or writing involved at any point

Watch out for

  • The debrief is the activity. If you are short on time, cut the build to seven minutes rather

than cutting the debrief

  • Competitive groups can get heated. Keep the prize meaningless
  • The person who got talked over may not want to say so publicly. Ask question 3 as "put your

hand up if" rather than asking someone to name it

  • Do not let a team blame one person for taking over. They took over because nobody had agreed

how to decide, which is a team problem

Behaviour, Not Adjective

8-10 mingamerespectrole-modelsicebreakeropenerleadershipfeedback

Type: game / opener · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the H step of FRM-019 W-H-O, and the Retention condition in FRM-026 Modelling.

The point: admiration is useless until you can say the exact thing the person does. This game makes that difficulty obvious in about four minutes, which is why it belongs before the worksheet.

How to run it

  1. Call out an adjective. "Respectful."
  2. The room shouts behaviours. Anything someone could actually watch you do. Take five or six

fast.

  1. Reject the ones that are still adjectives. "Considerate" is not a behaviour, it is another

adjective. Say so, cheerfully, and ask again. This is the game.

  1. Move to the next adjective. Six or seven of them, thirty to sixty seconds each.

The adjectives

Humble · Reliable · Respectful · A good listener · Fair · Approachable · A good leader

The last one is deliberately the hardest and it should be last.

What good answers sound like

AdjectiveNot a behaviourA behaviour
Humble"Doesn't big-note himself""Asks the apprentice what he thinks before giving his own view"
Reliable"You can count on her""Turns up ten minutes early, every time"
Respectful"Treats people well""Learns how to say your name properly and keeps using it"
A good listener"Really hears you""Puts the phone face down when you start talking"
Fair"Doesn't have favourites""Gives the good jobs out in rotation, and says so"
Approachable"Easy to talk to""Says 'got a minute?' back, instead of 'what is it?'"
A good leaderanything vaguewhatever they land on, and it will take the longest

The link back

Every single one of those adjectives is useless to you. You cannot copy "humble". You can copy "asks the apprentice first".

Then go straight into W-H-O and ACT-033 Who Is Someone You Respect?. The room has just practised the exact skill the H step needs.

Debrief

  • Which adjective was hardest to turn into a behaviour? (Usually "a good leader", and that is worth

sitting with for a moment)

  • What does that tell you about the feedback people usually get at work?
  • If someone told you "you're a great team player", would you know what to keep doing?

That last question is the one that lands. Most praise is adjectives, which means most praise teaches nobody anything.

Variations

  • Reverse version: call out a behaviour, the room names the adjective it earns. Quicker and

lighter

  • Pairs version: one person says an adjective, their partner has ten seconds to produce a

behaviour. Rotate. Higher energy, everyone talks

  • Feedback version: for teams, use it to fix how they praise each other. Everyone rewrites a

compliment they have given recently into a behaviour

  • Online: chat storm. Everyone types behaviours, the facilitator reads out the good ones and

gently rejects the adjectives

  • Low literacy: entirely spoken already

Watch out for

  • Keep the rejections light. "Nice try, that's still an adjective" with a grin. If it feels like

being marked wrong, the room stops shouting

  • Do not let it slow down. Sixty seconds per adjective. The pace is what makes it a game rather

than an exercise

  • Do not let people describe a real colleague negatively. Keep it to the positive adjectives on

the list

Name It In Ten Seconds

8-10 mingamerespecticebreakeropenernamescultureleadership

Type: game / energiser · Time: 8-10 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: high

What it sets up: the house example in FRM-019 W-H-O: greets people by name and checks pronunciation. The source uses it as an example of a respect behaviour. This turns it into something the room does rather than reads.

Why it matters more than it looks: for a lot of Pacific, Māori and migrant learners, having their name said properly, or not, is the most repeated respect experience of their working life. This game names that without making a speech about it.

How to run it

  1. Everyone stands in a circle.
  2. Round one, the mess (2 min). Go round. Everyone says their own name once, quickly. No

repeating, no help. Then ask the room to name five people. They cannot.

  1. Round two, properly (4 min). Go round again. This time each person says their name **twice,

slowly**, and the person to their left says it back. If they get it wrong, the owner corrects them and they try again until it is right. Nobody moves on until it is right.

  1. Round three, the test (2 min). Point at people at random. The room says the name together.
  2. Stop and ask the question below.

The link back

Ask, quietly:

Put your hand up if someone at work has been saying your name wrong for more than a month.

In most Zeducation rooms a lot of hands go up. Then:

Now put it up if you have ever corrected them.

Far fewer. Then land it:

That is what respect looks like at ground level. Not a value on a wall. Ten seconds of effort, from the person who has the easier job in that exchange.

Then go to W-H-O and the house example about greeting people by name and checking pronunciation.

Debrief

  • How did it feel to have the room say your name correctly?
  • Why do people stop correcting others? (Answers: did not want to make it awkward, gave up, it felt

rude, it happens too often to keep doing it)

  • Whose job is it to get someone's name right?
  • What else is like this? What other small thing signals respect or its absence?

Variations

  • Meaning version: each person says their name and one line about where it comes from or who

gave it to them. Slower, considerably warmer, and excellent with Pacific and Māori groups. Budget 15 minutes and never require it

  • Seated version: works fine around a table
  • Existing teams: run it with people who have worked together for years. The discovery that

someone has been mispronouncing a colleague's name for three years is the whole lesson, delivered for free

  • Online: works well. Everyone says their name, the next person repeats it. Also fix the display

names while you are there, which is a real and lasting outcome

  • Low literacy: nothing is read or written

Watch out for

  • Never single out one person's name as the difficult one. Everyone goes through the same

process, including the facilitator and including the shortest, most familiar names

  • The facilitator goes first, and gets their own name repeated back. It sets the tone and it

stops the exercise feeling like it is aimed at anyone

  • Do not let anyone laugh at a name. Shut it down immediately and without heat
  • Some people have chosen an easier "work name" because of exactly this problem. If it comes up,

it is a good conversation, not a failure. Let them keep whichever name they want

Whose Call Is It?

12-15 mingamedecision-makingleadershipicebreakeropenercollaborationstyles

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-028 Kurt Lewin's Three Decision-Making Styles.

Materials: three signs on three walls. MY WAY (autocratic), OUR WAY (democratic), YOUR WAY (laissez-faire).

How to run it

  1. Teach the three styles first, in three minutes. No more than that.
  2. Read a decision. Everyone walks to the wall for the style they think fits it best.
  3. Ask one person from each wall why. Never correct them. Some of these have no right answer.
  4. Ten decisions, eight minutes. Keep it fast.

The decisions

#The decisionUsually
1Someone is working at height without a harnessMy way, immediately
2What we call the new team chatYour way. It does not matter, so let them have it
3Changing the weekend rosterOur way, and this is the one people get wrong
4A customer is being abusive to a staff member right nowMy way
5How the team splits up the end-of-day jobsOur way, or your way if the team is solid
6Which supplier we use, when finance has set the budgetSplits. Often my way dressed up as our way
7Whether to change the shift start time by 30 minutesOur way. It is their lives
8How an experienced person does a job they have done for ten yearsYour way. Stop supervising them
9Cutting the team's overtime budgetSplits. The decision may be made, but the how is theirs
10What the team's values should beOur way, and only our way. Handed-down values are wallpaper

The link back

Two points, after the last one.

Nobody in this room has one style. You used all three in the last ten minutes, and you chose correctly most of the time. The skill is not having a favourite, it is choosing on purpose.

Then the harder one, on numbers 6 and 9:

The most damaging thing a leader can do is run a "our way" process on a "my way" decision. If the budget is already cut, do not ask people what they think about cutting the budget. Ask them how to do it. Fake consultation costs more trust than a straight decision ever does.

Debrief

  • Which one did the room split on most?
  • Number 6: have you ever been consulted about something that was already decided? What did that do

to your trust?

  • What is your default style when you are under pressure and short of time?
  • Which of these decisions does your manager get wrong?

Variations

  • Seated version: hold up one, two or three fingers. Same effect, lower energy, and it works with

limited mobility

  • Their own decisions: each person writes a real decision on a card and the room sorts it. This

is the best version with an intact leadership team

  • Time pressure round: rerun three of them with "and you have four minutes to decide". Watch how

many people move to My Way, then talk about what urgency does to consultation

  • Online: three-way poll per decision, then unmute one person per option

Watch out for

  • The room learning that democratic is the right answer. It is not, and if that is what they take

away the game has failed. Numbers 1, 4 and 8 exist to prevent it

  • Do not correct answers. Say "that's a defensible read" and ask why. Most of these genuinely

depend on the team

  • Do not let it become about a real manager's failings. One or two examples are fine, then move on

Used by

The Us And Them Hunt

10-12 mingamecollaborationsilosicebreakeropenerteamsblame

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-030 Collaborative vs Siloed Teams, and specifically the fastest diagnostic in it: the word "they".

How to run it

  1. Ask a simple question (2 min). *"What is one thing that makes your job harder than it needs to

be?"* Take five or six answers around the room. Do not comment on them, just collect them.

  1. Write them on the board as people say them, in their own words. Exactly their words. This

matters.

  1. Now go back and circle every "they", "them" and "that lot". In most rooms it is most of the

board.

  1. Count them out loud.
  2. Ask the question below.

The link back

Six answers, and we circled nine "theys". Not one person here is difficult and nobody said anything unfair. That is just what it sounds like from inside a silo.

Then the question that does the work:

Who is the "they" in this room, for somebody else?

Sit in the silence. Someone will eventually say it: every team is somebody else's "they". Head office is the regions' "they". The regions are head office's. Night shift and day shift are each other's.

Then land it on the framework: a siloed team is not a team that dislikes another team. It is a team that has stopped having reasons to talk to them, so all that is left is the times something went wrong.

Debrief

  • Which "they" on the board would change if you actually spoke to them next week?
  • When did you last have a conversation with that team about something that was not a problem?
  • What do they say about us?
  • What information do we have that they would find useful, that we have never sent?

That last question usually produces a real action, and it is often something that takes five minutes.

Variations

  • The week-long count: send everyone away to count how often they hear "they" about another team.

Report back next session. More honest than any engagement survey

  • Both sides in the room: run the same question in two groups, head office and regional,

separately, then show each group the other's board. Handled well it is the most useful ten minutes in the programme. Handled badly it starts a fight, so only do it with a group that has some trust

  • Swap version: each person has to argue the "they" side of one item on the board. Uncomfortable

and effective

  • Online: collect the answers in the chat, then paste them into a doc and highlight the pronouns

live

Watch out for

  • Do not let anyone be named. Teams and departments only. Stop it immediately if a person's name

goes on the board

  • Do not make people feel caught out. The framing is "this is what a silo sounds like", never

"look how negative you all are". Say explicitly that nobody said anything unreasonable

  • Some "theys" are legitimate. Sometimes another team genuinely is not doing its job. The point

is not that the complaint is wrong, it is that the complaint is being made in the wrong room

  • If the group is one intact team with a real grievance, this can open something bigger than the

session can hold. Have somewhere for it to go before you start

Who Does Everyone Ask?

10-12 mingameworkloadcollaborationburnouticebreakeropenerteamsnetworks

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, from 8 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: FRM-032 Collaborative Overload. It makes the hub effect visible in about six minutes, using the room's own answers.

The finding it demonstrates: 20 to 35% of value-added collaboration comes from 3 to 5% of people. Rooms rediscover this on their own, fast.

How to run it

  1. Everyone gets three sticky notes (1 min).
  2. Three questions, one per note (3 min). Write a name on each. Roles, not real names, if the

group is mixed.

    • Who do you go to when you are stuck on something?
    • Who do you go to when you need something done quickly and properly?
    • Who do you go to when something has gone wrong and you need advice?
  • Stick them all on the wall (2 min).
  • Group the duplicates out loud. The same two or three names will stack up.
  • Stand back and look at the shape.

The link back

Nine people, twenty-seven notes, and four names. That is what the research found across three hundred organisations. A small number of people carry most of it.

Then the question that changes the room:

Now: how do you think those four people are doing?

And the finding: the leaders rated by colleagues as the most in-demand collaborators had the lowest engagement and career satisfaction scores. The people everyone relies on are the ones most likely to be quietly looking for another job.

Debrief

  • Is anyone's own name up there? What is that like?
  • Why those people? (Answers: they know things, they always say yes, they never make you feel stupid)
  • What would happen to your workplace if the top name left tomorrow?
  • What would it take for one of those questions to have a different answer?
  • Whose job is it to fix this?

That last question matters. Most rooms answer "the hub's" and the honest answer is the organisation's.

Variations

  • Anonymous version: roles instead of names. Essential if the hubs are in the room and it might

embarrass them

  • Intact team version: genuinely revealing and it needs care. Done well it produces a real

redistribution conversation. Done badly it publicly labels one person as the bottleneck

  • The leader's version: managers map their own team. Most discover two people carrying it and are

surprised, because the hubs never complain

  • Online: three polls, or a shared board. The stacking effect is just as visible
  • Low literacy: spoken. Ask the three questions and tally names on the whiteboard as people call

them out

Watch out for

  • The hub in the room. Seeing your own name eleven times can feel like praise or like an

accusation, depending on the day. Frame it explicitly as a load problem the organisation created, never as "look how indispensable you are"

  • Do not let it become a popularity chart. The questions are about reliance, not regard, and

saying so up front keeps it clean

  • Never leave the notes up after the session
  • The person whose name appears nowhere. It is not a status ranking, and in a room of eight some

people will not be named. Say that before you start, lightly

Used by

Small Thing, Big Signal

12-15 mingamecultural-safetycultureicebreakeropenerinclusionleadership

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the "how cultural safety is broken" list in FRM-033 Cultural Safety, and the point underneath it: nearly every breach is small, defensible in isolation, and read instantly by the person on the receiving end.

How to run it

  1. Read a situation (30 seconds each).
  2. Everyone rates it 1 to 5 on their fingers, held at chest height. 1 = no big deal. 5 = serious.
  3. Look at the spread. Do not average it. The spread is the lesson.
  4. Ask two people at different numbers why. Never adjudicate.
  5. Eight situations, ten minutes.

The situations

#The situation
1A manager has been saying a staff member's name slightly wrong for six months. Nobody has corrected him
2A team photo is posted online. One person had said they would rather not be in it, and were in it anyway
3A meeting invite goes out for 6pm on a night when two staff have a regular church commitment
4Someone does an impression of a customer's accent in the break room. Everyone laughs, including the person the accent belongs to
5A bilingual staff member is asked to translate for a guest, for the fourth time this week, on top of her own job
6A cultural performance is added to the season launch. None of the staff from that culture were asked about it first
7The high performer makes a comment about someone's clothing. It is let go, because he is the high performer
8A visitor photographs a sacred site after being told not to. The guide says nothing, because the visitor is a paying customer

The link back

Two moves, in this order.

First, point at the spread:

Look at the range on number 4. Some of you said 1 and some said 5. Now think about which of those people is more likely to be the one it happens to.

Then the finding:

Every single one of those is small. Every one of them is defensible if you argue about it on its own. And every one of them teaches somebody that a part of who they are is a problem here. That is how cultural safety breaks. Not with a scandal, with eight small things nobody wrote down.

Then go into the eight named breaches on the framework page: token invites, assumption-led decisions, protocol theatre, name and language neglect, English-only spaces, culture as a joke, uneven consequences, invisible risks. Most of the room has just argued their way to all eight.

Debrief

  • Which one split the room most?
  • Number 4: does it change anything that the person laughed? (This is the hardest question in the

set. Laughing along is often the safest available response, not agreement)

  • Number 5: what would it take to fix that one? (It is usually the easiest to fix and the least often

noticed)

  • Number 7: whose job is it to say something?
  • Which of these has happened where you work in the last month?

Variations

  • Two-rating version: rate it twice. Once as the manager, once as the person it happened to. The

gap between a person's own two numbers is the whole topic, delivered privately

  • Add your own: each table writes one situation from their own workplace. Strongest version, and

it needs a room with trust

  • Online: poll per situation, show the distribution, then discuss the split ones
  • Low literacy: entirely spoken. Nothing is read or written by participants

Watch out for

  • Never ask anyone to speak as the target. People from the affected culture in the room are not

there to validate the exercise or to tell their story. If someone volunteers, that is theirs to choose

  • Do not adjudicate the ratings. The moment the facilitator supplies the "right" number, the room

stops being honest and starts guessing

  • Number 4 can sting if something like it happened recently in that workplace. Keep the pace up

and land the point rather than dwelling

  • Watch for the room deciding the low raters are bad people. They are not. Most breaches are

invisible from the side that is not experiencing them, which is exactly why the list exists

Used by

The Woven Mat

12-15 mingametalanoapacificcultural-safetyicebreakeropenerculturebelonging

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole class, from 6 up · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the source's own metaphor for FRM-035 Talanoa, made physical:

Cultural safety is a woven mat. Shared values are the strong warp threads, people's lived stories are the weft, and talanoa is the act of weaving those threads so the mat holds.

Materials: strips of paper or ribbon in two colours, about 20 of each. Or bring a real woven mat and use it, which is better if you can do it respectfully and it belongs to someone in the room who is happy to explain it.

How to run it

  1. Lay the warp (4 min). Hold up the first colour. These are the shared values, the things

this team says it stands for. Ask the room to name them and write one per strip. Respect. Safety. Manaakitanga. Whatever they actually say. Lay them out parallel on a table or the floor.

  1. Look at it. It is not a mat. It is a set of parallel lines that falls apart if you lift it.

Lift one end and let it come apart. This is the moment.

  1. Add the weft (5 min). Second colour. These are people's lived stories and knowledge. Ask

each person for one thing about how they do things, where they are from, or what they know that the team relies on. One per strip. Weave each one across the warp.

  1. Lift it again. Now it holds.

The link back

The values on their own were a poster. They did not hold anything, and you could see it. What made it a mat was people's actual stories going across them. Talanoa is the weaving. It is not a nice conversation you have if there is time. It is the thing that turns your values into something that can carry weight.

Then go into the three-part flow: teu le vā, ask open questions, listen and give back.

Debrief

  • Which values went down first? Who named them? (Often the most senior person, and that is worth

noticing out loud)

  • Whose story is not in the mat yet?
  • What happens to a mat when one thread is pulled out and never replaced?
  • Where does your workplace have plenty of warp and almost no weft?

That last question is the one to close on. Most organisations have values in abundance and have never asked anyone for a story.

Variations

  • Keep the mat. Photograph it, or leave it on the wall for the rest of the programme and add to

it. It becomes a record of the room

  • Repair version: partway through, quietly remove one weft strip. Later, ask what changed. Good

for talking about people leaving, or being excluded

  • Real mat version: if someone in the room has a mat, a tīvaevae, a tapa or a korowai and is

willing to bring it and speak to it, that is far better than paper. Ask, do not assume, and do not put anyone on the spot in front of colleagues. Ask privately, in advance, and accept no easily

  • Online: a shared board with two colours of note. It works, and it loses the physical moment

where the parallel strips fall apart, which is most of the value

  • Low literacy: say the values and stories aloud, facilitator writes the strips

Watch out for

  • Handle the metaphor with care, not decoration. Weaving is a real practice with real meaning

across the Pacific and in te ao Māori. Name where the metaphor comes from, credit the source, and do not turn a taonga into a craft activity

  • Never ask someone to be the cultural exhibit. The weft strips are about everyone's knowledge,

including the person who has worked there longest and knows how the till jams

  • Do not let the values list get long. Six or seven warp strips is plenty. Twenty makes a mess and

weakens the point

  • If you use a real mat, it does not go on the floor unless the person who brought it says so

Used by
