Two Hours A Week

10-12 mingameconflictconflict-resolutionicebreakeropenerteamscommunication

Type: game / opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole class, any size · Energy: medium

What it sets up: the cost of unresolved conflict, and the reframe that opens TOP-COM-007.

How to run it

  1. Ask everyone to think of one unresolved thing at work. Not a crisis. The low-level one: the

person they route around, the thing that comes up every few weeks and never gets settled, the conversation they keep not having. Nobody says it out loud.

  1. Ask them to estimate, privately, how many minutes a week it costs them. Thinking about it,

working around it, talking to someone else about it, redoing something because of it. Write the number down.

  1. Hands up by band. Under 15 minutes. 15 to 30. 30 to 60. More than an hour. More than two.
  2. Look at the room.
  3. Then give them the research.

The number

Across nine countries and 5,000 employees, the CPP Global Human Capital Report (2008) found workers spent an average of 2.1 hours a week dealing with conflict. That is over a hundred hours a year, per person.

📄 CPP Global Human Capital Report: Workplace Conflict (2008)

⚠️ Say what the study is. It is a large survey commissioned by CPP, a publisher of assessment tools, not a peer-reviewed study. The figure is widely cited and it is a vendor report. Learners trust you more, not less, when you say that.

⚠️ The source workbook also cites three further statistics from the same report: that a third of conflicts have led to attacks or personal injury, 20% to illness or absence, and 10% of projects have failed. Those three have not been verified against the primary report and should not be read out as fact until they are. The 2.1 hours figure is the one to use.

The link back

Nobody in this room put their hand up for zero. And most of you were thinking about one thing.

Then the turn, which is the actual opener for the topic:

Here is the part that matters. That two hours is not the cost of having conflict. It is the cost of not resolving it. Conflict that gets dealt with takes twenty minutes once. Conflict that gets avoided takes ten minutes a week, forever.

Then the reframe from the source: conflict is "an opportunity to engage in a conversation with someone who has a different viewpoint."

Debrief

  • Was your number higher than you expected?
  • What is the thing you keep not dealing with? (Nobody answers out loud. Just let them sit with it)
  • What would it take to resolve it? Is it actually that big?
  • What has it cost so far, beyond the time?

Variations

  • Sticky note version: everyone writes their number on a note, all notes go on the wall

anonymously. The spread is more striking than the show of hands

  • Team version: with an intact team, add up the room's total and convert to days a year. The

number is usually startling and it is the version managers remember

  • Cost version: for a commercial audience, multiply by an hourly rate. Blunt, effective, and it

makes conflict resolution a business case rather than a soft skill

  • Low literacy: entirely spoken and by show of hands

Watch out for

  • Nobody names the person. Say it clearly at step 1. This goes wrong fast if someone starts

describing a colleague

  • The room that says zero. Occasionally a group insists there is no conflict anywhere. That is

worth a gentle question about whether nobody disagrees, or whether nobody says so, which is fear of conflict and a better opener than the one you planned

  • Do not oversell the statistic. One verified number, honestly described, is worth more than four

dramatic ones

Leader Or Manager? The Sort

12-15 mingameleadershipmanagementopenergamesortingteams

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room, or teams of 4-5 · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-049 Kotter on Leadership and Management.

⚠️ Run this before you teach the framework. The argument is the activity. If people already know the answers there is nothing to argue about and nothing sticks.

The cards

Eighteen tasks. Cut them up. Teams sort into two piles: LEADERSHIP and MANAGEMENT.

Task
1Building next month's roster
2Telling the team why the new system is coming
3Checking the timesheets
4Deciding the shop will open on Sundays from March
5Ordering stock
6Sitting with someone who is thinking about leaving
7Working out how many staff the second site will need
8Being the first one to follow the new rule
9Running the Monday huddle
10Deciding which two of the five ideas the team will actually chase
11Fixing the till that keeps dropping out
12Telling the manager the documentation will not work for the night crew
13Writing the health and safety procedure
14Asking a quiet staff member what they think, by name, in advance
15Comparing this month's numbers to last month's
16Deciding the team is going to stop doing something it has always done
17Approving leave
18Noticing that the best person on the team is bored

The intended sort

Do not hand this out. It is for you.

Management (coping with complexity)Leadership (coping with change)
1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 172, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18

But the point is the arguments, not the score. Three cards reliably split a room:

  • Card 9, the Monday huddle. Running it is management. What you choose to say in it is

leadership. Same meeting

  • Card 7, staffing the second site. It is a spreadsheet, and deciding to open a second site at

all was the leadership act it depends on

  • Card 12, telling the manager the system will not work. Learners often file it as neither,

because "that's not my job". It is card 12 that makes it worth running this game

How to run it

  1. Teams of 4-5, cards face down (1 min). No teaching yet
  2. Sort, 5 minutes, timed. Every card has to go in a pile. No "both" pile. The refusal is the

engine of the activity

  1. Compare (3 min). Which cards did teams disagree on? Only discuss those
  2. Now teach Kotter (5 min). The room

already has the distinction. You are giving it a name and a source

  1. The closing question: "which pile is most of your week in?"

Debrief

  • Which card caused the biggest argument in your team?
  • Did anyone want a "both" pile? What was on it?
  • Look at the management pile. What happens to a team with none of it?
  • Now look at the leadership pile. What happens to a team with none of that?
  • The real one: if you disappeared for a month, which pile would nobody pick up?

Variations

  • Human sort: two sides of the room, read cards aloud, people walk to a side. Faster, louder,

and you can see who is unsure by who hesitates

  • Add your own: each team writes two cards from their own job before you start. These are always

the best cards

  • Rank instead of sort: put all eighteen in order of "what my team would miss most if I stopped".

Slower, and it goes somewhere different

  • Manager version: with actual supervisors, tally what they did last week against the two piles.

Most get 90/10, and the 10 is the conversation

  • Low literacy: read every card aloud, work as one group, sort physically on a table

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Do not let management become the losing pile. The framing that "leadership is the good one"

insults everyone in the room who is good at the other thing and it is not what Kotter said. Say explicitly: a team with no management fails faster than a team with no leadership

  • Teams that finish in two minutes. They have not argued. Send them back with the three splitting

cards

  • The "it depends" defence. True, and it stalls the game. Rule: pick a pile, then say what it

depends on

  • Status in the room. If some learners supervise and some do not, watch that the sort does not

turn into a ranking of people. Sort the tasks, not each other

What Kind Of Difference Is This?

12-15 mingamediversityteamsopenergamesortinginclusion

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-052 The Three Kinds of Diversity.

The trick of this game is that it is rigged. Learners sort statements into demographic, informational and values-based, and discover that most of what actually matters on a team is in the two piles nobody thinks about.

Set up

Three corners of the room, or three columns on a whiteboard:

DEMOGRAPHICINFORMATIONALVALUES
who we arewhat we knowwhat we're for

The statements

Read one at a time. The room moves, or points, or calls it out.

StatementAnswer
1"I'm 19, everyone else here is over 40"Demographic
2"I trained as a nurse in the Philippines"Informational (and people say demographic first)
3"I'm the only woman on the crew"Demographic
4"I've been doing this job for 22 years"Informational
5"I'm here to pay off my mum's house"Values
6"I use a wheelchair"Demographic
7"I want to be running my own crew in three years"Values
8"I'm the only one who's ever worked night shift"Informational
9"English is my third language"Both — demographic and informational. See below
10"I think the customer comes before the schedule"Values
11"I did a health and safety rep course last year"Informational
12"I don't want a promotion, I want my weekends"Values
13"I grew up here, everyone else moved in"Both
14"I think this whole approach is wrong"Values

The three moments the game exists for

Statement 2, the Filipino nurse. Rooms sort this as demographic almost every time, because they hear "Philippines". It is informational: this person has clinical training nobody else has. That mis-sort, live, in front of the room, is the best teaching moment in the activity.

➜ "You just heard where she's from and stopped listening to what she knows. That happens at work every day."

Statement 9, third language. Both, and it is worth sitting with. Someone who speaks three languages is demographically different and carries information the team does not have, and the workplace usually treats it purely as a deficit in the first language.

Statement 14, "this whole approach is wrong". Values diversity, and the room usually goes quiet because it does not feel like diversity at all. It feels like a difficult person. That is exactly the point: values diversity is the kind that produces the useful argument and the kind teams are least willing to call diversity.

How to run it

  1. Three corners, no teaching (1 min). Just the three headings
  2. Read the statements (8 min). People move. Do not correct immediately, ask why first
  3. Land the three moments above. Do not rush past statement 2
  4. Then teach FRM-052 (5 min), and the

evidence audit that goes with it

Debrief

  • Which pile did you find easiest? Which one did you never think of as diversity?
  • Statement 2: what did you assume, and how fast?
  • Which kind of diversity does a hiring process usually look at?
  • Which kind actually changes what a team decides?

Variations

  • Own-statement round: everyone writes one true statement about themselves on a card, unsigned.

Shuffle, read out, sort. Much stronger and it needs a group that already trusts each other

  • Team version: an intact team maps itself. Where are we diverse? Where are we all the same? Most

teams discover they are informationally identical

  • Fast version: just statements 2, 9, 10 and 14. Four minutes, and it still works
  • Low literacy: entirely read aloud, hands up or move to a corner. Nothing needs reading

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Nobody discloses anything they did not plan to. The printed statements are about

hypothetical people. The own-statement variation changes that, so only run it with a group you know, and make it genuinely optional

  • ⚠️ Statement 6 and disability. The library's Culture & Diversity pillar currently has almost

nothing on disability and accessibility. Do not improvise a session on it off the back of one card. Acknowledge and move on

  • The "everything is demographic" room. If people are sorting everything into the first column,

slow down and do statement 4 and statement 11 back to back

  • Turning it into a game of gotcha. The wrong answers are the content. Never make anyone feel

caught out, especially on statement 2

  • Skipping to the evidence. The sorting has to happen first. If you teach the model before the

game, the game is pointless

Say My Name

10-12 mingameopenernamesinclusiondiversityculturebelongingicebreaker

Type: opener · Time: 10-12 min · Group: whole room, up to about 20 · Energy: medium

What it practises: move 1 of FRM-055 Accommodating Diversity, and it is the fastest way into FRM-050 Tikanga Māori in Business.

The best opener in this library for a culture session, because it costs nothing, takes ten minutes, and something real happens in almost every room.

How it runs

Round the circle. Each person says three things:

  1. My name, the way it should be said.
  2. Where it comes from, if you know. Who gave it to you, what it means, who else has it
  3. What people usually get wrong, if anything

Then the room says it back. Together, out loud. If it is not right, the person says it again and the room goes again. Up to three times.

That is the whole activity.

Why the "say it back" step is not optional

Without it, this is a nice sharing exercise and nothing changes. With it, twenty people have physically practised somebody's name and got it wrong in front of them and been corrected and tried again.

➜ That is the lesson. Getting it wrong is fine. Not trying is the problem. Learners who have been quietly answering to a mangled version of their name for fifteen years watch the room work at it, and that is a different experience from being asked about it politely.

What tends to happen
Somebody's real name comes outPeople who have gone by a shortened, anglicised or nickname version at work for years sometimes give their actual name. Do not make a thing of it. Just use the name they gave you, for the rest of the programme
"It's fine, just call me…"The most common response, and it is worth one gentle push: "I'd rather learn it, if that's alright." If they say no, that is their call and drop it
A Pākehā learner says they have a boring nameOften untrue. Ask who they were named after. There is usually a grandparent in it
Somebody criesOccasionally. It means more than people expect

Debrief

Short. Do not overwork it.

  • Who has had their name shortened at work without being asked?
  • How long did you let it go?
  • What does it cost to ask?
  • The closing line: "Right. For the rest of this programme, we say each other's names properly.

Including mine."

Variations

  • Write it phonetically: everyone writes their name as it sounds on a card, and the cards stay on

the table for the session. Enormously helpful, and it de-loads people's memory

  • Facilitator goes last: better than going first. The room hears everyone else before they hear

you, and you have to have been paying attention

  • Roll-call round two: at the start of the next session, the facilitator names everyone from

memory. Get it right. If you cannot, do not attempt it

  • Team version: with an intact team who already know each other, the round is "what do you

actually want to be called at work, and is that what happens?" Different activity, same nerve

  • Large groups: tables of six rather than one circle. Loses some of the effect and still works
  • Big Zeducation cohorts: this pairs naturally with a mihi or pepeha round if that is appropriate

to the group and the facilitator is confident. It is not a substitute for one

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ The facilitator has to go first at getting it wrong. Model being corrected, cheerfully, at

least once. If the facilitator is precious about it, nobody else will risk it

  • ⚠️ Never make anyone explain their heritage. The question is about the name, not about

ethnicity. "Where does it come from" is answerable with "my nan" and that is a complete answer

  • ⚠️ Do not push someone who declines. Some people have complicated reasons for the name they use

at work. A trans learner, someone estranged from family, someone who changed it to get interviews. Offer once, accept the answer

  • Do not turn it into a pronunciation test. Nobody is being marked. Three attempts and move on
  • Then actually use the names. All programme. The activity is worthless if the facilitator

reverts to "mate" on day two

Seven Seconds

12-15 mingamecareer-readinesscvopenergamejob-searchwork-readiness

Type: game / opener · Time: 12-15 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-058 The CV That Gets Read.

Learners write CVs for a reader who does not exist: somebody with all the time in the world and a warm interest in them. This activity puts them in the actual reader's chair for ninety seconds and the point lands without anyone having to make it.

Set up

Print four sample CVs for the same fictional job. Make them deliberately different:

CVWhat is wrong or right with it
ABeautiful two-column design, photo, skills as little bar charts. Says almost nothing
BPlain, a wall of grey text, ten jobs since 2004, no headline
CPlain, a clear headline, four skill bullets with numbers, ticket listed at the top
DGood content, but the relevant licence is on page two

Do not label them. Nobody knows which is meant to be the good one.

How to run it

  1. Hand out all four to each small group, face down (1 min)
  2. "You are the hiring manager. You have forty CVs and a shift to run. You get seven seconds each."
  3. Timer. Seven seconds per CV. Then, immediately: "Yes pile or no pile?" No going back
  4. Count the room's verdicts on a whiteboard (3 min)
  5. Now give them two minutes with CV D and ask what they missed the first time
  6. Teach FRM-058 (5 min). The room has

already worked out most of it

What happens

Nearly every room does the same thing:

  • A gets rejected, and people are surprised, because it is the one that looks like effort
  • B gets rejected in about two seconds
  • C wins, and nobody expected the plainest one to win
  • D splits the room, which is the useful result. Two minutes later everyone can see it was a

decent candidate, and in seven seconds it was invisible

➜ The line to land it: "D wasn't a bad candidate. D was a bad top third."

⚠️ On the seven seconds

Say this out loud, because somebody will look it up:

"Seven seconds isn't a real measurement. The figures you see online come from recruitment companies selling something. What is true is that the first look is fast, and that software often reads it before a person does. We're using seven seconds to make a point, not to state a fact."

The library does not use unsourced statistics, and modelling that in front of learners is worth the thirty seconds it costs.

Debrief

  • What made you put one in the yes pile? Be specific
  • What did the pretty one actually tell you?
  • CV D: what would you move, and where?
  • The turn: how long do you think somebody spent on your CV last time you applied?

Variations

  • Their own CVs, anonymised: far more powerful, and only for a group that trusts each other.

Collect them the week before, strip names, run the same game

  • Software round: read the four out loud in a flat voice with no formatting, the way a parser

sees them. CV A becomes gibberish. Excellent and slightly cruel

  • Real ads: use a genuine Seek ad for the sector the group is heading into. Better than any

fictional job

  • Two minutes instead of seven seconds: run the whole thing slow first, then fast. The change in

verdicts is the lesson

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Never use a learner's real CV without their consent, and never one from this room

identifiably. Anonymise properly or use samples

  • The room that defends CV A. Let them. Then run the software round
  • Deflation. Somebody will realise their CV is a B or a D. Move straight into

ACT-097 so they leave having fixed it, not just having learned it was wrong

  • Do not moralise about design. A learner who made a lovely CV in Canva did the work. The problem

is the reader, not their effort

Who Do You Already Know?

20-25 mingamecareer-readinessnetworkingweak-tiesjob-searchwork-readinesshidden-job-market

Type: game · Time: 20-25 min · Group: whole room · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-061 How Jobs Are Actually Found and FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties.

Nearly everybody underestimates their own network by an order of magnitude. This activity makes it visible in about eight minutes, and most rooms are genuinely surprised.

Part 1 — the map (8 min, individual)

Big sheet. Your name in the middle. Then names, not categories.

CircleWho goes in it
FamilyIncluding cousins, in-laws, and the ones you only see at Christmas
Church, marae, communityEveryone whose name you know
Sport, club, culture groupTeam-mates, coaches, the parents on the sideline
School and studyOld classmates, tutors, people from this programme
Every job you have hadSupervisors, workmates, regular customers
Neighbours and aroundThe dairy, the barber, the school gate

Rule: write the name, even if you have not spoken in five years. Especially then.

Part 2 — count (2 min)

How many names? ______

Most people expect twenty and write sixty or more. Take a show of hands by range and put the spread on the board. The spread is the lesson.

Part 3 — the second question (6 min)

Now go back through and mark:

MarkWho
★Anyone who works somewhere, anywhere. Not a good job, any job
?Anyone whose workplace you could not describe

➜ Every ★ is a doorway into a workplace. Every ? is a five-minute conversation you have never had.

Part 4 — the sentence (6 min, pairs)

Say it out loud to your partner. Three parts, no more.

  1. What I'm looking for. Specific
  2. What I bring. One thing
  3. The ask. "If you hear of anything, would you let me know?"
"I'm looking for warehouse or storeperson work. I've got my F endorsement. If you hear of anything, would you flick me a text?"

My sentence: ______________________________________________

Then the commitment: "Who are three people you'll say that to this week, and when?"

WhoWhen

Debrief

  • How many names did you expect? How many did you get?
  • Who has a ★ they had never thought of as a work contact?
  • The one that lands: who is the last person you told that you're looking?
  • What stops you saying the sentence?

Variations

  • Room version: everyone says their sentence to the whole room, and anyone who knows something

says so on the spot. Jobs genuinely come out of this, and it is worth the ten minutes

  • Six degrees: pick a target employer. See how few steps it takes for anyone in the room to reach

somebody inside it. Usually two or three, and it is startling

  • Text-it-now: three minutes at the end, phones out, send the sentence to one person. Beats any

amount of intention

  • Employer mapping: for a group heading into one sector, map employers instead of people, then

work out who knows somebody at each

  • Low literacy: draw it, use first names only, or do it entirely spoken in pairs

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ "It's who you know" can land as confirmation the system is rigged, especially for learners

who already feel shut out. Turn it firmly the other way: you already have a network, it is bigger than you thought, and using it costs nothing. That is the whole point of doing the count before the sentence

  • ⚠️ Some people genuinely have a small map. New migrants, people out of a violent relationship,

people recently out of prison. Do not let the count become a competition. The room version helps, because the room itself becomes part of their map

  • Do not call it networking. The word closes people down. It is telling people what you are

looking for

  • The sentence that is too vague. "Anything going" gets nothing. Push for specific, because a

specific ask is the one people remember when they hear something

  • No date, no action. Part 4's table is the point. A sentence nobody says is worth nothing

The River Stones

15-20 mingamewellbeingresilienceopenergameactionmetaphorhouse-content

Type: game · Time: 15-20 min · Group: whole room · Energy: 🔥 high

What it practises: step C of FRM-064 The ABC Model, and the metaphor the SKILL UP Building Resilience guide closes on:

Some people can see the whole path across. Others can only see the rock in front of them. That's fine. Step onto it, and the next one shows up.

The metaphor was doing nothing on the last page of a PDF. This puts it on the floor, and it takes fifteen minutes.

Set up

Lay out eight to twelve sheets of paper across the floor in a wandering line. That is the river. Tape them down if the floor is slippery, because somebody will be moving with their eyes covered.

⚠️ Clear the space properly. Chairs, bags, cables. Check the floor is not wet.

Round 1 — the whole path (4 min)

One volunteer crosses the river. They can see every stone. They walk across. It takes eight seconds and it is completely boring.

Ask the room: "how did that feel to watch?" Somebody will say "easy". Good.

Round 2 — one stone at a time (8 min)

Second volunteer. Eyes covered, standing at the first stone.

A partner stands beside them and does one thing only: names the next stone.

"There's one about half a metre ahead, slightly to your left."

No route. No plan. No "then you'll go right twice." One stone, then the next, and only after the first foot lands.

⚠️ Hand on the elbow the whole way. Physical safety first, every time. Anyone can stop at any point and nobody explains why.

Do it twice so two people get the feeling.

Round 3 — the question (5 min)

Ask the person who went second:

  • "How far ahead could you see?" (One stone.)
  • "Did you get across?" (Yes.)
  • "When did you know the second stone was there?" (After they had stood on the first.)

Then to the room:

"So which one of them actually needed the whole plan?"

The line to land it on

Say it exactly like this, and then stop talking:

You don't need to see every step. You need the next one. Clarity comes from action, not the other way around.

➜ Go straight into step C of ACT-106 while the room is still standing up. Do not let them sit down first.

Debrief

  • Who in here has been waiting until they can see the whole path before they start?
  • What is the thing you have been not-starting because you cannot see how it ends?
  • Round 2 needed a partner naming the next stone. Who does that for you?
  • What did it feel like to move without the plan?

Variations

  • No blindfold: for a room where covering someone's eyes is a step too far, have them look at the

ceiling and rely entirely on the partner. Same lesson, nobody uncomfortable

  • Silent version: the partner may only point, not speak. Harder, funnier, and it makes the point

about needing people even sharper

  • Named stones: write a real step on each sheet. The room walks their own path across an actual

goal

  • Chairs version: for a room that cannot move around, do it as a thought exercise with two

volunteers describing what they would need. Weaker, and still worth doing

  • Outdoor version: if you have a courtyard and some chalk, this is much better outside

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Mobility, balance, vision and pregnancy. Ask for volunteers rather than picking anyone, and

never single somebody out. Have a seated role ready, because the partner naming the stones is the more interesting job anyway

  • ⚠️ Being blindfolded is not neutral for everyone. For some people it is a trauma trigger. Offer

the no-blindfold version first and let people choose without saying why

  • The partner who plans the whole route. They will. Stop them, restart, and let the room see the

difference. That correction is the activity

  • Do not over-explain before you run it. The game makes the point. A facilitator who explains the

metaphor first has spent it

  • Do not let it become a trust-fall session. It is about the next step, not about trust. Keep it

moving

Two Things — Reflection & Commitment

10-12 minreflectionreflectiongoal-settingcommitmentstar

Type: reflection · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the R in FRM-003 STAR. A generic closer that works for any topic, not just this one.

Materials: the learner's journal or the reflection page in the workbook, a pen.

How to run it

  1. Review (2 min). Put the learning outcomes back on the screen. Ask one learner to say the

purpose of the session in their own words. Not you. Them.

  1. Write (5 min). Silent. Everyone answers, in writing:
    • What is the one thing from today you will remember tomorrow?
    • What are 2-3 things you will do to be more assertive? (swap in the topic's skill)
    • Who will you use it with, and when?
  2. Share (3 min). Pairs read one of their commitments to each other. Reading it out loud to

another person is what makes it real.

  1. Close (2 min). Invite two or three to share with the room. Never force it.

Debrief

  • What made you choose that particular commitment?
  • What is likely to get in the way of it?
  • What would make it easier? Who could help?
  • How will you know it worked?

The point to land: a session you enjoyed and a session that changed something are different things. The difference is written down in front of you.

Variations

  • Follow-up: photograph the page, or have learners text their commitment to themselves. Open the

next session by asking who did it

  • Low literacy: voice note it on their phone instead of writing
  • Online: private chat to the facilitator, then volunteers share aloud
  • Team version: the group agrees one shared commitment and writes it on the wall
  • Programme version: collect the commitments each week. They become the evidence in the

end-of-programme report

Watch out for

  • Vague commitments ("be more confident") do nothing. Push for a person, a situation and a week
  • Do not skip this because you ran over time. It is the part that transfers
  • Never read someone's page without asking

ACT-013Activity · 03-Activities

Start, Stop, Continue

10-12 minreflectionreflectiongoal-settingcommitmentstar

Type: reflection · Time: 10-12 min · Group: individual, then pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the R in FRM-003 STAR. Topic-agnostic. Works as a closer for any session.

Materials: the reflection page, a pen.

How to run it

  1. Review (2 min). Learning outcomes back on the screen. Ask one learner to say the purpose of

the session in their own words.

  1. Write (5 min). Silent. Three boxes:
I want to start…something you are not doing yet
I want to stop…a habit that is costing you
I want to continue…something you already do well, name it so you keep it
  1. Share (3 min). Pairs read one box to each other. Most people find "stop" the hardest to say

out loud, which is usually the sign it is the right one.

  1. Close (2 min). Two or three share with the room. Never force it.

Debrief

  • Which box was hardest to fill in?
  • What makes the "stop" one hard to say out loud?
  • What is likely to get in the way of the "start" one?
  • Who will notice if you actually do it?

The point to land: most people only ever write the start list. The stop list is where the time comes from, and the continue list is what stops you throwing away something that already works.

Variations

  • Follow-up: photograph the page. Open the next session by asking who did their "start"
  • Team version: the group agrees one shared start, stop and continue and writes it on the wall
  • Low literacy: voice note it instead of writing
  • Online: private chat to the facilitator, volunteers share aloud
  • Programme version: collect them weekly. They become the evidence in the end-of-programme report

Watch out for

  • Vague entries ("stop being unclear") do nothing. Push for a specific behaviour in a specific

situation

  • The "continue" box gets rushed. It is the one that builds confidence, so protect the time for it
  • Do not read someone's page without asking

ACT-076Activity · 03-Activities

Conflict Resolution Presentation

5 min per learner, plus prepreflectionconflictconflict-resolutionassessed-taskhouse-contentpresentingreflectioncommitment

Type: filmed presentation, assessed · Time: maximum 5 minutes per learner, plus prep · Group: individual · Energy: medium

This is house content and an assessed task. From the Future Ready: Conflict Resolution facilitator guide (SRC-007), where it is Task 6.

📋 Assessment: evidence toward "Identify conflict resolution techniques and describe how they can improve leadership skills in the workplace". The facilitator films it and uploads it.

It is also the capstone of the whole micro-credential, and the only task where the learner speaks for themselves rather than filling in a box.

The brief

Make a short video, maximum 5 minutes, presenting on conflict resolution. It must include:

  1. You, introducing yourself: your name, where you were born, and your ethnicity
  2. Your role title at work, and what you do
  3. Two things you have learnt during the training
  4. One conflict resolution technique you have learnt, and how you will use it in the workplace

Items 1 and 4 are named twice in the source as mandatory. Make sure both are in.

How to run it

  1. Give the brief at the start of the programme, not the end. Learners who know the capstone is

coming pay differently to everything before it.

  1. Prep time, 15 minutes. Notes are fine. Reading a script to camera is not what is being

assessed and it produces the worst videos.

  1. Film somewhere quiet, one at a time. Not in front of the group unless the learner wants that.
  2. One retake offered as standard. Most people's second take is much better and nobody should

have to ask.

The structure to give them

SectionTimeWhat to say
Who I am45 secName, where you were born, ethnicity, your role and what you do
What I learnt90 secTwo things. Be specific: name the framework, not "communication"
The technique2 minOne technique. What it is, and the actual situation at work where you will use it
Close30 secWhen you will use it. A day, a person, a place

➜ Facilitator tip: the single biggest quality lift is insisting on a real, named situation in part 4. "I'll listen better" is not evidence. "When Sione comes to me about the roster on Monday, I'm going to use the three layers and ask what matters to him before I offer anything" is.

Why item 1 is not just admin

Asking learners to name where they were born and their ethnicity, at the front of a presentation about conflict, is a deliberate choice and worth understanding rather than treating as a form field. Conflict is read differently across cultures, and a programme delivered to Pacific, Māori and migrant learners that never asks who is in the room would be teaching one culture's conflict norms as neutral.

See FRM-033 Cultural Safety for why that matters.

Marking guidance

There is no rubric in the source. This is a suggested one, and it is not part of the official assessment.

EnoughNot yet
Technique namedA specific framework from the programme"Communication" or "listening"
ApplicationA real situation, person and timeA general intention
UnderstandingExplains why the technique worksDescribes the steps only
Leadership linkSays what changes for the people around themOnly about themselves

Watch out for

  • Camera fear is real. For many learners this is the hardest part of the micro-credential by a

wide margin. Offer the retake before they ask, let them hold notes, and film against a plain wall rather than in front of peers

  • Five minutes is a maximum, not a target. A tight three minute video that names a real situation

beats five minutes of padding

  • Consent and storage. The video goes to an assessor and contains the learner's name, birthplace

and ethnicity. Tell them where it goes, who sees it, and how long it is kept, before you film

  • Do not let it become a thank-you speech. Redirect to the technique
  • Accessibility: if a learner cannot present to camera, ask the assessor what alternative evidence

is acceptable before the day, not on it

ACT-087Activity · 03-Activities

Your Leadership Legacy

15-20 minreflectionleadershipreflectionlegacyvaluesself-awarenessgoal-setting

Type: reflection · Time: 15-20 min · Group: individual, then optional pairs · Energy: low

What it practises: the closing reflection for any leadership session. Pairs especially with FRM-048 and FRM-049.

The idea, from SRC-009: your leadership legacy has very little to do with your numbers. It is what people keep doing because they worked with you. And the test of it is what survives after you leave.

The reflection sheet

1. Think about a leader you worked for who is no longer in your life.

What do you still do, at work, because of them? ______________________________________________

What did you stop doing the moment they left? ______________________________________________

➜ The gap between those two answers is their real legacy. Not what they said. What stuck.

2. Now your own team.

If you left on Friday, what would they keep doing? ______________________________________________

What would go back to how it was within a month? ______________________________________________

3. The hard one.

What is one thing your team currently does because you are watching? ______________________________________________

4. What would have to change for that thing to survive you? ______________________________________________

5. Finish this sentence. One line. No jargon.

When people talk about what it was like to work with me, I want them to say ______________________________________________

How to run it

  1. Question 1 first, alone (5 min). Working from someone else's legacy before your own is easier

and it produces a better answer

  1. Questions 2 and 3 (5 min). Silent
  2. Questions 4 and 5 (5 min). Question 5 gets rewritten at least twice by most people
  3. Optional pairs (5 min). Share only question 5

Question 3 is the whole activity

"What does your team do because you are watching?"

Everyone has an answer and nobody enjoys it. The gloves that go on when you walk into the yard. The sign-off sheet that gets filled in properly on the days you are in.

That is not a failure of character in your team. It is Theory X showing up as a habit, and it means the standard belongs to you rather than to them. A standard that belongs to you leaves when you do.

They writePush with
"Nothing, my team are good""What happened the week you were on leave?"
"Wearing PPE properly""Do they know why, or do they know you check?"
"Filling in the sheets""Who else would notice if they stopped?"

Debrief

Room level. Nobody reports their own answers.

  • Did anyone's answer to question 1 surprise them?
  • What is the difference between a habit your team has and a rule you enforce?
  • Whose legacy is easier to build: a manager's or a leader's? Which one lasts?
  • Question 5: how many of you wrote something about results? How many about people?

Variations

  • End-of-programme version: run it on day one and again on the last day. People keep both sheets.

The change in question 5 is usually the best evidence of learning in the whole programme

  • Six-month letter: question 5 becomes a letter to yourself, sealed, and the facilitator posts it

in six months. Needs an address and a promise you will actually keep

  • Team version: the leader answers question 2, then the team answers it about them, anonymously.

Powerful, and only for a team that is already in decent shape

  • Whakataukī opener: open with Ki te kāhore he whakakitenga ka ngaro te iwi, "without foresight

or vision the people will be lost", attributed to Kīngi Tāwhiao. Then ask what they want people to see

  • Low literacy: entirely spoken in pairs, one person scribes for the other, or record it on a

phone

Watch out for

  • ⚠️ Not everyone in the room leads anyone. Reframe for them: what will the people you work

beside keep doing? A legacy does not require a title

  • Grandiosity. Question 5 attracts mission statements. Push for something a real person would

actually say about them in a smoko room

  • The learner who realises they have no legacy. Usually someone new, sometimes someone who has

been coasting. The answer is that question 5 is a decision, not a report

  • Do not force the pairs share. Question 5 is more personal than it looks

ACT-001Activity · 03-Activities

Four Styles Roleplay

25-35 minroleplayassertivenessroleplaycommunication-styles

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-35 min · Group: 3-5 per group · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-001 The 4 Communication Styles and FRM-002 The Assert Approach

Materials: one scenario card per group, a timer.

Set up

Groups of 3-5, spread around the room so they can rehearse without being overheard. Each group gets one scenario. Say up front: there is no perfect way to do this. The goal is to practise, learn and improve.

How to run it

  1. Each group takes or is given one scenario (below).
  2. As a group, they roleplay the same situation four times, once in each style: passive,

aggressive, passive-aggressive, assertive. 8 minutes to prepare.

  1. Each group performs to the class. They do not say which style is which.
  2. The rest of the class guesses the style after each version.
  3. Debrief the assertive version: what exactly made it assertive? Words, tone, or body language?

The scenarios

#SituationGoal
1Performance drop — a team member's work has slipped recently and it is affecting the teamHave a supportive conversation and reset expectations
2Running behind schedule — the team is behind and people are rushing and skipping stepsReset the team and give direction
3Unrealistic deadline — your manager asks for something that may not be realistic in the time givenCommunicate honestly about what is possible and discuss options
4Senior worker pushback — an experienced worker ignores the process and says "I've done this for years"Address it respectfully and maintain standards

Debrief

  • Which style was easiest to act? Which was hardest? Why?
  • What did the assertive version do that the others did not?
  • Which style did you recognise from your own workplace?
  • What changed in the room's body language between versions?

The point to land: assertive was not the loudest version. It was the clearest one. Clear and respectful at the same time is a skill, and it is trainable.

Variations

  • Youth: swap in scenarios about group chats, a friend borrowing money, a coach, a part-time job
  • Frontline / low literacy: read the scenario aloud, no written prep, straight into acting
  • Online: breakout rooms to prepare, perform in the main room with cameras on
  • Large group: each group performs only one assigned style, class assembles the full set
  • Short on time: run scenario 1 only, all groups, four styles

Watch out for

  • The aggressive roleplay can get personal if a group is acting out a real situation with a real

person in the room. Set the rule: no naming, no impressions of anyone here

  • Some learners will not want to perform. Give them the observer role: they call the style and

explain what gave it away

  • Keep the passive-aggressive version short. It is funny for about 30 seconds, then it is just

uncomfortable

ACT-003Activity · 03-Activities

DESC Rewrite Lab

25-30 minroleplayassertivenessdescdifficult-conversationspractice

Type: roleplay / structured practice · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-004 The DESC Script, built on FRM-002 "I" statements

Materials: a four-box card per learner (Describe / Express / Specify / Consequences), pens.

Set up

Pairs. Everyone brings one real, low-to-medium-stakes conversation they have been avoiding. Set the boundary early: nothing involving harassment, safety or anything that belongs with HR. Those are real conversations, but they need support, not a practice room.

How to run it

  1. Write (8 min). Each learner fills the four boxes for their own situation. Silent work.
  2. Swap and sharpen (5 min). Partners read each other's card and check three things:
    • Is Describe facts only, with no labels or "always"?
    • Is Specify one clear change the other person could actually do?
    • Are Consequences positive first, not a threat?
  3. Say it out loud (8 min). Partner A delivers their script to Partner B, who plays the other

person and pushes back once, reasonably. Then swap.

  1. Round two (5 min). Rewrite the line that did not land, and say it again.

Debrief

  • Which of the four boxes was hardest to fill in? (It is almost always Specify.)
  • What happened to your body when your partner pushed back?
  • What is different about hearing your own words out loud versus reading them?
  • When will you have the real conversation?

The point to land: you do not need to be braver, you need to be more prepared. Four lines written down beforehand is what turns avoiding into handling.

Variations

  • Youth: provide the situation rather than asking for a real one. Group chat left them out, a

friend borrowing money and not paying it back, a coach not playing them

  • Frontline / low literacy: facilitator writes one shared example on the board, everyone practises

the same script, then changes only the Specify line

  • Online: shared doc with the four boxes, breakout rooms in pairs
  • Advanced: partner pushes back twice, second time emotionally, to practise holding the line

Watch out for

  • Someone will bring a genuinely serious situation. Have a quiet word, and know your referral path

before the session starts

  • Pairs drift into venting about the person. Redirect to the card
  • Do not let anyone leave with a script they have written but never said aloud. Saying it is the

activity

ACT-009Activity · 03-Activities

Briefing Roleplay — What, Why, How

30-40 minroleplaybriefingtoolbox-talksafetyroleplayteamsclear-messaging

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-40 min · Group: 4-6 per group · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-007 The What-Why-How Briefing Framework

Materials: one briefing plan template per group, the scenario list.

Set up

Groups of 4-6. One person is the leader, everyone else is a crew member. Make the crew's job explicit before you start, because this is where most briefing practice falls over: the crew must contribute. They ask questions, confirm understanding, raise safety concerns, and share ideas.

Say the key line up front: a strong briefing is a team conversation, not a leader presentation.

How to run it

  1. Each group picks a scenario.
  2. The leader takes 5 minutes with the briefing plan template: What, Why, How, Risks, Team input.
  3. The leader delivers the briefing to their crew. 3-4 minutes.
  4. The crew does its job: questions, concerns, suggestions, confirming understanding.
  5. Swap the leader and run a second scenario, so more than one person practises.

The scenarios

#Situation
1Starting a task on a busy work site
2Conditions have changed before work begins
3A new worker joins the shift
4A safety risk is identified
5Equipment or vehicle movement creates hazards

Debrief

  • Leaders: which of the three questions was hardest to fill in?
  • Crew: at what point did you actually understand what you were doing?
  • Who raised something the leader had not thought of? What was it?
  • What would have happened on a real site if the Why had been left out?

The point to land: the Why is the part that gets skipped and the part that decides whether people adapt correctly when reality does not match the plan. And if nobody but the leader spoke, it was a presentation, not a briefing.

Variations

  • Non-site industries: swap in a kitchen service, a retail shift change, a call centre campaign,

an aged care handover. The structure does not change

  • Youth: briefing a team for a sports game or a community event
  • Online: breakout rooms, leader shares the template on screen
  • Harder version: give one crew member a hidden card — they know a hazard the leader does not,

and will only mention it if genuinely asked

  • Assessment version: use the template as evidence of competency for a health and safety unit

Watch out for

  • Crews going passive and just nodding. If it happens, stop and reset the expectation
  • Leaders who read the template out like a form. It is prompts, not a script
  • Do not let "any questions?" be asked while walking away. Ask it standing still, and wait through

the silence

ACT-014Activity · 03-Activities

Yes – No – Yes Lab

25-30 minroleplayboundariessaying-noassertivenesspracticeworkload

Type: worksheet then roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-008 The Positive No

Materials: a three-box card per learner (Yes / No / Yes), pens.

Set up

Pairs. Everyone brings one real request they find hard to turn down. Keep it to workload, shifts, favours and family asks. Anything involving bullying, safety or harassment is a real conversation that needs support, not a practice room.

Part 1 — Build your own (10 min)

Silent work. Each learner fills in three boxes for their own situation.

BoxPrompt
The requestWhat are you being asked to do?
YesWhat do you care about that makes this hard? The value, the priority, the person
NoYour clear limit. One sentence
YesA way forward you can genuinely offer

Then partners swap cards and check three things:

  • Is the middle line actually a no? Read it on its own. If it could be read as "maybe", it is not

done

  • Is the first Yes a value, not an apology? "Sorry, I'm just really busy" fails this
  • Is the last Yes something you can really do? A broken alternative costs more than the original no

Part 2 — Roleplay (12 min)

Person A is the asker. Pick one:

  • "Can you cover my shift this weekend?"
  • "I need you to take on this extra project, you're the only one who can."
  • "Can you stay back late again tonight?"

Person B answers using Yes – No – Yes.

Then the asker gives feedback:

#Question
1Did the no feel clear?
2Did you still feel respected?
3One thing to improve

Then swap roles.

Debrief

  • Which box was hardest to write? (Usually the first Yes. People reach for an excuse instead of a

value.)

  • How did it feel to say the middle line out loud, compared with writing it?
  • Askers: what made you accept it? What would have made you push?
  • Whose third Yes would you actually have taken?

The point to land: you are not rejecting the person, you are protecting something. Say what that something is and the no stops feeling like an insult, to them and to you.

Variations

  • Youth: provide the request rather than asking for a real one. A friend asking for money, a lift,

homework, or to cover for them

  • Frontline / low literacy: build one shared example on the board, everyone practises the same

three lines, then changes only the middle one

  • Online: shared doc with the three boxes, breakout rooms in pairs
  • Advanced: the asker does not accept the first answer. That is

ACT-015, and it works well run straight after this one

Watch out for

  • Long explanations. Learners pad the no with three reasons. One is enough. Time them if you have

to

  • The third Yes becoming the whole answer. Some learners will offer so much alternative that they

have effectively said yes. Point at the middle line and ask what they actually declined

  • Someone will bring a situation where the honest answer is that they cannot refuse, because of

immigration status, a probation period, or money. Do not push them to practise a no they cannot afford. Shift them to a lower-stakes example and name plainly that this is a real limit, not a personal failure

Used by

TopicPillarLink
TOP-COM-004 Boundaries Without GuiltCommunicationTOPIC.md
ACT-015Activity · 03-Activities

Hold The Line — Broken Record Roleplay

25-30 minroleplayboundariessaying-noassertivenesspressurepracticecustomer-service

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: high

What it practises: FRM-009 The Broken Record

Materials: a three-box card (Acknowledge / Appreciate / Explain priorities), pens.

Set up

This is the pressure activity. It works best straight after ACT-014 Yes – No – Yes Lab: they have just built a no, now someone refuses to accept it.

Demonstrate first. Ask a learner to push you three times while you hold one line. They need to see a calm third repetition before they will believe it is possible.

Part 1 — Build your own (8 min)

Think of a time someone kept pushing you to change your answer.

BoxPrompt
The situationWhat were they pushing for?
AcknowledgeSay back what they asked for
AppreciateValue their point or position, genuinely
Explain prioritiesYour reason, then your repeat line

The repeat line is the important box. One sentence. Write it down and underline it, because it is the thing that must not change under pressure.

Part 2 — Roleplay (15 min)

Person A is the pusher. Pick one, and keep pushing at least three times:

  • A customer demanding a discount
  • A teammate wanting you to rush a job
  • Someone pressuring you to say yes to extra work

Person B holds the line using the Broken Record. Stay calm, keep acknowledging, repeat the answer.

Feedback from Person A:

#Question
1Did Person B stay calm?
2Did the answer stay clear each time?
3Did they sound reasonable, not stubborn?

Then swap.

With an observer (threes): the third person's only job is to write down the repeat line each time it is said. Reading back the three versions is the most useful feedback in the activity, because drift is invisible to the person doing it.

Debrief

  • Pushers: what did you feel when the answer did not move? Did you give up, or get more creative?
  • Holders: at which push did you feel yourself starting to bend?
  • Did anyone's line change? What did it change into? (It almost always softens into a time or a

condition.)

  • What made the difference between sounding steady and sounding stubborn?
  • Where in your week will someone push you like this?

The point to land: you do not win by arguing better. You win by not needing to argue. The acknowledging is what keeps it respectful; the repetition is what keeps it yours.

Variations

  • Customer-facing teams: everyone holds the same organisational line (the price, the lead time,

the policy). Agreeing one shared repeat line as a team is a genuinely useful output

  • Youth: peer pressure scenarios. Someone wanting a lift, wanting them to skip class, wanting

their homework

  • Online: breakout rooms in threes with the observer role, which works better on video than pairs
  • Advanced: the pusher gets emotional on the third push, or brings a new argument that sounds

reasonable. That is the real test, and it sets up the "when not to use it" conversation

Watch out for

  • It gets loud. That is fine, but keep an eye on pairs where the pushing is landing personally.

Call time early on any pair that has stopped playing

  • Learners using it on a fair point. Debrief this deliberately: if the other person is raising

something you have not considered, the right move is to stop and listen, not to repeat. Holding a line you should have changed is not assertive

  • Sarcastic acknowledging. "I hear you" with an edge undoes the whole technique. Name it if you

hear it

Used by

ACT-018Activity · 03-Activities

Bad Listening, Then SOLER

15-20 minroleplaylisteningactive-listeningbody-languagepracticeempathy

Type: paired experience · Time: 15-20 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-010 Active Listening and SOLER

Materials: none. This is the best activity in the module and it costs nothing.

Why it goes first

Run this before you teach SOLER, not after. Being ignored for two minutes teaches more about listening than any diagram. The framework then arrives as the fix for something they have just felt.

How to run it

Round 1 — Bad listening (2 min)

Person A talks about their week. Person B listens badly on purpose: looks away, checks their phone, interrupts, changes the subject, hurries them along.

Give Person B the instruction privately or on a card if you can, so Person A gets the full effect.

Then talk (2 min): how did that feel for the speaker?

Round 2 — SOLER listening (4 min)

Swap. Now Person B listens using all five SOLER steps. No interrupting at all.

Then talk (3 min): what felt different?

Reflect (3 min)

Which SOLER step do you do well? Which one do you need to work on?

My strong step: _____________ My step to grow: _____________

Debrief

  • Speakers in round one: how long did it take before you wanted to stop talking?
  • Did anyone shorten what they were going to say? (This is the real cost. Bad listening does not just

feel bad, it changes what people tell you.)

  • Listeners in round one: how easy was it? Be honest. Most people find it uncomfortably familiar
  • In round two, what did the speaker do that they did not do in round one?
  • Where do you listen like round one without meaning to?

The point to land: you already know how to listen. The question is whether the other person can tell. Listening is invisible unless you show it.

Variations

  • Cultural adaptation, and say this out loud: in many Pacific, Māori and other cultures, direct

eye contact can be disrespectful, especially with elders. Offer the alternative from Stickley's SURETY critique: sit at an angle rather than square on, and rely on presence and stillness rather than eye contact. Nobody should leave thinking they listen wrongly because of how they were raised

  • Phone-based roles: run round two on the phone, back to back so they cannot see each other. Every

SOLER step has to be translated into voice, which makes the point sharply

  • Online: works fine in breakout rooms. Round one is easier to fake convincingly on video, which

is itself worth debriefing

  • Large or noisy rooms: threes with an observer, so the observer can report what they saw the

listener's body doing

Watch out for

  • Round one goes too far. Two minutes, hard stop. Some pairs get genuinely hurt if it runs long,

especially if the speaker chose something that mattered

  • Do not let anyone use round one on a topic that is actually sensitive. Say "your week" and keep

it light. If someone starts sharing something real, stop the round early

  • Overacting in round two. Learners lean in like they are about to headbutt each other. Say

"slightly" twice

  • Always debrief round one before running round two. Skipping that conversation wastes the activity

Used by

TopicPillarLink
TOP-COM-005 Listen To LeadCommunicationTOPIC.md
ACT-020Activity · 03-Activities

Reflect Before You Fix — Paraphrasing and De-escalation

20-25 minroleplaylisteningparaphrasingreflectingde-escalationpracticecustomer-service

Type: paired practice then roleplay · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-012 Paraphrasing and Reflecting

Materials: sentence-starter cards. Two lines are enough: "So what you're saying is…" and "It sounds like you felt…"

Part 1 — Paraphrase practice (5 min)

Person A talks for one minute about something on their mind. Person B replies with one paraphrase: "So what you're saying is…" Person A says whether it was right, or fixes it.

Was it accurate? ☐ Yes ☐ Close ☐ Off

Swap.

Part 2 — Reflect the feeling (5 min)

Person A shares something that annoyed or worried them. Person B names the feeling: "It sounds like you felt __________." Check whether it landed.

The feeling I named: _____________

Swap.

Part 3 — De-escalation roleplay (7-10 min)

Person A plays an upset customer or teammate. Pick one:

  • "I've been waiting all week and no one's called me back."
  • "You changed the roster again without asking me."

Person B must reflect the feeling first, before offering any fix. Stay calm.

This is harder than it sounds. The instinct to jump straight to the solution is strong, especially in people who are good at their jobs.

Feedback from Person A:

#Question
1Did you feel heard before they tried to fix it?
2One thing that helped

Then swap.

Debrief

  • Part 1: how many paraphrases came back "off"? What got lost?
  • Part 2: how did it feel to have your feeling named by someone else? Did anyone get it wrong, and

what happened when they did? (Being corrected is a good outcome. It means the other person is engaged and you now have better information.)

  • Part 3: how long did you last before you wanted to fix it?
  • Upset people: what did the reflect line do to your temperature?
  • Where in your job does someone arrive already upset?

The point to land: people cannot hear a solution until they feel heard. Reflecting first is not being soft, it is the fastest route to actually solving it. Clinical de-escalation guidance teaches the same order for exactly this reason.

Variations

  • Contact centres and reception: drill the opening reflect line until it is automatic. Ten

repetitions of the first sentence is worth more than one full roleplay

  • Second-language learners: the sentence-starter cards do the heavy lifting. Let them use the same

two openers every time. The skill is the noticing, not the phrasing

  • Advanced: the upset person does not settle after the first reflection. Person B has to reflect a

second time without repeating the same words. This is where it connects to ACT-015 Hold The Line

  • Online: works well, though reading feeling on video is harder. Debrief that as a finding, it sets

up TOP-COM-006

Watch out for

  • Parroting. Repeating exact words back sounds like a script and people hate it. Insist on their

own words

  • Reflect-then-fix in one breath. "That sounds frustrating, anyway what I'll do is…" is not

reflecting, it is a speed bump. Make them pause and let it land

  • Confident wrong labels. "You're angry" when someone is embarrassed makes it worse. Teach the

tentative form: "it sounds like…", "am I right that…"

  • Part 3 can get real if someone picks a live grievance. Keep them on the two scripted scenarios

Video Presence Dry Run

20-25 minroleplaydigital-communicationvideo-presencehybridmeetingspractice

Type: live practice · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: FRM-015 The Video Presence Checklist

Materials: a phone or laptop each. A projector helps a lot. The printed checklist.

Why it has to be live

Reading a checklist about video presence changes nothing. Seeing your own frame on a big screen changes everything, and it takes about four seconds.

Part 1 — The before shot (5 min)

Everyone joins a call from wherever they are sitting, with no adjustments at all. Whatever the device is doing right now.

Put two or three volunteers up on the projector. Ask the room, not the person:

  • Where is the camera compared with their eyes?
  • Where is the light coming from?
  • What can you see behind them?
  • How much of them is in frame?

Facilitator: be the first volunteer, with a deliberately bad setup. Nobody critiques a colleague's kitchen until you have shown them yours.

Part 2 — Fix it (7 min)

Everyone runs the setup half of the checklist on their own device.

☐Item
☐Camera at eye level. Books under the laptop, or prop the phone
☐Light in front, not behind. Turn to face the window
☐Quiet, tidy background. Whatever you can reasonably control
☐Head and shoulders in frame, a little space above your head
☐Hide your own self-view

Then the same three volunteers go back on the projector. The before-and-after is the activity.

Part 3 — Say something (8 min)

In pairs or threes on a call, each person delivers 60 seconds of something real: a project update, a safety brief, an introduction of themselves to a new client.

They practise the four during-the-call habits:

☐Item
☐Look at the lens when you speak
☐Mute when not talking
☐Use a name to bring someone in
☐Slow down and pause

Partner feedback, two questions only:

#Question
1Did it feel like they were looking at you?
2One thing that would make them easier to listen to

Debrief

  • What surprised you in the before shot?
  • Who had a light behind them and had never noticed?
  • What did hiding your self-view do? (Most people report they relaxed. That is Bailenson's mirror

anxiety, and naming it lands well.)

  • Speakers: what did looking at the lens feel like? (Unnatural. Say so, and say it looks completely

natural from the other end. That gap is the reason nobody does it.)

  • Which of these can you fix in the next five minutes?

The point to land: people judge your credibility in the first few seconds, before you have said anything worth hearing. Almost all of what they are judging is setup, not talent. Fix it once, and it is fixed for every call.

Variations

  • Phone-only groups: entirely fine and more realistic for many learners. Propping a phone against a

water bottle at eye level is the whole lesson

  • From a vehicle or a site: for learners who genuinely take calls from a ute, work the problem

rather than skipping it. Park facing away from the sun, use the headrest, do not take the important one while driving

  • Interview prep: run the 60 seconds as an interview answer. Very strong for

Employment & Work Readiness groups

  • No devices: if the room has no equipment, run the checklist as a discussion and demonstrate all

four states yourself on one laptop and the projector. Weaker, but it works

Watch out for

  • Backgrounds are a class issue. Some learners share a room, live with several families, or have

nowhere tidy. Never make a tidy background a standard people can fail. Say plainly: control what you reasonably can, and a virtual background or a plain wall is a perfectly good answer

  • The gear conversation. Somebody will want to talk about ring lights and microphones. Redirect:

books, a window, and a wall

  • Critiquing the person instead of the setup. Keep every comment about the frame, the light and the

angle. Never about how someone looks

  • Do not put a learner on the projector without asking them first

The Two Minute Introduction

20-25 minroleplaynetworkingrelationshipswork-readinessroleplaypracticeconfidence

Type: roleplay / live practice · Time: 20-25 min · Group: pairs, rotating · Energy: medium

What it practises: starting a conversation with someone you do not know, which is the one skill that turns FRM-024 The Strength of Weak Ties from an interesting fact into something you can use. Also the shy-starter practice in FRM-021.

Materials: a timer, and the scenarios below on a slide or read out.

How to run it

  1. Set it up (3 min). Everyone gets two minutes to start a conversation with a stranger and find

one thing they have in common and one thing they could help each other with. Two minutes only. That is the constraint that makes it work.

  1. Round one (2 min + 2 min debrief). Pairs, scenario 1. Swap who starts.
  2. Rotate. New partner, new scenario. Run three or four rounds.
  3. Keep the timer strict. When it goes off, they stop mid-sentence. That is realistic.

The scenarios

#Where you areWho they are
1Waiting for the induction to start on your first daySomeone else who is also new
2At a family functionYour cousin's friend, who works somewhere you would like to work
3Smoko room, you have been there three weeksSomeone from a different department you have never spoken to
4A community or church eventSomeone twenty years older who runs their own business
5A course or training dayThe tutor, in the ten minutes before it starts

The three moves to teach first

Give them this before round one. Two minutes is not long enough to improvise.

  1. Open with where you both are. "Have you done one of these before?" beats "so, what do you do?"

because it needs no courage and no preparation.

  1. Ask a question that cannot be answered with one word. "How did you get into that?" is the best

one in the language. People like telling that story.

  1. Leave a door open. "I'd be keen to hear how that goes" or "who should I talk to about that?"

That last question is how a single conversation becomes an introduction.

Debrief

  • Which opening line actually worked? Collect the good ones on the board
  • What did it feel like at the ten second mark, before anything was flowing?
  • Who found something in common they would never have guessed?
  • Which of the five scenarios would you avoid in real life? Why?

Variations

  • Confidence-first version: run round one as pairs who already know each other, playing the

scenario. It takes the sting out and nobody has to be brave twice

  • Online: breakout rooms of two, two minutes each, and the facilitator drops the scenario into

the chat before each round

  • Low literacy: read the scenarios out. Nothing needs to be read or written
  • Advanced: add a difficult partner. One person is distracted, checking their phone, giving short

answers. Debrief on what the other person did about it

  • Employer-facing groups: replace the scenarios with real ones from the industry they are

entering

Watch out for

  • This is genuinely hard for some learners, and it can be the most confronting thing in the

session. Name that at the start. Say that two minutes is deliberately short so nobody is stuck

  • The pair that just chats. Bring them back to the two goals: one thing in common, one thing you

could help each other with

  • Do not force anyone to perform in front of the room. Everyone works in pairs at the same time.

There is no audience, and that is the point

  • Watch for the rotation excluding someone. Count the pairs before you start

Bad News First

25-30 minroleplaytrustpsychological-safetyroleplayleadershiplisteningfeedback

Type: roleplay · Time: 25-30 min · Group: pairs, or threes with an observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: the third leader move in FRM-023 Psychological Safety, responding productively to bad news. It is the move that actually decides whether a team is safe, and almost nobody practises it.

Materials: the five scenarios below, on cards or a slide.

How to run it

  1. Set it up (4 min). Say the finding plainly: people are not testing what you say about

openness. They are watching what happened to the last person who was open. This session is that moment, practised.

  1. Round one, deliberately badly (5 min). Person A brings the bad news. Person B reacts the way

people actually react: sighs, asks why they did not catch it sooner, starts problem-solving over the top of them. Debrief for two minutes: how likely is A to bring the next one?

  1. Teach the three moves (3 min). Thank them first. Ask a question before you react. Separate the

news from the person who brought it.

  1. Round two, properly (5 min). Same scenario, same pair, swapped roles.
  2. Debrief (8 min).

The scenarios

#The bad newsBrought by
1"I've made a mistake on the order and it's already gone out"A staff member, on their fourth week
2"The team don't trust the new roster and they've been talking about it"Someone senior, who nearly did not tell you
3"I don't think we're going to hit Friday"A team lead, three days out
4"I saw someone skip the safety check"Someone reporting on a workmate they like
5"Honestly? The way you spoke in that meeting put people off"Someone giving you feedback about yourself

Scenario 5 is the hardest and the most valuable. Save it for the end, and only run it in a group where trust is already reasonable.

The three moves to teach

  1. Thank them, first, before anything else. "Thanks for telling me." Four words, said before your

face has time to do anything else.

  1. Ask before you react. One question. "What happened?" or "How did you find it?" It buys you the

three seconds that stop the sigh.

  1. Separate the news from the messenger. Deal with the problem later. Right now the only thing

happening is whether this person brings you the next one.

Debrief

  • In round one, what did B do that made A want to stop talking? Collect the specific behaviours
  • What was the hardest to hold back?
  • Scenario 4: what happens in a workplace where nobody reports what they saw?
  • Think of a time you brought someone bad news and it went badly. What did you do differently the

next time? (This is the question that produces the real stories)

Variations

  • Observer version: threes, with one person watching only B's face and body for the first five

seconds. That five seconds is the whole activity

  • Phone version: run it as a call, so tone carries everything. Good for contact centre teams
  • Online: breakout rooms of two. Note that on video the first-five-seconds effect is even

stronger, because the face fills the screen

  • Low literacy: read the scenarios out. Nothing needs to be written

Watch out for

  • Round one can sting if someone is playing a version of their real manager. Keep it short and

move to the teaching quickly

  • Do not let B defend themselves in the debrief. The question is not whether their reaction was

fair, it is what it taught A

  • Scenario 5 needs a safe room. If you are unsure, cut it. Running it badly does more damage than

not running it

  • Nobody roleplays a real named person. Say so at the start

Storming On Purpose

30-35 minroleplayteamsconflictstormingroleplayleadershipnorms

Type: roleplay · Time: 30-35 min · Group: threes, two in role and one observer · Energy: medium

What it practises: running a Storming conversation instead of avoiding it (FRM-018), and landing it on an agreement (FRM-027 Team Charter).

Why it exists: Tuckman tells you storming is normal and then says nothing about what to do while you are in it. This is the missing half.

How to run it

  1. Set it up (4 min). The goal is not to win the disagreement. It is to get the team to an

agreement they will both keep. That is what moves a team from Storming to Norming.

  1. Teach the four moves (4 min). Below.
  2. Round one (7 min). Two in role, one observing against the four moves.
  3. Observer feedback (3 min). Which moves happened? Which got skipped?
  4. Rotate roles and scenarios. Run two or three rounds.
  5. Whole class debrief (8 min).

The four moves

#MoveWhat it sounds like
1Name the stage, not the person"I think we're just working out how this team runs, rather than you and me having a problem"
2Make it about the work"The thing I actually need is to know who's locking up"
3Ask for their version before you argue yours"How are you seeing it?" and then be quiet
4Land on a rule, not a truce"So from Monday, whoever's on late shift locks up and messages the group. Yes?"

Move 4 is the one that separates this from an argument that goes quiet. A truce lasts until next week. A rule survives it.

The scenarios

#The disagreementThe complication
1Who is responsible for the end-of-day cleanOne of you has been doing it for a month without being asked
2A new person is doing the job "wrong"Their way is actually faster, just different
3Someone keeps changing the roster in the group chatThey have a genuine reason and never explained it
4Two shifts blame each other for what gets left undoneNeither has ever spoken to the other directly
5You and a peer both think you are leading the projectNobody ever said who was

Debrief

  • Which of the four moves was hardest?
  • Did anyone land a rule, or did most pairs end on a truce? (Most end on a truce. That is the finding)
  • What happened when someone asked for the other version first? Did it change the conversation?
  • Scenario 5: whose job is it to sort that out?
  • What is the cost of leaving any of these for another three months?

Variations

  • Difficult partner: brief one person to get defensive early. Realistic and much harder
  • Leader version: a third person plays the supervisor who has to step in. Practises the presence

move from Tuckman's storming row

  • Cross-team version: for TOP-LEA-005,

make the two roles head office and a regional site, and run it with 3C instead of the four moves

  • Online: breakout threes. The observer keeps their camera on and the two in role do the talking
  • Low literacy: read the scenario to each three rather than handing out cards

Watch out for

  • Real disputes leaking in. If two people in the room have this exact argument in real life, do

not pair them. Check before you form the threes

  • The polite roleplay. Some pairs will agree in ninety seconds to avoid discomfort, which teaches

nothing. Give the observer permission to say "that was too easy, run it again with more push"

  • Winning. Remind them there is no winner. There is a rule at the end or there is not
  • Do not let it become a complaint about a real manager. Redirect to the scenario
